cards.answer: It showed people preferred capitalism to communism, and the departing skilled workers weakened East Germany's economy.

cards.front: Name the three main categories that metal shaping processes are grouped into.
cards.answer: Wastage (material removed) / Deforming/reforming (reshaped without removal) / Fabricating (joining)

cards.front: Name the four operations that can be carried out on a lathe.
cards.answer: Rough turning / Facing / Parting off / Thread cutting

cards.front: Why must a hacksaw blade have at least three teeth in contact with the material at all times?
cards.answer: If fewer teeth are in contact the teeth can snag on the material and break.

cards.front: Why is die casting only economical for high-volume production?
cards.answer: Because the reusable steel die is very expensive, so its cost must be spread over many thousands of parts to be worthwhile.

cards.front: What three things is a 16-mark thematic essay marked on?
cards.answer: Knowledge of specific evidence across all eras / Analysis using second-order concepts / Substantiated judgement
items: Knowledge of specific evidence across all eras

cards.front: What three mistakes do low-scoring thematic essays typically make?
cards.answer: List events chronologically without analysis / Cover only one or two eras / Describe changes without weighing against continuity
items: Cover only one or two eras
Describe changes without weighing against continuity

cards.front: Why is the acceptance of germ theory in the 1860s–1880s described as a genuine turning point?
cards.answer: Because it overturned the entire theoretical framework that had governed medicine since antiquity, not just an incremental improvement.

cards.front: Why do physicians wearing beak-shaped masks in the 1665 plague show continuity in disease theory?
cards.answer: Because over 300 years after the Black Death, physicians still believed in miasma theory despite other medical advances.

title: The Story: The Phone Call to Autumn
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What six seasons does the play move through in order, according to the original producing company's synopsis?
cards.answer: Winter in London / Summer in Adelaide / Autumn / Winter / Spring / Summer

cards.front: Which four children open a seasonal section with their own monologue, and where is each one set?
cards.answer: Rosie in Berlin / Pip in the garden / Mark remembering the gum tree / Ben remembering his parents dancing

cards.front: Why is the gap between what Bob fears and what the phone call turns out to be about structurally important?
cards.answer: The opening call trains the audience to fear for one of the four children, but it is actually about Fran, creating a built-in reversal.

cards.front: Why does the staging remove the furniture and put Pip on the ground for her autumn confession?
cards.answer: A chair would be an easy resting place for the actor, so removing it keeps the moment tense and exposed, showing the power shift over Pip.

cards.front: Name the six global biomes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Polar regions / Coral reefs / Hot deserts / Grasslands / Temperate forests / Tropical rainforests

cards.front: Name the four vegetation layers of a tropical rainforest.
cards.answer: Emergents / Canopy / Under-storey / Ground layer

cards.front: How does cutting down a rainforest tree show interdependence in an ecosystem?
cards.answer: It dries the soil faster, slows the water cycle, removes animal habitat and starves bacteria in the leaf litter.

cards.front: Why does the equator get heavy convectional rainfall almost daily?
cards.answer: The sun heats the air and ocean intensely all year, so warm air rises and cools, producing heavy convectional rainfall.

title: British Values and the Principles of Society
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson, name the four levels at which identity is shaped.
cards.answer: Individual level / Group level / National level / Global level

cards.front: The lesson lists four things covered by political rights. What are they?
cards.answer: Right to vote / Right to stand for election / Right to join a political party / Right to take part in free and fair elections
items: Right to join a political party
Right to take part in free and fair elections

cards.front: Why is freedom of expression a qualified right rather than an absolute one?
cards.answer: It can be lawfully restricted to protect national security, prevent disorder, or protect others' reputation, if the restriction is lawful, necessary and proportionate.

cards.front: Why do some critics argue that labelling certain principles as 'British values' is problematic?
cards.answer: It can imply other cultures lack these values and can be used to single out communities, especially Muslims, for scrutiny.

title: Conventions of Pop: Rock 'n' Roll of the 1950s and 1960s
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the four musical styles that fused together to create rock 'n' roll.
cards.answer: African-American rhythm and blues / Gospel / Boogie-woogie piano / Country music

cards.front: Name the five instruments in a typical rock 'n' roll line-up.
cards.answer: Electric guitar / Piano / Saxophone / Double bass or electric bass / Drum kit

cards.front: Why did the 12-bar blues become the shared musical language of early rock 'n' roll?
cards.answer: It uses only three chords in a fixed order, letting musicians from different backgrounds play together easily and improvise confidently.

cards.front: Why were most rock 'n' roll songs kept short, often under three minutes?
cards.answer: This reflected the time limits of 45rpm singles and radio airplay, keeping songs immediate and memorable for repeated play.

title: Practical and Ethical Issues in Research
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the three practical issues the lesson identifies as constraints on sociological research.
cards.answer: Time / Cost / Access

cards.front: Name the three ethical issues named at GCSE level in sociological research.
cards.answer: Informed consent / Confidentiality / Harm to participants

cards.front: Why does cost limit the scale and type of sociological research that can be carried out?
cards.answer: Large-scale surveys need funding from research councils, so independent researchers are often limited to small local studies or cheaper online methods.

cards.front: Why might consent given by participants in a prison, school or workplace not be truly voluntary?
cards.answer: Participants in these settings may feel unable to refuse without consequences, even if they are technically told they can withdraw.

cards.front: Name the three things about Silas that made the Raveloe villagers find him strange and frightening.
cards.answer: His cataleptic fits / His solitary habits / His knowledge of herbal remedies

cards.front: According to the lesson, Silas retreated from four things that had given his life meaning. What are they?
cards.answer: Faith / Friendship / Community / Love

cards.front: Why did Silas's cataleptic fits change from being seen as holy at Lantern Yard to being seen as evidence of guilt?
cards.answer: Because the deacon's money went missing during one of his fits, so the congregation reinterpreted the same condition as guilt rather than holiness.

cards.front: Why does Eliot suggest Silas's loss of faith is really a loss of trust in people rather than in God?
cards.answer: Because the Lantern Yard congregation claimed to speak for God, but their judgement was manipulated by William Dane's deceit.

title: Obedience: Milgram and the Authoritarian Personality
subject: psychology-aqa

cards.front: Why did obedience drop when Milgram made the experimenter's authority less clear (e.g. replaced by an ordinary person)?
cards.answer: The authority figure seemed less legitimate, so participants felt less obliged to obey and obedience fell considerably.

cards.front: How does Adorno explain why authoritarian personalities are hostile towards out-groups?
cards.answer: A harsh upbringing made them fear and resent power, so they displace their anxieties downward onto weaker groups while submitting upward to authority.

title: Hollywood Then and Now: Studio System to Modern Blockbuster
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five studios that made up Hollywood's 'Big Five' in the classical era.
cards.answer: MGM / Paramount / Warner Bros. / RKO / 20th Century-Fox

cards.front: Name the four types of content the Hays Code prohibited in Hollywood films.
cards.answer: Explicit sexuality / non-marital relationships shown sympathetically / graphic violence / material challenging organised religion or government
items: material challenging organised religion or government

cards.front: How did the Hays Code shape the endings of 1930s and 1940s horror films?
cards.answer: It demanded moral resolution, so the monster as sexual threat had to be destroyed and the heroine restored to domestic safety.

cards.front: Why did the Paramount decree lead to the collapse of the studios' long-term contract system?
cards.answer: Losing guaranteed cinema outlets removed the reliable assembly-line market for studio films, increasing risk and ending the need for permanent contracted staff.

cards.front: Name the three fears Juliet voices in her Act 4 Scene 3 soliloquy before drinking the potion.
cards.answer: The mixture might not work at all / It might be a poison meant to kill her / She might wake before Romeo arrives
items: The mixture might not work at all
It might be a poison meant to kill her
She might wake before Romeo arrives

cards.front: Name the five figures the lesson says share blame for the tragedy.
cards.answer: The feuding families / Capulet's tyranny / Friar Lawrence's failed plan / Fate (the plague) / The lovers' haste

cards.front: Why is Juliet's conversation with Paris in Act 4, Scene 1 dramatically ironic?
cards.answer: Paris believes Juliet is speaking as his loving bride, but her equivocating words secretly refer to her devotion to Romeo.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Juliet drinking the potion as her bravest moment?
cards.answer: She imagines horrific visions of suffocation and Tybalt's corpse yet drinks the potion anyway despite her terror.

cards.front: Name the three example activities the lesson gives for the pulse-raising phase.
cards.answer: Jogging around the pitch / Light cycling / Steady swimming

cards.front: Name the three example mobility exercises given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arm circles / Hip rotations / Ankle rolls

cards.front: How does mobility work reduce the risk of joint injury during a warm up?
cards.answer: Mobility work increases synovial fluid production, which lubricates joint surfaces and reduces friction that could otherwise cause cartilage wear.

cards.front: Why is controlling arousal levels an important psychological benefit of a warm up?
cards.answer: A nervous performer can use techniques like controlled breathing or imagery during the warm up to regulate their activation level to an optimum state.

cards.front: Name the four social functions the lesson says monasteries performed.
cards.answer: Hospitality for travellers / Education for some boys / Medical care for the poor and elderly / Relief for beggars at their gates
items: Medical care for the poor and elderly
Relief for beggars at their gates

cards.front: Name the five types of matters the lesson says Church courts had jurisdiction over.
cards.answer: Conduct of the clergy / Probate of wills / Marriage disputes / Cases of immorality (fornication, heresy) / Debt cases where an oath was sworn
items: Debt cases where an oath was sworn

cards.front: Why could Henry VIII use popular anticlericalism to attack Church jurisdiction without most people expecting a Protestant Reformation?
cards.answer: Anticlericalism was resentment of the institution, not rejection of faith, so critics still attended mass and sought sacraments.

cards.front: Why did the 'mortmain' problem frustrate gentry families?
cards.answer: Land given to the Church was held in perpetuity, so it could never be recovered by the original family through inheritance or purchase.

cards.front: Name the three properties scientists consider when choosing a radioactive isotope for a particular use.
cards.answer: Type of radiation emitted / Half-life / Toxicity

cards.front: Name the six safety precautions workers use when handling radioactive sources.
cards.answer: Minimise exposure time / Maximise distance from source / Use shielding / Wear protective equipment / Monitor exposure with dosimeters / Use tongs

cards.front: How does a smoke alarm use alpha radiation to detect smoke?
cards.answer: Alpha particles ionise air creating a current; smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.

cards.front: Why is a beta emitter with a longer half-life preferred for industrial thickness gauges?
cards.answer: So the source does not need frequent replacement.

title: Conservation of Energy, Stores and Transfers
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Why does doubling an object's speed quadruple its kinetic energy?
cards.answer: Because kinetic energy depends on speed squared (Ek = ½mv²), so doubling speed multiplies energy by four.

cards.front: Why is no work done if you push hard against a wall that doesn't move?
cards.answer: Work done equals force × distance moved (W = Fs), and since the wall moves zero distance, no energy is transferred.

cards.front: Name the three main types of audience segmentation used by media organisations.
cards.answer: Demographic segmentation / Psychographic segmentation / Geographic segmentation

cards.front: Name the six NRS social grades in order from highest to lowest.
cards.answer: A / B / C1 / C2 / D / E

cards.front: Why do media organisations invest heavily in audience research and categorisation?
cards.answer: Because advertisers want to know audience details like age, income, values and habits, not just total viewer numbers, to justify ad space and production budgets.

cards.front: Why might a low BARB share for a programme on a Friday night not mean the content was poor?
cards.answer: It might indicate poor scheduling rather than poor content.

cards.front: Name the three main skills tested in the Germany 1919–1939 exam.
cards.answer: Knowledge and understanding (recall and understanding) / Historical analysis (explanation and analysis) / Source and interpretations work (source/interpretation analysis)

cards.front: Name the four things interpretations of Germany 1919–1939 often differ on.
cards.answer: Hitler's personal role / How ordinary Germans related to the regime / Whether economic recovery was genuine or illusory / The degree of terror versus consent
items: How ordinary Germans related to the regime
Whether economic recovery was genuine or illusory
The degree of terror versus consent

cards.front: Why can a source still be very useful even if it is biased?
cards.answer: Because the bias itself can tell us something important about the attitudes or aims of the time.

cards.front: Why do most students lose marks in the exam despite having enough knowledge?
cards.answer: They apply the wrong skill to the wrong question type instead of matching their answer to what's asked.

cards.front: Name the four key techniques Shelley uses in 'England in 1819'.
cards.answer: Subversive use of sonnet form / Accumulation of grievances / Violent imagery / Dramatic volta

cards.front: Name the three key techniques khan uses in 'pot'.
cards.answer: Everyday object as vehicle for ideas / Anaphora and short single-line stanzas / Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern
items: Everyday object as vehicle for ideas
Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern

cards.front: How does pathetic fallacy work in Eliot's 'In a London Drawingroom'?
cards.answer: The grey sky mirrors the emotional and spiritual greyness of Victorian conformity.

cards.front: Why does khan repeat 'or / did they say' when listing how the pot arrived in Britain?
cards.answer: The repetition makes each explanation for the pot's arrival sound like an excuse, exposing the dishonesty behind its looting.

title: Engineering Developments — Bicycles, Theme-Park Rides & Smart Phones
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Besides frame material, name the three other structural improvements to bicycles given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pneumatic tyres (comfort and grip) / Geared drivetrain (choose ratio for hills/flat) / Hydraulic disc brakes on mountain bikes
items: Hydraulic disc brakes on mountain bikes

cards.front: Name the three key developments the lesson gives for how mechanical design in theme-park rides improved.
cards.answer: Three-sided wheel-and-rail system preventing derailment / Shift from wooden to steel structural frames / Electronic launch and braking systems replacing mechanical control
items: Shift from wooden to steel structural frames
Electronic launch and braking systems replacing mechanical control

cards.front: Why did structural steel replace wood as the frame material for roller coasters?
cards.answer: Steel allowed taller, more complex track layouts that could withstand repeated loading cycles without fatigue failure.

cards.front: How did digital signal processing improve on analogue radio in mobile phones?
cards.answer: It replaced analogue radio and allowed more calls to share the same radio spectrum.

title: London at war 1939: target, port and government capital
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three types of gas mask were issued, matched to age group?
cards.answer: Black rubber mask with metal filter for adults / Brightly coloured 'Mickey Mouse' mask for small children / Helmet-and-pump gas helmet for babies
items: Black rubber mask with metal filter for adults
Brightly coloured 'Mickey Mouse' mask for small children

cards.front: What were the three waves of evacuation from London mentioned in the lesson?
cards.answer: First wave from September 1939 / Second wave after Black Saturday, September 1940 / Third wave in 1944 with the V1 attacks
items: Second wave after Black Saturday, September 1940
Third wave in 1944 with the V1 attacks

cards.front: Why did the Home Office initially ban Londoners from sheltering in Tube stations?
cards.answer: It feared a 'deep shelter mentality' — that civilians who went underground would refuse to come up and work would stop.

cards.front: Why did Anderson shelters work less well in the East End during Black Saturday?
cards.answer: Flat-roofed terraced backyards there were less practical for burying a shelter than the suburban semi-detached gardens the shelters were designed for.

cards.front: Name the four main ways Christians interpret the Bible.
cards.answer: Literal / Conservative / Symbolic / Biblical myth

cards.front: In the parable of the sheep and goats, what four actions decide the final judgement?
cards.answer: Fed the hungry / Welcomed strangers / Clothed the poor / Visited prisoners

cards.front: Why do Quakers and the Salvation Army not use sacraments?
cards.answer: They believe God's grace needs no outward sign.

cards.front: How is Confirmation understood in relation to baptism?
cards.answer: It is a personal completion of baptism, where the candidate affirms their faith and receives a strengthening of the Holy Spirit.

title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: The lesson names three pillars of Sikh teaching. What are they?
cards.answer: Honest work (kirat karni) / Sharing with others (vand chakna) / Meditating on God's name (nam japna)

cards.front: The lesson gives four dietary restrictions from different faiths that explain why langar is vegetarian. What are they?
cards.answer: Muslims require halal meat / Jews require kosher food / Hindus may not eat beef / Many Buddhists are vegetarian

cards.front: Why does the akhand path reading never have any gaps, even during the night?
cards.answer: Because when one reader finishes their section, the next begins immediately, keeping the reading continuous and unbroken.

cards.front: Why is the akhand path timed to end just before a wedding ceremony begins?
cards.answer: So the final words are read right before the key event, placing it under the eternal Guru's guidance at that moment.

title: Library Modules: random, math, time and turtle
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four library modules the PLS says you must know.
cards.answer: random / math / time / turtle

cards.front: What are the four common mistakes listed for using these library modules?
cards.answer: Forgetting to import the module / Using the wrong range in random.randint / Using a turtle subprogram not in the PLS / Leaving out turtle.done()
items: Using the wrong range in random.randint
Using a turtle subprogram not in the PLS

cards.front: Why does math.floor(-3.5) return -4 instead of -3?
cards.answer: Because math.floor always rounds down towards negative infinity, not towards zero.

cards.front: Why does the filled square program only need one begin_fill() and one end_fill(), even though its loop repeats four times?
cards.answer: Because the fill colour applies to everything drawn between begin_fill() and end_fill(), covering all four sides the loop draws.

cards.front: List the three types of radiation from most to least ionising.
cards.answer: Alpha particles / Beta particles / Gamma rays

cards.front: What three observations did Rutherford make in the gold foil experiment?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through / Some particles were deflected / A few bounced straight back
items: Most alpha particles passed straight through

cards.front: Why does higher ionising power mean lower penetrating power for radiation?
cards.answer: Radiation with higher ionising power transfers its energy quickly, so it cannot travel far before losing all its energy.

cards.front: Why must you subtract the background count rate when measuring a radioactive source's activity?
cards.answer: This gives a corrected count rate that represents radiation from the source alone, not the environment around it.

title: Physical Indicators of Health & Interpreting Data
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five physical indicators of health that students must know.
cards.answer: Blood pressure / Peak flow / Body mass index (BMI) / Waist-to-hip ratio / Pulse rate (resting and recovery)

cards.front: Name the four contributing factors considered when interpreting physical health indicators.
cards.answer: Age / Sex / Lifestyle / Environment

cards.front: Why is a peak flow reading 50% or below an asthma patient's usual reading significant?
cards.answer: It signals a severe asthma attack requiring immediate treatment.

cards.front: Why does regular blood pressure monitoring matter even if someone feels fine?
cards.answer: Many people have hypertension without experiencing any symptoms, so regular checks are needed to detect it.

cards.front: What four forms of racism does the play show?
cards.answer: Formal colour bar (employment discrimination) / Informal exclusion (housing, social spaces) / Casual everyday hostility (verbal abuse, suspicion) / Internalised effects (self-doubt, fear, proving worth)

cards.front: According to the lesson, in what four ways does Odimba present unity across difference?
cards.answer: Without erasing difference / As earned rather than given / As historically grounded / As fragile

cards.front: How do characters resist casual, everyday hostility in the play?
cards.answer: Through dignity and pride — refusing to be diminished, using cultural expression, self-naming (Princess), and asserting their presence.

cards.front: How does Princess resist the internalised effects of racism?
cards.answer: Through imagination — her imaginative world resists the psychological damage of being told she is less than, making dreaming itself an act of defiance.

cards.front: Name the four events that make up the Paschal Mystery.
cards.answer: Suffering of Jesus / Death of Jesus / Resurrection of Jesus / Ascension of Jesus

cards.front: Name the five 'last things' covered by Catholic eschatology.
cards.answer: Resurrection / Judgement / Heaven / Hell / Purgatory

cards.front: Why does Luke 24 show that Jesus' resurrection was a bodily event, not just a spiritual symbol?
cards.answer: Because it describes the risen Jesus walking, talking and eating with his disciples, not merely appearing as a spirit.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching hold that hell is a real possibility?
cards.answer: Because God respects human freedom, even allowing individuals who freely and completely reject him to remain separated from him.

title: Metamorphic Rocks: Heat, Pressure and Texture
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the two types of metamorphism described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Contact metamorphism / Regional metamorphism

cards.front: Name the four metamorphic rocks covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Slate / Schist / Marble / Metaquartzite

cards.front: Why is contact metamorphism driven mainly by heat rather than pressure?
cards.answer: Because within the metamorphic aureole pressure is not significantly elevated, so heat from the intrusion is the main agent of change.

cards.front: How can you tell metaquartzite apart from sandstone by how each rock breaks?
cards.answer: In metaquartzite fresh breaks pass through the quartz grains because recrystallisation destroyed grain boundaries, whereas in sandstone breaks go around grains.

cards.front: Name the six typical pop ballad features the lesson lists to listen for.
cards.answer: Slow tempo / Expressive vocal with vibrato and melisma / Piano or guitar-led opening that builds in texture / Slow harmonic rhythm / Verse-chorus form with a contrasting middle eight / Key change before the final chorus
items: Expressive vocal with vibrato and melisma
Piano or guitar-led opening that builds in texture
Verse-chorus form with a contrasting middle eight
Key change before the final chorus

cards.front: Which three artists' versions of 'Make You Feel My Love' does the lesson compare?
cards.answer: Bob Dylan / Billy Joel / Adele

cards.front: Why do pop ballads typically use a slow harmonic rhythm?
cards.answer: Chords change infrequently, creating a stable harmonic backdrop so the melody and vocal ornamentation can be heard clearly.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the middle eight in a pop ballad's structure?
cards.answer: It breaks the repeating verse-chorus pattern, offering contrast through new harmony, a rise in register, or a changed accompaniment texture.

title: Break-Even and the Importance of Cash
subject: cambridge-nationals-enterprise-and-marketing

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for a start-up running out of cash.
cards.answer: Customers paying late / Paying suppliers upfront / High stock levels / Seasonal demand

cards.front: Name the three assumptions the break-even formula makes.
cards.answer: Selling price stays constant for every unit / Variable cost per unit does not change / Every unit produced is sold
items: Selling price stays constant for every unit
Variable cost per unit does not change

cards.front: Why does a rise in variable cost per unit increase the break-even quantity?
cards.answer: Each unit contributes less towards covering fixed costs, so more units must be sold to break even.

cards.front: Why does the total revenue line on a break-even graph start at zero?
cards.answer: Because if no units have been sold yet, there is no revenue at all.

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for choosing the right scale of production.
cards.answer: How many products are needed / How much can be spent on tooling / How much customisation the customer wants
items: How much can be spent on tooling
How much customisation the customer wants

cards.front: Name the three mass-production processes the lesson gives for shaping metals.
cards.answer: Casting and forging / Pressing and stamping / Robotic welding

cards.front: Why is unit cost high in one-off production?
cards.answer: It uses general-purpose tools and hand skills, so labour and set-up time aren't shared across other products.

cards.front: How does quality control usually work on a mass-production line?
cards.answer: It is often automated, with sensors checking dimensions and finish as products move along the line.

title: Newspapers: The Sun — Industry and Audience
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four roles involved in the pre-press stage of producing The Sun.
cards.answer: Journalists (newsgathering) / Editor (sets agenda, signs off content) / Sales team (sells advertising space) / Page designer (lays out stories/adverts)

cards.front: Name the four sources of revenue the lesson gives for how The Sun is funded.
cards.answer: Advertising / Advertorials / Digital subscriptions / Diversification into gambling brands

cards.front: Why is The Sun written using bold text, strong visuals and short chunks of copy?
cards.answer: To make it accessible and quick to skim for readers with weaker literacy or those reading on a commute.

cards.front: Why do rival publishers dispute whose online newspaper audience is really the biggest?
cards.answer: Because reach figures alone don't show engagement, so rivals like MailOnline instead compare total reading minutes to claim a bigger audience.

cards.front: Name the four types of reason the lesson gives for why performers use PEDs.
cards.answer: Desire for competitive advantage / Financial reward and career pressure / Cultural and peer pressure / win-at-all-costs culture / To recover from injury and train harder
items: Cultural and peer pressure / win-at-all-costs culture
To recover from injury and train harder

cards.front: Name the three counter-points the lesson gives against the 'level playing field' argument for PED use.
cards.answer: Not all athletes dope, so refusers are disadvantaged / Wealthier athletes/nations can dope more effectively / Normalising doping raises health risks for everyone
items: Not all athletes dope, so refusers are disadvantaged
Wealthier athletes/nations can dope more effectively
Normalising doping raises health risks for everyone

cards.front: Why can an athlete be banned even if they didn't know they'd taken a prohibited substance?
cards.answer: Athletes have strict liability, so a positive test result leads to a ban regardless of the performer's knowledge or intent.

cards.front: Why can anabolic steroid use permanently reduce adult height in adolescent users?
cards.answer: It causes premature closure of growth plates in adolescents, stopping bones from growing further before full height is reached.

title: Changes of State and Internal Energy
subject: science-ocr

cards.front: Name the five changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting (solid to liquid) / Freezing (liquid to solid) / Evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas) / Condensation (gas to liquid) / Sublimation (solid directly to gas)

cards.front: Why does evaporation cause cooling of a liquid?
cards.answer: The fastest-moving particles escape from the surface, reducing the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind.

cards.front: Why is the specific latent heat of vaporisation always greater than the specific latent heat of fusion for the same substance?
cards.answer: Because particles must completely overcome the intermolecular forces between them to become a gas.

cards.front: Name the three British historical figures Agard says he was taught about in school.
cards.answer: Dick Whittington / Lord Nelson / Florence Nightingale

cards.front: What are the three stages 'London' moves through across its four stanzas?
cards.answer: Observation (stanza 1) / Analysis (stanzas 2-3) / Devastating conclusion (stanza 4)

cards.front: Why does Blake use synaesthesia in 'the hapless Soldier's sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls'?
cards.answer: It turns a sigh into blood on the walls, creating a horrifying image that directly blames the monarchy for soldiers' deaths.

cards.front: How does the 'youthful Harlot's curse' line show poverty's effect on future generations in 'London'?
cards.answer: The prostitute's suffering destroys even a newborn's innocence, showing poverty corrupts everything, even the next generation.

cards.front: Name the three locations where Nigeria's government has set up Free Trade Zones.
cards.answer: Lekki / Calabar / Lagos

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson gives for why TNCs are attracted to Nigeria.
cards.answer: Oil reserves / A vast consumer market / English as the language of business
items: English as the language of business

cards.front: Why does turning raw materials into manufactured goods add more value for Nigeria?
cards.answer: Raw cocoa beans sold unprocessed earn one price, but chocolate bars made from them in Nigeria earn far more.

cards.front: Why did the Nigerian government set up Free Trade Zones?
cards.answer: To attract factories by offering low taxes and reliable electricity.

title: UK Weather Hazards: The Storm Desmond Floods
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that combined to make Storm Desmond so extreme.
cards.answer: Saturated ground from a wet November / Steep relief forcing air upwards (orographic rainfall) / An atmospheric river of tropical moisture / Climate change adding extra water vapour
items: Saturated ground from a wet November
Steep relief forcing air upwards (orographic rainfall)
An atmospheric river of tropical moisture
Climate change adding extra water vapour

cards.front: Name the five types of UK weather hazard the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Wind storms / Heavy rain and flooding / Snow and ice / Heatwaves / Drought

cards.front: Why did Cumbria flood again so soon after the 2009 floods, even though defences had been raised?
cards.answer: Desmond's rainfall was so far above the 2009 totals that the newly raised flood defences were overwhelmed.

cards.front: How did climate change make Storm Desmond's rainfall worse?
cards.answer: Warmer Atlantic waters held more water vapour, making a downpour like Desmond about 40% more likely.

title: Wool, Banks and the Royal Purse
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three pillars did Edward I's royal finance rest on?
cards.answer: The wool customs (maltolt) / Loans from Italian banking houses / Parliamentary grants of taxation

cards.front: Which four regions fed the flocks that produced England's wool in the thirteenth century?
cards.answer: The Cotswolds / Lincolnshire / The Welsh borders / The Yorkshire moors

cards.front: Why did the Riccardi banking house collapse in 1294?
cards.answer: French officers seized their Paris assets while Edward froze their English accounts, so they lost income from both ends and went bankrupt.

cards.front: How did the 1279-80 re-coinage make it harder to clip coins?
cards.answer: New pennies were struck on a heavier flan with a larger inscription that made any clipping obvious.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Why is the live wire dangerous even when the switch is off?
cards.answer: It is still at 230 V relative to earth, so touching it creates a potential difference that drives current through your body.

cards.front: Why does increasing the transmission voltage reduce the current in the National Grid cables?
cards.answer: Since P = IV, if power stays the same, increasing the voltage means the current must decrease.

title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things the amount of internal energy in a substance depends on.
cards.answer: Temperature / Mass / What material it's made from

cards.front: Name the four changes of state described in the particle model explanation.
cards.answer: Melting (solid to liquid) / Boiling (liquid to gas) / Condensing (gas to liquid) / Freezing (liquid to solid)

cards.front: Why does a metal spoon heat up quickly in hot soup compared to the water around it?
cards.answer: Metals generally have lower specific heat capacities than water, so they need less energy to heat up.

cards.front: How does the particle model explain why gases take up much more space than liquids or solids?
cards.answer: During boiling, energy completely overcomes the forces between particles, letting them move freely and spread far apart.

cards.front: How did Malotki's 1983 research challenge Whorf's claim about the Hopi language?
cards.answer: Malotki found Hopi actually has tense and extensive time vocabulary, undermining Whorf's claim that Hopi speakers conceptualise time differently.

cards.front: How does learning new words later in childhood challenge Piaget's view that language depends on thought?
cards.answer: Learning a new word can introduce a new concept, suggesting language can shape thought rather than only expressing existing thoughts.

cards.front: What are the three regular past participle endings for -er, -ir and -re verbs in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: -er verbs end in -é / -ir verbs end in -i / -re verbs end in -u

cards.front: Name the five time phrases given for signalling the past tense in French.
cards.answer: l'année dernière (last year) / l'été dernier (last summer) / la semaine dernière (last week) / hier (yesterday) / il y a deux ans (two years ago)
items: il y a deux ans (two years ago)

cards.front: Why do verbs of movement and reflexive verbs use être instead of avoir in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: They belong to a specific group of verbs, mainly verbs of movement, that take être as their auxiliary rather than avoir.

cards.front: How does the past participle change when the subject of an être verb is feminine plural?
cards.answer: Add -es to the past participle to agree with the feminine plural subject, e.g. elles sont allées.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says resource exploitation changes the environment where it happens.
cards.answer: Overfishing collapses food chains / Intensive farming erodes soil and depletes aquifers / Mining and drilling pollute air and water / Deforestation removes habitat and releases stored carbon
items: Intensive farming erodes soil and depletes aquifers
Mining and drilling pollute air and water
Deforestation removes habitat and releases stored carbon

cards.front: What are the four PEEL steps for describing a choropleth resource map?
cards.answer: Pattern - where is the highest band / Exception - which country breaks the pattern / Explain - what factor causes that / Link - how it connects to another map
items: Pattern - where is the highest band
Exception - which country breaks the pattern
Link - how it connects to another map

cards.front: Why does the UK's north-west receive far more rain than the south-east?
cards.answer: South-westerly winds carry moist Atlantic air, which rises over uplands, cools and releases relief rainfall, leaving little moisture by the south-east.

cards.front: Why did Russia's gas exports give it political influence over Europe?
cards.answer: Populous, resource-poor European countries depended on Russia's gas exports, giving Russia geopolitical leverage over European energy security until 2022.

title: Cell Structure, Microscopy and Specialised Cells
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four adaptations of the sperm cell described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Streamlined head with acrosome containing enzymes / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Long flagellum for propulsion / Nucleus carrying haploid genetic information
items: Streamlined head with acrosome containing enzymes
Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the five organelles found in an animal cell, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Nucleus / Cytoplasm / Cell membrane / Mitochondria / Ribosomes

cards.front: Why do muscle cells contain more mitochondria than other cells?
cards.answer: Muscle cells have high energy demands, so they need more mitochondria to carry out aerobic respiration.

cards.front: Why does the plant cell wall stop the cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: The cellulose cell wall provides structural strength that resists the pressure created as water enters the cell.

cards.front: Name the four things Gothic fiction thrives on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Isolated settings / Supernatural terror / Psychological dread / The idea the past cannot be escaped
items: The idea the past cannot be escaped

cards.front: Name the four familiar Gothic elements Hill uses in The Woman in Black.
cards.answer: Fog / Marshland / A decaying house / A vengeful spirit

cards.front: Why did Hill choose to write in the traditional ghost story form?
cards.answer: She admired James's restraint and psychological complexity and wanted to prove the classic ghost story could still terrify a modern reader.

cards.front: Why does Kipps choose to write down his story rather than tell it aloud?
cards.answer: Writing lets him control the narrative and impose order on an experience that shattered his understanding of the world.

cards.front: Name the six qualities (the 6Cs) that enable practitioners to deliver person-centred values.
cards.answer: Care / Compassion / Competence / Communication / Courage / Commitment

cards.front: Name the three person-centred values that together form the 'empowerment cluster'.
cards.answer: Independence / Choice / Encouraging decision making

cards.front: How do independence, choice and encouraging decision making combine to produce empowerment?
cards.answer: Independence lets service users do things themselves, choice gives them options, and encouraging decision making builds confidence to use those options.

cards.front: Why does a community nurse close the door before discussing medication even when the patient lives alone?
cards.answer: Because the habit of maintaining privacy protects the service user's dignity, regardless of whether anyone else could actually overhear.

title: Political change, 1960-2000: from Kennedy to Clinton
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four goals of Kennedy's New Frontier programme.
cards.answer: Tackle poverty / Extend civil rights / Invest in education / Create Medicare

cards.front: Name the four effects Watergate had on American political life.
cards.answer: Public trust in government collapsed / War Powers Act passed (1973) / Campaign finance reform legislation passed / The suffix '-gate' entered the language

cards.front: Why did Kennedy struggle to pass his New Frontier programme through Congress?
cards.answer: He faced a conservative Congress that blocked much of his ambitious domestic agenda.

cards.front: Why did the federal deficit increase substantially under Reagan despite economic growth?
cards.answer: Because Reagan's tax cuts outpaced the reductions in government spending.

cards.front: Name the four layers of the Earth's structure, from outer to inner.
cards.answer: Crust / Mantle / Outer core / Inner core

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that affect hazard risk.
cards.answer: Population density / Wealth / Frequency of the hazard / Type of hazard / Climate change

cards.front: Why do richer countries usually have a lower death toll from natural hazards?
cards.answer: They can afford early-warning systems, stronger buildings and well-funded emergency services.

cards.front: Why do intraplate earthquakes happen even though most hazards occur at plate boundaries?
cards.answer: They are caused by ancient faults reactivating or a magma plume punching through the plate from below.

title: The Origin of Evil and the Problem of Suffering
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: According to Catholic teaching, what three things does Original Sin damage in human nature?
cards.answer: A tendency towards self-centredness / A weakening of the will / A darkening of the intellect

cards.front: Why do Catholic thinkers treat moral evil and natural evil differently when explaining the problem of evil?
cards.answer: Moral evil can be traced to human freedom being misused, but natural evil is harder to explain without reference to God's purposes.

cards.front: How does the Irenaean 'soul-making' view explain why evil and suffering exist?
cards.answer: It sees humanity as created immature, so evil and suffering are conditions for moral and spiritual growth, not just consequences of sin.

title: Britain in the early 1950s: austerity and rationing
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six goods that still required ration books by 1951, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Meat / Butter / Cooking fats / Sugar / Tea / Cheese

cards.front: What were the three weekly adult ration allowances given in the lesson for the early 1950s?
cards.answer: 13 ounces of meat / 1½ ounces of cheese / 6 ounces of butter

cards.front: Why was sterling convertibility suspended within weeks of being restored in 1947?
cards.answer: Restoring convertibility triggered a run on the pound, showing how fragile Britain's finances were, so it was quickly suspended.

cards.front: Why did young couples often wait five or more years for council housing in the early 1950s?
cards.answer: Despite government building programmes, demand for housing consistently outpaced the supply of new homes being built.

title: The Five-Year Plans and Soviet Industry
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives four reasons why Stalin pushed rapid industrialisation. Name them.
cards.answer: Defence against industrial powers / Autarky (self-sufficiency) / Ideology (need an industrial working class) / Succession (defining himself against Bukharin)

cards.front: How did factory managers respond to quota pressure under the planning system, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Hoarding raw materials / Padding workforce numbers / Ignoring quality / Faking returns

cards.front: Why can't Five-Year Plan output figures be treated as accurate measurements of growth?
cards.answer: Output was measured in inconsistent units, padded by managers to fulfil quotas, and over-fulfilment was reported as a political survival tactic during the Terror.

cards.front: Why were around 10,000 foreign engineers hired during the First Five-Year Plan?
cards.answer: To install machinery, train Soviet workers and run the new plants until Soviet engineers could take over.

cards.front: Name the three linked moves Mao used between 1962 and 1966 to prepare his comeback against the party.
cards.answer: Socialist Education Movement to attack rural cadres / Lin Biao's PLA cult of Mao / Campaign in education and culture against 'bourgeois' thinking
items: Socialist Education Movement to attack rural cadres
Lin Biao's PLA cult of Mao
Campaign in education and culture against 'bourgeois' thinking

cards.front: What four things did Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping do to run the recovery after the Great Leap Forward?
cards.answer: Scaled back the communes / Allowed peasants small private plots / Restored material incentives in factories / Rebuilt the bureaucracy

cards.front: Why did Mao see Liu and Deng's recovery policies as a betrayal of the revolution?
cards.answer: They looked like the Soviet Union under Khrushchev, with the revolution quietly buried under managers, technicians and bonuses.

cards.front: Why did Mao attack examinations in his reform of education?
cards.answer: He argued they restored privilege, filtering out peasants' sons in favour of pupils taught bourgeois entrance tests by middle-class teachers.

cards.front: What four primary research techniques does the lesson describe for designers?
cards.answer: Market research & interviews / Ergonomics & anthropometric data / Focus groups / Product analysis

cards.front: What secondary research sources does the lesson name?
cards.answer: Published books / Academic journals / Manufacturer datasheets / Government statistics / Online databases

cards.front: Why are interviews often more useful than written surveys for design research?
cards.answer: The designer can ask follow-up questions and observe body language, giving richer data than a survey alone.

cards.front: Why do designers usually combine secondary research with primary research?
cards.answer: Secondary research is quick and cheap for background knowledge, then primary research fills gaps it doesn't cover.

cards.front: Name the eight main energy stores the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Chemical / Nuclear / Kinetic / Gravitational potential / Elastic potential / Thermal / Electrostatic / Electromagnetic

cards.front: What three wires does a home appliance's three-core cable contain?
cards.answer: Live / Neutral / Earth

cards.front: Why does double-glazing reduce heat loss through a window?
cards.answer: It traps a layer of air or gas between two panes, and air is a poor thermal conductor, so less heat transfers across.

cards.front: How does a generator in a power station produce electricity?
cards.answer: A turbine, driven by the fuel source, spins a magnet near a coil of wire, which generates electricity.

cards.front: What five reasons does the lesson give for why a business needs finance?
cards.answer: Establishing a new business / Funding expansion / Running the business / Recruitment / Marketing

cards.front: What four factors does the lesson say suitability of a finance source depends on?
cards.answer: How much is needed / How quickly it's needed / How long it's needed for / How established the business is

cards.front: Why is retained profit a low-risk source of finance for a business?
cards.answer: It costs nothing in interest, doesn't need repaying, and doesn't cause loss of control to outsiders.

cards.front: Why is a bank loan better than an overdraft for a large one-off purchase like a delivery van?
cards.answer: A loan gives a fixed sum repaid over an agreed period, while an overdraft is only meant to cover short-term cash-flow problems.

cards.front: The lesson names four volcanic hazards that can kill people. What are they?
cards.answer: Pyroclastic flows / Lava flows / Lahars / Ash clouds

cards.front: Name the six social and economic factors the lesson says increase a community's vulnerability.
cards.answer: High population density / Low income / Poor building quality / Limited emergency services / Lack of education/drills / Weak government/infrastructure

cards.front: Why did the 2010 Haiti earthquake kill far more people than the much more powerful 2011 Tōhoku earthquake?
cards.answer: Japan had stronger buildings and a tsunami warning system, while Haiti had weak buildings and limited emergency services, so vulnerability was lower in Japan.

cards.front: How does Japan's Earthquake Early Warning system reduce risk during an earthquake?
cards.answer: It uses fast primary waves from the rupture to send a warning before slower damaging surface waves arrive, letting trains brake and surgeons pause.

cards.front: The lesson tracks Elizabeth's growth through five specific moments in the novel. What are they?
cards.answer: Amused defiance at the assembly / Trust in Wickham / Shock at Darcy's letter / Humility at Pemberley / Mature love in the second proposal
items: Mature love in the second proposal

cards.front: Name the four character contrasts the lesson says Austen uses to build her characters.
cards.answer: Wickham's charm vs Darcy's awkwardness / Elizabeth's wit vs Jane's gentleness / Mrs Bennet's anxiety vs Mr Bennet's detachment / Collins's obsequiousness vs Elizabeth's independence
items: Mrs Bennet's anxiety vs Mr Bennet's detachment

cards.front: Why does Jane's goodness almost cost her Bingley?
cards.answer: Her inability to think ill of anyone makes her too reserved, so her true feelings for Bingley stay invisible to him.

cards.front: How does Lady Catherine's interrogation of Elizabeth at Rosings reveal her worldview?
cards.answer: It shows she believes her rank entitles her to dictate others' marriages and behaviour, enforcing social rules as rigidly as law.

cards.front: Name the three conditions collision theory says must be met for a reaction to occur.
cards.answer: Particles must collide with each other / Collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy) / Collide with the correct orientation
items: Particles must collide with each other
Collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy)

cards.front: Name the four main factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration / Pressure / Surface area

cards.front: Why can a fine powder of a combustible material in air cause a dust explosion?
cards.answer: The surface area is so enormous that the reaction rate becomes dangerously fast.

cards.front: Why can 1/t be used as a measure of reaction rate?
cards.answer: A shorter time (t) to complete a set amount of reaction means a faster rate, so 1/t is proportional to rate.

cards.front: Name the three areas of social treatment the lesson says this scene deepens.
cards.answer: Race / Gender / Class

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson describes Jo and the Boy doing together that show their innocence.
cards.answer: Play together / Tease each other / Share physical closeness

cards.front: How does the Boy's departure differ from Helen's earlier abandonment of Jo?
cards.answer: The Boy leaves with genuine regret, whereas Helen leaves Jo with barely a backward glance.

cards.front: Why is Act 1 Scene 2 structurally crucial to the rest of the play?
cards.answer: It creates the pregnancy that drives the second half, giving Geof a reason to stay and Helen a reason to return.

title: The Structure and Function of the Brain
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four lobes that the cerebral cortex is divided into.
cards.answer: Frontal lobe / Temporal lobe / Parietal lobe / Occipital lobe

cards.front: Why does cerebellum damage cause jerky, poorly timed movement instead of stopping movement completely?
cards.answer: The cerebellum refines and times movement by comparing intended and actual movement, rather than switching movement on or off.

cards.front: Why is understanding a spoken sentence not the job of just one lobe?
cards.answer: It draws on the temporal lobe to recognise words and the frontal lobe to work out meaning and form a response, working as a network.

title: Catholic Social Teaching, Mission and Funeral Rite
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What are the six core principles of Catholic Social Teaching named in the lesson?
cards.answer: Dignity of the human person / The common good / Solidarity / Subsidiarity / Preferential option for the poor / Care for creation

cards.front: What are the three areas of work CAFOD carries out?
cards.answer: Emergency relief / Long-term development / Justice and advocacy

cards.front: Why does the Sheep and Goats parable make serving the poor a matter of justice rather than optional charity?
cards.answer: Jesus says whatever is done for the poor is done for him, making service of the vulnerable a criterion of the Last Judgment.

cards.front: How does the Catholic funeral rite differ from most Protestant funeral rites regarding the Eucharist?
cards.answer: The Catholic rite includes a full Requiem Mass centred on the Eucharist, while most Protestant funerals focus on Scripture, hymns and preaching instead.

cards.front: Why does Wells never explain the science behind the Heat-Ray?
cards.answer: Because the weapon is simply beyond human understanding, showing Martian technology's overwhelming superiority.

cards.front: How does the narrator's clinical detachment create dramatic irony in the novel?
cards.answer: It makes the reader feel the horror of events that the narrator himself suppresses while describing them scientifically.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three common methods the lesson gives for measuring the rate of a reaction.
cards.answer: Collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water / Measuring the loss of mass on a balance / Timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque
items: Collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water
Measuring the loss of mass on a balance
Timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

cards.front: Why does changing the temperature or concentration alter the steepness of a rate graph but not the final volume of gas produced?
cards.answer: These changes only affect how fast particles collide, not the amount of reactant present, so the same total gas forms if the amount of reactant is unchanged.

cards.front: Name the four customer needs the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Price / Quality / Choice / Convenience

cards.front: Name the four sources of secondary research given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Internet / Published market reports / Government statistics / Industry trade bodies

cards.front: Why can getting price and quality wrong threaten a business's survival?
cards.answer: The wrong price loses customers to cheaper rivals or cuts profit, while poor quality drives customers away and spreads negative reviews.

cards.front: Why does market research reduce risk when launching a new product?
cards.answer: It gives evidence of what customers want before money is spent on production, narrowing uncertainty even though it can't eliminate risk entirely.

title: Gender, Stereotypes and the Mulvey Male Gaze
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three example stereotypes the lesson gives to show how stereotypes work as cognitive shortcuts.
cards.answer: A gruff older male detective / A vain teenage girl obsessed with looks / A nerdy male computer scientist
items: A vain teenage girl obsessed with looks

cards.front: Name the three examples of counter-types given in the lesson.
cards.answer: A male nurse / A female action hero / An older woman shown as professionally authoritative
items: An older woman shown as professionally authoritative

cards.front: Why do most contemporary media scholars favour social constructionism over essentialism?
cards.answer: Because it can explain why gender representations change over time and vary across cultures.

cards.front: How do stereotypes become naturalised so audiences see them as reality rather than construction?
cards.answer: Through repetition across hundreds of media products, genres, platforms and time periods until audiences stop noticing the construction.

title: The Nervous System and Reflex Arc
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the five parts of the brain named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cerebrum / Cerebellum / Medulla oblongata / Hypothalamus / Pituitary gland

cards.front: Name the four variables the lesson says could affect ruler drop reaction time results.
cards.answer: Caffeine / Fatigue / Distractions / Practice

cards.front: Why do synapses only allow impulses to travel in one direction?
cards.answer: Because neurotransmitters are released from the pre-synaptic side only, and receptors are only present on the post-synaptic side.

cards.front: Why is the ruler drop test a measure of voluntary reaction rather than a true reflex?
cards.answer: Because the information passes through the brain (visual cortex to motor cortex) rather than being processed only in the spinal cord.

cards.front: Name the three irreversible losses Golding uses to track the loss of innocence.
cards.answer: Percival forgets his name and address / The unnamed littlun dies in the first fire / Simon is murdered by the group
items: Percival forgets his name and address
The unnamed littlun dies in the first fire
Simon is murdered by the group

cards.front: What five-step pattern does the lesson give for analysing the printed extract?
cards.answer: Point / Quotation / Analysis of language / Effect on reader / Link to Golding's purpose

cards.front: Why do most of the boys choose to follow Jack rather than Ralph?
cards.answer: Following a strong leader is simpler than thinking for themselves; authoritarianism offers protection, belonging and excitement, while democracy demands effort and self-discipline.

cards.front: How does Roger's story arc support Golding's claim that evil is innate?
cards.answer: Roger moves from throwing stones to deliberately missing to committing murder, showing civilisation's taboo alone restrained his cruelty, and once removed, violence became inevitable.

cards.front: Name the three combined factors the lesson gives for why UK landscapes vary.
cards.answer: Geology (hard upland rocks vs softer lowland rocks) / Climate (wetter, cooler in north and west) / Human activity (farming, settlement and tourism)
items: Geology (hard upland rocks vs softer lowland rocks)
Climate (wetter, cooler in north and west)

cards.front: Name the three management strategies used in the Lake District National Park to handle tourist pressure.
cards.answer: Footpath repair / Visitor management / Planning controls

cards.front: How did glaciers shape the Lake District's landscape?
cards.answer: Glaciers carved deep U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes such as Windermere, and sharp ridges.

cards.front: Why do cereals and root crops thrive in the Norfolk Broads?
cards.answer: Drier continental air brings only about 600mm of rain a year onto deep, fertile soils.

title: The Revolt of the Earls & William’s Legacy
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five effects the 1075 revolt had on the rebel earls and their earldoms.
cards.answer: Roger's lands forfeited and imprisoned for life / Ralph's estates confiscated / Earldom of Hereford abolished / Earldom of Norfolk abolished / William never let earls hold such power again
items: Roger's lands forfeited and imprisoned for life
William never let earls hold such power again

cards.front: What four traits does the lesson use to describe William the Conqueror's character?
cards.answer: Ruthless / Politically shrewd / Militarily brilliant / Deeply religious

cards.front: Why did the 1075 revolt collapse so quickly?
cards.answer: The rebels could not join forces: Roger was blocked at the River Severn, Ralph fled, and a Danish fleet arrived too late.

cards.front: How did William Rufus defeat Odo's 1088 revolt?
cards.answer: He secured the loyalty of the English people and key Norman barons by promising good government and lower taxes.

title: England before 1066 and the Norman impact on migration
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three claimants to the English throne after Edward the Confessor died in 1066.
cards.answer: Harold Godwinson / Harald Hardrada of Norway / William, Duke of Normandy

cards.front: What four things did Norman migrants bring with them to England after 1066?
cards.answer: their language (Norman French) / their legal customs / their building techniques / their ecclesiastical networks

cards.front: Why did William I launch the Harrying of the North in 1069-70?
cards.answer: Danish forces had allied with English rebels in 1069 to challenge William's authority, so he responded with deliberate destruction.

cards.front: Why is the Domesday Book's category of 'Frenchmen' significant evidence of Norman impact?
cards.answer: It recorded Frenchmen as a distinct legal category on hundreds of manors, showing rapid replacement of the English landowning class with a French elite.

title: Bush, Thatcher and Building the Coalition
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Arab contributions to the coalition described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Egypt sent two divisions / Syria sent one division / Saudi Arabia provided forces and bases
items: Saudi Arabia provided forces and bases

cards.front: Name the four financial contributions to the $61 billion Gulf War cost given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Saudi Arabia paid about $16 billion / Kuwait-in-exile paid about $16 billion / Germany paid about $6 billion / Japan paid about $13 billion

cards.front: Why was it crucial for the coalition to include visible Arab support?
cards.answer: Without Arab cover the operation would look like a colonial war by Christian powers on a Muslim country, letting Saddam's pan-Arab framing gain support.

cards.front: Why did Gorbachev's refusal to veto the UN resolutions matter for the coalition?
cards.answer: It showed Soviet acquiescence despite Iraq being a former client, denying Saddam the cover of superpower rivalry.

cards.front: Name the five design strategies given in the specification.
cards.answer: Collaboration / User-centred design / Systems approach / Iterative design / Avoiding design fixation

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for avoiding design fixation.
cards.answer: Brainstorming / Mind mapping / SCAMPER / Looking at the problem from different perspectives
items: Looking at the problem from different perspectives

cards.front: How does user-centred design reduce the risk of a product failing in practice?
cards.answer: By gathering data through interviews, observation and usability testing, then designing specifically around those findings.

cards.front: Why do designers use physical models as well as drawings?
cards.answer: Physical models help test form, proportion and ergonomics in ways that drawings cannot.

title: Religious Life and Catholic Forms of Expression
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three monastic orders described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Benedictines / Cistercians / Trappists

cards.front: Name the three mendicant orders described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Franciscans / Dominicans / Carmelites

cards.front: Why are the evangelical counsels seen as freeing rather than just a sacrifice?
cards.answer: They liberate the religious from anxiety about possessions, divided loyalties and self-will, making them wholly available for God and others.

cards.front: Why does Michelangelo's Creation of Adam show God reaching to touch Adam's finger?
cards.answer: It visually shows that human life is a gift from God and that humans are made in the divine image.

cards.front: Name the three boys stranded on the island in Ballantyne's The Coral Island.
cards.answer: Ralph / Jack / Peterkin

cards.front: How does Simon's encounter with the Lord of the Flies in Chapter 8 show Golding's view on evil?
cards.answer: The beast tells Simon it cannot be hunted and killed, revealing that evil lives inside every boy, not as an external monster.

cards.front: Why did Golding set Lord of the Flies during an unspecified nuclear war?
cards.answer: To show adults have already destroyed the world through the same violence the boys will replicate on the island.

title: Sacraments, Mission and Evangelisation in Britain
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four steps in the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
cards.answer: Confession of sins to a priest / Contrition (genuine sorrow) / Penance (prayer or service) / Absolution given in Christ's name
items: Confession of sins to a priest

cards.front: Name the four Catholic groups the lesson gives as promoting mission in Britain.
cards.answer: CAFOD / Catholic Education Service / Missio / St Vincent de Paul Society

cards.front: Why do Catholics celebrate Mass for the dead?
cards.answer: Because of the Catholic belief in purgatory and the communion of saints.

cards.front: How does the Anointing of the Sick help a person who is seriously ill or dying?
cards.answer: It strengthens the person spiritually, may restore physical health if God wills it, and prepares them for eternal life.

cards.front: Name the three people who carry out the attack on Adam.
cards.answer: Josh / Logan / Paul

cards.front: What four things make up the long aftermath of the attack that Blackman insists on showing, instead of skipping to recovery?
cards.answer: Hospitalisation / Depression / Withdrawal / Suicidal ideation

cards.front: How does Blackman make Josh's violence psychologically coherent rather than simple hatred?
cards.answer: His violence comes from shame, not hatred, as he attacks the version of himself he cannot accept.

cards.front: Why is Adam's depression after the attack presented as a rational response rather than weakness?
cards.answer: It is a reaction to being severely beaten by someone he trusted while those who might have protected him could not help.

cards.front: What three safety precautions does the lesson give for investigating Hooke's Law?
cards.answer: Do not overload the spring / Use a clamp stand secured to the bench / Place a cushion or tray below the masses
items: Use a clamp stand secured to the bench
Place a cushion or tray below the masses

cards.front: What three types of material does the lesson describe different density-measuring methods for?
cards.answer: Regular solid / Irregular solid / Liquid

cards.front: Why does deforming an object (stretching, bending or compressing) require at least two forces?
cards.answer: A single force would simply accelerate the object rather than change its shape, so two opposing forces are needed.

cards.front: Why does ice float on liquid water even though it is a solid?
cards.answer: Ice has a more open crystal lattice structure than liquid water, making it less dense despite being solid.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence for evolution given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Fossils / Antibiotic-resistant bacteria / Comparative anatomy

cards.front: Name the seven levels of Linnaeus's classification system, from broadest to narrowest.
cards.answer: Kingdom / Phylum / Class / Order / Family / Genus / Species

cards.front: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria show natural selection happening?
cards.answer: Resistant bacteria survive antibiotic exposure and reproduce, so resistance becomes more common, showing selection in action.

cards.front: Why does comparative anatomy support the idea that species share common ancestors?
cards.answer: Similar bone structures found in different species suggest those species evolved from the same ancestor.

cards.front: The lesson says the Roman forum was 'at once' four things. Name them.
cards.answer: A marketplace / A law court / A political meeting place / A religious precinct

cards.front: According to the Key Fact, which four things stood around the Pompeii forum?
cards.answer: Temple of Jupiter / The basilica / The comitium / Offices of magistrates

cards.front: Why was the macellum built as a separate building from the rest of the forum?
cards.answer: To separate the messier business of food retail from the more formal civic activities at the forum's centre.

cards.front: What does the fruit sellers' electoral inscription reveal about civic life in Pompeii?
cards.answer: It shows tradespeople actively took part in local elections and highlights how competitive those elections were.

cards.front: Name the five major themes that essays on Frankenstein connect to.
cards.answer: Dangerous knowledge and ambition / Creation and responsibility / Monstrosity and prejudice / Isolation and companionship / Nature versus nurture

cards.front: What are the three assessment strands your response to the 19th-century novel question is judged on?
cards.answer: AO1: critical response with well-chosen references / AO2: analysis of the writer's methods / AO3: understanding of context
items: AO1: critical response with well-chosen references
AO2: analysis of the writer's methods

cards.front: Why does the passive phrasing 'it breathed hard' distance Victor from responsibility for the Creature?
cards.answer: The passive construction removes Victor as the active subject of the sentence, distancing him from responsibility for the being he created.

cards.front: How does Shelley's own biography connect to Victor's rejection of the Creature in the creation scene?
cards.answer: Shelley's own mother died in childbirth, making her deeply aware that creation carries moral obligations, which Victor evades.

cards.front: Name the five stages the argument moves through across the stanzas of 'Decomposition'.
cards.answer: Description of the photograph / Dehumanising stone and fossil imagery / The indifferent crowd / The speaker's original pride in his composition / His present-day reconsideration
items: The speaker's original pride in his composition

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson pairs with Ghose's 'Decomposition'.
cards.answer: War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy / Disabled by Wilfred Owen / Remains by Simon Armitage
items: War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy

cards.front: Why does Ghose's plain, documentary style make the final confession in 'Decomposition' land more powerfully?
cards.answer: It breaks sharply from the detached, matter-of-fact tone used throughout the rest of the poem.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'Decomposition' mirror the way memory works?
cards.answer: The speaker isn't just describing an old photograph but re-examining it, so his understanding changes stanza by stanza.

cards.front: Name the three functions Russell's songs serve in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Windows into characters' inner lives / Vehicles for Russell's political argument / Structural bridges that compress time

cards.front: Name the three parallel scenes Russell uses to make the class divide visible on stage.
cards.answer: Policeman aggressive with Johnstones, polite with Lyons / Mickey gets a factory job, Eddie goes to university / Mickey made redundant, Eddie becomes a councillor
items: Policeman aggressive with Johnstones, polite with Lyons
Mickey gets a factory job, Eddie goes to university
Mickey made redundant, Eddie becomes a councillor

cards.front: How does the cyclical structure reinforce the play's theme of fate?
cards.answer: It makes the tragic outcome feel inevitable, just as the class system makes Mickey's downfall feel inevitable.

cards.front: How does the cross-cutting between storylines in the final act affect the audience?
cards.answer: It creates a sense of accelerating catastrophe as multiple storylines converge, making the audience feel powerless to stop the inevitable ending.

title: Earth Hazards: Earthquakes, Eruptions, Landslides and Tsunamis
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four triggers of landslides given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Earthquake shaking / Volcanic activity loading slopes with ash and lava / Heavy rainfall saturating soils / Undercutting by rivers or coastal erosion
items: Volcanic activity loading slopes with ash and lava
Undercutting by rivers or coastal erosion

cards.front: Name the three causes of subsidence given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Withdrawal of groundwater or hydrocarbons / Dissolving limestone (sinkholes) / Mining

cards.front: Why does a magnitude 7 earthquake release far more energy than a magnitude 6 earthquake?
cards.answer: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic, so each whole number increase means roughly 32 times more energy released.

cards.front: Why does low-viscosity basaltic magma produce effusive eruptions instead of explosive ones?
cards.answer: Its low viscosity lets gases escape gradually, so pressure doesn't build up and lava flows out rather than exploding.

title: Brahman and the Three Features of the Divine
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three similar-sounding words the lesson distinguishes and what each means.
cards.answer: Brahman - ultimate reality, ground of all being / brahman (lower case) - sacred power in Vedic ritual / Brahmin - the priestly caste of Hindu society
items: Brahman - ultimate reality, ground of all being
brahman (lower case) - sacred power in Vedic ritual
Brahmin - the priestly caste of Hindu society

cards.front: Why do Hindus honour a murti (sacred image) in a mandir?
cards.answer: Because the murti represents divine reality, so worshippers are reaching towards Brahman, not worshipping a piece of stone.

cards.front: How does the ocean-and-waves analogy explain the relationship between the universe and Brahman?
cards.answer: The universe emanates from Brahman like waves from the ocean - the waves are real, but ultimately made of ocean.

cards.front: What four groups did Hitler tailor his promises to during the Depression, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The unemployed — jobs and economic recovery / Middle classes and farmers — protection of property and anti-communism / Nationalists — national greatness and revenge for Versailles / Those who saw coalitions as weak — strong leadership
items: The unemployed — jobs and economic recovery
Middle classes and farmers — protection of property and anti-communism
Nationalists — national greatness and revenge for Versailles
Those who saw coalitions as weak — strong leadership

cards.front: What four social consequences of the Depression does the lesson describe in Germany?
cards.answer: Hunger / Poverty / Family breakdown / A pervasive sense of hopelessness

cards.front: How did the Wall Street Crash trigger economic collapse in Germany?
cards.answer: American banks recalled the short-term loans underpinning Germany's recovery, so factories lost credit, banks failed, and unemployment rocketed.

cards.front: How did the political violence of 1932 damage support for the Weimar Republic?
cards.answer: Hundreds of political killings showed Weimar couldn't protect citizens, discrediting democracy and pushing voters towards parties promising decisive action.

cards.front: List the four groups seated in the Colosseum, from front to back.
cards.answer: Senators / Equestrian class / Ordinary male citizens / Women and the poor

cards.front: Name the three major types of gladiator described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Murmillo / Retiarius / Thraex

cards.front: Why did the seating arrangement inside the Colosseum matter beyond just seating people?
cards.answer: The tiers corresponded to social rank, making the amphitheatre a visual map of Roman society.

cards.front: Why might an editor choose to spare a defeated gladiator instead of having him killed?
cards.answer: Killing a well-trained gladiator unnecessarily was costly, whereas keeping him alive meant he could fight again.

cards.front: Name the three groups of characters Syal uses to populate Tollington.
cards.answer: The nosy neighbours / The struggling families / The men who drink at the pub while women hold everything together
items: The men who drink at the pub while women hold everything together

cards.front: What three things do the early comic episodes show Meena doing?
cards.answer: Steals the charity tin and lets another child take the blame / Tells outrageous stories to get attention / Navigates the village's social minefield with bravado and desperation
items: Steals the charity tin and lets another child take the blame
Tells outrageous stories to get attention
Navigates the village's social minefield with bravado and desperation

cards.front: Why does Meena feel embarrassed by the Aunties' gatherings?
cards.answer: She sees them through English eyes and cringes at how different they seem, not yet realising this is a source of strength.

cards.front: How does Syal's early comic writing serve a serious purpose in the novel?
cards.answer: It makes Meena sympathetic to the reader, so the later darker themes of racism and betrayal hit with greater emotional impact.

title: Spitalfields: site introduction and Huguenot weavers
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three streets the lesson says Huguenot weavers settled along in Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Fournier Street / Princelet Street / Elder Street
