cards.answer: A game has no fixed running time, so the music must loop indefinitely and react to whatever the player is doing right now.

cards.front: How does an ostinato build tension in a film score?
cards.answer: A short pattern repeats unchanged while more instruments are added on top, making the texture thicker and louder over time.

title: The Arms Race and the Space Race
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three early Soviet space race achievements that gave the USSR the lead before Apollo 11.
cards.answer: Sputnik 1 (1957) / Gagarin's first crewed flight (1961) / Leonov's spacewalk (1965)

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things did the Moon landings NOT change about the Cold War?
cards.answer: Thousands of warheads still pointed at each other / The Berlin Wall still stood / The Vietnam War was still raging
items: Thousands of warheads still pointed at each other
The Vietnam War was still raging

cards.front: Why did Kennedy pledge in May 1961 to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out?
cards.answer: To let the West reclaim the symbolism the Soviets had captured with Sputnik and Gagarin, since the Soviets led in spectacular firsts.

cards.front: How did MIRVs, deployed by 1970, make arms control harder?
cards.answer: MIRVs let one rocket carry several warheads, so the count that mattered became cheaper-to-produce warheads rather than rockets.

title: Music for Ensemble 3: Musical Theatre and Chamber Groups
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: What three techniques let four string players create a texture as full as a small orchestral section?
cards.answer: Spacing chords across the full pitch range / Double-stopping (playing two notes at once) / Interweaving countermelodies so no moment sounds thin
items: Spacing chords across the full pitch range
Interweaving countermelodies so no moment sounds thin

cards.front: What three techniques does a wind quintet use to avoid gaps in the texture?
cards.answer: Horn sustains harmony notes or extends the bass register / Bassoon doubles or reinforces the bass line / Upper woodwind share melodic material through imitation or alternating register
items: Horn sustains harmony notes or extends the bass register
Bassoon doubles or reinforces the bass line
Upper woodwind share melodic material through imitation or alternating register

cards.front: Why does a homophonic duet in musical theatre suggest agreement or romantic unity between two characters?
cards.answer: Both voices move together in the same rhythm, often in thirds or sixths, showing the characters are aligned.

cards.front: Why do wind quintet composers often write dialogue-like passages where instruments answer or interrupt each other?
cards.answer: The five instruments have strikingly different timbres, so composers exploit that contrast instead of blending them into one sound.

cards.front: What three things does choosing the right data type decide?
cards.answer: Which operations are allowed / How much memory is used / Whether invalid data can be caught early
items: Whether invalid data can be caught early

cards.front: Why does adding two numbers typed as input without casting give "23" instead of 5?
cards.answer: Because the inputs are read as strings, and adding strings joins them end-to-end rather than performing arithmetic.

cards.front: Why are arrays and loops so often used together?
cards.answer: Because a single loop can visit each index in turn, so the same few lines work whether there are 30 items or 3000.

title: Increasing Food Supply: Strategies & Sustainable Futures
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the six key strategies the lesson gives for increasing food supply.
cards.answer: Irrigation / Aeroponics and hydroponics / New Green Revolution (biotechnology/GM crops) / Appropriate technology / Organic farming / Urban farming

cards.front: What features make sand dams an example of appropriate technology?
cards.answer: Use simple materials (concrete, rock, labour) / Need no electricity or pumps / Can be maintained by the community without engineers / Last 50 years or more / Fit the landscape by using seasonal sand rivers
items: Can be maintained by the community without engineers
Fit the landscape by using seasonal sand rivers

cards.front: Why did the original 1960s-70s Green Revolution fail to fully solve food insecurity?
cards.answer: It relied on expensive inputs poor smallholders couldn't afford, favoured irrigated lowlands over rain-fed uplands, and damaged soils and water tables through chemical overuse.

cards.front: Why is the Indus Basin Irrigation System vulnerable in the long term?
cards.answer: It partly relies on meltwater from Himalayan glaciers, which are retreating due to climate change, threatening future water availability.

cards.front: Familiaris Consortio names four tasks of the family. What are they?
cards.answer: Forming a community of persons / Serving life / Participating in the development of society / Sharing in the life and mission of the Church
items: Participating in the development of society
Sharing in the life and mission of the Church

cards.front: What five types of family structure does the Church recognise as existing in 21st-century society?
cards.answer: Nuclear / Single-parent / Same-sex parent / Extended / Blended

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching say artificial contraception violates the full meaning of the sexual act?
cards.answer: Because it deliberately removes the procreative dimension, artificially separating it from the unitive dimension which cannot be split apart.

cards.front: Why is the family called 'the domestic church' in Catholic teaching?
cards.answer: Because it is the first place where faith is lived and passed on to children.

title: Citizens in Action: Two Case Studies
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the four methods disability rights organisations used to campaign for stronger equality protections.
cards.answer: Direct advocacy to MPs and ministers / Evidence submissions to parliamentary committees / Public awareness campaigns / Legal challenges under existing equality legislation
items: Direct advocacy to MPs and ministers
Legal challenges under existing equality legislation

cards.front: Name the three citizenship principles the lesson says the Hillsborough case illustrates.
cards.answer: Ordinary citizens can challenge state institutions and win justice / Legal processes are an important route alongside political pressure / Meaningful change in complex cases takes decades of perseverance
items: Ordinary citizens can challenge state institutions and win justice
Legal processes are an important route alongside political pressure
Meaningful change in complex cases takes decades of perseverance

cards.front: How did the disability rights campaign combine insider and outsider tactics?
cards.answer: They used insider tactics like formal consultations and committee evidence alongside outsider tactics like public campaigns and demonstrations.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to judge citizenship campaigns as either fully succeeding or fully failing?
cards.answer: Campaigns can partially succeed, such as changing awareness without changing law, so outcomes should be judged in nuanced terms.

title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven renewable energy resources given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Solar / Wind / Hydroelectric / Tidal / Geothermal / Wave power / Biofuels

cards.front: Name the three types of home insulation the lesson gives that reduce thermal energy loss.
cards.answer: Loft insulation / Cavity wall insulation / Double glazing

cards.front: How does double glazing reduce heat loss from a house?
cards.answer: A layer of gas between two panes of glass reduces energy transfer by conduction and convection.

cards.front: Why is a mix of energy resources needed to ensure a reliable electricity supply?
cards.answer: Because many renewable resources are weather- or location-dependent, so they can't always supply enough energy alone.

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of Newton's Third Law pairs in action.
cards.answer: Pushing a wall (wall pushes back equally) / Gravity pulling you down (you pull Earth up equally) / Swimmer pushing water back (water pushes swimmer forward)
items: Pushing a wall (wall pushes back equally)
Gravity pulling you down (you pull Earth up equally)
Swimmer pushing water back (water pushes swimmer forward)

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson says air resistance depends on.
cards.answer: Speed / Surface area / Shape

cards.front: Why does a falling skydiver eventually stop accelerating and reach terminal velocity?
cards.answer: As speed increases air resistance increases until it equals weight, making resultant force zero.

cards.front: Why does a skydiver slow down when their parachute opens?
cards.answer: The bigger surface area makes air resistance suddenly much greater than weight, decelerating the skydiver.

cards.front: Name the three rules for drawing electric field lines given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Field lines run from positive to negative / Field lines never cross each other / Closer lines together mean a stronger field
items: Field lines run from positive to negative
Field lines never cross each other
Closer lines together mean a stronger field

cards.front: Name the four practical applications of static electricity described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Electrostatic paint spraying / Inkjet printers / Photocopiers and laser printers / Electrostatic precipitators

cards.front: Why does a charged comb attract small, uncharged pieces of paper?
cards.answer: The charge on the comb induces a redistribution of charge in the paper, attracting the opposite charge on the near side.

cards.front: How does lightning form in a thundercloud?
cards.answer: Colliding ice crystals and water droplets transfer charge, making the cloud base negative and the ground below positive; the air ionises and discharges when the potential difference is large enough.

cards.front: What are the five stages of Scrooge's emotional arc, one per stave?
cards.answer: Isolation and cruelty (Stave 1) / Regret and emotional vulnerability (Stave 2) / Guilt and growing compassion (Stave 3) / Terror and repentance (Stave 4) / Joy, generosity, and redemption (Stave 5)

cards.front: Name the five characters the lesson says act as contrasting foils to Scrooge, and the quality each highlights.
cards.answer: Bob in generosity / Fred in warmth / Fezziwig in employer kindness / Belle in emotional openness / Marley as a warning

cards.front: Why does Dickens show us Scrooge's lonely childhood in Stave 2?
cards.answer: To present Scrooge as a product of his experiences rather than simply a villain.

cards.front: Why is it significant that Tiny Tim 'did NOT die' after Scrooge changes?
cards.answer: It shows that individual generosity can save lives, reversing the fatal consequences of neglecting the poor.

cards.front: Name the four metal finishing processes described for protecting metal from corrosion.
cards.answer: Dip coating / Powder coating / Galvanising / Anodising

cards.front: Name the five factors that decide which finish to choose for a product.
cards.answer: Material category / Product's environment (indoor/outdoor, wet/dry) / Desired appearance / Cost / Whether it needs to be food-safe
items: Whether it needs to be food-safe

cards.front: How does galvanising protect steel from rusting?
cards.answer: The zinc coating acts as a sacrificial layer, corroding before the steel underneath can rust.

cards.front: How does anodising increase aluminium's resistance to corrosion?
cards.answer: It is an electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium, making it harder and more corrosion resistant.

cards.front: Name the four main printing methods used to apply colour to fabric described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Block printing / Screen printing / Digital (inkjet) printing / Sublimation printing

cards.front: Name the four barriers stopping smart/e-textiles becoming mainstream.
cards.answer: Electronics must survive washing, bending and sweat / Data privacy concerns from biometric monitoring / High costs from small production volumes / Hard to separate electronics from fabric for recycling
items: Electronics must survive washing, bending and sweat
Data privacy concerns from biometric monitoring
High costs from small production volumes
Hard to separate electronics from fabric for recycling

cards.front: Why must disperse dyes be applied under high temperature and pressure for polyester?
cards.answer: The dye molecules have to physically enter the fibre structure, which polyester only allows under heat and pressure.

cards.front: Why does quilting improve the warmth of a fabric?
cards.answer: Two fabric layers are stitched together with wadding in between, and the wadding traps air, providing insulation.

title: Second Civil War, Pride's Purge and regicide
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three regions where Royalist uprisings broke out in the Second Civil War (1648).
cards.answer: Kent / Essex / Wales

cards.front: Why did the Rump Parliament proceed with Charles I's trial without the House of Lords?
cards.answer: The Lords refused to participate in setting up the High Court of Justice, so the Rump went ahead without them.

cards.front: How did Charles I's refusal to plead affect the fairness of his trial?
cards.answer: Because he refused to acknowledge the court, no defence was mounted, making the proceedings one-sided.

cards.front: What four impulsive actions show Romeo's hamartia driving the tragedy?
cards.answer: Falls in love instantly / Marries within 24 hours / Kills Tybalt in rage / Commits suicide without checking Juliet is truly dead
items: Commits suicide without checking Juliet is truly dead

cards.front: What three things should you examine when analysing Romeo and Juliet's characters?
cards.answer: Their language changes / Their interactions with other characters / How they respond to conflict

cards.front: How does dramatic irony affect the audience's experience of Romeo and Juliet's story?
cards.answer: The audience already knows their fate from the Prologue, which adds poignancy to the lovers' hopes and plans.

cards.front: How does Juliet's relationship with her parents change as the play progresses?
cards.answer: She starts respectful and obedient but becomes increasingly defiant as her love for Romeo grows, reflecting generational conflict.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says the Fitzgeralds provide Alem with.
cards.answer: Warmth / Stability / A sense of belonging

cards.front: Name the three things Alem learns as he adjusts to life in England.
cards.answer: The rhythms of school / The Fitzgeralds' household routines / The social codes that confused him
items: The social codes that confused him

cards.front: Why do Mustapha and Alem stand together against Sweeney?
cards.answer: Because Mustapha has also been bullied by Sweeney, so the two boys share the experience of hostility and support each other.

cards.front: Why is the Fitzgeralds' relationship with Alem always complicated, despite their love for him?
cards.answer: Because it is temporary — Alem's future depends on the asylum hearing, not on the Fitzgeralds' love for him.

cards.front: Name the six stages of the novel's progressive collapse from order to chaos, in order.
cards.answer: Conch establishing order / Signal fire going out / Jack's tribe splitting / Simon's murder / Piggy's death and conch destruction / The manhunt

cards.front: What are the four parts of the PEAC essay paragraph structure?
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Analysis / Context

cards.front: Why does Jack's authoritarian leadership prove more effective than Ralph's democratic leadership?
cards.answer: Democratic leadership needs people to consent, whereas Jack offers simple answers, exploits fear, and punishes dissent without needing consent.

cards.front: Why does fear give Jack more power than Ralph and Piggy's reasoning?
cards.answer: Fear is a more powerful motivator than logic, so Jack's promise to hunt the beast attracts followers away from rational reassurance.

title: Vietnamisation, Paris and Why the US Lost, 1969-75
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four overlapping reasons the lesson gives for why the United States lost the Vietnam War.
cards.answer: Strengths of North Vietnam and the Vietcong / Failure of US tactics / Political weakness of South Vietnam / Impact of opposition at home
items: Strengths of North Vietnam and the Vietcong

cards.front: What four terms did the January 1973 Paris Peace Agreement set out?
cards.answer: US forces withdraw within sixty days / American POWs returned / A ceasefire in place / Political talks among the Vietnamese parties
items: US forces withdraw within sixty days
Political talks among the Vietnamese parties

cards.front: Why did Vietnamisation fail to solve South Vietnam's strategic problem despite ARVN growing to around 1.1 million men?
cards.answer: South Vietnam still had no rural legitimacy and the ARVN was riven by corruption, desertion and politically appointed officers who broke in combat.

cards.front: Why did South Vietnam collapse so quickly to the North Vietnamese offensive in 1975?
cards.answer: Watergate forced Nixon's resignation, Congress slashed aid to Saigon, and ARVN units collapsed as officers abandoned their men.

cards.front: Name the five types of constraint the lesson says investigations can face.
cards.answer: Time constraints / Cost constraints / Ethical issues / Confidentiality concerns / Convenience

cards.front: Name the three strategies the lesson gives for reducing non-response.
cards.answer: Keep questionnaires short / Offer an incentive / Follow up with reminders

cards.front: Why might a study on seasonal behaviour give misleading results if data collection is limited to one month?
cards.answer: Behaviour like ice cream sales or flu cases varies across the year, so a short collection window misses the full seasonal picture.

cards.front: Why is convenience a constraint on some investigations?
cards.answer: The ideal population may not be realistically accessible, such as surveying a random sample of all UK secondary school students.

cards.front: Name the three everyday examples of exothermic reactions given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Combustion (e.g. burning methane) / Neutralisation (acid + alkali) / Hand warmers (iron reacting with oxygen)

cards.front: Name the three ways given to reduce error when measuring temperature change in a calorimetry experiment.
cards.answer: Use a lid on the cup / Take readings quickly / Use a digital thermometer
items: Use a lid on the cup

cards.front: Why does even an exothermic reaction need an initial energy input to start?
cards.answer: Because bonds in the reactants must first be broken, which requires energy, before new bonds can form and release energy.

cards.front: How do you calculate the overall energy change of a reaction using bond energies?
cards.answer: Subtract the total energy released making bonds in the products from the total energy needed to break bonds in the reactants.

title: Europe in 1894: Empires, Alliances and the Long Fuse
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson's key fact, what distinct national interest did each of the five Great Powers pursue in 1894?
cards.answer: British empire and naval supremacy / French recovery of Alsace-Lorraine / German industrial expansion / Austro-Hungarian unity of a multi-ethnic empire / Russian access to the Mediterranean
items: Austro-Hungarian unity of a multi-ethnic empire

cards.front: Why did Bismarck deliberately keep Germany's ambitions modest and avoid major colonial expansion?
cards.answer: He feared a 'nightmare of coalitions' where France gained powerful allies and Germany faced a war on two fronts.

cards.front: Why did France and Russia form an alliance in 1894 despite being very different political systems?
cards.answer: A shared interest in containing Germany pulled them together, reinforced by French capital funding Russian railway and industrial projects.

cards.front: Name the three main tools governments have for managing the economy.
cards.answer: Fiscal policy (spending and taxation) / Monetary policy (interest rates) / Supply-side policies

cards.front: What is the five-step chain of reasoning linking education and training investment to higher real GDP?
cards.answer: Better training / Higher productivity / Lower average costs for firms / Lower prices and greater competitiveness / Higher real GDP

cards.front: Why does privatisation tend to improve the efficiency of a business that used to be state-owned?
cards.answer: Private firms are driven by the profit motive, giving them stronger incentives to cut costs, improve efficiency and respond to consumers than government-run enterprises.

cards.front: Why can deregulation increase competition and lower prices in a market?
cards.answer: Removing rules that raise firms' costs lowers barriers to entry, attracting new firms, increasing competition and consumer choice.

title: Ethical, Cultural, Environmental and Privacy Impacts
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three ethical issues that appear regularly in extended-response computing questions.
cards.answer: Privacy / AI bias / Automation's impact on employment

cards.front: Name the three contexts in which the lesson says the digital divide exists.
cards.answer: International, between high- and low-income countries / Domestic, between urban and rural areas / Domestic, between older and younger generations
items: International, between high- and low-income countries
Domestic, between urban and rural areas
Domestic, between older and younger generations

cards.front: Why do civil liberties organisations object to mass surveillance by governments?
cards.answer: Because monitoring everyone rather than targeting suspects chills free expression and presumes guilt rather than innocence.

cards.front: How does the energy mix used by a data centre affect its environmental impact?
cards.answer: Data centres powered by renewable sources have a much lower carbon footprint than those powered by coal or gas.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says pathogens can be transmitted between organisms.
cards.answer: Air (droplets) / Water (contamination) / Direct contact / Vectors (e.g. mosquitoes)

cards.front: Name the four measures the lesson gives for reducing the spread of communicable diseases.
cards.answer: Hygiene measures / Destroying vectors / Isolation of infected individuals / Vaccination

cards.front: How does vaccination give immunity without causing the disease?
cards.answer: It introduces dead or inactive pathogen, stimulating white blood cells to make antibodies and memory cells without illness.

cards.front: How does overuse and misuse of antibiotics lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
cards.answer: Overuse and misuse of antibiotics drives the evolution of bacteria that survive treatment, creating resistant 'superbugs'.

cards.front: Name the three cephalopod groups used as zone fossils, based on suture-line complexity.
cards.answer: Goniatites / Ceratites / Ammonites

cards.front: Why can biostratigraphy be used to correlate rock outcrops on different continents?
cards.answer: The same zone fossil, with its short time range, appears in rocks worldwide, acting as a time stamp regardless of location.

cards.front: How does using two overlapping zone fossil ranges improve the precision of dating a rock bed?
cards.answer: The bed's age must fall within the overlap of both fossils' ranges, narrowing the estimate more than either fossil alone.

title: Invasion of the Body Snatchers and E.T.: Aliens and Anxiety
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names four filmic techniques Invasion of the Body Snatchers uses to construct the alien as a threat. What are they?
cards.answer: Monochrome photography / Static framing / Silence / Gradual reveal

cards.front: The lesson names four filmic techniques E.T. uses to construct the alien as a source of transcendence. What are they?
cards.answer: Warm colour cinematography / Child's-eye-view camera / Non-diegetic orchestral maximalism / Iconic silhouette

cards.front: Why does Siegel stage the first pod reveal at the Belicec house gradually rather than as a shock cut?
cards.answer: Because the horror lies not in the sight itself but in the implication of what the pod means for everyone the characters know.

cards.front: Why does Carmen Dragon's score drop out entirely at the moment of the pod's discovery?
cards.answer: To replace music with near-silence broken by an unsettling ambient hum, making the internal, invisible threat feel more unnerving.

cards.front: Name the four contact forces given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Friction / Tension / Normal contact force / Air resistance

cards.front: Name the three non-contact forces given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gravity / Magnetism / Electrostatic attraction

cards.front: How do you find the resultant force when two forces act in opposite directions on an object?
cards.answer: Subtract the smaller force from the larger one; the resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

cards.front: Why does a heavy truck accelerate much less than a bicycle when the same resultant force is applied?
cards.answer: The truck has far greater inertial mass, so the same resultant force produces much less acceleration.

cards.front: In her Act 4 potion soliloquy, what three terrifying possibilities does Juliet consider before drinking?
cards.answer: The potion might not work, forcing marriage to Paris / The Friar might be poisoning her to hide the secret marriage / She might wake too early and go mad in the tomb
items: The potion might not work, forcing marriage to Paris
The Friar might be poisoning her to hide the secret marriage
She might wake too early and go mad in the tomb

cards.front: What four steps make up Friar Lawrence's plan in Act 4, Scene 1?
cards.answer: Juliet drinks a potion faking death for 42 hours / Her family places her in the Capulet tomb / The Friar sends a letter to Romeo in Mantua / Romeo returns to rescue her when she wakes
items: Juliet drinks a potion faking death for 42 hours
Her family places her in the Capulet tomb
The Friar sends a letter to Romeo in Mantua
Romeo returns to rescue her when she wakes

cards.front: How does Capulet's grief over Juliet's apparent death create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The audience knows Juliet is alive, so his praise of her as a lost flower exposes the hypocrisy of the man who threatened to let her starve.

cards.front: How does the Friar's line 'She's not well married that lives married long' work as dramatic irony?
cards.answer: It seems a general comment on death but secretly describes the truth: Juliet is married to Romeo and will die young, understood only by the audience.

cards.front: What three things happened to a baby left at the Foundling Hospital, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Given a new name / Educated / Trained for employment

cards.front: Why does Gavin include Toby, a Black child, at the Foundling Hospital?
cards.answer: To remind readers that exploiting children was part of a wider culture treating human beings as property, broadening who counted as fully human.

cards.front: How does the Foundling Hospital contrast with what actually happens to the babies Otis Gardiner collects?
cards.answer: The Hospital saves children like Aaron, while Otis and Meshak actually bury most of the babies rather than delivering them there.

cards.front: Why did Gavin choose to set Coram Boy in 18th-century England?
cards.answer: To invite modern readers to see parallels between historical and contemporary attitudes to children, poverty and race.

cards.front: Name the four levels of isolation the lesson identifies in The Woman in Black.
cards.answer: Physical isolation / Social isolation / Psychological isolation / Emotional isolation

cards.front: Name the four stages of the model paragraph structure for extract analysis.
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Analysis / Effect

cards.front: How does Arthur's rationalism cause his psychological isolation?
cards.answer: His refusal to believe in ghosts isolates him from understanding events and stops him taking the danger seriously until too late.

cards.front: Why does Hill spread guilt across the whole community rather than one person?
cards.answer: The townspeople's silence, Alice Drablow's adoption of Nathaniel, and Sam Daily's unclear warning all contribute, showing collective inaction lets evil persist.

cards.front: Name the three types of prototype designers use, depending on what they need to test.
cards.answer: Appearance models / Functional prototypes / Production prototypes

cards.front: What are the six things a well-developed prototype must do, according to the specification?
cards.answer: Satisfy the requirements of the brief / Respond to client wants and needs / Demonstrate innovation / Be functional / Consider aesthetics / Be potentially marketable
items: Satisfy the requirements of the brief
Respond to client wants and needs

cards.front: How does rapid prototyping speed up the iterative design process?
cards.answer: A designer can turn a CAD model into a physical prototype in hours, test it, modify the digital file, and print an improved version the same day.

cards.front: Why does the testing-and-improvement cycle for a prototype keep repeating?
cards.answer: Because it continues until the product meets all specification requirements or the best possible compromise is reached.

cards.front: Name the three settings multiplied together to work out a sound file's size in bits.
cards.answer: Sample rate / Duration / Bit depth

cards.front: Why does a low-resolution image look blocky when stretched across a large screen?
cards.answer: Each pixel is enlarged until you can see the individual coloured squares.

cards.front: How does a greater bit depth make a sound recording cleaner?
cards.answer: It lets each sample record the amplitude more precisely, giving a wider range of volumes.

cards.front: What three things drive Enid's fierce protectiveness of her daughters, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Her experience of an abusive marriage / Her mother's death and their estrangement / Her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant
items: Her experience of an abusive marriage
Her mother's death and their estrangement
Her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant

cards.front: What six dramatic techniques does the lesson say to analyse alongside language in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Naturalistic dialogue / Code-switching / Dual settings / Obeah scenes / Silence / Stagecraft

cards.front: Why does the title 'Leave Taking' capture the play's theme of belonging?
cards.answer: It refers to Enid's departure from Jamaica, the daughters' departure from her values, and leaving shame behind.

cards.front: Why does Pinnock avoid staging dramatic racist incidents in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Because racism works as pervasive structural pressure shaping every character's choices, which is more realistic and powerful.

cards.front: Name the five stages of the five-act structure Shakespeare uses in Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Exposition (Act 1: feud, lovers meet) / Rising action (Act 2: balcony, marriage) / Turning point (Act 3: Mercutio and Tybalt die, banishment) / Falling action (Act 4: potion plan) / Catastrophe (Act 5: deaths and reconciliation)
items: Turning point (Act 3: Mercutio and Tybalt die, banishment)

cards.front: Name the four key structural techniques Shakespeare uses in the play.
cards.answer: Prologue as a structural frame / Five-act structure with turning point at centre / Mirrored scenes (ball/tomb, opening/closing) / Compressed four-day timeline
items: Five-act structure with turning point at centre

cards.front: Why does the Prologue's dramatic irony make the play more emotional rather than less suspenseful?
cards.answer: We watch the lovers' joy knowing it cannot last, which makes it both more beautiful and more painful.

cards.front: How does the play's compressed four-day timeline help cause the tragedy?
cards.answer: It creates breathless urgency so the lovers have no time to reflect or reconsider, making the speed that excites us also make tragedy inevitable.

title: Specialist Writing on Film: Reviews, Theory, Cinematography
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of specialist writing on film described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Film review / Film criticism / Writing on cinematography

cards.front: Which three critics does the lesson name as widely referenced writers of film reviews?
cards.answer: Pauline Kael / Roger Ebert / Mark Kermode

cards.front: Why does simply mentioning a specialist term like 'continuity editing' earn nothing in extended writing?
cards.answer: Because the term only counts if the rest of the sentence explains what that technique does in the specific sequence, making an argument about meaning.

cards.front: How should auteur theory be used to analyse a director's choices in this unit?
cards.answer: By pointing to specific, repeated formal choices across a director's films, such as Gerwig's persistent two-shot, and naming that formal evidence.

cards.front: Name the six tasks the lesson says pre-production includes.
cards.answer: Commissioning / Writing and developing the script / Casting performers / Scouting locations / Drawing up a production schedule / Agreeing a budget

cards.front: Name the five things the lesson says post-production includes for film and television.
cards.answer: Editing / Colour grading / Adding visual effects / Mixing the soundtrack / Creating titles and credits

cards.front: Why do production team sizes vary so much between different media products?
cards.answer: Because the size of the team, available technology and working environment depend on budget and form, from hundreds of crew to one person.

cards.front: How does streaming-first commissioning change the structure of a series' narrative?
cards.answer: Because episodes are often released all at once, binge-viewing audiences tolerate different pacing than audiences watching weekly, changing narrative structure.

cards.front: Name the four ways everyone abandons Juliet by the end of Act 3 Scene 5.
cards.answer: Romeo is banished / Capulet threatens to disown her / Lady Capulet refuses to intervene / The Nurse advises marrying Paris

cards.front: Why does Romeo refuse to fight Tybalt when Tybalt insults him?
cards.answer: Romeo is secretly married to Juliet, making Tybalt family, so he refuses to fight him despite the insult.

cards.front: How does Romeo's refusal to fight Tybalt lead to Mercutio's death?
cards.answer: Mercutio, not knowing about the marriage, sees Romeo's refusal as cowardice and fights Tybalt himself, and Romeo's attempt to separate them lets Tybalt stab Mercutio.

cards.front: Name the four English leaders who submitted to William at Berkhamsted in December 1066.
cards.answer: Edgar the Aethling / Archbishop Stigand / Earl Edwin / Earl Morcar

cards.front: Name the three locations where William created Marcher earldoms.
cards.answer: Chester / Shrewsbury / Hereford

cards.front: Why did William raid and burn parts of southern England instead of marching straight to London after Hastings?
cards.answer: To intimidate potential opponents into submitting rather than resisting his advance.

cards.front: How did rebellions from 1068 onwards speed up the replacement of English lords with Normans?
cards.answer: Each rebellion gave William a pretext to confiscate rebels' lands and redistribute them to loyal Normans.

cards.front: Name the three strategies (the 'three Rs') the lesson gives for reducing the use of finite resources.
cards.answer: Reduce / Reuse / Recycle

cards.front: Name the three disposal options the lesson gives for a product at the end of its life.
cards.answer: Landfill / Incineration / Recycling

cards.front: Why can the 'use' stage of a car have a larger environmental impact than its manufacture?
cards.answer: Because the car burns fuel and produces exhaust emissions throughout its whole working life, releasing far more CO2 than was released during construction.

cards.front: Why does extracting metals from ore cause environmental damage?
cards.answer: It requires large amounts of energy and mining damages landscapes, causes noise and dust, and destroys habitats.

cards.front: What three motivations drive Shylock to pursue the bond against Antonio?
cards.answer: Revenge for years of abuse / Financial justice for the bond legally owed / Retribution for Jessica's betrayal
items: Financial justice for the bond legally owed

cards.front: Name the three ways patriarchal society constrains Portia.
cards.answer: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test) / Cannot practise law openly / Must submit to male authority
items: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test)

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare complicate Portia's character despite her eloquent mercy speech?
cards.answer: She makes racist remarks about Morocco and shows no mercy to Shylock, despite preaching mercy so eloquently.

cards.front: How does the ring plot in Act 5 demonstrate Portia's power?
cards.answer: She outwits Bassanio over the ring he gave away, proving she controls the relationship.

cards.front: Name the three weapons a legionary used in sequence during a battle.
cards.answer: Pilum, thrown to disrupt the enemy line / Gladius, used for close-combat stabbing / Pugio, a dagger for last resort
items: Pilum, thrown to disrupt the enemy line
Pugio, a dagger for last resort

cards.front: What three things could a legion construct to besiege a fortified town?
cards.answer: Approach ramps of earth and timber / Artillery platforms for ballistae and onagri / Covered corridors to advance soldiers under fire
items: Approach ramps of earth and timber
Artillery platforms for ballistae and onagri
Covered corridors to advance soldiers under fire

cards.front: Why did Roman armies build a fully fortified camp every single night on campaign?
cards.answer: So the army could never be caught completely unprepared by a night attack, giving a huge strategic advantage.

cards.front: How did a volley of pila thrown just before the charge help the legion?
cards.answer: It created shock, disorder and disadvantage in the enemy line before the legionaries closed in with their swords.

title: The Road Back to the Throne: Restoration of the Monarchy 1660
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What were the four promises Charles II made in the Declaration of Breda (1660)?
cards.answer: A free pardon for most who fought against the Crown / Liberty to tender consciences in religion / Payment of the army's arrears / A settlement of disputed land titles
items: A free pardon for most who fought against the Crown
Liberty to tender consciences in religion
A settlement of disputed land titles

cards.front: What three things did the 1660 Restoration settlement actually bring back?
cards.answer: The monarchy itself / The House of Lords / The Church of England with its bishops
items: The Church of England with its bishops

cards.front: Why did the Protectorate collapse in the sixteen months after Cromwell's death?
cards.answer: Richard Cromwell had no military reputation or army support and resigned within nine months, leaving rival regimes, falling trade and rising taxes that exhausted the country.

cards.front: How did the Declaration of Breda let Charles II return without conquering England?
cards.answer: It passed every difficult decision — pardons, religion, army pay, land disputes — to Parliament, so Charles returned by invitation rather than by force.

cards.front: Name the three ways a cool down helps reduce the risk of DOMS.
cards.answer: Maintains blood flow through muscles for longer / Static stretching may reduce inflammatory swelling / Prevents sudden loss of oxygen/nutrient supply to damaged fibres
items: Maintains blood flow through muscles for longer
Static stretching may reduce inflammatory swelling
Prevents sudden loss of oxygen/nutrient supply to damaged fibres

cards.front: Why is lactic acid no longer considered the main cause of DOMS?
cards.answer: Lactic acid is cleared from muscles within an hour of exercise ending, but DOMS soreness lasts 24-72 hours due to the inflammatory repair of damaged muscle fibres.

cards.front: How can skipping a cool down affect an athlete psychologically before their next session?
cards.answer: A rushed exit without a cool down can contribute to elevated anxiety and poor readiness for the next training session.

cards.front: Name the three stages of Jewish persecution that intentionalists cite as evidence Hitler was following a fixed plan.
cards.answer: Boycotts (1933) / Nuremberg Laws (1935) / Kristallnacht (1938)

cards.front: Name the four competing agencies functionalist historians say jostled for Hitler's favour in the Nazi state.
cards.answer: The SS / The SA / Various party offices / State ministries

cards.front: How did Ian Kershaw combine the intentionalist and functionalist interpretations?
cards.answer: He argued Hitler's ideology was real and consistent, but policy radicalised through officials working towards the Führer rather than direct step-by-step orders.

cards.front: Why do functionalist historians read Mein Kampf differently from intentionalists?
cards.answer: Functionalists argue Mein Kampf should be seen as political propaganda rather than a master blueprint Hitler systematically followed.

title: Physics on the Move: Stopping Distances and Momentum
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson gives that increase thinking distance.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Alcohol / Drugs / Distractions such as mobile phone use
items: Distractions such as mobile phone use

cards.front: Name the three safety features the lesson describes that reduce injury by extending the time momentum changes over.
cards.answer: Crumple zones / Seatbelts / Airbags

cards.front: How does an airbag reduce the force on an occupant in a crash?
cards.answer: It inflates and deflates as the occupant hits it, spreading the impact force over a larger area and longer time.

cards.front: Why do wet or icy roads increase braking distance?
cards.answer: There is less friction between the tyres and the road, giving less braking force to stop the car.

cards.front: Name the three social forces that drive the tragedy in Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Patriarchal authority / The blood feud / Honour culture

cards.front: Name the three moments the lesson gives as examples of honour culture's destructive pattern.
cards.answer: The opening brawl (Act 1, Scene 1) / Tybalt's aggression at the ball (Act 1, Scene 5) / Mercutio's death (Act 3, Scene 1)
items: Tybalt's aggression at the ball (Act 1, Scene 5)

cards.front: Why does the Nurse advise Juliet to marry Paris even though Juliet is already secretly married to Romeo?
cards.answer: It shows the Nurse's pragmatism and how limited women's options were, unable to imagine defying male authority outright.

cards.front: How did Shakespeare change the tone of Arthur Brooke's source poem when adapting it?
cards.answer: Brooke blamed the lovers for disobeying their parents, but Shakespeare makes them sympathetic, blaming the feud and social forces instead.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says technology benefits performers.
cards.answer: More precise training monitoring (wearables, GPS, video analysis) / Improved equipment design (swimwear, running shoes) / Faster feedback on technique
items: More precise training monitoring (wearables, GPS, video analysis)

cards.front: Name the three types of broadcast infrastructure the lesson says make global live footage delivery possible.
cards.answer: Satellite uplinks / Fibre optic cables / Compression technology

cards.front: Why can relying too heavily on data feedback from devices harm a performer's development?
cards.answer: It can make it harder for the performer to develop their own intrinsic awareness of their body's movement and technique.

cards.front: Why might officiating technology still produce disputed decisions?
cards.answer: Because the technology has tolerances and thresholds, and results still depend on human interpretation of the footage.

cards.front: Name the three immediate problems the new Israeli government faced in 1949.
cards.answer: Securing diplomatic recognition / Mass immigration / Constant cross-border raids

cards.front: Which three armed groups were merged to form the IDF in May 1948?
cards.answer: Haganah / Irgun / Lehi

cards.front: How did the IDF respond to fedayeen cross-border attacks?
cards.answer: It used disproportionate reprisal raids, hitting the raiders' home territory with far greater force than the original attack.

cards.front: Why did the US keep its early support for Israel limited rather than full?
cards.answer: It balanced backing Israel with protecting its oil interests and Cold War alliances in the Arab world.

cards.front: Name the three main principles computational thinking is built on.
cards.answer: Abstraction / Decomposition / Algorithmic thinking

cards.front: What four sub-problems does the quiz app example break down into?
cards.answer: Store the questions with correct answers / Display one question at a time / Collect and check the player's answer / Keep score and show the final result
items: Store the questions with correct answers
Display one question at a time
Collect and check the player's answer
Keep score and show the final result

cards.front: Why is Harry Beck's Underground map more useful for passengers than a geographically accurate map?
cards.answer: It drops true distances and station positions, keeping only station order, line, and connections, which is all a passenger needs.

cards.front: Why does a vague instruction like 'check the answers' fail as an algorithm step?
cards.answer: A computer follows instructions exactly, so an unclear or out-of-order step produces the wrong result.

cards.front: Name the three factors that determine which method is used to shape a polymer.
cards.answer: Whether it's thermoforming or thermosetting / The shape of the final product / The scale of production
items: The shape of the final product

cards.front: Name the three limitations of FDM 3D printing given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Relatively slow build speed / Visible layer lines (lower surface finish) / Anisotropic mechanical properties (weaker along layers)

cards.front: Why can't blow moulding produce solid shapes or components with internal features?
cards.answer: Air is blown into the parison to expand it outward against the mould, so it only forms hollow shapes.

cards.front: Why does line bending only produce straight bends rather than curves?
cards.answer: A strip heater heats only a localised straight line, softening the material there so it bends only along that line.

title: The Eightfold Path and Buddhist Ethics
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things Right Speech tells a Buddhist to avoid.
cards.answer: Lying / Harsh speech / Gossip / Divisive speech

cards.front: In metta bhavana (loving-kindness meditation), name the five groups goodwill is extended to, in order.
cards.answer: Oneself / Family and friends / Strangers / Difficult people / All living beings

cards.front: Why does stealing (breaking the second Precept) create negative kamma, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because the intention to take what isn't given expresses and reinforces greed, one of the Three Poisons, deepening the conditions that perpetuate suffering.

cards.front: How does sila on the Eightfold Path differ from the Six Perfections in their approach to ethics?
cards.answer: Sila is mainly about restraint (not harming, stealing or deceiving), while the Six Perfections actively cultivate positive qualities like generosity and patience that benefit all beings.

cards.front: Name the three obsessions of James I that the lesson says drive the plot of Macbeth.
cards.answer: Witches / Regicide / Divine Right of Kings

cards.front: Name the three ways Shakespeare 'darkens' the real Macbeth story from Holinshed's Chronicles.
cards.answer: Compresses the timeline / Invents the witches' prophecies / Makes Duncan saintly rather than weak
items: Makes Duncan saintly rather than weak

cards.front: Why is Macbeth's murder of Duncan presented as sacrilege, not just murder?
cards.answer: Because Divine Right meant Duncan was appointed by God, so killing him was an offence against God as well as a man.

cards.front: How do the Weird Sisters' powers reflect James I's view of witches in Daemonologie?
cards.answer: They can predict and manipulate but never compel — their prophecies only come true through Macbeth's own willing action.

cards.front: Name the five BBFC film classification categories given in the lesson.
Name the three Creative Commons licence types described in the lesson.
cards.answer: CC BY / CC BY-NC / CC BY-ND

cards.front: Why must media creators get a model release or location release before using someone's image?
cards.answer: Without them, the creator could face legal claims under privacy law or data protection legislation.

cards.front: How can repeated stereotyping in media cause real harm?
cards.answer: Repeated use of oversimplified, inaccurate images of a group can reinforce prejudice against that group.

cards.front: Name the four types of retail location described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Town centre/high street / Shopping centre / Out-of-town retail park / Online

cards.front: What four options does a retailer have if its physical location is underperforming?
cards.answer: Negotiate a rent review / Sublet part of the space / Relocate when the lease expires / Shift more sales online

cards.front: How does clustering with complementary shops create 'agglomeration'?
cards.answer: Shops attracting the same type of customer combine their footfall, so the cluster generates more total visitors than each shop alone.

cards.front: Why do out-of-town retail parks have lower footfall but higher conversion rates than town centres?
cards.answer: Customers arrive by car specifically intending to buy something, so fewer visitors browse but more of them actually purchase.

cards.front: Name the four separation techniques the lesson describes for separating mixtures (excluding chromatography).
cards.answer: Filtration / Crystallisation / Simple distillation / Fractional distillation

cards.front: How does crystallisation produce pure, dry crystals of a salt from a solution?
cards.answer: The solution is heated gently to evaporate the solvent until crystals begin to form, then left to cool so more crystals grow.

cards.front: How does fractional distillation separate a mixture of liquids with different boiling points?
cards.answer: The mixture is heated with a fractionating column; the liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates first and is collected, then each liquid is collected in turn as the temperature rises.

cards.front: How does filtration separate an insoluble solid from a liquid?
cards.answer: The mixture is poured through filter paper so the liquid passes through as the filtrate while the solid stays behind as the residue.

title: Media Industries: Ownership, Funding and Regulation
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three funding models the lesson describes for media organisations.
cards.answer: Publicly funded (e.g. licence fee) / Commercially funded (advertising/sponsorship) / Not-for-profit (grants, donations, membership)

cards.front: Name the four platforms/technologies the lesson says convergence brings content across.
cards.answer: Broadcast / Streaming / Social media / Mobile

cards.front: How does vertical integration keep money inside the same organisation?
cards.answer: Because the company owns every stage of the supply chain, so it doesn't have to pay independent suppliers at each stage.

cards.front: How can a single film franchise create synergy across a conglomerate?
cards.answer: It can drive a video game tie-in, a streaming spin-off, a soundtrack and merchandise, all reinforcing one another's marketing.

cards.front: Name the four types of research method the lesson lists for sociologists researching education.
cards.answer: Observation (participant or non-participant) / Interviews (structured, unstructured or focus group) / Questionnaires / Secondary data (e.g. official statistics, league tables)
items: Secondary data (e.g. official statistics, league tables)

cards.front: What are the three key ethical issues in sociological research on education?
cards.answer: Informed consent / Confidentiality / Harm to participants

cards.front: Why can headteachers acting as gatekeepers distort research data on schools?
cards.answer: They may refuse access to poor lessons and only allow researchers to observe 'good' lessons, distorting the data.

cards.front: Why can requiring parental consent introduce class bias into research samples of pupils?
cards.answer: It reduces the sample to pupils whose parents are engaged and willing to respond, skewing who takes part.

cards.front: What are the three key contexts for Silas Marner given in the lesson?
cards.answer: The Industrial Revolution and decline of rural communities / Victorian religion: Dissenting chapels vs Church of England / The rigid Victorian class system and attitudes towards outsiders
items: The Industrial Revolution and decline of rural communities
Victorian religion: Dissenting chapels vs Church of England
The rigid Victorian class system and attitudes towards outsiders

cards.front: Name the three members of the Cass family described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Squire Cass / Dunsey / Godfrey

cards.front: Why did Eliot set Silas Marner in the rural village of Raveloe?
cards.answer: To explore what holds close-knit rural communities together and what tears them apart as industrialisation caused their decline.

cards.front: Why is the novel's subtitle 'The Weaver of Raveloe' significant?
cards.answer: Weaving was a cottage industry destroyed by factory mechanisation, so Silas represents dying pre-industrial craftsmanship overtaken by progress.

cards.front: What four demands did Hungarian students make when they marched in Budapest on 23 October 1956?
cards.answer: Free elections / An end to censorship / Withdrawal of Soviet troops / Return of Imre Nagy

cards.front: What three factors pinned down Western governments and stopped them intervening in Hungary in 1956?
cards.answer: The simultaneous Suez Crisis / Fear of nuclear war with the Soviet Union / Hungary's location inside the Soviet sphere agreed at Yalta
items: Fear of nuclear war with the Soviet Union
Hungary's location inside the Soviet sphere agreed at Yalta

cards.front: Why did Khrushchev order the Soviet invasion of Hungary on 4 November 1956?
cards.answer: Hungary leaving the Warsaw Pact would set a precedent that could unravel Soviet control across Eastern Europe.

cards.front: Why did reformers across Eastern Europe feel encouraged to demand change after Khrushchev's Secret Speech leaked?
cards.answer: They concluded the rules had changed and that Soviet control might soften, making demands for independence seem tolerable.

title: Media Language: Semiotics, Codes and Conventions
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three things a newspaper front page is expected to follow as conventions.
cards.answer: Masthead placement / Headline hierarchy / Column structure

cards.front: Name the six mechanisms the lesson says a student should name when analysing a poster's meaning.
cards.answer: Denotation / Connotation / Code / Convention / Anchorage / Intertextuality

cards.front: Why do producers add anchorage text, like a headline, to an image?
cards.answer: Because images are polysemic and open to more than one reading, so text steers the audience towards one intended meaning.

cards.front: How does intertextuality add extra meaning to a media product without extra words or images?
cards.answer: It deliberately references another text the audience already knows, inviting them to bring existing associations to the new product.

cards.front: Name the four phases shown on a heart rate graph during exercise.
cards.answer: Anticipatory rise before exercise / Steep rise at onset of exercise / Plateau during steady exercise / Recovery curve after exercise stops
items: Steep rise at onset of exercise

cards.front: Name the three linked measurements used to describe how efficiently the heart pumps blood.
cards.answer: Stroke volume / Heart rate / Cardiac output

cards.front: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker, more muscular wall than the right ventricle?
cards.answer: It must generate much higher pressure to push blood all the way around the whole body.

cards.front: Why is it inadvisable to exercise vigorously straight after a large meal?
cards.answer: Because the digestive system and the working muscles are competing for the same blood supply.

title: Health and Safety Law and Risk
subject: l12-construction-built-environment

cards.front: Name the five steps in the hierarchy of control, in priority order from most to least preferred.
cards.answer: Eliminate the hazard / Substitute with something safer / Engineering controls (e.g. guarding, extraction) / Administrative controls (e.g. safe systems of work) / PPE
items: Administrative controls (e.g. safe systems of work)

cards.front: Name the four hazardous substances found on construction sites mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cement dust / Silica dust / Solvent fumes / Asbestos fibres

cards.front: Why can a worker inhale a dangerous amount of silica dust without realising it?
cards.answer: The particles are extremely fine and invisible to the naked eye, so a worker can breathe in a lot without noticing.

cards.front: Why does ignoring procedures, such as removing safety barriers around a floor opening, increase the risk of a serious accident?
cards.answer: It removes the protective control that was put in place, so the risk of a serious accident increases significantly.

title: Rump Parliament and the rise of Cromwell 1649-1653
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three reasons did Cromwell have for dissolving the Rump Parliament in 1653?
cards.answer: Refused to dissolve itself and hold elections / Blocked godly reform of the law and church / Acted out of narrow self-interest
items: Refused to dissolve itself and hold elections
Blocked godly reform of the law and church

cards.front: Why did critics see the killings at Wexford in October 1649 as worse than those at Drogheda?
cards.answer: Soldiers stormed the town and killed many civilians before Cromwell had given orders, going beyond even brutal wartime norms.

cards.front: Why did Cromwell's dissolution of the Rump in April 1653 matter for England's constitution?
cards.answer: It destroyed the constitutional continuity of the republic, so governance now rested openly on military power rather than Parliament.

cards.front: Name the four main factors sociologists identify as affecting criminal behaviour.
cards.answer: Social class / Gender / Ethnicity / Age

cards.front: What three explanations do sociologists give for the overrepresentation of ethnic minorities in crime statistics?
cards.answer: Interactionist labelling and selective policing / Marxist institutional racism / Structural poverty and deprivation

cards.front: How does Merton's strain theory explain why working-class people are more likely to commit crime?
cards.answer: A mismatch between the shared goal of material success and unequal access to legitimate means pushes some towards 'innovation', using illegal methods to achieve success.

cards.front: How do functionalists explain why men commit more crime than women?
cards.answer: Boys are socialised to be tough, assertive and risk-taking, while girls are socialised towards conformity and domestic roles, making male deviance more likely.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that increase braking distance.
cards.answer: higher speed / wet or icy roads / worn tyres / worn brakes

cards.front: Name the four key points about Newton's third law pairs of forces.
cards.answer: equal in magnitude / opposite in direction / act on different objects / same type of force

cards.front: Why does opening a parachute cause a skydiver to decelerate to a new, lower terminal velocity?
cards.answer: Opening it increases drag so drag exceeds weight, giving an upward resultant force that decelerates the skydiver until drag equals weight again.

cards.front: In the F = ma core practical, why must total system mass be kept constant while varying force?
cards.answer: If mass added to the hanger wasn't removed from the trolley, both force and mass would change at once, making the results meaningless.

title: Pressure groups, Thatcher and challenges to Parliament
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three pressure groups specifically studied for this period (1958 onwards).
cards.answer: CND / Greenpeace / NUM

cards.front: What three factors weakened the NUM's position during the Miners' Strike?
cards.answer: Divided communities / Hardship among miners' families / Lack of a national ballot

cards.front: How did Thatcher's government prepare for the confrontation with the miners?
cards.answer: It stockpiled coal, arranged alternative fuels, and deployed police from across the country to manage picket lines.

cards.front: Why was Thatcher removed as Prime Minister in November 1990?
cards.answer: She was removed by her own MPs over the poll tax and European policy.

title: Coastal Management & a Distinctive UK Coastline
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: Name the four options a shoreline management plan can choose for a stretch of coast.
cards.answer: Hold the line / Advance the line / Manage realignment / Take no active intervention

cards.front: Name the five stakeholder groups involved in deciding coastal management, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Residents at risk / Farmers losing fields / Environmental groups / Engineers / Government agencies

cards.front: How did the 1991 Mappleton defences cause erosion at Cowden?
cards.answer: The groynes trapped longshore-drift sediment, starving beaches to the south, so erosion at Cowden sped up to 10m a year.

cards.front: Why are coastal defences usually only funded for towns and not farmland?
cards.answer: Defences are usually only funded where the value of property at risk exceeds the build and maintenance cost.

cards.front: Name the three main arc-based welding processes.
cards.answer: MIG welding / TIG welding / Arc welding (MMA)

cards.front: Name the three types of temporary fastener for joining metal.
cards.answer: Nuts and bolts / Machine screws / Self-tapping screws

cards.front: How does arc welding (MMA) protect the weld pool without using a shielding gas?
cards.answer: The flux coating on the electrode melts and forms a protective slag over the weld pool.

cards.front: Why is a soldered joint weaker than a brazed joint?
cards.answer: Soldering bonds by adhesion and limited diffusion, whereas brazing bonds metallurgically to the base metal.

cards.front: Name the five possessive adjectives the lesson says you need for GCSE.
cards.answer: mein (my) / dein (your) / sein (his) / ihr (her/their) / unser (our)

cards.front: Name the six relationship status words given in the lesson.
cards.answer: verheiratet (married) / geschieden (divorced) / getrennt (separated) / ledig (single) / in einer Beziehung (in a relationship) / in einer zivilen Partnerschaft (in a civil partnership)
items: in einer zivilen Partnerschaft (in a civil partnership)

cards.front: Why does 'mein' change to 'meinen' in 'Ich liebe meinen Vater'?
cards.answer: Vater is masculine and is the direct object (accusative), so mein takes the ending -en to become meinen.

cards.front: How does the word order work inside a Relativsatz like 'Ich habe einen Bruder, der Tom heißt'?
cards.answer: The relative pronoun matches the noun's gender and the verb is pushed to the end of the clause.

title: Reducing Tectonic Risk: Monitoring, Prediction, Protection, Planning
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four Ps geographers use to group tectonic risk-reduction strategies.
cards.answer: Monitoring / Prediction / Protection / Planning

cards.front: Name the three pieces of equipment used to monitor volcanoes.
cards.answer: Seismometers / GPS sensors / Gas sniffers

cards.front: How does Japan's earthquake early-warning system manage to warn people before shaking hits?
cards.answer: Sensors detect the fast harmless P-waves, calculate the quake's size, and send alerts before the slower destructive S-waves arrive.

cards.front: Why is reducing tectonic risk seen as a development problem, not just a science problem?
cards.answer: Low-income countries must choose between spending on hazard management or on health, education and roads, unlike richer countries.

title: Marxist, Interactionist and Feminist Theories of Crime
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Heidensohn identified three domains of patriarchal control that limit women's opportunities to offend. Name them.
cards.answer: Control in the home / Control in public spaces / Control at work

cards.front: In the Saints and Roughnecks study, name the three factors that made the Saints less visible to police.
cards.answer: Respectable appearance / Access to cars (mobility) / Middle-class presentation

cards.front: How can a moral panic increase the visible scale of a social problem?
cards.answer: Media, police and public respond disproportionately to a perceived threat, and this exaggerated attention itself amplifies the problem's visible scale.

cards.front: Why is Becker's labelling theory criticised from a Marxist perspective?
cards.answer: It fails to explain why labels fall disproportionately on the working class without reference to class power in society.

title: The Farewell: Representation and Diaspora Grief
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five key sequences the lesson identifies for micro/representation analysis in The Farewell.
cards.answer: Opening Billi-and-Nai-Nai phone call / Airport-arrival and family-greeting sequence / Wedding-banquet hall set piece / Hospital scan-results sequence / Closing slow-motion street-walk

cards.front: What four formal techniques does Wang's representational strategy in The Farewell rely on?
cards.answer: Long static takes / Wide ensemble framing during family meals / A score used sparingly / Language-shift cuts between Mandarin and English
items: Wide ensemble framing during family meals
Language-shift cuts between Mandarin and English

cards.front: Why do the language-shift cuts in The Farewell position the spectator inside the bilingual world rather than as an outsider?
cards.answer: There is no subtitle change or visual shift when the language switches, refusing to mark Chinese as needing translation for an English-speaking viewer.

cards.front: Why is asking whether The Farewell is an 'accurate' portrait of Chinese culture not the right representation question?
cards.answer: Representation asks how a group is constructed for the spectator through specific filmic choices, not whether those choices match lived experience.

cards.front: Name the four natural polymers the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: DNA / Starch / Cellulose / Proteins

cards.front: Name the three toxic gases the lesson says can be released when polymers are burned.
cards.answer: Carbon monoxide / Hydrogen chloride / Hydrogen cyanide

cards.front: Why does bromine water stay orange-brown when mixed with an alkane?
cards.answer: Alkanes have no carbon-carbon double bond, so there is nothing for the bromine to react with.

cards.front: Why is cracking needed to make addition polymers?
cards.answer: Cracking breaks down larger hydrocarbons to produce alkenes, giving enough monomers to meet plastic production demand.

cards.front: Name the three layers used in a Tetra Pak milk carton, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Paperboard for structure and printing / Polyethylene to bond layers and seal against liquid / Aluminium foil to block light and oxygen
items: Polyethylene to bond layers and seal against liquid
Aluminium foil to block light and oxygen

cards.front: Name the three physical characteristics the lesson gives for describing paper and board.
cards.answer: Density / Transparency / Surface texture

cards.front: Why is titanium difficult to machine even though it is light, strong and corrosion-resistant?
cards.answer: It work-hardens quickly and generates a lot of heat when cut.

cards.front: Why are metals chosen for wiring and heat sinks while polymers and timbers are chosen as insulators?
cards.answer: Metals conduct heat and electricity well, whereas polymers and timbers resist conducting, protecting people from heat or electric shock.

title: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan and divided Germany
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four powers that controlled the occupation zones of Germany after 1945.
cards.answer: USA / USSR / Britain / France

cards.front: What were the three aims of the Marshall Plan?
cards.answer: Rebuild war-shattered economies / Create stable markets for American goods / Remove poverty and unemployment where communism might flourish
items: Create stable markets for American goods
Remove poverty and unemployment where communism might flourish

cards.front: Why did the introduction of the Deutschmark in June 1948 push Germany towards permanent division?
cards.answer: Stalin saw the new currency as a step towards a permanent Western German state hostile to the USSR.

cards.front: Why did Stalin order the Berlin Blockade in June 1948?
cards.answer: He gambled that the West would rather abandon Berlin than risk war, hoping to force the Western powers out.

cards.front: Name the three internal stakeholder groups.
cards.answer: Owners / Managers / Employees

cards.front: Name the four external stakeholder groups.
cards.answer: Customers / Suppliers / Local community / Government

cards.front: How does a higher rate of corporation tax affect a business?
cards.answer: It lowers the profit the business keeps (retained profit) after paying tax to the government.

cards.front: Why did Morrisons cutting 150 management jobs split stakeholder reactions?
cards.answer: Shareholders welcomed the cost savings, while affected employees lost income and morale fell across the remaining workforce.

title: Staging and Design: World-Building on a Bare Stage
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four contrasting locations the lesson identifies as key staging moments in Noughts and Crosses.
cards.answer: Beach scene / Cross school scene / Prison and interrogation scenes / Execution scene

cards.front: What three colour associations might a lighting designer establish across the production?
cards.answer: Warm amber for private moments of hope / Cool white-blue for institutional or state power / Neutral white for narration
items: Warm amber for private moments of hope
Cool white-blue for institutional or state power

cards.front: Why does minimal staging suit the political intent of Noughts and Crosses?
cards.answer: It stops the audience settling into a recognisable domestic world, keeping focus on relationships and power dynamics rather than period detail.

cards.front: Why might a designer make the Cross school uniform slightly off-fitting on Callum?
cards.answer: To suggest the institutional garment, and the institution itself, was not made for his body or truly meant to include him.

cards.front: Name the four human activities the lesson gives for raising greenhouse gas concentrations since the Industrial Revolution.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels for electricity and transport / Clearing forests for farming / Industrial farming (cattle release methane) / Cement manufacture
items: Burning fossil fuels for electricity and transport

cards.front: What three uncertainties does the lesson give for why future warming projections range so widely?
cards.answer: Future emissions depend on political/economic choices / Feedback loops are hard to model / Natural variability masks short-term trends
items: Future emissions depend on political/economic choices
Feedback loops are hard to model

cards.front: What caused the Medieval Warm Period and the Little Ice Age, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Both were caused by a mix of changes in solar output and volcanic activity.

cards.front: Why can't natural causes explain the rapid warming seen since 1970?
cards.answer: Natural causes explain past climate cycles, but today's warming is about ten times faster than the natural warming that ended the last ice age.

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why UK manufacturing has declined relative to services?
cards.answer: Global competition from lower-wage countries / Automation replacing manual workers / Rising incomes shifting spending towards services
items: Rising incomes shifting spending towards services

cards.front: Which four UK regions does the lesson name as hit hardest by deindustrialisation?
cards.answer: The Midlands / South Wales / The North East / Parts of Scotland

cards.front: How does automation contribute to deindustrialisation?
cards.answer: Robots and computer-controlled machinery replace manual workers, so the same output can be produced with fewer employees.

cards.front: Why does rising income shift demand towards the tertiary sector?
cards.answer: As people become wealthier they spend a higher proportion of income on services like holidays and healthcare rather than extra manufactured goods.

title: Roles & Responsibilities in the Music Business
subject: music-technology

cards.front: Name the four main creative roles in the music business.
cards.answer: Musical artist / Composer/songwriter / Lyricist / Arranger

cards.front: Name the three key technical roles in the music business.
cards.answer: Producer / Technician / Engineer

cards.front: Why do recording studios rely on session musicians?
cards.answer: Studios bring them in for their expertise on a particular instrument to add professional-quality parts to tracks.

cards.front: How does A&R connect the two sides of a record label?
cards.answer: A&R acts as the bridge between the creative and commercial sides of a record label.

cards.front: Name the four ways rivers erode, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Abrasion / Attrition / Hydraulic action / Solution

cards.front: Name the four ways rivers transport their load, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Traction / Saltation / Suspension / Solution

cards.front: Why can the same river erode in winter but deposit in summer?
cards.answer: Heavy rainfall raises discharge and energy so the river can erode, but with less discharge energy only just moves the water, causing deposition.

cards.front: Why do levees build up alongside a river channel?
cards.answer: Repeated flooding drops the coarsest sand close to the channel, and this builds up over time into low ridges.

title: Formal & Informal Support When Milestones Aren't Reached
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of nurse the lesson identifies as supporting different life stages.
cards.answer: Health visitor / School nurse / District nurse

cards.front: Name the four additional forms of support (beyond formal and informal care) the lesson describes for people who haven't reached milestones.
cards.answer: Training and development / Equipment and resources / Financial support / Support groups

cards.front: Why is financial support significant for individuals who have not reached expected milestones?
cards.answer: Without it, the cost of specialist equipment, therapies, and adapted housing falls entirely on the individual and family, creating an economic barrier to development.

cards.front: How does advocacy support an individual's PIES development?
cards.answer: It protects the individual's right to have their needs accurately represented in decisions about their own care.

cards.front: Name the three poems explored in this lesson on power and control in relationships.
cards.answer: My Last Duchess / Valentine / The Manhunt

cards.front: The lesson says power operates differently in each of the three poems — through what three means?
cards.answer: Through murder / Through language / Through emotional withdrawal

cards.front: How does the single unbroken stanza of 'My Last Duchess' reflect the Duke's character?
cards.answer: It mirrors his refusal to allow interruption, showing he controls the conversation just as he controlled the Duchess.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'The Manhunt' mirror Laura's process of reconnecting with her husband?
cards.answer: The couplets move from external wounds to internal trauma, mirroring her slow journey towards the hidden psychological damage.

title: Establishing Law and Order on the Plains
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three pressures the lesson gives for why federal authority grew westward after the Civil War.
cards.answer: Railroads needed national protection / Territorial governments answered directly to Washington / The army was redeployed across the Plains after 1865
items: Territorial governments answered directly to Washington
The army was redeployed across the Plains after 1865

cards.front: Name the four states admitted to the Union in 1889, the single year with the most admissions in this period.
cards.answer: North Dakota / South Dakota / Montana / Washington

cards.front: Why was Henry Plummer's case so unsettling for the frontier system of law?
cards.answer: The elected sheriff may have secretly led the outlaw gang he was meant to stop, and no other institution was close enough to check him.

cards.front: How did the Johnson County War of 1892 show that statehood alone didn't end frontier crime?
cards.answer: Even though Wyoming had been a state for two years, large landowners could still hire private gunmen and outrun local sheriffs.

title: Modern crime: drugs, driving and race crimes
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three offences created by the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
cards.answer: Unauthorised access ('hacking') / Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence / Unauthorised modification of data
items: Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence

cards.front: Which three drugs could be bought legally over the counter in British chemists' shops in 1900?
cards.answer: Cocaine / Opium / Cannabis

cards.front: Why did the 1993 Stephen Lawrence case lead to wider hate-crime protections?
cards.answer: The racist murder and the 1999 Macpherson Inquiry that followed pushed Parliament to extend protection to religion, sexual orientation, disability and transgender status.

cards.front: Why is drug crime described as a change in legal classification rather than a new type of behaviour?
cards.answer: Drugs like cocaine and opium were legal and openly sold in 1900, so the acts themselves didn't change but their legal status flipped from legal to criminal.

title: Data Compression: Huffman and Run-Length Encoding
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why compressing data is useful.
