cards.answer: Files download faster / Costs less to transmit over a network / Consumes less storage space
items: Costs less to transmit over a network

cards.front: Name the four types of data the lesson gives where lossless compression is essential.
cards.answer: Text files / Program code / Medical images / Database backups

cards.front: Why does RLE increase file size when data alternates frequently, e.g. 010101?
cards.answer: Because each single value needs its own count-value pair, so the number of stored values doubles instead of shrinking.

cards.front: Why is RLE effective on simple bitmap images but not on photographic images?
cards.answer: RLE relies on long runs of the same value; bitmaps have solid colour areas but adjacent pixels in photos rarely match.

title: Electronic Systems and the Input-Process-Output Model
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four sensors described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Light-dependent resistor (LDR) / Thermistor / Microswitch / Moisture sensor

cards.front: Name the four output devices described in the lesson.
cards.answer: LED / Buzzer / Motor / Relay

cards.front: How does a buzzer turn an electrical signal into sound?
cards.answer: It converts electrical pulses into sound by vibrating a disc inside it.

cards.front: Why can an open-loop toaster produce toast that isn't actually done properly?
cards.answer: It has no feedback, so it heats for a fixed time regardless of whether the bread is actually toasted.

cards.front: Name the three biased perspectives the reader must weigh in Frankenstein's nested narrative.
cards.answer: Walton hero-worships Victor / Victor blames the Creature / The Creature seeks sympathy

cards.front: What three things does Victor do to isolate himself while creating the Creature at Ingolstadt?
cards.answer: Stops writing to his family / Neglects his health / Works in secret

cards.front: Why does Shelley structure the novel so Victor's story is told to Walton?
cards.answer: So Victor's story serves as a warning to Walton, and to the reader, that unchecked ambition destroys the ambitious.

cards.front: Why does Shelley give Walton the last word in the novel?
cards.answer: Because when his crew demand they turn back, Walton agrees, making him the one man who heeds the warning in time.

cards.front: Name the three prescribed material sources for Greek warfare mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: South frieze of Temple of Athena Nike / Lenormant Trireme relief / Triptolemos Painter kylix
items: South frieze of Temple of Athena Nike

cards.front: Name the four Roman monuments or objects the lesson gives as sources for Roman warfare.
cards.answer: Trajan's Column / Arch of Trajan at Benevento / Relief of Actium in the Vatican Museum / Mark Antony Legionary denarius
items: Relief of Actium in the Vatican Museum

cards.front: Why did all three banks of rowers on a trireme need to stroke in precise rhythm?
cards.answer: To generate the burst of speed needed for an effective ramming run against enemy ships.

cards.front: Why was the Mark Antony Legionary denarius more than just currency?
cards.answer: It was struck to pay soldiers before Actium, so it also worked as propaganda advertising Antony's fleet and strength.

cards.front: Name the three spirits Marley says will visit Scrooge.
cards.answer: Ghost of Christmas Past / Ghost of Christmas Present / Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
items: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

cards.front: Name the six items Marley's chain 'forged in life' is made of.
cards.answer: Cash-boxes / Keys / Padlocks / Ledgers / Deeds / Heavy purses

cards.front: Why does Dickens say 'external heat and cold had little influence on Scrooge'?
cards.answer: Because his inner coldness and greed are worse than any winter weather could be.

cards.front: How does Fred's visit to Scrooge's office create contrast in Stave 1?
cards.answer: His warmth and generous view of Christmas as kind and charitable set up the moral alternative to Scrooge's cruelty.

cards.front: Name the five indicative active tenses the passage may use.
cards.answer: Present / Future / Imperfect / Perfect / Pluperfect

cards.front: What three changes usually need to be made when polishing a literal draft into natural English?
cards.answer: Move the verb earlier / Add articles such as 'a' or 'the' / Choose an idiomatic subject-verb-object order

cards.front: Why should you always translate in two stages rather than going straight into polished English?
cards.answer: The literal stage checks every grammatical detail, while the polished stage produces accurate natural English without losing or adding meaning.

cards.front: How does mixing up a present active participle and a perfect passive participle change a sentence's meaning?
cards.answer: It changes both the timing of the action (same time vs already finished) and its direction (doing it vs having it done to you).

cards.front: Name the four types of jobs the lesson says women worked in significant numbers by 1910.
cards.answer: Teachers / Nurses / Secretaries / Factory workers

cards.front: What four new social spaces/technologies gave young women new freedoms in the 1920s?
cards.answer: The speakeasy / The cinema / The radio / The gramophone

cards.front: Why were many women pushed out of their jobs after the First World War ended?
cards.answer: Returning soldiers reclaimed the jobs women had taken on during the war.

cards.front: Why was Margaret Sanger prosecuted multiple times in the 1910s and 1920s?
cards.answer: Because contraception was still illegal in many states, making her campaigning controversial.

cards.front: Name the three parallel developments that drive the crisis in Scenes 4–7.
cards.answer: Del deepens her relationship with Mai and moves into her bedsit / Del's pregnancy becomes apparent / Viv walks out of an A-level exam
items: Del deepens her relationship with Mai and moves into her bedsit
Viv walks out of an A-level exam

cards.front: Why does Pinnock use parallel crises for Del and Viv in Scenes 4–7?
cards.answer: To show that both sisters ultimately reject the identity Enid tried to impose on them, just in different ways.

cards.front: What does Mai's advice to Enid in Scene 6 mean for the play's ending?
cards.answer: Mai tells Enid that being at peace with yourself means being at home anywhere, opening the way for reconciliation.

cards.front: Name the three comparative structures given in the lesson for comparing subjects.
cards.answer: más + adjective + que (more... than) / menos + adjective + que (less... than) / tan + adjective + como (as... as)

cards.front: Name the six negative opinion phrases the lesson gives for talking about school subjects.
cards.answer: No me gusta(n) / No me gusta(n) nada / Odio / Detesto / Me aburre(n) / No aguanto / No soporto / Me da igual

cards.front: Why does the verb change between 'Me gusta el español' and 'Me gustan las matemáticas'?
cards.answer: The verb ending agrees with the subject noun (singular or plural), not with the person speaking.

cards.front: Why don't adjectives like 'interesante' and 'difícil' change for gender when describing school subjects?
cards.answer: Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant stay the same for both masculine and feminine subjects.

cards.front: Name the five 'Giant Evils' identified in Beveridge's 1942 report.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Name the four Liberal reforms (1906–1911) that expanded state welfare.
cards.answer: 1906 free school meals / 1907 school medical inspections / 1908 old age pensions / 1911 National Insurance Act

cards.front: How did Florence Nightingale reduce the death rate at Scutari?
cards.answer: She overhauled sanitation, organised laundry, improved diet and established cleanliness routines, cutting deaths from preventable infection.

cards.front: Why did the British Medical Association oppose the creation of the NHS?
cards.answer: Doctors feared losing income and professional independence under a state-run health service.

cards.front: Name the four types of guidance used in coaching.
cards.answer: Visual guidance / Verbal guidance / Manual guidance / Mechanical guidance

cards.front: Give the four disadvantages of mechanical guidance.
cards.answer: Creates dependency on the aid / Alters the feel of the movement / Aids can be expensive and unavailable / Elite performers rarely need it
items: Alters the feel of the movement
Aids can be expensive and unavailable

cards.front: Why is manual guidance rarely appropriate for elite performers?
cards.answer: It interrupts the automatic motor programme they have spent years developing.

cards.front: Why is mechanical guidance well suited to closed skills but not open skills?
cards.answer: Closed skills happen in predictable environments so movement can be rehearsed with an aid, but aids can't replicate an unpredictable open-skill environment.

title: Railroads and the Pacific Railroad Act
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four transcontinental railroad lines that crossed the US by 1893.
cards.answer: Union Pacific–Central Pacific (1869) / Southern Pacific (1881) / Northern Pacific (1883) / Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe (1883)

cards.front: Name the four standard time zones the US railroads imposed in 1883.
cards.answer: Eastern / Central / Mountain / Pacific

cards.front: Why was Congress able to pass the Pacific Railroad Act in 1862?
cards.answer: Southern senators had left Congress for the Civil War, letting the Republican majority finally agree a northern route.

cards.front: Why did US railroads introduce standard time zones in 1883?
cards.answer: Trains running on coast-to-coast schedules made towns' different local times dangerous, risking collisions between trains.

cards.front: Name the three categories that prevention measures fall into.
cards.answer: Physical / Logical / Secure destruction

cards.front: Name the five Acts of IT legislation covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Computer Misuse Act / Copyright, Designs and Patents Act / Data Protection Act / Freedom of Information Act / Health and Safety at Work Act
items: Health and Safety at Work Act

cards.front: How does magnetic wipe (degaussing) destroy data on a traditional hard drive?
cards.answer: It uses a powerful magnet to disrupt the magnetic patterns on the drive, rendering the data unreadable.

cards.front: Why should organisations maintain logs of access attempts under the Computer Misuse Act?
cards.answer: To detect and prove unauthorised access to their computer systems.

cards.front: Name the four steps in the chain from fuel to electricity in most power stations.
cards.answer: Fuel heats water / Steam turns a turbine / Turbine drives a generator / Generator produces AC electricity

cards.front: Why does a generator produce alternating current rather than direct current?
cards.answer: As the coil spins in the magnetic field, the direction of the induced current reverses every half turn.

cards.front: Why can the National Grid supply electricity from one part of the country to areas of high demand elsewhere?
cards.answer: It is a national system, so electricity generated anywhere can be directed to where it's needed, making supply reliable.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use masks at the masquerade ball?
cards.answer: To literalise the play's theme that everyone hides behind a performance, with truth revealed when masks slip.

cards.front: Why is it significant that Don Pedro woos Hero on Claudio's behalf?
cards.answer: It shows Hero being negotiated between men at the ball with little regard for her own feelings.

cards.front: Name the three main meals in France, from morning to evening.
cards.answer: le petit déjeuner (breakfast) / le déjeuner (lunch) / le dîner (dinner/evening meal)

cards.front: What are the four forms of the partitive article and when is each used?
cards.answer: du - before masculine nouns / de la - before feminine nouns / de l' - before vowels / des - before plural nouns

cards.front: How does the partitive article change in a negative French sentence?
cards.answer: After a negative, du/de la/des/de l' all change to de (or d' before a vowel), e.g. je ne mange pas de viande.

cards.front: Why is it useful to add opinions and connectives when describing food in French?
cards.answer: Adding opinions with connectives lets you express personal views and build longer, more complex sentences for higher marks.

title: The Power Struggle to Succeed Lenin
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five plausible heirs to Lenin who were contenders in 1924.
cards.answer: Leon Trotsky / Joseph Stalin / Grigori Zinoviev / Lev Kamenev / Nikolai Bukharin

cards.front: Name the three stages of Stalin's tactical alliances used to defeat his rivals between 1924 and 1929.
cards.answer: Allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev to crush Trotsky (1924-25) / Allied with Bukharin to crush Zinoviev and Kamenev (1925-27) / Turned on Bukharin and the Right Deviation (1928-29)
items: Allied with Zinoviev and Kamenev to crush Trotsky (1924-25)
Allied with Bukharin to crush Zinoviev and Kamenev (1925-27)
Turned on Bukharin and the Right Deviation (1928-29)

cards.front: Why did Stalin's rivals underestimate him in 1924?
cards.answer: He lacked their obvious talents, spoke with a heavy accent and seemed a dull administrator, so while rivals fought publicly he quietly built control over appointments.

cards.front: How did Stalin's role as General Secretary help him defeat his rivals?
cards.answer: It let him control appointments of officials at every level, so Congress delegates and new members owed their positions and loyalty to him, not his rivals.

title: Hitler's foreign policy and the road to war
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: How did the lack of Allied response to the Rhineland reoccupation affect Hitler's position?
cards.answer: It boosted his confidence and domestic prestige, secured Germany's western frontier, and freed him to plan expansion eastward.

cards.front: Why did Hitler sign the Nazi-Soviet Pact in August 1939?
cards.answer: To neutralise the Soviet threat to his eastern flank, giving him a free hand to invade Poland in the west.

cards.front: Name the three literary forms that combine in Animal Farm.
cards.answer: Allegory / Satire / Fable

cards.front: Name the four features that characterised Stalin's dictatorship, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Purges / Show trials / Secret police (NKVD) / Cult of personality

cards.front: Why did Orwell choose to write Animal Farm as a fable rather than a political essay?
cards.answer: Giving animals human qualities let him satirise Stalin's regime without naming it, reaching a wider audience than an essay could.

cards.front: How does the pigs sleeping in beds 'with sheets' show Animal Farm working as a satire?
cards.answer: It uses dark comedy — the pigs changing the commandment — to expose the absurdity and hypocrisy of totalitarianism.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that shape UK climate at the regional scale.
cards.answer: Latitude / Altitude / Distance from the sea / Ocean currents (North Atlantic Drift)

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for the urban heat island effect.
cards.answer: Dark surfaces storing heat / Waste heat from cars and buildings / Sheltered streets reducing wind / Lack of vegetation to cool the air
items: Waste heat from cars and buildings
Lack of vegetation to cool the air

cards.front: Why do average July temperatures fall from about 20°C in southern England to 13°C in north-west Scotland?
cards.answer: Further north the sun's angle is lower, so each square metre of ground receives less heat.

cards.front: Why does the summit of Ben Nevis get snow while lower ground nearby stays frost-free?
cards.answer: Temperature drops about 1°C for every 100 m of altitude, making the 1,345 m summit far colder.

cards.front: Name the four magical feats Prospero lists in his renunciation speech before giving up magic.
cards.answer: Dimmed the sun / Raised storms / Opened graves / Commanded spirits

cards.front: Which four characters does the lesson say move towards freedom by the play's end?
cards.answer: Ferdinand from his test / Alonso from his guilt / Caliban from servitude / Ariel from obligation

cards.front: How does The Tempest's ending differ from Shakespeare's tragedies like Hamlet and Macbeth?
cards.answer: Those tragedies end in death, but Prospero chooses mercy over revenge so his story ends in release instead.

cards.front: Why is it ironic that Ariel prompts Prospero's decision to forgive his enemies?
cards.answer: A non-human spirit says even it would feel tender compassion if human, teaching the human Prospero about mercy.

cards.front: Name the four ways à combines with the definite article in 'avoir mal à' expressions.
cards.answer: à + le = au / à + la = à la / à + l' = à l' / à + les = aux

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson gives for coping with stress.
cards.answer: Do yoga / Sleep enough / Go to bed early / Talk to friends / Meditate

cards.front: Why does 'Elle s'est reposée' have an extra -e on the past participle?
cards.answer: Because reflexive verbs use être in the passé composé and the past participle agrees with the subject, showing it is feminine.

cards.front: Why do you say 'J'ai mal au ventre' but 'J'ai mal à la tête'?
cards.answer: Because à contracts with the masculine article le to become au, but stays separate as à la before a feminine noun.

cards.front: Name the six issues the lesson says can be used to evaluate any study of perception.
cards.answer: Validity / Reliability / Generalisability / Ethics / Objectivity / Subjectivity

cards.front: How does emotion create a perceptual set when judging a stranger's facial expression?
cards.answer: An anxious person may perceive an ambiguous expression as more threatening than a calm person, because emotion directs attention toward mood-congruent information.

cards.front: Why did Carmichael, Hogan and Walter include a control group that heard no verbal label?
cards.answer: So the effect of the label on drawing accuracy could be isolated from other factors.

cards.front: Name the five major types of non-communicable disease given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cardiovascular diseases (heart disease and stroke) / Cancer / Lung diseases (e.g. bronchitis) / Liver diseases (e.g. cirrhosis) / Type 2 diabetes

cards.front: Name the four risk factors for cancer given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Smoking / UV radiation / Certain viruses (e.g. HPV) / Genetic predisposition

cards.front: Why does smoking increase the risk of cardiovascular disease?
cards.answer: It damages the lining of arteries, leading to atherosclerosis, which narrows arteries and reduces blood flow.

cards.front: How do malignant tumours differ from benign tumours in how they spread?
cards.answer: Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissues and spread to other organs via the blood (metastasis), while benign tumours do not spread.

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in a 16-mark period essay.
cards.answer: Narrative without argument / Listing without weighing / Sitting on the fence / Forgetting SPaG

cards.front: What are the three parts of the structure that works for a 16-mark essay?
cards.answer: Introduction (2-3 sentences) / Two or three analytical paragraphs / Conclusion (3-5 sentences)

cards.front: Why does simply listing factors (Factor A, Factor B, Factor C) fail to show analysis?
cards.answer: It shows knowledge but not analysis, because it does not compare factors and say which was more important.

cards.front: Why must every paragraph in a 16-mark essay link back to the question?
cards.answer: Without linking back, the essay becomes narrative retelling of events rather than an argument answering the question.

title: Film Music: Creating Mood, Time and Place
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: What four things does a composer gradually increase across a cue to build tension?
cards.answer: Rising pitch / Thickening texture / Increasing dynamics / Mounting dissonance

cards.front: What are the four stages of a typical climax-and-resolution shape in an exam extract?
cards.answer: Calm, thinly textured opening / Middle section thickens with more dissonance / Climax with full orchestration and maximum volume / Resolve into a calmer, consonant closing passage
items: Middle section thickens with more dissonance
Climax with full orchestration and maximum volume
Resolve into a calmer, consonant closing passage

cards.front: Why does brass scoring often suggest heroism, royalty or ancient battle in film music?
cards.answer: Because brass instruments have long been used for ceremonial and military music.

cards.front: Why are pentatonic scales often used to suggest East Asian settings in film music?
cards.answer: Because pentatonic scales are genuinely common in folk music from that region.

cards.front: Name the four steps the lesson gives for structuring extract analysis.
cards.answer: Read the extract to identify Dickens's purpose / Select 3-4 key quotations / Analyse each quotation's language and effect / Link analysis to the wider novel
items: Read the extract to identify Dickens's purpose
Analyse each quotation's language and effect
Link analysis to the wider novel

cards.front: Name the four-part pattern each paragraph should follow in a wider text essay.
cards.answer: Point / Quotation / Analysis of language / Link to writer's purpose

cards.front: How does the criminal justice system in the novel expose class hypocrisy?
cards.answer: Compeyson, a gentleman, receives a lighter sentence than Magwitch for the same crimes, showing the law separates rich from poor, not guilty from innocent.

cards.front: Why does Dickens present Joe's love for Pip as the only love that truly heals him?
cards.answer: Because it is unconditional — it never wavers, never demands repayment, and never depends on Pip's class or gratitude.

cards.front: Name the six connectives given in the lesson for linking descriptions in Spanish.
cards.answer: y / pero / también / sin embargo / además / aunque

cards.front: Name the four forms of a Spanish adjective ending in -o, using alto as the example.
cards.answer: alto / alta / altos / altas

cards.front: Why is 'tiene el pelo largo' translated as 'has long hair' even though it literally says 'has the hair'?
cards.answer: Spanish uses the structure 'has the hair' with a definite article, rather than 'has ... hair' as in English.

cards.front: Why don't mayor and menor change when describing an older or younger sibling?
cards.answer: These words for older/younger family members do not change for gender, staying the same for masculine and feminine nouns.

title: Sociological Theories of the Role of the Family
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four perspectives the lesson covers in the conflict versus consensus debate on the family.
cards.answer: Functionalism / Marxism / Feminism / New Right

cards.front: What three structural causes do feminists say the New Right ignores when blaming lone parent families?
cards.answer: Poverty / the gender pay gap / lack of affordable child care

cards.front: Why does Oakley say working women face a 'double shift'?
cards.answer: Because when women take paid jobs, domestic duties don't get reduced, so they simply gain a second shift of work on top.

cards.front: How does the New Right argue the welfare state has caused family breakdown?
cards.answer: It has made it economically rational for women to raise children alone, removing the incentive for male responsibility in the family.

cards.front: What are the four factors that increase the rate of diffusion?
cards.answer: Steeper concentration gradient / Larger surface area / Thinner membrane / Higher temperature

cards.front: What are the four main components of blood?
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Why does a red blood cell burst when placed in a very dilute solution?
cards.answer: It has no cell wall, so water entering by osmosis makes it swell until it bursts (lysis).

cards.front: Why is having a double circulation useful for mammals?
cards.answer: It lets blood pressure stay high in both circuits, supporting the high metabolic rate needed for warm-blooded activity.

cards.front: Name the five stages, in order, that the atomic model went through from Dalton to Chadwick.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere / Thomson's plum pudding model / Rutherford's nuclear model / Bohr's electron shells / Chadwick's discovery of the neutron

cards.front: Name the four pieces of experimental evidence the lesson says forced changes to the atomic model.
cards.answer: Cathode rays / Alpha scattering / Emission spectra / Neutron bombardment

cards.front: Why did Rutherford's nuclear model have a stability problem that Bohr's model solved?
cards.answer: Classical physics predicted orbiting electrons would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, making atoms unstable, unless they stayed in fixed energy levels.

cards.front: Why does each element produce its own unique spectrum of light, according to Bohr's model?
cards.answer: Electrons jump between fixed energy levels, absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy as light unique to that element.

cards.front: Name the four things sold at German Christmas markets according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Glühwein (mulled wine) / Lebkuchen (gingerbread) / Stollen (sweet bread with dried fruit) / gebrannte Mandeln (roasted almonds)

cards.front: Name the three traditional Silvester (New Year's Eve) activities in Germany.
cards.answer: Bleigießen (melting wax to predict the future) / Watching Dinner for One on TV / Eating Berliner (jam doughnuts)
items: Bleigießen (melting wax to predict the future)
Watching Dinner for One on TV

cards.front: Why is 3rd October celebrated as Tag der Deutschen Einheit in Germany?
cards.answer: It celebrates the reunification of East and West Germany in 1990 and is Germany's national holiday.

cards.front: How is Bleigießen used on Silvester to predict the future?
cards.answer: You melt a small piece of wax and pour it into water, and the shape formed is used to predict the future.

title: Public Health & Fighting Cholera in the 19th Century
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four years the lesson gives for cholera's arrival and major outbreaks in Britain.
Name the four factors the lesson gives that combined to make the 1875 Public Health Act possible.
cards.answer: Science and technology (Germ Theory) / Individuals (Snow and Chadwick's evidence) / Government attitudes (1867 Reform Act) / Public pressure (outbreaks and Great Stink)

cards.front: Why did progress in public health reform remain uneven across Britain?
cards.answer: Wealthier areas improved faster than poorer ones, so many slum areas stayed unhealthy well into the 20th century.

cards.front: How did clean water and sewerage reforms improve life expectancy?
cards.answer: Clean water, proper sewerage and Medical Officers of Health cut death rates from waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid, raising life expectancy.

cards.front: Name the four other poems in the Conflict cluster that 'Thirteen' is compared with in this lesson.
cards.answer: Boat Stealing / Honour Killing / Flag / Songs for the People

cards.front: The lesson names four short phrases from 'Thirteen' precise enough to memorise and quote. What are they?
cards.answer: horizon in the east / stars / black holes / thirteen

cards.front: How does opening each stanza in the future tense reflect the poem's theme of prejudice?
cards.answer: It makes the boy's fate feel fixed before it happens, echoing how prejudice pre-judges a person before they act.

cards.front: Why does Femi compare the boy's future to a supernova?
cards.answer: A supernova looks like a star's brightest moment but is actually its visible death, showing the boy's predicted brilliance really signals his destruction.

title: Life during the Second World War
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What three changes did Goebbels' 'total war' policy bring to German society from 1943?
cards.answer: Longer working hours / more women in factories / severe reductions in consumer goods

cards.front: Name the six death camps established in occupied Poland.
cards.answer: Auschwitz-Birkenau / Treblinka / Sobibor / Belzec / Chelmno / Majdanek

cards.front: Why did the Nazi regime try to shield German civilians from hardship in the early years of the war?
cards.answer: They feared excessive hardship would undermine popular support, having studied how the Home Front collapsed in 1918.

cards.front: How did Allied bombing weaken Germany's war effort beyond causing civilian casualties?
cards.answer: It disrupted industrial production, forced factories to disperse, and consumed anti-aircraft resources diverted from the front.

cards.front: What three things did a Roman sanctuary include?
cards.answer: The temple itself / An open altar standing outside in front of it / Often a grove of sacred trees
items: An open altar standing outside in front of it
Often a grove of sacred trees

cards.front: What were the three ten-year stages of a Vestal Virgin's thirty years of service?
cards.answer: First ten years learning her duties / Next ten years performing them / Final ten years teaching new Vestals
items: First ten years learning her duties
Final ten years teaching new Vestals

cards.front: Why did King Numa create the office of flamen Dialis, according to Livy?
cards.answer: He feared future kings, being more warlike than himself, would neglect Jupiter's royal rituals while away at war.

cards.front: Why did the pontifices punish a Vestal Virgin whose sacred fire went out?
cards.answer: Because the Romans believed a continually burning fire was essential to the safety of the city.

title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names three types of tanhā (craving). What are they?
cards.answer: Craving for sensory pleasure / Craving for existence (clinging to life) / Craving for non-existence (wishing for annihilation)

cards.front: Name the three practices that make up samādhi (the meditation section) of the Eightfold Path.
cards.answer: Right effort / Right mindfulness / Right concentration

cards.front: Why did Siddhattha develop the idea of the Middle Way?
cards.answer: He found that neither his earlier life of luxury nor his later extreme asceticism led to liberation, so he sought a balanced path avoiding both.

cards.front: Why is the Deer Park Sermon an important event in Buddhism?
cards.answer: It was the Buddha's first teaching, setting out the Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path, and marked the beginning of the sangha.

cards.front: Name the three stages the lesson says are always involved in turning a design into a working prototype.
cards.answer: Shaping raw material into the right form / Fabricating or joining separate parts together / Assembling everything into a finished product
items: Shaping raw material into the right form
Fabricating or joining separate parts together
Assembling everything into a finished product

cards.front: Name the seven timber joints named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Butt / Dowel / Lap / Housing / Mitre / Mortise and tenon / Dovetail

cards.front: Why does vacuum forming produce thinner walls in deep shapes and sharp corners?
cards.answer: The sheet thins wherever it is stretched most, so deeper shapes and sharper corners stretch and thin more than flat areas.

cards.front: Why is CAM used across metals, polymers, timbers and papers instead of hand tools alone?
cards.answer: It gives greater accuracy and repeatability, so the same digital file can be reproduced identically many times.

title: Organisational Structures and Ways of Working
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five barriers to effective communication in organisations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Physical barriers (noise, poor internet, time zones) / Jargon and technical language / Too many layers in the chain of command / Cultural differences between team members / Overloaded managers failing to pass on information
items: Physical barriers (noise, poor internet, time zones)
Too many layers in the chain of command
Overloaded managers failing to pass on information

cards.front: Name the six ways of working the lesson describes for organising employment.
cards.answer: Full-time employees / Part-time employees / Flexible hours arrangements / Permanent contracts / Temporary contracts / Freelancers

cards.front: Why might a wide span of control fail to work well as a flat-structure business grows?
cards.answer: A wide span of control only works well when employees are highly skilled and need little supervision, so managers get overstretched otherwise.

cards.front: Why can too much communication harm a business, not just too little?
cards.answer: Excessive meetings, email chains and sign-offs slow down operations and frustrate employees just as much as insufficient communication.

cards.front: Name the three contextual forces the lesson says drive Othello's tragedy.
cards.answer: Racial prejudice (Othello permanently 'othered') / Patriarchal honour (male identity tied to female chastity) / Jacobean attitudes to marriage (wives as property)
items: Patriarchal honour (male identity tied to female chastity)
Jacobean attitudes to marriage (wives as property)

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson says use racist language to attack Othello.
cards.answer: Iago / Brabantio / Roderigo

cards.front: How does the shift from Venice to Cyprus help Iago manipulate Othello?
cards.answer: Cyprus is isolated from Venice's legal and social structures, so rumour replaces evidence and Othello's self-doubt can grow unchecked.

cards.front: How does Desdemona's elopement break Jacobean patriarchal marriage rules?
cards.answer: She marries without her father's consent and marries a Black man, violating the system twice.

title: Edward the Lawgiver: The Statutes of Westminster, Gloucester and Mortmain
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four great Edwardian statutes issued between 1275 and 1290.
cards.answer: Westminster I (1275) / Gloucester (1278) / Mortmain (1279) / Westminster II (1285)

cards.front: What four abuses did the First Statute of Westminster deal with?
cards.answer: Corrupt sheriffs / Bullying of jurors / Over-use of distraint / Exploitation of widows and minors

cards.front: Why did the spread of mortmain worry Edward I financially?
cards.answer: Land held by the church never passed to an heir, so the king lost feudal incidents like reliefs, wardships and marriages he could normally collect.

cards.front: How did Quia Emptores simplify the structure of land tenure?
cards.answer: Buyers of land held it from the seller's lord rather than the seller, stopping the creation of new layers of feudal lordship.

cards.front: Name the three social classes the lesson describes in Victorian England.
cards.answer: Aristocracy and landed gentry / Middle class (merchants, lawyers, bankers) / Working class and the poor

cards.front: Name the three stages Great Expectations is divided into, in order.
cards.answer: Stage one: childhood on the marshes / Stage two: life as a gentleman in London / Stage three: disillusionment and moral redemption
items: Stage one: childhood on the marshes
Stage two: life as a gentleman in London
Stage three: disillusionment and moral redemption

cards.front: How does Pip's version of 'self-improvement' differ from Samuel Smiles's idea in Self-Help?
cards.answer: Pip's self-improvement is about becoming richer and more refined, not morally better, making him snobbish and ashamed of Joe.

cards.front: How did serialisation shape the structure of Great Expectations?
cards.answer: Each weekly instalment ended with a cliffhanger to keep readers buying, shaping dramatic reveals like Magwitch's return.

title: The Activation Synthesis Theory of Dreaming
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Name the three features independent judges used to rate bizarreness in Williams et al. (1992).
cards.answer: Incongruity (things not fitting together) / Discontinuity (sudden unexplained changes) / Vagueness

cards.front: Name the three main structures of the brain mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cerebrum / Cerebellum / Brainstem

cards.front: Why do people often wake from a vivid dream in the early hours of the morning, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: REM sleep periods become longer and more frequent towards morning, increasing the chance of waking during a vivid dream.

cards.front: How do supporters of activation synthesis theory respond to the criticism that dream content often relates meaningfully to real life?
cards.answer: They argue the cortex draws on the dreamer's own memories and concerns to build the story, even though it starts from random signals.

cards.front: The lesson says the five-act structure controls the play's emotional rhythm. Name the three stages it describes.
cards.answer: Acts 1 and 2: love and hope / Act 3: conflict and death / Acts 4 and 5: accelerate towards tragic conclusion
items: Acts 4 and 5: accelerate towards tragic conclusion

cards.front: Name the three stages of classical tragedy structure that Romeo and Juliet follows.
cards.answer: Initial happiness / Complications / Final catastrophe

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use asides in Romeo and Juliet?
cards.answer: Asides let characters share thoughts with the audience while others remain unaware, adding humour and character insight, as with the Nurse and Mercutio.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare vary verse and prose to reflect character and mood?
cards.answer: Lovers speak lyrical verse emphasising the beauty and intensity of their relationship, while the Nurse and Mercutio use prose for naturalistic, humorous dialogue.

title: Methods of Training and Their Effects
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six key training methods covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Continuous training / Fartlek training / Interval training / Circuit training / Weight/resistance training / Plyometric training

cards.front: Name the four fitness class formats covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Body pump / Aerobics / Pilates / Yoga

cards.front: Why would a marathon runner make little progress by only doing heavy weight training?
cards.answer: Heavy weight training builds strength, not the aerobic endurance a marathon runner needs to perform.

cards.front: Why is it hard to monitor overload in fartlek training?
cards.answer: Because pace and terrain are varied spontaneously, so intensity is harder to measure precisely.

cards.front: Name the three South African place names Hardy uses in 'Drummer Hodge' to create disorientation.
cards.answer: kopje / veldt / Karoo

cards.front: Name the four anthology poems the lesson pairs with 'Drummer Hodge' for comparison.
cards.answer: Disabled (Owen) / Remains (Armitage) / Kamikaze (Garland) / I Shall Return (McKay)

cards.front: Why does Hardy never give the soldier a first name, calling him only 'Drummer Hodge'?
cards.answer: So he stands for thousands of anonymous war dead, showing war strips ordinary soldiers of their individual identity.

cards.front: Why does Hardy's regular, controlled ABABAB structure create an unsettling effect in the poem?
cards.answer: Its orderly, hymn-like pattern contrasts with Hodge's chaotic, undignified death, giving him a formal memorial denied in reality.

cards.front: Name the five most likely extract topics to prepare for in the Henry V exam.
cards.answer: The Prologue/Chorus (the 'wooden O') / The tennis balls response / The Harfleur speech / The St Crispin's Day speech / The wooing of Katherine

cards.front: Name the four captains in Henry V who are meant to represent British unity.
cards.answer: English / Welsh / Scottish / Irish

cards.front: Why is the unity of the four captains shown to be fragile in Henry V?
cards.answer: Macmorris asks 'What ish my nation?', revealing underlying tension about Irish identity within the supposed 'band of brothers'.

cards.front: How does the Epilogue undercut the play's patriotic narrative?
cards.answer: It reminds the audience that everything won by Henry was later lost, undermining the earlier celebration of conquest.

cards.front: Name the four types of reactions between acids and other substances that make a salt (as given in the lesson).
cards.answer: Acid + metal / Acid + metal oxide / Acid + metal hydroxide / Acid + metal carbonate

cards.front: Name the three everyday examples of neutralisation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Farmers adding limestone/quicklime to acidic soil / Indigestion remedies neutralising stomach acid / Toothpaste neutralising acids from mouth bacteria
items: Farmers adding limestone/quicklime to acidic soil
Toothpaste neutralising acids from mouth bacteria

cards.front: Why is a digital pH probe more accurate than universal indicator for measuring pH?
cards.answer: A pH probe gives a numerical reading to several decimal places, whereas universal indicator only gives an approximate colour-matched reading.

cards.front: Why is a titration repeated until two concordant results are obtained?
cards.answer: Repeating until results agree within 0.10 cm³ and averaging them ensures the titre is accurate.

title: Practitioner Application: Physical Theatre and Ensemble Storytelling
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three practitioner traditions the lesson identifies as directly relevant to staging this play.
cards.answer: Frantic Assembly / Complicite / Music-hall and circus tradition

cards.front: Name the three elements of Frantic Assembly's signature vocabulary given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Round-by-through exercises / Chair duets and contact choreography / Lifts that serve narrative rather than spectacle
items: Lifts that serve narrative rather than spectacle

cards.front: Why is Frantic Assembly's approach suited to the elephant, train and ship sequences in this play?
cards.answer: Because the whole ensemble is more than the sum of its parts, so the audience reads a collective physical decision as a single image.

cards.front: Why would a Frantic Assembly-influenced lighting designer avoid overilluminating the elephant sequence?
cards.answer: To trust the physical storytelling, keeping the design clean and powerful so it serves the movement without competing with it.

title: Staging and Design: Two Worlds, One Stage
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four areas of design the lesson covers for creating class contrast in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Set design / Lighting design / Sound design / Costume design

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things must a good lighting design answer specify?
cards.answer: The type of lantern / The direction of the light / The colour gel / The effect on the audience

cards.front: How does the gobo effect on the Johnstone kitchen wall reinforce the play's theme of entrapment?
cards.answer: It casts a grid of shadows that reads as both a domestic window and prison bars, without any dialogue.

cards.front: Why does the lesson recommend cross-fading rather than sudden blackouts for the play's time leaps?
cards.answer: Cross-fading creates smooth transitions that preserve the dream-like, retrospective quality of Russell's storytelling.

cards.front: Name the four scalar quantities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Speed / Distance / Mass / Energy

cards.front: Name the four vector quantities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Velocity / Displacement / Force / Acceleration

cards.front: Why does doubling a car's speed more than double its stopping distance?
cards.answer: Because braking distance depends on kinetic energy, which grows with speed squared, so braking distance grows faster than speed increases.

cards.front: What are the two parts that make up a vehicle's stopping distance?
cards.answer: Thinking distance, covered during the driver's reaction time, plus braking distance, covered while decelerating to rest.

cards.front: Name the four major pollutants produced by burning fossil fuels.
cards.answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) / Sulfur dioxide (SO2) / Oxides of nitrogen (NOx) / Particulates

cards.front: Name the four human activities the lesson gives that increase greenhouse gas emissions.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Deforestation / Agriculture (cattle and rice paddies) / Landfill sites

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide toxic to the body?
cards.answer: It binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, so the blood cannot carry oxygen properly.

cards.front: How did the formation of the ozone layer allow life to colonise land?
cards.answer: Accumulating oxygen formed the ozone layer, which blocked harmful ultraviolet radiation, allowing life to survive on land.

cards.front: What are the four things the lesson says the novel's ending does NOT resolve?
cards.answer: Racism has not been defeated / Sam is not punished / Tollington has not changed / The motorway is still being built
items: The motorway is still being built

cards.front: On what three levels is Meena's scholarship significant, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Educationally - confirms she is intelligent and capable / Socially - separates her from Anita and the village / Symbolically - represents social mobility
items: Educationally - confirms she is intelligent and capable
Socially - separates her from Anita and the village

cards.front: Why do Nanima's stories of Partition change how Meena sees her parents' quiet behaviour?
cards.answer: They reveal her parents have survived far worse than Tollington's racism, so their quietness is resilience, not passivity.

cards.front: Why does the final image of Meena leaving Tollington feel bittersweet rather than triumphant?
cards.answer: She gains understanding and opportunity through the scholarship, but is also losing Tollington, which was still home.

cards.front: Name the four physiological indicators of health covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Resting heart rate / Heart rate recovery after exercise / Blood pressure / Body mass index (BMI)

cards.front: Name the six risk factors for high blood pressure given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Obesity / High salt intake / Lack of exercise / Stress / Smoking / Excessive alcohol consumption

cards.front: Why does a lower resting heart rate generally show better cardiovascular fitness?
cards.answer: Because the heart pumps more blood per beat, so it doesn't need to beat as often to circulate blood.

cards.front: Why is slow heart rate recovery after exercise a warning sign for health?
cards.answer: It shows the heart and circulatory system aren't working efficiently, indicating poor fitness and increased risk of heart disease.

cards.front: Name the four deserts the lesson gives as examples created by sinking Hadley-cell air.
cards.answer: Sahara / Arabian / Atacama / Australian

cards.front: What three things should you focus on when describing a climate graph?
cards.answer: Temperature range (highest minus lowest) / Total annual rainfall / Pattern of wet and dry seasons
items: Pattern of wet and dry seasons

cards.front: How does the North Atlantic Drift affect winter temperatures in the British Isles?
cards.answer: It carries tropical heat polewards, making British winters 5–10°C warmer than parts of Canada at the same latitude.

cards.front: Why does the UK experience changeable weather from day to day?
cards.answer: The UK sits where the Ferrel cell meets the polar front, causing frequent changes in weather.

title: Black Consciousness, Durban strikes and trade unions
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the two reasons the lesson gives for why the Durban strikes were significant.
cards.answer: Showed black workers could organise despite no legal recognition and banned strikes / Forced employers and government to see low wages and the pass system as unsustainable
items: Showed black workers could organise despite no legal recognition and banned strikes
Forced employers and government to see low wages and the pass system as unsustainable

cards.front: Name the four sectors affected by the 1973 Durban strike wave.
cards.answer: Docks / Factories / Transport / Municipal services

cards.front: Why did the black universities created under Bantu Education become centres of political organising?
cards.answer: Bantu Education universities were designed to restrict black education, but by concentrating black students together they ironically allowed SASO to spread rapidly.

cards.front: How did the Durban strikes affect the development of black trade unions?
cards.answer: They accelerated trade union organising, leading to embryonic independent black trade unions that became the basis for COSATU, founded in 1985.

cards.front: Name the four factors that determine which joining method to use for an assembly.
cards.answer: Whether the joint needs to be dismantled later / The materials being joined / The load the joint must carry / The cost of the process
items: Whether the joint needs to be dismantled later
The load the joint must carry

cards.front: Name the seven steps of the riveting sequence in order.
cards.answer: Mark out / Centre-punch each position / Clamp the sheets together / Drill the rivet holes / De-burr the holes / Insert the rivet / Form the tail

cards.front: Why is a joint centre-punched before drilling in the riveting sequence?
cards.answer: Centre-punching each marked position stops the drill bit from wandering off the correct spot.

cards.front: How does capillary action allow solder or brazing filler to join two pieces of metal?
cards.answer: The heated filler metal melts and is drawn into the narrow gap between the closely fitted parts, filling it without melting the parent metal.

cards.front: Name the four risks the lesson gives for coastal fieldwork.
cards.answer: Cliff falls / Rip currents / Slippery rocks / Tides cutting off access

cards.front: Name the four mitigations the lesson gives for managing fieldwork risks.
cards.answer: Checking river-level gauges and tide tables / Working in groups / Wearing wellies and gloves / Never wading above knee depth
items: Checking river-level gauges and tide tables

cards.front: Why is secondary data required alongside your own primary fieldwork data?
cards.answer: Because one day's primary data is rarely enough on its own, so secondary data sets it in a wider context.

cards.front: Why must a method justification link back to the enquiry question in two parts?
cards.answer: You must state what the method measures and how that measurement directly answers the question, not just describe the method.

cards.front: What three aspects does the lesson compare between Dickinson's and Hannah's poems?
cards.answer: Tone / Voice / Form

cards.front: Why does Dickinson's simple hymn metre create an unsettling effect in 'I started Early – Took my Dog'?
cards.answer: Because its nursery-rhyme-like, song-like rhythm contrasts with the disturbing content of the speaker being pursued by the sea.

cards.front: Why is the distance between Hannah and her persona essential for the satire in 'Postcard from a Travel Snob' to work?
cards.answer: The reader must recognise Hannah is mocking, not endorsing, the speaker, so the self-important voice exposes the speaker's own arrogance.

cards.front: Name the six causes the lesson gives for rising poverty in Elizabethan England.
cards.answer: Population growth / Rising prices / Sheep enclosures replacing arable farming / Dissolution of the monasteries / Bad harvests in the 1580s / Demobilisation of soldiers

cards.front: Name the three currents the lesson gives for why attitudes to the poor began to soften.
cards.answer: Towns pioneering local schemes / Protestant clergy preaching about the poor / Visibility of unemployed able-bodied men
items: Protestant clergy preaching about the poor

cards.front: How did enclosure reduce the number of labouring jobs on the land?
cards.answer: One shepherd could manage land that had previously employed a dozen ploughmen.

cards.front: Why did price inflation hit wage labourers hardest?
cards.answer: Because their wages rose much more slowly than the rising cost of bread.

cards.front: Name the four zones in Mumbai's urban land-use pattern, moving from the coast inland.
cards.answer: Central Business District (Nariman Point and Fort) / Inner city (older industry and Dharavi) / Suburbs (e.g. Bandra and Andheri) / Urban-rural fringe (new airport and satellite towns)
items: Central Business District (Nariman Point and Fort)
Urban-rural fringe (new airport and satellite towns)

cards.front: Name the three types of work the lesson says pull migrants to Mumbai.
cards.answer: Textiles / Construction / Domestic service

cards.front: Why can bulldozers clear slum neighbourhoods in Mumbai with little notice?
cards.answer: Many slum residents have insecure property rights, so they have no legal protection against eviction.

cards.front: Why is there such stark inequality within Mumbai?
cards.answer: Skilled, English-speaking workers gained far more from growth than unskilled migrants, and peninsula land scarcity pushed property prices to extreme levels, excluding the poor.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says to consider when comparing the injury risk of different sporting activities.
cards.answer: Contact level / Speed of movement / Use of implements / The natural environment involved

cards.front: Name the four categories of equipment discussed as extrinsic factors affecting injury risk.
cards.answer: Protective equipment / Performance equipment / Clothing / Footwear

cards.front: Why does an excessively hard artificial playing surface increase the risk of stress fractures and shin splints?
cards.answer: A hard surface increases ground-reaction forces on the joints, raising the risk of stress fractures and shin splints.

cards.front: How can a hostile crowd increase injury risk during a match?
cards.answer: A hostile crowd can increase a performer's anxiety, which in turn can lead to reckless play and injury.

cards.front: What four push factors from rural Maharashtra and Bihar drive migration to Mumbai?
cards.answer: Small landholdings / Drought / Low rural wages / Limited rural healthcare

cards.front: What four downsides of the informal economy in Mumbai does the lesson give?
cards.answer: Workers earn very little / Conditions are dangerous / Tax revenue is missed / Women exposed to harassment

cards.front: Why do some Londoners move out of the city in their thirties?
cards.answer: High housing costs push people out when they start families.

cards.front: How does the informal economy help new arrivals in Mumbai?
cards.answer: It provides cheap goods and services and creates work for new arrivals who would otherwise be unemployed.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says subroutines make programs easier.
cards.answer: Easier to write (tackle one task at a time) / Easier to test (check each block in isolation) / Easier to reuse (call the same subroutine many times) / Easier to maintain (change one block without breaking others)
items: Easier to write (tackle one task at a time)
Easier to test (check each block in isolation)
Easier to reuse (call the same subroutine many times)
Easier to maintain (change one block without breaking others)

cards.front: What three steps does the lesson say to follow when asked to write a subroutine?
cards.answer: Start with the signature (name and parameters) / Write the body / Add RETURN at the end if it is a function
items: Start with the signature (name and parameters)
Add RETURN at the end if it is a function

cards.front: In a banking app, how does making the balance a local variable make it easier to find bugs than using a global variable?
cards.answer: Only the subroutine that owns the local variable can change it, so any fault is isolated to that one subroutine.

cards.front: How do local variables let a hundred users run the same login check at once without interfering with each other?
cards.answer: Each user gets their own isolated local copy of the username and password that only exists while that subroutine runs.

title: Improving Processes: Metals, LCAs and Recycling
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the six factors that a life cycle assessment (LCA) considers.
cards.answer: Energy consumption at each stage / Raw material use / Water use / Emissions to air and water / Waste produced / Potential for recycling or reuse

cards.front: Name the four factors that affect decisions about whether to recycle a material.
cards.answer: Cost of collection and sorting / Energy needed to process recycled material compared to making new material / Market value of the recycled product / Public willingness to separate and recycle materials
items: Energy needed to process recycled material vs new material
Market value of the recycled product
Public willingness to separate and recycle

cards.front: Why is electrolysis used to extract aluminium instead of reduction with carbon?
cards.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide, meaning electrolysis must be used instead.

cards.front: Why should LCA evidence be evaluated critically rather than accepted at face value?
cards.answer: LCAs involve subjective judgement on hard-to-quantify factors, and companies sometimes use selective LCA data to support marketing claims.

cards.front: Name the five uses of glucose produced by photosynthesis in a plant.
cards.answer: Respiration / Starch storage / Cellulose for cell walls / Amino acids and proteins / Lipids for energy storage

cards.front: Name the three main factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis eventually level off as light intensity keeps increasing?
cards.answer: Because carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor, so extra light no longer increases the rate.

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis decrease at temperatures below the enzyme's optimum?
cards.answer: Molecules have less kinetic energy, so they collide less frequently with enzyme active sites, slowing the reaction.

cards.front: Name the five dry cooking methods the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Roasting / Baking / Grilling / Frying / Dry-frying

cards.front: Name the five moist cooking methods the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Boiling / Steaming / Poaching / Braising / Stewing

cards.front: Why does over-working a pastry dough make it tough and chewy instead of short and crumbly?
cards.answer: Over-working activates the gluten network too strongly, producing a tough, chewy result instead of a short, crumbly texture.

cards.front: Why does a meringue foam collapse if fat gets into the egg whites?
cards.answer: Fat destroys the protein film that wraps around and stabilises the tiny air bubbles, causing the foam to collapse.

title: Modern policing, the death penalty and the Bentley case
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three types of exemption a WWI tribunal could grant to a Conscientious Objector.
cards.answer: Absolute exemption (rare) / Conditional exemption (alternative civilian work) / Non-combatant service (RAMC or Non-Combatant Corps)

cards.front: Name the five non-custodial sentencing options that existed in Britain by 2000, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Probation / Community service / Suspended sentences / Fines / Electronic tagging

cards.front: How did the alleged words 'Let him have it, Chris' make Bentley legally guilty of murder?
cards.answer: The Crown argued they were an instruction to shoot, making Bentley guilty of murder under joint enterprise even though Craig fired the shot.

cards.front: Why did the Bentley case not lead straight to the abolition of the death penalty in 1953?
cards.answer: It took twelve more years, further controversial executions like Ruth Ellis, and four attempts by Silverman before Parliament abolished capital punishment in 1965.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says you should annotate in an unseen poem.
cards.answer: Language / Structure / Form

cards.front: Name the three common mistakes the lesson warns against in unseen poetry answers.
cards.answer: Retelling the poem / Feature-spotting / Ignoring form and structure

cards.front: How does the 'How' stage of the What-How-Why method work?
cards.answer: You quote the poet's specific words and analyse them closely, looking at word choices, sounds, rhythms and patterns.

cards.front: Why should you summarise a poem's message in one sentence before writing your response?
cards.answer: It keeps your response focused, so every paragraph you write connects back to that central interpretation.

cards.front: Name the four types of research businesses combine with location factors when actually deciding where to locate.
cards.answer: Customer demographics / Planning permission / Transport access / Rival activity

cards.front: Name the four business types and the location factor each weighs most heavily, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Service businesses – proximity to market / Materials-heavy manufacturers – availability of materials / Warehouses/fulfilment centres – costs and motorway access / Knowledge-based businesses – availability of labour
items: Warehouses/fulfilment centres – costs and motorway access

cards.front: Why is the location decision described as an operations decision first and foremost?
cards.answer: Because it affects how the business produces, supplies and serves customers every single day.

cards.front: How does being close to suppliers improve a factory's operations?
cards.answer: It creates shorter supply chains, giving faster restocking and more reliable delivery to the business's own customers.

cards.front: Name the five main material categories covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Papers and boards / Timbers / Metals / Polymers / Textiles

cards.front: Name the three alloys named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Brass / Stainless steel / High speed steel (HSS)

cards.front: Why is plywood strong in all directions?
cards.answer: Because it is made from layers of veneer glued together at right angles to each other.

cards.front: Why is copper used for electrical wiring and plumbing?
cards.answer: Because copper is an excellent electrical conductor.

title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the six features of the alveoli that make gas exchange efficient.
cards.answer: Large total surface area / moist walls only one cell thick / short diffusion distance / large capillary network / large blood supply / maintained concentration gradient (high O2, low CO2)
items: Moist walls only one cell thick
Maintained concentration gradient (high O2, low CO2)

cards.front: Name the four lung volumes shown on a spirometer trace at rest.
cards.answer: Inspiratory reserve volume / tidal volume / expiratory reserve volume / residual volume

cards.front: How do the intercostal muscles help cause inhalation at rest?
cards.answer: They contract to raise the rib cage upward and outward, increasing chest cavity volume and lowering lung air pressure so air rushes in.

cards.front: Why can't you increase oxygen delivery to muscles just by trying harder to breathe?
cards.answer: Diffusion rate depends on surface area and concentration gradients, which effort alone cannot increase, though exercise raises breathing rate and opens more capillaries.

cards.front: Name the four social engineering techniques described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phishing / Pretexting / Baiting / Vishing

cards.front: Name the three types of hacker in the colour-coded classification.
cards.answer: White hat / Black hat / Grey hat

cards.front: Why does stealing intellectual property damage a business's competitive advantage?
cards.answer: Competitors can replicate the stolen designs or research without the original investment, destroying the creator's market edge.

cards.front: Why can a business struggle to recover even after a data breach is technically fixed?
cards.answer: Customers lose confidence and partners withdraw, causing lasting reputational damage beyond the initial technical problem.

cards.front: Name the four human activities the lesson identifies as reducing biodiversity.
cards.answer: Deforestation / Pollution / Global warming / Overexploitation

cards.front: Name the five strategies the lesson gives for maintaining biodiversity.
cards.answer: Breeding programmes for endangered species / Protection of rare habitats / Reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins / Seed banks / Reducing deforestation and carbon emissions
items: Reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins

cards.front: How does deforestation reduce biodiversity?
cards.answer: Clearing forests for agriculture and building destroys habitats, reducing the space and resources available for species.

cards.front: How do decomposers release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere?
cards.answer: They break down dead organic material from dead organisms and release CO2 through respiration.

cards.front: Name the three predictions Birling makes that turn out to be wrong (his dramatic irony).
cards.answer: The Titanic is 'unsinkable' / There will be no war / Prosperity will keep 'steadily increasing'

cards.front: Name the three things Sheila does by the end of the play that show her transformation.
cards.answer: Returns the engagement ring / Defies her parents / Adopts the Inspector's moral perspective

cards.front: Why is Mrs Birling arguably more culpable than any other character in the play?
cards.answer: She represents institutional failure, corrupting the charity that was Eva's last safety net with class prejudice, causing her death.

cards.front: Why does Priestley make Eric more sympathetic than his parents despite his terrible crimes?
cards.answer: Because Eric accepts what he has done, unlike his parents who try to escape blame and refuse responsibility.

cards.front: Name the six types of financial information the lesson lists for measuring performance.
cards.answer: Revenue / Costs / Profit and loss / Gross and net margins / Average rate of return / Cash flow figures

cards.front: What are the four steps the lesson gives for structuring a synoptic answer?
cards.answer: Identify at least two functions involved / Link them together / Use the numbers given / Make a supported judgement
items: Identify at least two functions involved

cards.front: Why would the vegan sausage roll launch have stalled if finance underestimated demand?
cards.answer: Finance would have run out of cash to pay for ingredients, causing the launch to stall halfway through January.

cards.front: Why is financial information described as a feedback loop between the four functions?
cards.answer: Only financial data can confirm whether marketing, operations or pricing claims actually worked, showing what to adjust next.

cards.front: Name the three assumptions Sandra holds when she first arrives at Mrs Rutter's cottage.
cards.answer: Old ladies are kind / Boys like Kerry are undesirable / The world is readable by its surface appearances
items: The world is readable by its surface appearances

cards.front: Why does Kerry not undergo the same moral revelation that Sandra does?
cards.answer: He simply knows immediately that leaving the airman to die was wrong, unlike Sandra, whose moral understanding develops more slowly.

cards.front: How does Mrs Rutter's character subvert traditional expectations of elderly women?
cards.answer: She appears to be a gentle, nurturing grandmother figure but is shown to be capable of cruelty and feels no remorse about it.

cards.front: Name Piaget's four stages of cognitive development, in order.
cards.answer: Sensorimotor / Pre-operational / Concrete operational / Formal operational

cards.front: Why does a pre-operational child say there is more water after it's poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin one?
cards.answer: They lack conservation, so they judge quantity by appearance (height) rather than understanding the amount stayed the same.

cards.front: Why do concrete operational children struggle with a logic puzzle that has no physical objects?
cards.answer: Their logical thinking only works when applied to real, tangible objects, not to purely abstract or hypothetical reasoning.

cards.front: Name the four key themes the lesson identifies in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Class and Inequality / Nature vs Nurture / Superstition and Fate vs Free Will / Violence
items: Superstition and Fate vs Free Will

cards.front: What four-part pattern should each body paragraph of a modern text essay follow?
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Analysis / Context

cards.front: Why does Russell use superstition as a theme in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: It acts as a metaphor for the false explanations society uses to justify inequality, while class remains the real cause.

cards.front: Why does Mickey become violent in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: Not because he is a bad person but because the class system has left him with nothing, driven by poverty and desperation.

cards.front: Name the four contact forces listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Friction / Air resistance / Tension / Normal contact force

cards.front: Name the three non-contact forces listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gravitational force / Electrostatic force / Magnetic force

cards.front: Why does a book resting on a table stay still?
cards.answer: Its weight acting downwards and the normal contact force acting upwards are equal, giving a zero resultant force.

cards.front: How do you find the resultant of two forces that don't act along the same line using a scale drawing?
cards.answer: Draw the forces as arrows tip-to-tail to scale; the resultant runs from the start of the first to the end of the second; measure its length and angle.

cards.front: Name the three things Hitler did to secure the two-thirds majority needed to pass the Enabling Act.
cards.answer: Arrested Communist deputies / Intimidated Social Democrat deputies / Secured Catholic Centre Party support

cards.front: Name the three institutions whose collaboration helped the Nazis consolidate power in 1933.
cards.answer: The army / Civil servants / The Catholic Church

cards.front: How did the army's oath of loyalty on 2 August 1934 make it harder for officers to resist Hitler later?
cards.answer: It bound soldiers personally to Hitler himself rather than to Germany or the constitution, making resistance psychologically and legally harder.

cards.front: Why did the Catholic Church sign the Concordat with Hitler in July 1933?
cards.answer: To gain legal protection for the Church in exchange for accepting Nazi political supremacy and withdrawing from politics.

title: Engineering Maths II — Areas, Volumes, Estimation & Scale
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four length unit conversions given in the lesson.
cards.answer: 1 m = 1000 mm / 1 km = 1000 m / 1 foot = 12 inches / 1 inch ≈ 25.4 mm

cards.front: What are the four common engineering drawing scales given in the lesson?
cards.answer: 1:1 full size / 1:2 half size / 1:10 one tenth of real size / 2:1 twice real size

cards.front: Why can the cylinder volume formula be applied to any prism shape?
cards.answer: Because it is the area of the constant cross-section multiplied by the length, which works for any prism.

cards.front: How can an engineer quickly estimate the cost of materials before ordering?
cards.answer: Round all values to one or two significant figures, calculate mentally, then refine with a calculator if needed.

cards.front: Name the seven variables Townsend's deprivation index scored households on.
cards.answer: Diet / Fuel / Clothing / Housing / Health / Education / Social activities

cards.front: Name the three industries the lesson says were relocated to South and East Asia due to globalisation.
cards.answer: Car production / Steel production / Textile production

cards.front: Why do lone parents face a high risk of poverty?
cards.answer: They combine childcare responsibility with a single, often part-time or lower-paid, income, worsened by the gender pay gap and childcare costs.

cards.front: How does the cycle of deprivation reinforce poverty across generations?
cards.answer: Poor childhood health limits educational attainment, which restricts employment prospects, which creates low income and material deprivation for the next generation.

cards.front: Name the five fundamental tasks the lesson says the operating system handles.
cards.answer: Manages the CPU / Allocates RAM to running programs / Controls input and output devices / Manages the file system / Provides the user interface

cards.front: Name the five examples of utility software given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Anti-malware software / Disk defragmenters / File compression tools / Backup software / Disk cleanup tools

cards.front: How does firmware prepare a computer when it first starts up?
cards.answer: Firmware such as BIOS/UEFI runs a Power-On Self Test before handing control over to the operating system.

cards.front: Why is specialist software usually more expensive than general applications software?
cards.answer: It is developed for a narrower market with specific requirements and usually requires specialist training to use.

cards.front: Name the four common timber defects described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Knots / Shrinkage and warping / Shakes / Fungal attack

cards.front: Name the four types of manufactured board named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Plywood / MDF / Chipboard / Hardboard

cards.front: Why is balsa classed as a hardwood even though it feels soft?
cards.answer: Because hardwood/softwood is a botanical classification based on the tree (balsa comes from a deciduous tree), not physical hardness.

cards.front: Why do manufactured boards overcome most of the defects found in solid timber?
cards.answer: Their manufacturing process removes directional grain dependence, large knots and growth-related stresses that cause defects.

cards.front: Name the three experimental designs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Independent groups / Repeated measures / Matched pairs

cards.front: Name the three types of experiment based on setting described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Laboratory experiment / Field experiment / Natural experiment

cards.front: Why can experiments establish cause and effect, unlike other methods?
cards.answer: Because they directly manipulate one variable while keeping everything else constant, then measure its effect on another variable.

cards.front: Why is a natural experiment lower in control than laboratory or field experiments?
cards.answer: Because the researcher does not choose the IV, so participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions.

title: Worsening Relations: Taxation, Plot of 1212 and Bouvines 1214
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three things broke the relationship between John and the barons between 1212 and 1215?
cards.answer: Relentless financial pressure / A baronial plot John never forgave / The catastrophe of Bouvines in July 1214
items: A baronial plot John never forgave
The catastrophe of Bouvines in July 1214

cards.front: Beyond scutage, name the four ways the lesson says John exploited feudal incidents.
cards.answer: Charging punitive reliefs on inheritance / Selling heiresses to the highest bidder / Forcing widows to pay fines to avoid remarriage / Auctioning wardships of orphaned heirs
items: Selling heiresses to the highest bidder
Forcing widows to pay fines to avoid remarriage

cards.front: According to modern historians like W. L. Warren, why did the barons actually rebel against John?
cards.answer: Not because he was a bad administrator but because he was a good one whose methods were arbitrary and squeezed them harder than any king before.

cards.front: Why did John's southern advance towards Bouvines fail before the main battle even happened?
cards.answer: His advance stalled at the siege of La Roche-aux-Moines because his Poitevin allies refused to fight a pitched battle.

cards.front: Name the five 'Giant Evils' Beveridge identified in his 1942 report.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Name the six industries nationalised by Attlee's government (1945-51).
cards.answer: Coal / Railways / Electricity / Gas / Steel / Bank of England

cards.front: Why was Britain's entry into the EEC in 1973 controversial for parliamentary sovereignty?
cards.answer: EEC membership meant Community law was superior to Acts of Parliament in areas like trade, agriculture and competition.

cards.front: Why did the Conservatives keep the NHS and most nationalised industries after returning to power in 1951?
cards.answer: Keeping them suggested the welfare settlement had wide public support across the political spectrum.

cards.front: What three drawbacks of celluloid film stock does the lesson give as limitations directors faced?
cards.answer: Expensive to buy / Expensive to process / Limited in quantity (finite takes)

cards.front: What three visual qualities does the lesson give as the recognisable look of DV footage?
cards.answer: Specific colour response / Softness / Visible grain in low light

cards.front: Why did digital cinematography change the economics and culture of film production?
cards.answer: Digital sensors recorded to memory cards or hard drives, footage could be reviewed instantly, and takes were essentially free.

cards.front: Why did Tangerine (2015) have its distinctive intimate, close-up visual look?
cards.answer: The iPhone's wide-angle lens made faces fill the frame, backgrounds fall into soft-focus, and the camera move through streets with immediacy.

title: Social Challenges in Africa & South Asia
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main social challenges the lesson identifies for sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
cards.answer: Getting girls through school / Ending child labour / Supporting refugees / Reducing infant mortality

cards.front: What six stubborn reasons does the lesson give for girls dropping out of school?
cards.answer: School fees / Cost of uniforms and books / Long unsafe walks to class / Lack of girls' toilets / Early marriage / Assumption boys' education is more valuable
items: Assumption boys' education is more valuable

cards.front: Why does educating girls tend to lower infant mortality in the next generation?
cards.answer: Better-educated mothers are more likely to vaccinate children, less likely to die in childbirth, and less likely to lose a baby in its first year.

cards.front: Why is child labour so hard to tackle even though it harms children?
cards.answer: It is woven into household survival, as families depend on children's income and a missed school year often means missing school forever.

cards.front: What are the three offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
cards.answer: Unauthorised access to computer material / Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences / Unauthorised modification of computer material
items: Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences

cards.front: What three rights does GDPR give individuals over their personal data?
cards.answer: Right to access data held about them / Right to correct inaccurate data / Right to request deletion (right to be forgotten)
items: Right to access data held about them
Right to request deletion (right to be forgotten)
