cards.front: Why is the monitoring of individuals an ethical issue rather than just a legal one?
cards.answer: Something can be legal yet still ethically questionable, so an employer legally reading staff emails without telling them can still breach trust.

cards.front: Why do companies need strong security as well as privacy protections when collecting personal data?
cards.answer: Collecting large amounts of data creates a responsibility to protect it, and poor security can cause breaches exposing people to identity theft, fraud and harassment.

cards.front: Name the three German adverbs used to show how much you like an activity, from least to most.
cards.answer: gern (like doing) / lieber (prefer doing) / am liebsten (like doing most of all)
items: am liebsten (like doing most of all)

cards.front: What are the six present tense verb endings used for regular German verbs like spielen?
cards.answer: -e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en

cards.front: How do you form the present tense of a regular German verb such as spielen?
cards.answer: Remove -en from the infinitive to get the stem (spiel-), then add the correct ending for the subject.

cards.front: How does using weil or obwohl to give a reason change the word order of a German sentence?
cards.answer: The verb moves to the end of the clause, which is called subordinate word order.

cards.front: Name the four types of sentence available to Youth Courts for offenders aged 10-17.
cards.answer: Youth cautions / Referral orders / Youth rehabilitation orders / Detention and training orders

cards.front: Name the four main types of sentence available to courts.
cards.answer: Custodial sentence / Community order / Fines / Conditional discharge

cards.front: Why can higher levels of policing in an area make crime appear more concentrated there than it really is?
cards.answer: More policing leads to more recorded offences in that area, which can make crime seem concentrated when the reality may be more complex.

cards.front: Why do official crime statistics undercount offences like domestic violence and sexual offences?
cards.answer: Underreporting means these offences are often not reported to police, so they are missed from recorded crime figures.

cards.front: Name the three main types of waste/excess substances the kidneys filter from the blood to form urine.
cards.answer: Urea / Excess water / Excess mineral ions (such as sodium)

cards.front: According to the lesson, what are the four drawbacks of dialysis compared with a transplant?
cards.answer: Time-consuming / Requires repeated sessions / Restricts diet and quality of life / Does not cure kidney failure
items: Restricts diet and quality of life

cards.front: How are nephron tubule cells adapted to maximise selective reabsorption?
cards.answer: They have microvilli to increase surface area and many mitochondria to provide energy for active transport.

cards.front: Why is dialysis fluid carefully formulated to contain the correct concentrations of glucose and mineral ions?
cards.answer: So that glucose and mineral ions are not lost from the blood by diffusion during dialysis.

cards.front: Name the six key themes that every Anita and Me exam question connects to.
cards.answer: Identity / Racism / Friendship / Family / Class / Growing Up

cards.front: What five-part pattern does a strong comparative paragraph follow?
cards.answer: Point about the studied text / Quotation + AO2 analysis / Comparison with unseen text / Quotation + AO2 analysis / Link to context (AO3)

cards.front: Why does Syal argue that the community's silence is as damaging as racism itself?
cards.answer: Because that silence enables racism to continue unchallenged at every level, from casual comments to violent attacks.

cards.front: Why is Tollington's class status significant for the novel's class theme?
cards.answer: The Kumars are middle-class in education and aspiration but live in working-class Tollington, showing class intersecting with race.

cards.front: Name the six tools an IDE typically includes.
cards.answer: Code editor / Syntax error detection / Debugger / Breakpoint / Variable watch / Memory inspector

cards.front: Name the five compilation stages in order.
cards.answer: Lexical analysis / Syntax analysis / Semantic analysis / Code generation / Code optimisation

cards.front: Why does an interpreted program run more slowly than a compiled program?
cards.answer: Because an interpreter translates each line every time the program runs, instead of translating once beforehand like a compiler.

cards.front: Why are logic errors the hardest type of error to find?
cards.answer: Because the program runs without crashing and appears to work, even though it produces the wrong result.

cards.front: What four main things does the biosphere provide for people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Food / Medicine / Building materials / Fuel

cards.front: Name the four types of UK terrestrial ecosystem given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Moorland / Heathland / Woodland / Wetland

cards.front: Why do mountainsides show the same sequence of biomes as travelling from the equator to the poles?
cards.answer: Every 100m of altitude is roughly equivalent to moving 100km polewards, so height recreates the global climate pattern in miniature.

cards.front: Why is the biosphere described as a regulator as well as a resource?
cards.answer: Plants remove CO2 and release oxygen and water vapour, so damaging ecosystems releases stored carbon and reduces the planet's ability to recycle gases.

title: Characters: Mercutio, Tybalt and the Nurse
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three ways Mercutio, Tybalt and the Nurse each directly cause the tragedy.
cards.answer: Mercutio's death provokes Romeo to kill Tybalt / Tybalt's aggression causes Romeo's banishment / The Nurse's betrayal pushes Juliet to the Friar's plan
items: Mercutio's death provokes Romeo to kill Tybalt
The Nurse's betrayal pushes Juliet to the Friar's plan

cards.front: Why does it matter that Mercutio is neither a Montague nor a Capulet when he dies?
cards.answer: His death can't be blamed on either family, showing that the feud itself, not one side, kills him.

cards.front: Why does the Nurse tell Juliet to marry Paris after Romeo's banishment?
cards.answer: She prioritises Juliet's physical safety and social security over romantic love, seeing it as practical advice.

cards.front: Name the three main parts of a sperm cell.
cards.answer: Head containing the nucleus / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Tail (flagellum) for propulsion
items: Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the four stages a fertilised egg goes through from zygote to implantation.
cards.answer: Cleavage (repeated division) / Morula (solid ball of cells) / Blastocyst (hollow ball with fluid cavity) / Implantation into the endometrium

cards.front: How is the sex of a baby determined at fertilisation?
cards.answer: The egg always contributes an X chromosome; a Y sperm makes a male (XY) embryo, an X sperm makes a female (XX) embryo.

cards.front: Why does menstruation happen if fertilisation does not occur?
cards.answer: Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall, causing the thickened uterine lining to break down and be shed.

title: Trophic Levels and Transfer of Biomass
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why biomass is lost between trophic levels.
cards.answer: Not all parts of organisms are eaten (e.g. roots, bones, feathers) / Material lost in excretory products (faeces, urine, carbon dioxide) / Biomass used in respiration, released as heat
items: Not all parts of organisms are eaten (e.g. roots, bones, feathers)
Material lost in excretory products (faeces, urine, carbon dioxide)
Biomass used in respiration, released as heat

cards.front: Name the three intensive farming methods the lesson gives for increasing energy transfer efficiency to animals.
cards.answer: Restricting movement / Controlling temperature / Using high-energy feeds

cards.front: How does controlling temperature in factory farming increase energy efficiency?
cards.answer: Heated or insulated buildings mean animals lose less energy keeping warm, so more energy goes into growth.

cards.front: Why does a human get less energy from eating grain-fed meat than from eating the grain directly?
cards.answer: Eating the animal adds an extra trophic level, so about 90% of the grain's energy is lost before it reaches the human.

title: Crime, Punishment and the Aims of Justice
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main aims of punishment given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Justice / Retribution / Deterrence / Reformation

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why most Humanists oppose capital punishment.
cards.answer: Execution is irreversible / Miscarriages of justice cannot be corrected / Evidence for deterrence is weak
items: Miscarriages of justice cannot be corrected

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching call the death penalty 'inadmissible' even though it accepts the state's right to defend society?
cards.answer: Because the death penalty attacks human dignity, according to the Catechism of the Catholic Church.

cards.front: Why does ahimsa make capital punishment a problem for many Hindus?
cards.answer: Because taking a life, even a criminal's, creates negative karma, so many Hindus see it as wrong.

cards.front: Name the five common social indicators of development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Life expectancy / Infant mortality / Literacy rate / Mean years of schooling / Access to clean water

cards.front: Name the four extra indicators the lesson gives for measuring inequality and poverty beyond GDP and HDI.
cards.answer: Gini coefficient / Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) / Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) / Gender Inequality Index

cards.front: Why do countries with persistently low Corruption Perceptions Index scores develop more slowly?
cards.answer: Economic gains get captured by elites and public services collapse, which slows broader development.

cards.front: Why do geographers usually combine several development indicators rather than rely on just one?
cards.answer: A single indicator gives only a partial picture, so combining measures reveals what each one misses.

cards.front: Name the four purposes the lesson gives for why Orwell wrote Animal Farm.
cards.answer: To warn against totalitarianism / To show how propaganda enables dictatorship / To criticise the complacency of the masses / To satirise the Soviet Union specifically
items: To show how propaganda enables dictatorship
To criticise the complacency of the masses
To satirise the Soviet Union specifically

cards.front: How does Squealer's use of language help the pigs stay in power?
cards.answer: He manipulates language, rewriting the commandments and distorting the truth, showing that controlling language means controlling thought.

cards.front: Why does Orwell criticise the ordinary animals' behaviour in Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Their failure to question authority lets the pigs seize power unchecked, suggesting ordinary people must stay vigilant.

title: Vikings, Anglo-Saxons and the Danelaw, c800–c1066
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three pull factors the lesson gives for Vikings settling in Britain.
cards.answer: Fertile land / Weak political resistance after Anglo-Saxon infighting / Coastline studded with rich monasteries
items: Weak political resistance after Anglo-Saxon infighting

cards.front: Name the three areas of lasting Viking impact on England the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Language / Law / Economy

cards.front: Why did Old English and Old Norse mingle rather than clash?
cards.answer: Because Anglo-Saxons and Vikings both spoke languages from the same Germanic family.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat Anglo-Saxons as the original 'native' population set against foreign Vikings?
cards.answer: Anglo-Saxons were themselves migrants who arrived from Germany and Denmark in the fifth and sixth centuries, only becoming 'British' later.

title: Cinematography: Shot, Angle, Movement and Lighting
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five core shot distances the lesson identifies, from closest to furthest.
cards.answer: extreme close-up / close-up / medium shot / long shot / extreme long shot

cards.front: Name the four camera angles the lesson describes.
cards.answer: high angle / low angle / Dutch tilt / aerial shot

cards.front: Why is the medium shot the most common distance for dialogue scenes?
cards.answer: It shows characters from the waist up, which feels like a natural conversational distance.

cards.front: How does handheld camerawork affect the spectator during action scenes?
cards.answer: It introduces tremor and unpredictability, placing the spectator in nervous proximity to the action.

title: The Citizen and the State: A Thematic Toolkit, c1170-Present
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven factors AQA tests across this unit.
cards.answer: War / Religion / Chance / Government / Communication / The economy / Ideas

cards.front: Name the four question types always asked, in order, on Paper 2 Section A.
cards.answer: 8-mark how useful is the source / 8-mark explain the significance / 8-mark explain two ways similar or different / 16-mark factors essay
items: 8-mark explain two ways similar or different

cards.front: How did the Black Death (1348–49) make the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 possible?
cards.answer: It reshaped the labour market, creating the conditions that allowed the revolt to happen.

cards.front: How did the First World War affect women's suffrage?
cards.answer: The war accelerated the granting of women's suffrage in 1918.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three rights does an advocate help uphold for a service user?
cards.answer: Right to choice / Right to consultation / Right to dignity

cards.front: Name the four types of service user the lesson gives as needing special methods of communication.
cards.answer: A person who is profoundly deaf / A person with a learning disability / A patient with little English / A resident who is blind
items: A person who is profoundly deaf
A person with a learning disability

cards.front: Why should a practitioner arrange a qualified BSL interpreter instead of using gestures or written notes for a Deaf patient?
cards.answer: BSL is a full language with its own grammar, so without an interpreter the patient may consent to a procedure they haven't fully understood, risking their health and rights.

cards.front: Why does Hassan need a professional interpreter at every clinical appointment?
cards.answer: Without one he cannot describe his symptoms accurately, consent meaningfully to treatment, or understand his care plan.

cards.front: Name the three types of legitimate authority identified by Weber.
cards.answer: Traditional authority / Charismatic authority / Rational-legal authority

cards.front: Name the four examples of informal power given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Economic power (employer dismissing/rewarding workers) / Social influence through cultural or media prestige / Patriarchal power within families / Social closure by status groups
items: Social influence through cultural or media prestige

cards.front: Why is a popularly elected Prime Minister's authority rational-legal rather than charismatic?
cards.answer: Because their power rests on formal electoral rules and constitutional office, not on personal devotion from followers.

cards.front: How can a monarch hold charismatic authority alongside traditional authority?
cards.answer: If followers are personally devoted to the monarch as an individual, this creates charismatic authority existing alongside their inherited traditional authority.

cards.front: Name the five items that made up a hoplite's panoply, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hoplon (large round shield) / Doru (spear) / Helmet (usually Corinthian type) / Breastplate (thorax or linothorax) / Bronze greaves

cards.front: Why did poorer Athenian citizens gain political influence when Athens built its fleet to fight Persia at Salamis?
cards.answer: They rowed the triremes in the large fleet, which gave them a claim to political influence they had never previously held.

cards.front: Why did Greek helmet designs become more open later in the fifth century BC?
cards.answer: City-states began valuing better hearing and awareness in larger, more complex battles over the full protection of enclosed helmets.

cards.front: Name the five personality traits Priestley establishes for the Birlings and Gerald at the start of Act 1.
cards.answer: Arthur: pompous and self-important / Sybil: cold and class-conscious / Sheila: light-hearted but shows flashes of intelligence / Eric: nervous and drinks too much / Gerald: polished and well-connected
items: Sheila: light-hearted but shows flashes of intelligence
Eric: nervous and drinks too much

cards.front: What three things does Birling dismiss or boast about in his speech just before the Inspector arrives?
cards.answer: Dismisses community as 'nonsense' / Mocks the possibility of war / Boasts the Titanic is 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable'
items: Boasts the Titanic is 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable'

cards.front: Why does Birling's use of the word 'awkward' reveal his selfishness?
cards.answer: It reduces the profound moral question of caring for others to a matter of minor inconvenience, showing he can't think beyond his own comfort.

cards.front: Why did Birling sack Eva Smith from his factory?
cards.answer: She was one of several workers who asked for a pay rise, so he sacked the ringleaders, including her, to stop further demands.

cards.front: Name the four features shared by Shakespeare's late romances.
cards.answer: Fathers separated from children / Sea voyages / Apparent loss followed by miraculous reunion / Endings that favour forgiveness over revenge
items: Apparent loss followed by miraculous reunion
Endings that favour forgiveness over revenge

cards.front: Name the three plots to seize power by force in The Tempest.
cards.answer: Antonio overthrowing Prospero / Antonio and Sebastian plotting to murder Alonso / Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plotting to murder Prospero
items: Antonio and Sebastian plotting to murder Alonso
Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plotting to murder Prospero

cards.front: How does Shakespeare undercut Gonzalo's idealistic commonwealth speech in Act 2?
cards.answer: Antonio and Sebastian mock him throughout, and the play shows that power struggles and treachery persist even on the island.

cards.front: Why does Prospero abruptly end the wedding masque in Act 4?
cards.answer: Because he suddenly remembers Caliban's conspiracy to murder him.

cards.front: Name the four key locations where the British sector saw major engagements on the Western Front.
cards.answer: The Ypres salient / The Somme / Arras / Cambrai

cards.front: Name the five stages of the chain of evacuation, in order from the battlefield.
cards.answer: Stretcher bearers / Regimental Aid Post / Dressing stations / Casualty Clearing Stations / Base hospitals

cards.front: Why was wound infection such a constant danger in Flanders and the Somme?
cards.answer: The farmland soil was heavily manured, so shrapnel drove bacteria deep into wounds.

cards.front: How did soldiers catch trench fever?
cards.answer: It was spread by body lice that infested soldiers' clothing and bedding.

cards.front: Name the four natural resources the lesson says gave the United States a head start before the First World War.
cards.answer: Coal / Iron / Oil / Timber

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says did not share in the 1920s economic boom.
cards.answer: Farmers / Black Americans / Recent immigrants / Unskilled industrial workers

cards.front: How did the self-reinforcing 'virtuous circle' drive the 1920s consumer boom?
cards.answer: Higher factory productivity lowered prices, letting more people buy goods, which raised output and gave more workers wages to spend.

cards.front: Why did the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 end up damaging the American economy in the longer term?
cards.answer: It protected American industry short-term but raised duties so high it damaged international trade, contributing to later economic fragility.

cards.front: Name the three topics Leah talks about in her monologues to Phil.
cards.answer: Bonobos (peaceful apes) / The nature of happiness / What it means to be alive
items: What it means to be alive

cards.front: Name the three behaviours the group shows while panicking in the wood.
cards.answer: Argue / Blame each other / Talk over one another

cards.front: Why did Phil's cover-up plan go wrong in Act 2?
cards.answer: Cathy took DNA from a real postman instead of a stranger, so police matched an innocent man fitting Brian's description and arrested him.

cards.front: How does Phil's silence during Leah's monologues affect her role as the play's conscience?
cards.answer: His refusal to respond reduces Leah to a voice heard by the audience but ignored by the one person she wants to reach.

cards.front: Name the three rules the lesson gives for forming a Relativsatz (relative clause).
cards.answer: Relative pronoun must match the noun's gender (der/die/das) / Always place a comma before the relative pronoun / The verb goes to the end of the clause
items: Relative pronoun must match the noun's gender (der/die/das)
Always place a comma before the relative pronoun
The verb goes to the end of the clause

cards.front: Name the three common adjectives the lesson gives that add an Umlaut in the comparative.
cards.answer: alt → älter / jung → jünger / groß → größer

cards.front: Why should you use a wide variety of personality adjectives instead of repeating 'nett' in your writing or speaking?
cards.answer: Using varied vocabulary rather than repeating one word shows range, which earns credit for vocabulary variety.

cards.front: How do you form a comparative adjective in German to compare two people's personalities?
cards.answer: Add -er to the adjective and follow it with als (than), e.g. lustiger als.

title: Medicines, Monoclonal Antibodies and Lifestyle Disease
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three phases of clinical trials described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers to test safety / Phase II: patients test effectiveness and side effects / Phase III: large-scale randomised controlled trial
items: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers to test safety
Phase II: patients test effectiveness and side effects
Phase III: large-scale randomised controlled trial

cards.front: Name the three uses of monoclonal antibodies given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pregnancy testing / Cancer diagnosis / Cancer therapy

cards.front: Why can preclinical testing not fully predict how a drug will affect humans?
cards.answer: Because it only tests cells, tissues and animals, not humans, so it filters dangerous compounds but can't guarantee human safety.

cards.front: Why do stents give only temporary relief for cardiovascular disease?
cards.answer: They mechanically prop open the narrowed artery but don't stop fatty plaque building up in other vessels, so disease can still progress.

title: Discipleship: The Call, the Cost and Living It Today
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four types of soil/ground in the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1-20).
cards.answer: The path – no response / Rocky ground – initial enthusiasm withers / Thorny ground – choked by wealth and worries / Good soil – bears fruit
items: Thorny ground – choked by wealth and worries

cards.front: Name the three modern Christians studied as examples of costly discipleship.
cards.answer: Dietrich Bonhoeffer / Oscar Romero / Mother Teresa

cards.front: Why were the disciples unable to drive out the spirit from the boy in Mark 9:14-29?
cards.answer: Because they relied on their own authority instead of prayer; Jesus says 'this kind can come out only by prayer.'

cards.front: Why is Peter's denial of Jesus in Mark 14:66-72 significant for understanding discipleship?
cards.answer: Because Peter, despite confidently declaring Jesus the Messiah, denied him under pressure, showing discipleship depends on grace, not strength.

cards.front: Name the three features used to compare RAM and ROM.
cards.answer: Whether it is volatile / Whether it can be written to / What it stores
items: Whether it can be written to

cards.front: How does a computer use ROM and RAM to start up?
cards.answer: The CPU runs the bootstrap instructions stored in ROM, which test the hardware and copy the operating system from secondary storage into RAM.

cards.front: Why is RAM usually much larger than ROM?
cards.answer: RAM must hold everything currently in use, while ROM only needs enough room for a small boot-up program.

cards.front: Name the four environmental problems the lesson links to rapid urbanisation.
cards.answer: Increased traffic / Air pollution / Water shortages / Waste-disposal problems

cards.front: Name the four contemporary challenges the lesson says Lagos faces.
cards.answer: Housing shortages and spreading informal settlements / Traffic congestion / Waste collection problems / Flooding
items: Housing shortages and spreading informal settlements

cards.front: Why have some megacities, like Tokyo, stopped growing or started shrinking?
cards.answer: Because birth rates in these cities have fallen.

cards.front: Why is urbanisation happening fastest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia?
cards.answer: Because populations there are young and rural-to-urban migration is high.

title: Pilgrimage, Catholic Social Teaching and Mission
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four pilgrimage sites specified in this unit.
cards.answer: Jerusalem / Lourdes / Rome / Walsingham

cards.front: What three purposes does the Catholic funeral rite serve?
cards.answer: Communion with the deceased through prayer / Supporting the bereaved community / Proclaiming eternal life and the resurrection
items: Communion with the deceased through prayer
Proclaiming eternal life and the resurrection

cards.front: Why are many Protestants sceptical about the practice of pilgrimage?
cards.answer: The Reformation rejected the idea that visiting a physical place earns spiritual merit, teaching instead that God can be encountered anywhere.

cards.front: How does Pope Francis link mission (proclamation) and social action in Evangelii Gaudium?
cards.answer: He insists authentic faith always involves a deep desire to change the world, so proclaiming the Gospel and serving the poor cannot be separated.

cards.front: Name the five areas of public debate about crime covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Concerns over violent crime / Sentencing / Treatment of young offenders / The prison system / Media coverage of crime

cards.front: Name the four goals of sentencing debated by sociologists.
cards.answer: Retribution / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: Why do Marxists argue that focusing public debate on violent street crime is misleading?
cards.answer: It diverts attention from corporate and state harms like unsafe workplaces, pollution and financial misconduct, which may cause more damage overall.

cards.front: How does the functionalist perspective explain public concern about violent crime?
cards.answer: It serves an integrative function, where collective outrage, law enforcement and sentencing reinforce shared values and social solidarity.

cards.front: Name the five categories of characters covered by standard ASCII's 128 codes.
cards.answer: Upper-case letters A-Z / Lower-case letters a-z / Digits 0-9 / Punctuation and special symbols / Control characters

cards.front: Name the three common Unicode encodings the lesson describes.
cards.answer: UTF-8 / UTF-16 / UTF-32

cards.front: Why did extended ASCII cause compatibility problems between different computer systems?
cards.answer: Different manufacturers implemented the extra codes 128-255 differently, so the same code could mean a different character on different systems.

cards.front: Why does mojibake (garbled text) appear when a file is opened?
cards.answer: It happens when a file saved in one encoding is opened assuming a different encoding, so bytes are misread as the wrong characters.

title: Mountain Men, the Donner Party and the Mormon Trek
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four US states where the Mormons faced persecution before settling in Salt Lake Valley.
cards.answer: New York / Ohio / Missouri / Illinois

cards.front: Name the three differences the lesson gives for why the Mormons succeeded where the Donner Party failed.
cards.answer: Leadership / Planning / Geography

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Donner disaster was not just about freak weather?
cards.answer: The storm was the final blow, but the real danger came from earlier choices: trusting an untested guidebook, taking the cutoff, losing weeks in the Wasatch, and splitting the train in the desert.

cards.front: Why did neighbouring communities react violently to the early Mormons?
cards.answer: Their distinct beliefs and practice of polygamy outraged neighbours, while their political and economic power frightened them.

cards.front: Name the four steps used to extract DNA from strawberries.
cards.answer: Mash the fruit / Add salt water and washing-up liquid / Filter the mixture / Layer ice-cold ethanol on top
items: Add salt water and washing-up liquid

cards.front: Name the four potential applications of the Human Genome Project mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying genes linked to diseases / Developing personalised medicines / Understanding human evolution and migration / Creating genetic tests for inherited condition risk
items: Creating genetic tests for inherited condition risk

cards.front: How does fertilisation determine whether a baby is male or female?
cards.answer: Eggs always carry an X chromosome; if an X-carrying sperm fertilises it the offspring is female, if a Y-carrying sperm does it's male.

cards.front: Why are salt water and washing-up liquid added when extracting DNA from strawberries?
cards.answer: They break open the fruit's cells so that the DNA inside is released.

cards.front: Name the three things Japanese Buddhist memorial services are held on after a death.
cards.answer: The seventh day / The forty-ninth day / The death anniversary each year

cards.front: Name the three things loved ones do at a dying Buddhist's bedside to support their mental state.
cards.answer: Recite texts / Chant / Create a calm and focused environment
items: Create a calm and focused environment

cards.front: Why is cremation the traditional funeral practice in most Theravada Buddhist communities?
cards.answer: It follows the example of the Buddha, whose own body was cremated after his parinibbana.

cards.front: Why does Parinirvana Day remind Buddhists of impermanence?
cards.answer: Even the Buddha, who had attained Enlightenment, still died, showing all conditioned existence is transient.

title: Origins of the Universe, the Sanctity of Life and Abortion
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five things Genesis 1-2 describes God creating in stages.
cards.answer: Light / Land / Sea / Plants / Animals

cards.front: In the abortion debate, name the four viewpoints the lesson says show sanctity of life in action.
cards.answer: Pro-life Christians defend the unborn as made in God's image / Pro-choice Christians may apply situation ethics to hard cases / Non-religious critics focus on a woman's right to choose / Christians respond by reasserting all human life has God-given worth
items: Pro-life Christians defend the unborn as made in God's image
Pro-choice Christians may apply situation ethics to hard cases
Non-religious critics focus on a woman's right to choose
Christians respond by reasserting all human life has God-given worth

cards.front: Why do some Christians see a conflict between the Big Bang theory and Genesis?
cards.answer: They read Genesis literally as a six-day creation, which conflicts with the Big Bang's account of the universe's origin.

cards.front: Why do most Christians reject treating the universe purely as a commodity?
cards.answer: The universe is God's creation reflecting his goodness, so exploiting it dishonours his ownership and ignores humanity's responsibility to care for it.

cards.front: Name the five steps for structuring a strong modern-text essay response given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Engage with the quotation / Explore the theme across the play / Embed context throughout / Analyse dramatic techniques / Write precisely
items: Explore the theme across the play

cards.front: Name the three levels at which prejudice operates in Refugee Boy.
cards.answer: Personal / Institutional / Societal

cards.front: How does the play show that identity is constructed by others as much as by the individual?
cards.answer: Alem is the same person wherever he is, but is treated differently depending on who defines him — rejected by Ethiopia and Eritrea, seen as an outsider in England.

cards.front: Why does the asylum tribunal fail to represent true justice in the play?
cards.answer: It follows legal rules, but those rules cannot fully account for human suffering, making the process feel cold, impersonal and arbitrary.

cards.front: Name the four research methods the lesson says sociologists use to research education.
cards.answer: Observation (participant or non-participant) / Interviews (structured or unstructured) / Questionnaires / Secondary data (official statistics, league tables, Ofsted reports)
items: Secondary data (official statistics, league tables, Ofsted reports)

cards.front: Name the three key ethical issues in sociological research on education.
cards.answer: Informed consent / Confidentiality / Harm to participants

cards.front: Why can requiring parental written consent introduce class bias into a study's sample?
cards.answer: It may reduce the sample to pupils whose parents are engaged and able to respond, excluding others.

cards.front: Why might a headteacher acting as gatekeeper limit how representative research data is?
cards.answer: Headteachers may only allow observation of 'good' lessons, so the data does not represent everyday school life.

cards.front: The lesson gives four corporate/business terms the Headmaster uses to describe education. Name them.
cards.answer: results / shelf / display / selling points

cards.front: What three steps does Irwin's method involve for arguing against the obvious?
cards.answer: Find a proposition / invert it / look around for proofs

cards.front: Why did the Headmaster fail to act on Hector's inappropriate behaviour until it became a problem?
cards.answer: He knew about it but only acted once it became publicly embarrassing, caring about institutional reputation rather than child protection.

cards.front: Why does Bennett draw a parallel between Irwin's intellectual and sexual dishonesty?
cards.answer: Irwin performs heterosexuality by hiding his attraction to Dakin just as he performs historical argument without genuine conviction.

cards.front: Name the four main factors that shape where a business locates.
cards.answer: Proximity to the market / Proximity to labour / Proximity to materials / Proximity to competitors

cards.front: Name the four elements of the marketing mix (the four Ps).
cards.answer: Product / Price / Promotion / Place

cards.front: Why might a business choose to locate near its competitors, like car dealerships?
cards.answer: Clustering together can attract more customers to the area, although it also intensifies rivalry between the businesses.

cards.front: Why did some businesses lose sales when shoppers shifted to buying groceries online during lockdowns?
cards.answer: Because they could not adjust their 'place' strategy to sell online, so more agile rivals took their customers.

cards.front: Name the three isotope pairs used in radiometric dating.
cards.answer: Uranium-238 to lead-206 / Potassium-40 to argon-40 / Carbon-14 to nitrogen-14

cards.front: Why is radioactive decay considered a reliable geological clock?
cards.answer: Because it happens at a fixed, predictable rate regardless of temperature, pressure or chemical environment.

cards.front: Why can't carbon-14 be used to date material older than about 50,000 years?
cards.answer: After about 10 half-lives so little carbon-14 remains that measurements become unreliable.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the Apollo spacecraft.
cards.answer: Command Module / Service Module / Lunar Module

cards.front: Name the four challenges of crewed deep-space missions the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Radiation exposure beyond the magnetosphere / Bone, muscle and cardiovascular changes from microgravity / Psychological isolation over months or years / Life-support systems must be highly reliable with minimal resupply
items: Bone, muscle and cardiovascular changes from microgravity
Psychological isolation over months or years
Life-support systems must be highly reliable with minimal resupply

cards.front: Why are fly-by missions used for distant targets instead of orbiters?
cards.answer: Because the fuel cost of slowing down to enter orbit around a distant target would be too high.

cards.front: Why can a human geologist identify interesting rocks much faster than a robotic rover?
cards.answer: Astronauts can make real-time decisions on the spot, while rovers face communication delays of minutes to hours.

title: The Origins of the Weimar Republic 1918–19
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three things did the armistice of 11 November 1918 require Germany to do?
cards.answer: Withdraw troops from occupied territories / Surrender its navy and heavy weapons / Allow Allied forces to occupy the Rhineland
items: Surrender its navy and heavy weapons
Allow Allied forces to occupy the Rhineland

cards.front: What five strengths did the Weimar Constitution have?
cards.answer: Universal suffrage for men and women over 20 / A Bill of Rights protecting individual freedoms / President directly elected by the people / Reichstag could pass laws and government was accountable to it / Länder kept local powers
items: Universal suffrage for men and women over 20
A Bill of Rights protecting individual freedoms
President directly elected by the people
Reichstag could pass laws and government was accountable to it

cards.front: How did the mutiny at Kiel turn into a full-scale revolution across Germany?
cards.answer: Workers and soldiers formed councils like the Russian soviets and seized control of cities such as Hamburg, Bremen and Munich, demanding peace and change.

cards.front: Why had political change become inevitable in Germany by October 1918?
cards.answer: Germany faced military defeat, mass starvation from the British blockade, and collapsing morale among soldiers and civilians all at once.

cards.front: Name the four sources of background radiation the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Radon gas from granite rocks / Cosmic rays from space / Radioactive isotopes in food and water / Radiation from medical procedures
items: Radioactive isotopes in food and water

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that determine how severe a radiation health risk is.
cards.answer: Type of radiation (ionising ability) / Half-life of the isotope / Whether it's irradiation or contamination

cards.front: Why does a gamma source pose an external irradiation risk even from a distance?
cards.answer: Gamma rays have low ionising ability but high penetrating power, needing thick lead or concrete to block them, so they pass easily through air to the body.

cards.front: Why do control rods keep a nuclear fission chain reaction steady?
cards.answer: Control rods absorb neutrons so that on average only one neutron from each fission goes on to cause the next fission.

title: In Paris With You — James Fenton
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the three famous Paris landmarks the speaker says they will skip in the poem.
cards.answer: The Louvre / Notre Dame / The Champs Elysées

cards.front: Name the four other anthology poems the lesson compares with 'In Paris With You'.
cards.answer: Lochhead's 'I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine' / Browning's 'Now' / Jordan's 'Poem for My Love' / Antrobus's 'The Perseverance'
items: Lochhead's 'I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine'

cards.front: Why does the speaker dismiss the Louvre, Notre Dame and the Champs Elysées in one breath?
cards.answer: Naming and rejecting all three shows he has no interest in tourism; the person in front of him matters more than the city's monuments.

cards.front: How does the closing refrain let the speaker admit happiness without using the word 'love'?
cards.answer: By ending stanzas on 'I'm in Paris with you', presence and place replace the romantic vocabulary he claims to distrust.

cards.front: Why do most psychologists reject strict linguistic determinism?
cards.answer: People can think thoughts for which they have no word and then coin a new word, which would be impossible if language fully controlled thought.

cards.front: Why is it hard to test Vygotsky's claim about when thought and language merge?
cards.answer: Very young children cannot easily report on their own thinking, making the exact age and process difficult to test directly.

title: Diurnal Motion, Circumpolarity and Observing Conditions
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key moments in a star's path across the sky each day.
cards.answer: Rising / Upper transit (culmination) / Lower transit

cards.front: According to the lesson, where does a star rise depending on its declination (three cases)?
cards.answer: Dec = 0° rises due east / Positive declination rises north of east / Negative declination rises south of east
items: Positive declination rises north of east
Negative declination rises south of east

cards.front: Why is lower transit invisible for stars that rise and set, unlike circumpolar stars?
cards.answer: For stars that rise and set, lower transit occurs below the horizon, so it cannot be seen.

cards.front: Why is Arcturus (Dec +19°11′) not circumpolar as seen from Edinburgh (56°N)?
cards.answer: Its declination of 19° is less than the circumpolar limit at 56°N, which is 34°, so it rises and sets.

title: Challenges for Religion in a Secular Society
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: What three types of secularisation does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Institutional secularisation (laws, schools, hospitals no longer religiously controlled) / Individual secularisation (ethical decisions made without religious teaching) / Cultural secularisation (religious symbols/festivals become commercial)
items: Institutional secularisation (laws, schools, hospitals no longer religiously controlled)
Individual secularisation (ethical decisions made without religious teaching)

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say Humanists UK has campaigned for?
cards.answer: Removal of bishops from the House of Lords / An end to compulsory acts of worship in schools / Inclusive sex education
items: Removal of bishops from the House of Lords
An end to compulsory acts of worship in schools

cards.front: Why are religious organisations not required to conduct same-sex marriages in Britain?
cards.answer: When same-sex civil marriage was legalised in 2014, religious organisations were given an explicit exemption from having to conduct them.

cards.front: Why does therapeutic gene editing receive more religious support than 'designer baby' selection?
cards.answer: Therapeutic gene editing corrects inherited diseases, whereas selecting non-medical traits treats embryos as raw material and undermines their dignity.

cards.front: Name the four irregular adjectives given in the lesson, showing their feminine forms.
cards.answer: bon → bonne / beau → belle / nouveau → nouvelle / vieux → vieille

cards.front: What are the three past participle agreement endings for the perfect tense with être, based on the subject?
cards.answer: add -e for feminine subject / add -s for masculine plural subject / add -es for feminine plural subject

cards.front: Why do verbs like aller and sortir use être instead of avoir in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: Because they belong to a group of verbs of movement that use être as the auxiliary verb instead of avoir.

cards.front: How does the feminine form of an adjective ending in -eux change, such as ennuyeux?
cards.answer: Adjectives ending in -eux change to -euse in the feminine, so ennuyeux becomes ennuyeuse.

title: Russia in 1917: Empire at Breaking Point
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three crises collided in Russia by February 1917?
cards.answer: Military disaster on the Eastern Front / Peasant land hunger since the 1861 Emancipation / Strike wave in Petrograd over food and fuel
items: Military disaster on the Eastern Front
Peasant land hunger since the 1861 Emancipation
Strike wave in Petrograd over food and fuel

cards.front: What three groups of ministers did Tsarina Alexandra replace at speed in just over a year?
cards.answer: Four prime ministers / Five interior ministers / Three war ministers

cards.front: Why could a concentrated urban working class bring down the tsar while a scattered peasantry could not?
cards.answer: Workers were packed into a few Petrograd districts, so when Putilov workers struck, half of working Petrograd joined within days.

cards.front: Why did rumours about Rasputin damage the dynasty more than his actual influence did?
cards.answer: His real power over policy was modest, but public belief he was the Tsarina's lover and choosing ministers destroyed the dynasty's respectability.

title: Al-Qaeda: Aims, Beliefs and Bin Laden
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What four aims did bin Laden state for al-Qaeda?
cards.answer: Remove Western/American troops from Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world / Topple corrupt Arab governments, starting with Saudi Arabia and Egypt / Destroy Israel / Restore a unified Islamic caliphate under strict Wahhabism
items: Remove Western/American troops from Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world
Topple corrupt Arab governments, starting with Saudi Arabia and Egypt
Restore a unified Islamic caliphate under strict Wahhabism

cards.front: What three attacks before 9/11 established al-Qaeda as a global threat?
cards.answer: East African embassy bombings, 7 August 1998 / Failed Millennium plot at Los Angeles airport, December 1999 / USS Cole bombing, 12 October 2000
items: Failed Millennium plot at Los Angeles airport, December 1999

cards.front: Why did the 9/11 Commission conclude pre-2001 warnings about al-Qaeda were missed?
cards.answer: The failures were of imagination, structure and information sharing rather than effort — agencies were watching for a different kind of attack.

cards.front: How did al-Qaeda's structure make it both hard to destroy and capable of major attacks?
cards.answer: It was decentralised enough to survive losing any single cell, yet coordinated enough to plan a synchronised four-airliner attack.

title: The Origin of Evil and Suffering
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What three qualities must God have for the problem of evil to arise as a challenge?
cards.answer: omnipotent (all-powerful) / omniscient (all-knowing) / omnibenevolent (perfectly good)

cards.front: What three gunas does the Bhagavad Gita describe, where dominance of the lower ones leads to suffering?
cards.answer: goodness / passion / ignorance

cards.front: Why does the free-will defence struggle to explain natural evil such as earthquakes and disease?
cards.answer: Natural evil is not caused by human choices, so blaming misuse of free will fails to account for it.

cards.front: Why do critics find the soul-making theodicy morally troubling?
cards.answer: It seems to require extreme suffering to be justified by the spiritual growth it produces, which many find unacceptable.

cards.front: Name the four guerrilla tactics the lesson gives for how the Vietcong fought.
cards.answer: Ambushes / Booby traps / Hit-and-run raids / Underground tunnel network at Cu Chi
items: Underground tunnel network at Cu Chi

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson say made continued US involvement in Vietnam untenable by 1973?
cards.answer: Domestic political pressure / The Tet Offensive's psychological impact / Credibility damage from My Lai and the Pentagon Papers
items: Credibility damage from My Lai and the Pentagon Papers

cards.front: Why did the Tet Offensive shatter American public confidence even though it was militarily repulsed?
cards.answer: Westmoreland had assured the public the war was being won, so the offensive proved the enemy was far from defeated.

cards.front: Why was it so difficult for US forces to identify the enemy in Vietnam?
cards.answer: Vietcong fighters were indistinguishable from civilians, making identification of the enemy extremely difficult.

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives for choosing a supplier.
cards.answer: Price / Quality / Reliability / Delivery speed / Payment terms

cards.front: Name the five impact criteria the lesson gives for logistics and supply decisions.
cards.answer: Time / Length of supply chain / Reliability of supply / Costs / Customer service

cards.front: Why does delivery speed matter more for bakeries and florists than for other businesses?
cards.answer: Their products have short shelf-lives, so slow delivery leaves shelves empty or goods spoiled before sale.

cards.front: How do long payment terms, like 60 days credit, help a buyer's cash flow?
cards.answer: They let the business sell goods and collect cash before paying the supplier, acting like an interest-free loan.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: What four factors can be altered to change the rate of a chemical reaction?
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases) / Surface area of solid reactants / Using a catalyst
items: Concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases)

cards.front: What three methods can be used to measure the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: Collecting gas in a syringe or over water / Measuring mass loss on a balance / Timing a colour change (e.g. disappearing cross)
items: Collecting gas in a syringe or over water
Measuring mass loss on a balance
Timing a colour change (e.g. disappearing cross)

cards.front: Why does increasing temperature or concentration change the steepness of a rate graph but not the final volume of gas produced?
cards.answer: The same amount of reactant is used, so the same total gas forms, just faster; only the rate changes.

cards.front: Why does increasing the amount of reactant increase the total volume of gas produced on a rate graph?
cards.answer: More reactant means more product can form before the reaction finishes, increasing the total gas volume.

cards.front: Name the four types of diagnostic technology the lesson gives that let doctors see inside the body without surgery.
cards.answer: X-rays / CT scans / MRI scans / Ultrasound

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why penicillin took so long to develop.
cards.answer: Fleming lacked chemistry skills to purify it / Funding was limited in the 1930s Depression / Only WWII gave the motivation and funding for mass production
items: Fleming lacked chemistry skills to purify it
Funding was limited in the 1930s Depression
Only WWII gave the motivation and funding for mass production

cards.front: Why did the experience of the Second World War create strong public support for a free NHS?
cards.answer: The government had organised emergency healthcare during the war, and the 1942 Beveridge Report had called for a welfare state.

cards.front: How were antibiotics like penicillin different from earlier 'magic bullets' like Salvarsan and Prontosil?
cards.answer: Antibiotics were natural substances made by moulds or fungi that could kill a wide range of bacteria, unlike targeted magic bullets.

title: The First Crusade: Antioch and Jerusalem
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six leaders of the First Crusade army mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Godfrey de Bouillon / Baldwin / Bohemond of Taranto / Tancred / Raymond of Toulouse / Robert of Normandy

cards.front: Name the three hardships the crusaders suffered during the eight-month Siege of Antioch.
cards.answer: Famine killed thousands / Desertion was a constant problem / Foraging parties were ambushed by Seljuk relief forces
items: Foraging parties ambushed by Seljuk forces

cards.front: Why did the crusaders defeat Kerbogha's much larger relief army outside Antioch in June 1098?
cards.answer: Kerbogha's coalition was fragile because individual Muslim commanders had their own rivalries and withdrew during the battle.

cards.front: How did having no single commander affect the First Crusade's campaign?
cards.answer: It weakened coordination among the leaders but also stopped the whole crusade collapsing when any one leader failed.

cards.front: Name the five standard stock forms that metals are supplied in, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sheet / Bar (flat/square) / Rod (round bar) / Tube / Angle

cards.front: Name the four methods the lesson gives for protecting metals from corrosion.
cards.answer: Galvanising / Powder coating / Painting / Anodising

cards.front: Why does the green patina that forms on copper actually protect it?
cards.answer: The patina is a layer of copper carbonate that protects the underlying metal from further corrosion.

cards.front: Why is recycling aluminium preferred over producing virgin aluminium from bauxite?
cards.answer: Recycling aluminium uses only around 5% of the energy needed to smelt virgin aluminium from bauxite.

cards.front: Name the six classic examples of high-risk foods given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cooked poultry / Cooked rice / Custards and cream-based desserts / Soft cheeses / Cooked shellfish / Egg-based dishes such as quiche

cards.front: Name the three ways given to control enzymic browning in fruit.
cards.answer: Adding acids like lemon juice / Blanching with heat / Covering to minimise oxygen exposure

cards.front: Why is a cooled cooked chicken breast left at room temperature considered higher-risk than raw chicken about to be roasted?
cards.answer: The cooked breast will be eaten as-is, so any bacteria multiplying in the danger zone go straight into the body, unlike raw chicken which will still be cooked.

cards.front: Why can vacuum-packed meat still carry a food safety risk?
cards.answer: Some bacteria are anaerobic and grow without oxygen, so removing air doesn't stop them multiplying if temperature control fails.

cards.front: Name the three different forms in which an algorithm can be expressed.
cards.answer: Pseudo-code / Flowchart / Actual program code

cards.front: Name the four sub-problems the NHS GP appointment booking system is decomposed into.
cards.answer: Patient login / Show available slots / Book slot / Send confirmation

cards.front: Why does a sat-nav system abstract away road surface physics, the Highway Code and car mechanics?
cards.answer: Keeping only position, destination, road connections and speeds means less detail to process, so routes are calculated faster and more clearly.

cards.front: How is abstraction applied in the school login system algorithm?
cards.answer: It ignores how passwords are stored, the server's operating system and network details, keeping only username, password, stored credentials and match/no-match.

cards.front: What are the three genotype ratios produced from a Bb × Bb cross?
What three arguments does the lesson give about embryo screening?
cards.answer: it prevents suffering / it is unethical to select embryos / it could lead to designer babies
items: it is unethical to select embryos
it could lead to designer babies

cards.front: How does cystic fibrosis affect the body?
cards.answer: It causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.

cards.front: How does the Y chromosome cause a baby to develop as male?
cards.answer: It carries the SRY gene, which triggers male development.

cards.front: Name the four rules of binary addition given in the lesson.
Name the four SI decimal units of data storage used on this course, smallest to largest, and what each equals.
cards.answer: kilobyte (kB) = 1,000 bytes / megabyte (MB) = 1,000 kilobytes / gigabyte (GB) = 1,000 megabytes / terabyte (TB) = 1,000 gigabytes

cards.front: Why do computers store and process all data as binary rather than another number system?
cards.answer: A transistor is either conducting electricity or not, and this two-state physical reality maps perfectly onto binary's two digits.

cards.front: Why can a right binary shift by 1 lose information from a number?
cards.answer: It performs integer division by 2, so any remainder is lost as the last bit shifts beyond the boundary.

title: Mechanical Systems: Motion, Linkages and Cams
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of motion that mechanical systems use.
cards.answer: Rotary motion / Linear motion / Reciprocating motion / Oscillating motion

cards.front: Name the four named cam profiles covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pear cam / Eccentric (circular) cam / Snail (drop) cam / Heart cam

cards.front: How does a crank and slider mechanism turn rotary motion into reciprocating motion?
cards.answer: A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider by a connecting rod, so as the crank rotates the slider moves back and forth.

cards.front: Why is the cam profile in an aero-engine fuel valve unit machined to very tight tolerances?
cards.answer: Because any deviation in the profile changes the valve timing, which affects the engine's thrust output.

title: Organic Chemistry: Hydrocarbons, Alcohols and Polymers
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the six main fractions crude oil is separated into by fractional distillation.
cards.answer: Refinery gases / Petrol (gasoline) / Kerosene / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen

cards.front: Name the first four alkanes in order.
cards.answer: Methane / Ethane / Propane / Butane

cards.front: Why are alkenes far more reactive than alkanes?
cards.answer: The C=C double bond is a site of high electron density, so molecules like hydrogen, water or bromine can add across it, breaking the bond.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to breathe in?
cards.answer: It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen from being transported around the body.

cards.front: Name the four great Anglo-Saxon earldoms that existed before William reduced the power of earls.
cards.answer: Wessex / Mercia / Northumbria / East Anglia

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says the feudal system worked through to give William control.
cards.answer: Homage / Knight service / Forfeiture

cards.front: Why did William need to appoint regents to govern England?
cards.answer: Because William spent roughly half his reign in Normandy, so trusted men had to govern England in his absence.

cards.front: Why did William's system of using regents create a risk for him?
cards.answer: A regent who abused his power could cause resentment and rebellion, as Odo of Bayeux later proved.

cards.front: What three classical authors did Elizabethan grammar school students study?
cards.answer: Plutarch / Cicero / Seneca

cards.front: Name the four key contextual threads for exam analysis of Julius Caesar given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Roman republican ideal against absolute power / Elizabethan succession crisis and fear of instability / the divine right debate over legitimacy of power / Shakespeare's use of Plutarch for historical authority
items: Roman republican ideal against absolute power
Elizabethan succession crisis and fear of instability
the divine right debate over legitimacy of power
Shakespeare's use of Plutarch for historical authority

cards.front: How did Shakespeare turn Plutarch's biography into a gripping political thriller?
cards.answer: He compressed timelines, invented dialogue, and gave far more dramatic weight to moments like the soothsayer's warning.

cards.front: Why did Rome share power between two consuls rather than one ruler?
cards.answer: Power was deliberately shared between two annually elected consuls to prevent any one person becoming a king.

cards.front: Name the five xerophyte adaptations for reducing water loss given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Thick waxy cuticle / Reduced or modified leaves (spines) / Sunken stomata / Rolled leaves / Water storage tissue

cards.front: Name the three hydrophyte adaptations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Aerenchyma (air spaces) / Broad flat floating leaves / Flexible stems

cards.front: Why does a root bend downward in response to gravity (positive gravitropism)?
cards.answer: Auxin accumulates on the lower side, but root cells are sensitive to it, so high auxin inhibits elongation there, bending the root down.

cards.front: How does rolling its leaves inward help marram grass reduce water loss?
cards.answer: Rolling leaves inward traps humid air inside the leaf, reducing the humidity gradient and slowing water vapour loss.

cards.front: What four theatrical spectacles does Prospero stage on the island?
cards.answer: The storm / The masque / The harpy banquet / The spirits

cards.front: What three roles does the Epilogue simultaneously perform?
cards.answer: A character's plea / An actor's curtain call / A playwright's farewell

cards.front: Why does Prospero's magic move Antonio emotionally but fail to make him genuinely repent?
cards.answer: Art can move people emotionally but cannot change their fundamental nature, shown by Antonio never apologising despite Prospero's illusions.

cards.front: How does the play's tight structure of the unities reflect Prospero's control over the island?
cards.answer: The single overarching plan within one place and short time mirrors Prospero's orchestration, making others seem like performers hitting his marks.

cards.front: The lesson groups electronic system components into three jobs. Name them.
cards.answer: Sensing what is happening / Controlling what happens next / Producing an output

cards.front: Name the three control devices between the sensor and output described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Switch / Transistor / Resistor

cards.front: Why must a resistor connected to an LED have exactly the right value, not too low or too high?
cards.answer: Too little resistance damages the LED, while too much resistance makes the output too dim or weak.

cards.front: Why can a transistor let a weak sensor signal control a powerful output like a motor or bright lamp?
cards.answer: A small current or voltage at one connection switches a much larger current, controlling power the sensor alone couldn't drive.

cards.front: How does Ralph betray Piggy's trust in Chapter 1?
cards.answer: He reveals Piggy's hated nickname to the other boys after Piggy specifically asked him not to.

cards.front: Why does enthusiasm for shelter-building and the fire fade by Chapter 3?
cards.answer: Hunting offers immediate, exciting satisfaction, while maintaining the fire and shelters is boring and requires discipline and sacrifice.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Macbeth's character arc across the play.
cards.answer: Loyal warrior / Tempted nobleman / Guilt-stricken murderer / Paranoid tyrant / Nihilistic villain

cards.front: What three pieces of evidence support reading Macbeth as a tragic hero deserving pity?
cards.answer: He hesitates / He feels guilt / He recognises what he has lost
items: He recognises what he has lost

cards.front: Why don't the witches' prophecies actually create Macbeth's ambition?
cards.answer: They reveal an ambition that already existed within him, shown by the phrase 'horrid image' in Act 1 Scene 3.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare bring Banquo's ghost back in Act 3 Scene 4?
cards.answer: To make Banquo the play's symbol of inescapable guilt and of legitimate succession through his descendants.

cards.front: Name the three targets the lesson gives that Vikings attacked far inland in Britain.
cards.answer: Lindisfarne / York / London

cards.front: Name the three Anglo-Dutch Wars periods given in the lesson.
How did Nelson's tactics at Trafalgar differ from the traditional line of battle?
cards.answer: He attacked in two columns perpendicular to the enemy line, cutting it in three and forcing close-quarters fighting where British gunnery won.

cards.front: Why did the Spanish Armada suffer its greatest losses in 1588?
cards.answer: As it tried to return home around Scotland and Ireland, storms wrecked about 63 ships, far more than were lost in battle.

title: UK Population Distribution & a Major UK City
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things that make Manchester an important city within the UK, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Major financial centre (Spinningfields) / Home to four universities including University of Manchester / Manchester Airport, third-busiest in the UK / BBC's second hub at MediaCityUK
items: Home to four universities including University of Manchester
Manchester Airport, third-busiest in the UK

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why Manchester became 'Cottonopolis'.
cards.answer: Wet climate suited cotton spinning / Fast-flowing Pennine streams powered mills / Coal from Lancashire fed steam engines
items: Coal from Lancashire fed steam engines

cards.front: How does cumulative causation explain why London and the south-east became so densely populated?
cards.answer: A navigable Thames and fertile lowlands helped a financial centre grow, which then attracted jobs, transport links and universities, drawing in more people.

cards.front: Why did the Manchester Ship Canal help Manchester's development?
cards.answer: Opened in 1894, it let ocean-going ships reach Manchester directly, bypassing Liverpool and boosting trade.

cards.front: Name the four festivals covered in this lesson on Spanish festivals.
cards.answer: Las Fallas / La Tomatina / Semana Santa / El Día de los Muertos

cards.front: What four things are ofrendas decorated with during El Día de los Muertos?
cards.answer: photographs / flowers (marigolds/cempasúchil) / candles / favourite foods of the deceased

cards.front: How does El Día de los Muertos combine two different cultural traditions?
cards.answer: It combines indigenous Aztec traditions with Catholic beliefs brought by Spanish colonists.

cards.front: Why is El Día de los Muertos a joyful celebration rather than a sad one?
cards.answer: It celebrates the lives of family members who have died, and Mexicans believe their spirits return to visit.

title: Sources of Authority and Muslim Identity
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four architectural features of a mosque given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Mihrab (prayer niche facing Makkah) / Minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons) / Minaret (tower for call to prayer) / Area for wudu (ritual washing)

cards.front: Name the four main Sunni legal schools of Shari'ah Law.
cards.answer: Hanafi / Maliki / Shafi'i / Hanbali

cards.front: Why did the Sunni-Shi'a split over religious authority arise after the Prophet's death?
cards.answer: Shi'a Muslims believe Ali and the Ahl-ul-Bayt were the divinely appointed rightful authorities, while Sunnis respect Ali as a caliph but not divinely appointed.

cards.front: Why was ibn al-Arabi's concept of wahdat al-wujud (Unity of Being) controversial?
cards.answer: It suggested all existence reflects Allah's being, which some orthodox scholars felt blurred the distinction between Creator and creation.

title: Civil Rights: Segregation, Martin Luther King and the 1964 Act
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four civil-rights leaders the lesson says mattered only because mass action made their leadership consequential.
cards.answer: Martin Luther King / Malcolm X / Rosa Parks / Stokely Carmichael

cards.front: Name the three US Civil Rights Acts passed between 1964 and 1968.
cards.answer: Civil Rights Act, 1964 / Voting Rights Act, 1965 / Fair Housing Act, 1968

cards.front: Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock in 1957?
cards.answer: Governor Faubus used the National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine, so Eisenhower sent paratroopers to enforce desegregation.

cards.front: Why did Congress pass the 1964 Civil Rights Act?
cards.answer: Televised images of Bull Connor's police using dogs and fire hoses on child protestors in Birmingham shocked the nation and pushed Congress to act.

cards.front: Name the three narrative techniques the lesson says Wells uses in The War of the Worlds.
cards.answer: Journalistic register / Direct address / Scientific language for the Martians

cards.front: Name the five escalating threats that structure Book 1 of The War of the Worlds.
cards.answer: Cylinder / Heat-Ray / Tripods / Black Smoke / Exodus

cards.front: Why does the pacing change so dramatically between Book 1 and Book 2 of The War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Book 1 is fast-paced action showing public spectacle, while Book 2 slows to show private, claustrophobic psychological survival.

cards.front: How does the structural mirroring of Book 1 expanding and Book 2 contracting reflect Wells's argument?
cards.answer: Book 1's escalating threats mirror growing public crisis, while Book 2's shrinking setting mirrors the shift to private survival.

cards.front: Name the six fixed costs the lesson gives as typical for a start-up.
cards.answer: Rent / Insurance / Advertising / Salaries / Utilities / Loan interest

cards.front: Name the three rearranged formulas the lesson says to practise for calculation questions.
cards.answer: Find selling price (Revenue ÷ Quantity sold) / Find quantity sold (Revenue ÷ Selling price) / Find variable cost per unit (Total variable costs ÷ Quantity produced)
items: Find variable cost per unit (Total variable costs ÷ Quantity produced)

cards.front: Why is flour a variable cost for a baker who makes more loaves?
cards.answer: Because making twice as many loaves means using twice as much flour, so the cost rises directly with output.

cards.front: Why is it useful for a start-up to identify a loss early?
cards.answer: It helps the entrepreneur decide whether to adjust prices, cut costs, or both before the problem grows.

title: Immigration: Windrush, race riots and Enoch Powell
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names three groups whose hostility Caribbean migrants faced in Britain. What were they and how did each act?
cards.answer: Landlords who refused rooms to Black tenants / Employers who paid lower wages / Neighbours who objected to their presence
items: Landlords who refused rooms to Black tenants
Neighbours who objected to their presence

cards.front: The lesson lists five types of institutions migrant communities built for themselves. What were they?
cards.answer: Temples / Mosques / Churches / Social clubs / Newspapers

cards.front: Why was the Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1968 seen by critics as racially discriminatory?
cards.answer: It targeted East African Asians who held British passports by requiring them to prove a 'substantial connection' with Britain before entry.

cards.front: Why did the reaction to Powell's 1968 speech reveal a gap between politicians and the public?
cards.answer: Heath sacked Powell for the speech, yet opinion polls showed over 70% of the public agreed with his concerns about immigration.

title: The Second Cold War: Afghanistan & Reagan’s SDI
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four punitive measures Carter took against the USSR after the invasion of Afghanistan.
cards.answer: Withdrew SALT 2 from Senate consideration / Imposed a grain embargo on the USSR / Increased US defence spending / Boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics
items: Imposed a grain embargo on the USSR

cards.front: What are the two historian views on whether SDI helped end the Cold War?
cards.answer: SDI pressured the USSR into arms reduction talks it couldn't afford to match / The Cold War ended due to Soviet internal weakness and Gorbachev's reforms, not SDI
items: SDI pressured the USSR into arms reduction talks it couldn't afford to match
The Cold War ended due to Soviet internal weakness and Gorbachev's reforms, not SDI

cards.front: Why did Brezhnev send Soviet troops into Afghanistan in 1979?
cards.answer: He feared that if the communist government fell, it would encourage anti-Soviet movements in the USSR's own Muslim-majority Central Asian republics.

cards.front: How did Reagan's increased defence spending aim to defeat the Soviet Union?
cards.answer: He believed the USA could outspend the USSR in an arms race, forcing it to choose between military spending and economic collapse.

title: The Elizabethan theatre and attitudes towards it
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three connected factors the lesson gives for why Elizabethan theatre boomed.
cards.answer: Noble patronage protecting actors from vagrancy laws / Rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income / Elizabeth's personal taste for plays at court
items: Noble patronage protecting actors from vagrancy laws
Rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income
Elizabeth's personal taste for plays at court

cards.front: What four reasons did the City of London Corporation give for banning public playhouses?
cards.answer: Spread plague by drawing crowds / Attracted pickpockets, prostitutes and brawlers / Pulled apprentices away from honest work / Encouraged immorality
items: Pulled apprentices away from honest work

cards.front: Why did the Privy Council sometimes order playhouses closed during serious plague outbreaks?
cards.answer: Partly to control infection by stopping crowds gathering, and partly to placate the City of London and the Puritans.

cards.front: How did royal licensing by the Master of the Revels from 1581 protect acting companies?
cards.answer: A licensed play could not be banned by the City of London Corporation, so licensing shielded companies as well as censoring them.

title: Culture and fashion in Edwardian Britain
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four major authors the lesson credits with publishing important works during the Edwardian period (1890–1914).
cards.answer: Thomas Hardy / George Bernard Shaw / H.G. Wells / Beatrix Potter

cards.front: Why did Thomas Hardy stop writing novels after 1896?
cards.answer: He gave up fiction following the hostile reception to his novel Jude the Obscure.

cards.front: Why did women's fashion shift towards straighter, less restrictive styles by around 1907–1910?
cards.answer: Partly due to the suffragette movement's critique of restrictive clothing, and partly the rise of active leisure like cycling and golf.

cards.front: Name the three common mistakes the lesson warns about when calculating image file size.
cards.answer: Forgetting to multiply by colour depth / Leaving the answer in bits when bytes are asked for / Dividing by 1,000 instead of 8 to convert bits to bytes
items: Forgetting to multiply by colour depth
Leaving the answer in bits when bytes are asked for
Dividing by 1,000 instead of 8 to convert bits to bytes

cards.front: Name the three problems the lesson says happen when there aren't enough bits to represent data accurately.
cards.answer: Colour banding in images / Quantisation noise in sound / Lost high-frequency detail from low sample rate
items: Lost high-frequency detail from low sample rate

cards.front: Why does increasing colour depth allow more possible colours per pixel?
cards.answer: Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel, and the number of possible colours equals 2 to the power of that bit count.

cards.front: Why does a lower sample rate cause loss of high-frequency detail in a recorded sound?
cards.answer: Fewer samples per second means rapid wave variations happen faster than the gaps between samples, so they get missed.

title: Stock Control and Working with Suppliers
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three types of stock a manufacturing business might hold.
cards.answer: Raw materials / Work in progress / Finished goods

cards.front: Name the four key values shown on a bar gate stock graph.
cards.answer: Maximum stock level / Minimum stock level / Re-order level / Re-order quantity

cards.front: Why might a business using just-in-time stock control miss out on volume-purchase discounts?
cards.answer: It orders smaller quantities more frequently instead of buying in bulk, so it misses discounts for large orders.

cards.front: How can poor supply chain decisions, like relying on a single supplier, affect a business?
cards.answer: They raise costs, create delays and damage the business's reputation.

title: Staging and Design: Sea, State Apartment and Searchlight
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four specific choices the lesson says should be specified when designing cold lighting for the North Korea scenes.
cards.answer: Which lantern type (profile spot or Fresnel) / What intensity (e.g. 70%) / What colour gel (e.g. Full C.T. Blue) / What directional angle (e.g. steep top-light)
items: Which lantern type (profile spot or Fresnel)
What colour gel (e.g. Full C.T. Blue)

cards.front: Name the three elements the lesson gives as North Korea's design vocabulary.
cards.answer: Flat, harsh overhead light / Institutional walls / Absence of the natural world

cards.front: Why does the play use a minimalist set instead of a naturalistic one?
cards.answer: The play spans 24 years and two countries, so a realistic set would need constant scene changes that would fatally slow its momentum.

cards.front: Why does the sound designer move the sea sound from binaural speakers to a mono centre speaker as the play progresses?
cards.answer: To suggest the sea has retreated into memory, marking how far Hanako has moved from her original loss.

cards.front: According to mainstream Islamic scholarship, what four conditions must be met for armed (Lesser) Jihad to be legitimate?
cards.answer: Declared by legitimate authority / Must be the last resort / Civilians and non-combatants must be protected / Must cease when the enemy seeks peace
items: Civilians and non-combatants must be protected
Must cease when the enemy seeks peace

cards.front: In classical Islamic jurisprudence, what three circumstances allow Lesser Jihad to be waged?
cards.answer: Muslim community under attack / Innocent people being oppressed / Evil cannot be removed by other means
items: Evil cannot be removed by other means

cards.front: Why do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims mark Ashura in such different ways?
cards.answer: For Shi'a it mourns Hussayn's martyrdom at Karbala, while for Sunni it marks Moses's rescue from Pharaoh, so Sunni Muslims fast instead.

cards.front: Why do Sunni Muslims not observe Eid-ul-Ghadeer?
cards.answer: They do not share the Shi'a belief that Muhammad designated Ali as his rightful successor at Ghadir Khumm.

title: Violence, War and Just War Theory
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the four causes of terrorism the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Political grievances / Economic marginalisation / Cultural humiliation / Extremist ideologies claiming divine sanction
