cards.answer: Carbon taxes / Plastic bag charges / Mandatory recycling / Right-to-repair laws

cards.front: Why does e-waste still end up in places like Ghana or Nigeria despite stricter international rules?
cards.answer: The Basel Convention has reduced flows, but poor recycling infrastructure means much e-waste still ends up where it shouldn't.

cards.front: How do HIC consumer choices reshape environments in LICs, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Through palm-oil deforestation, food-mile emissions and shipped e-waste, connecting supermarket choices to ecosystems on the other side of the world.

title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four consequences of global warming given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sea level rise / More extreme weather events / Changes to ecosystems and species distribution / Impacts on agriculture
items: Changes to ecosystems and species distribution

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson gives to reduce a carbon footprint.
cards.answer: Use renewable energy / Improve energy efficiency / Carbon capture and storage / Reduce meat consumption / Reduce travel

cards.front: How did the oceans form from Earth's early atmosphere?
cards.answer: Water vapour in the early atmosphere condensed as the Earth cooled, forming the oceans.

cards.front: How did the ozone layer form and why was this important for life?
cards.answer: As oxygen levels increased, the ozone layer formed, shielding life on Earth from UV radiation.

title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the four atomic models covered in the lesson, in the order they were proposed.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere model (1803) / Thomson's plum pudding model (1897) / Rutherford's nuclear model (1909) / Bohr's electron shell model (1913)

cards.front: Name the three types of particles that make up an atom.
cards.answer: Protons / Neutrons / Electrons

cards.front: Why did Rutherford's gold foil results show that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but some bounced back, showing a small, dense, positively charged region.

cards.front: Why don't neutrons affect an atom's chemical properties?
cards.answer: Neutrons are neutral particles with no charge, so they only add mass and aren't involved in chemical bonding.

title: Treating Depression and Addiction: CBT and Drugs
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four lenses used to evaluate treatments for depression and addiction.
cards.answer: Validity / Reliability / Generalisability / Ethics

cards.front: How does behavioural activation help treat depression in CBT?
cards.answer: It gradually reintroduces activities the person has withdrawn from because of low mood.

cards.front: Why can CBT's effects outlast a course of medication?
cards.answer: Because CBT teaches skills the client can keep using after treatment ends.

cards.front: What three stages make up the novel's Bildungsroman arc, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Innocence — the early comic chapters / Experience — the racism, the betrayal, the broken leg / Maturity — the break with Anita and the grammar school place
items: Experience — the racism, the betrayal, the broken leg
Maturity — the break with Anita and the grammar school place

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say Meena has that Anita does not?
cards.answer: A loving family / A rich cultural heritage / The intellectual ability to imagine a different future
items: The intellectual ability to imagine a different future

cards.front: Why does Syal present Anita's fate with sorrowful understanding rather than condemnation?
cards.answer: Because Anita is shaped by her environment — the neglect, poverty and lack of aspiration in the Rutter family, showing class harms as much as racism.

cards.front: Why is Meena's rejection of Anita described as self-assertion rather than anger?
cards.answer: Because it is a quiet, decisive choice to stop seeking validation from someone who will never truly offer it.

cards.front: Name the six output devices listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lamp / LED / Buzzer / Solenoid / Motor / Servo / Loudspeaker

cards.front: Name the three common errors students make with block diagrams.
cards.answer: Mixing up stages / Inventing blocks not needed / Omitting the transducer driver

cards.front: Why does the security light example use an AND gate rather than a single sensor?
cards.answer: The light must only turn on when it is dark AND movement is detected, so the AND gate output is HIGH only when both sensor inputs are HIGH.

cards.front: Why would a designer use a latch instead of a simple logic gate for an output that must stay on?
cards.answer: A latch holds its output HIGH or LOW until told to change, so the output stays on even after the trigger signal is removed.

title: The Cavalier Parliament and the Religious Settlement
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four statutes of the Clarendon Code in the order they were passed (1661–1665).
cards.answer: Corporation Act 1661 / Act of Uniformity 1662 / Conventicle Act 1664 / Five Mile Act 1665

cards.front: Name the four main Dissenting groups targeted by the Clarendon Code.
cards.answer: Presbyterians / Independents (Congregationalists) / Baptists / Quakers

cards.front: Why did the Great Ejection of 1662 create a permanent body of Protestant Dissenters?
cards.answer: Around 2,000 ministers refused to conform and were expelled, but kept their congregations, preaching in private houses, barns and woods without churches.

cards.front: Why did Charles II's need to ask Parliament for money give MPs leverage over his religious policy?
cards.answer: His voted income of about £1.2 million was roughly two-thirds of what he needed, so he had to ask Parliament for extra funds for war or court.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson says affect an individual's daily energy requirement.
cards.answer: Age / Gender / Height / Energy expenditure (exercise level)

cards.front: Name the three non-energy roles of fat given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Insulates the body / Protects organs / Carries fat-soluble vitamins

cards.front: Why does the body switch from fat back to carbohydrate as exercise intensity increases?
cards.answer: Because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the energy demand at higher exercise intensities.

cards.front: How does dehydration affect the nervous system during performance?
cards.answer: Dehydration slows reaction time and worsens decision-making, for example causing a basketball player to make slower, poorer decisions.

title: Data, Information and Fit for Purpose
subject: l12-ict

cards.front: Name the six file properties every file has, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: File name / File type (extension) / File size / Date created / Date modified / Author or owner

cards.front: Name the five common file types the lesson gives, with their purpose.
cards.answer: Text files for written documents / Image files for photographs and graphics / Audio files for sound / Video files for moving images / Spreadsheet files for numerical data
items: Image files for photographs and graphics

cards.front: Why does repeatedly saving a JPEG photo make it degrade in quality over time?
cards.answer: Each save uses lossy compression which permanently discards more data, so quality is lost further with every save.

cards.front: How have advances in ICT hardware improved data storage and retrieval?
cards.answer: SSDs retrieve data far faster than old spinning hard drives, and cloud storage removes the limit of on-site hardware capacity.

title: Exam Practice: Performer, Director and Designer
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four design elements a student can choose to answer about in the designer question on the set-play paper.
cards.answer: Lighting / Sound / Set / Costume

cards.front: The lesson names five types of command word used in set-play exam questions. What are they?
cards.answer: Identify or name / Define or what is meant by / Explain or describe the effect of / How would you interpret / Analyse the playwright's intentions
items: Define or what is meant by
Explain or describe the effect of

cards.front: How would staging Abdul's kneeling in the final Tilbury scene on a thrust stage affect the audience's response, compared to a proscenium arch?
cards.answer: On a thrust stage, audience on three sides makes the kneeling feel exposed and communal, like a public farewell shared with everyone.

cards.front: Why might a costume designer dress Rani in a plain, sombre English nanny's uniform once Georgina employs her?
cards.answer: It visually erases her own identity, mirroring how real ayahs were recorded in ship's papers only under their employer's name.

title: Medieval Migrants: Hanseatic Merchants, Jews & Lombards
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five English towns where medieval Jewish communities grew after 1070.
cards.answer: London / York / Lincoln / Norwich / Oxford

cards.front: Name the six goods Hanseatic merchants imported from the Baltic and North Sea.
cards.answer: Timber / Wax / Fur / Grain / Pitch / Tar

cards.front: Why did Edward I decide to expel the Jews from England in 1290?
cards.answer: He had already taxed Jewish wealth past the point of usefulness, and richer Italian bankers were arriving to replace them.

cards.front: Why did English merchants resent the Hanseatic League by the fifteenth century?
cards.answer: Hanseatic merchants paid lower tolls than English merchants and were free from many local taxes, giving them an unfair advantage.

cards.front: Name the four bodies that can designate protected areas in the UK.
cards.answer: Natural England / Natural Resources Wales / NatureScot / DAERA in Northern Ireland

cards.front: What are the three categories of true costs of sending construction waste to landfill?
cards.answer: Financial costs (gate fees) / Environmental costs (greenhouse gases, land loss) / Social costs (traffic, noise, smells)

cards.front: How does using wood as a structural material help reduce carbon dioxide levels?
cards.answer: Timber stores carbon absorbed during the tree's growth, locking it away for the life of the building.

cards.front: Why must developers protect wildlife even on sites that aren't officially designated as protected?
cards.answer: Developers have a responsibility to reduce their impact on nature, such as tunnels for newts or replacement bat roosts.

cards.front: What four things does the play's resolution involve releasing or resolving?
cards.answer: Ariel is freed / Caliban is released / The nobles are sent home / Prospero asks the audience to 'set me free'
items: Prospero asks the audience to 'set me free'

cards.front: Name the three contextual lenses the strongest whole-play essays use.
cards.answer: Jacobean (hierarchy, legitimate authority) / Postcolonial (Prospero as coloniser) / Autobiographical (Prospero as Shakespeare)

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Prospero's forgiveness of Antonio as a difficult choice rather than a natural one?
cards.answer: His language towards Antonio ('infect my mouth') shows forgiveness does not erase anger, making virtue over vengeance require effort.

cards.front: Why might a Jacobean audience have read Prospero differently to a modern postcolonial audience?
cards.answer: They lacked a postcolonial framework, so might have seen Prospero as a civilising force bringing order to chaos, not a coloniser.

title: Nature of crimes: industrial to modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four new offences the lesson says were created by the spread of the motor car.
cards.answer: Speeding / Drink-driving / Driving without insurance / Vehicle theft

cards.front: Name the three types of crime the lesson says were hosted by overcrowded Victorian slums.
cards.answer: Gangs of pick-pockets / Prostitution networks / Receivers of stolen goods (fences)

cards.front: Why did highway robbery decline by the late eighteenth century?
cards.answer: Improved roads, better banking and organised thief-taking reduced the number of highwaymen.

cards.front: Why was smuggling difficult for the authorities to police in eighteenth-century England?
cards.answer: Policing was thin along the coastline and local communities often sympathised with or took part in the trade.

title: Trace Tables, Error Types and Algorithm Evaluation
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the two most common trace-table errors made in exams.
cards.answer: Adding extra rows for iterations that did not happen / Forgetting to update a counter variable every iteration
items: Adding extra rows for iterations that did not happen
Forgetting to update a counter variable every iteration

cards.front: Name the three questions you should ask to evaluate an algorithm.
cards.answer: Is it correct? / Is it efficient? / Does it use memory wisely?

cards.front: Why did the grading program crash when a new enrolment had taken zero assessments?
cards.answer: It tried to divide the total marks by zero assessments, an operation the processor cannot complete, so it crashed.

cards.front: Why does bubble sort need many more passes to sort a list of 100 items than a list of 10?
cards.answer: Because the number of passes through the loop grows as the size of the problem increases.

cards.front: The lesson gives four classic examples of fixed costs for a coffee shop. Name them.
cards.answer: Rent / Manager's salary / Insurance / Business rates

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says managers use cost, revenue and profit numbers.
cards.answer: Setting prices / Spotting a problem early / Talking to lenders and investors

cards.front: Why is a market-stall sandwich seller less risky than a cinema in a quiet week?
cards.answer: It has low fixed costs, so if sales fall it doesn't have big fixed costs to cover, unlike the cinema.

cards.front: How can watching revenue and cost figures let a manager spot a problem early?
cards.answer: If revenue stays flat but total costs creep up month after month, profit is being quietly eaten, so a manager can act before it becomes a crisis.

cards.front: Name the four other anthology poems this lesson compares with Out, Out.
cards.answer: Midnight on the Great Western / Happy Birthday Moon / Prayer / Equilibrium

cards.front: Why does Frost write in blank verse with no rhyme scheme in Out, Out?
cards.answer: So there is nothing to soften events or signal an ending, making the horror arrive unpredictably like the accident itself.

cards.front: How does Frost's use of enjambment make the accident feel more shocking?
cards.answer: It creates an unhurried, conversational tone that makes the sudden violence feel more shocking by contrast.

title: National Governing Bodies & Technology in Sport
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-studies

cards.front: Name the five functions of a National Governing Body given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Promoting participation / Developing coaching and officiating / Organising competitions / Amending rules / Supporting anti-doping

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says technology in sport affects.
cards.answer: Athletes / Officials / Spectators / The sport itself

cards.front: Why did rugby union's law-makers restrict high tackles?
cards.answer: To improve player safety by reducing dangerous contact with the head and upper body.

cards.front: How do instrumented mouthguards help protect rugby players?
cards.answer: They measure head impacts and alert medical staff to a possible concussion.

cards.front: Name the six drivers of counter-urbanisation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Rising car ownership / Motorway expansion (M25) / Early home computing / Desire for cheaper houses / Better schools / Quieter quality of life

cards.front: Name the four drivers of re-urbanisation since 2000 given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Inner-city regeneration projects / Rise of knowledge-economy jobs / Lifestyle preference for short commutes / Conversion of warehouses, mills and offices into apartments

cards.front: Why did suburbanisation hollow out city-centre high streets?
cards.answer: Retail and services followed people out to the suburbs, leaving city centres emptier.

cards.front: Why did Manchester's inner-city population fall from 766,000 in 1931 to 393,000 by 2001?
cards.answer: The city lost manufacturing jobs from the 1970s, while suburbanisation and counter-urbanisation pulled families and professionals out.

cards.front: Name the six selection methods the lesson describes businesses using to choose new staff.
cards.answer: CV / Application form / Interview / Tests / Group activities / References

cards.front: Name the four areas of employment law the lesson says all UK businesses must follow.
cards.answer: Protection from discrimination / Right to a contract / Holidays / Hours of work

cards.front: Why do businesses often use several selection methods together rather than just one interview?
cards.answer: Because a single interview can miss bad hires — good talkers are not always good workers.

cards.front: Why does good staff development improve employee retention?
cards.answer: Because employees see a future in the business, giving them a reason to stay rather than leave.

cards.front: Name the three key groups of Roman religious officials the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Pontifices — guardians of religious law and calendar / Augures — readers of the auspices / Haruspices — readers of entrails
items: Pontifices — guardians of religious law and calendar

cards.front: Name the three extraordinary legal privileges the lesson says Vestal Virgins received.
cards.answer: Could own property / Could make wills / Could travel in public without a male guardian
items: Could travel in public without a male guardian

cards.front: Why did the college of augurs effectively have the power to veto public actions in Rome?
cards.answer: Because no significant Roman undertaking, like a battle or election, could proceed without favourable auspices declared by the augurs.

cards.front: Why do some scholars think the Pythia's trance at Delphi had a genuine physical cause?
cards.answer: Geological surveys found fault lines and ethylene gas traces in the spring water, a substance that can induce hallucination.

title: Religious Experience, Design and Cosmological Arguments
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: According to al-Ghazali, what four qualities must the cause of the universe have?
cards.answer: Timeless / Uncaused / Immensely powerful / Personal

cards.front: What three things do Muslims point to as evidence that religious experience is a real encounter with Allah, not just imagination?
cards.answer: Consistency of experience across cultures and centuries / Moral transformation it produces / Extraordinary lives it has galvanised
items: Consistency of experience across cultures and centuries

cards.front: Why does Richard Dawkins argue that religious experiences aren't evidence for a real divine agent?
cards.answer: The human brain evolved to detect patterns and agency, producing vivid experiences of presence even when no real agent exists.

cards.front: How is the Islamic design argument different from Paley's watchmaker analogy?
cards.answer: Paley's is a philosophical argument from analogy, but the Islamic argument is grounded in Qur'anic theology — Allah states creation is his sign.

cards.front: Name the three real-world examples of forgiveness given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gee Walker forgiving her son's killers / The Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa / The Amish school shooting forgiveness
items: Gee Walker forgiving her son's killers
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa

cards.front: Name the two names of Allah relating to forgiveness given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) / Ar-Rahman (the Most Merciful)

cards.front: Why do some Christians distinguish between forgiveness and reconciliation?
cards.answer: Because forgiveness is always required, but reconciliation may not be possible or safe, so a victim can forgive without rebuilding the relationship.

cards.front: How can forgiveness and justice coexist according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Forgiveness is a personal decision to let go of anger, while justice holds people accountable, so a criminal can be forgiven yet still serve their sentence.

title: The Battle of Stirling Bridge: Historic Environment 2027
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three ground features of the Stirling Bridge site the lesson says you must describe.
cards.answer: Narrow wooden bridge over the Forth / Soft carse inside a loop of the river / Abbey Craig, a mile north of the bridge
items: Narrow wooden bridge over the Forth
Soft carse inside a loop of the river
Abbey Craig, a mile north of the bridge

cards.front: What three consequences followed the Scottish victory at Stirling Bridge, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Wallace became Guardian of Scotland / Andrew Moray died from his wounds / Edward returned and beat Wallace at Falkirk
items: Andrew Moray died from his wounds
Edward returned and beat Wallace at Falkirk

cards.front: Why did Wallace and Moray wait until half the English army had crossed the bridge before attacking?
cards.answer: So seizing the bridgehead would cut the English army in two, trapping the vanguard on the soft carse with no help.

cards.front: Why were the English knights unable to fight effectively once trapped inside the river loop?
cards.answer: Their warhorses floundered on the soft carse, the causeway couldn't hold formation, and the river hemmed them in on three sides.

cards.front: Name the five sections of the recommended essay structure for the exam response.
cards.answer: Introduction / Paragraph 1 - the quotation itself / Paragraph 2 - wider evidence / Paragraph 3 - context and purpose / Conclusion

cards.front: Name the three levels on which isolation operates in the novel.
cards.answer: Physical - Eel Marsh House cut off by the causeway and marshes / Emotional - Kipps isolated by the community's refusal to explain / Psychological - his supernatural experiences set him apart from others
items: Physical - Eel Marsh House cut off by the causeway and marshes
Emotional - Kipps isolated by the community's refusal to explain
Psychological - his supernatural experiences set him apart from others

cards.front: Why does Hill present secrets as dangerous throughout the novel?
cards.answer: Secrets fester and grow more powerful with time, always eventually surfacing, shown through Mrs Drablow's papers and the hidden truth about Nathaniel.

cards.front: How does Jennet's grief create a moral paradox in the novel?
cards.answer: Jennet kills children because she lost her own child, replicating on others the very suffering that destroyed her.

cards.front: Name the four ways the main characters respond to the impending raid in Act 2.
cards.answer: Osborne: quiet acceptance / Stanhope: fierce control / Hibbert: desperate evasion / Raleigh: naïve willingness

cards.front: Why does Stanhope quietly decide not to censor Raleigh's letter after all?
cards.answer: Hearing the letter's genuine admiration moves him, letting his guard down despite the war making vulnerability feel dangerous.

cards.front: What personal function does reading Alice's Adventures in Wonderland serve for Osborne right before the raid?
cards.answer: It lets him escape into a fantasy world rather than face the reality of the next day's danger.

cards.front: Name the four pathways the lesson gives for energy transferring between stores.
cards.answer: Heating / Radiation / Electrical working / Mechanical working

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says engineers can improve a device's efficiency.
cards.answer: Lubrication (reducing friction) / Streamlining (reducing air resistance) / Thermal insulation

cards.front: How can you find the speed of an object falling from height h, ignoring air resistance?
cards.answer: Set GPE lost equal to KE gained (mgh = ½mv²); the masses cancel, giving v = √(2gh).

cards.front: Why is a falling object's real speed slightly less than the value calculated using v = √(2gh)?
cards.answer: Air resistance dissipates some of the energy as thermal energy in the air, so less converts to kinetic energy.

cards.front: Name the four benefits a motivated workforce gives a business, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Higher productivity / Better staff retention / Improved quality / Stronger customer service

cards.front: Name the four non-financial methods of motivation the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Management style / Greater responsibility / Training / Fringe benefits

cards.front: Why can high pay alone fail to keep staff motivated long-term?
cards.answer: Once pay covers basic needs, workers usually want interesting work, respect and the chance to grow, not just money.

cards.front: How does poor motivation increase costs for a business?
cards.answer: It causes higher absenteeism, higher staff turnover and more scrap or rework, all of which cost money.

cards.front: Name the three contemporary poems studied in this Home & Place lesson, with their poets.
cards.answer: Peckham Rye Lane by Amy Blakemore / In Wales, Wanting to be Italian by Imtiaz Dharker / Us by Zaffar Kunial
items: Peckham Rye Lane by Amy Blakemore
In Wales, Wanting to be Italian by Imtiaz Dharker

cards.front: Name the three different tones the lesson describes across Blakemore, Dharker and Kunial's poems.
cards.answer: Blakemore: exuberant and sensory / Dharker: wry and self-deprecating / Kunial: quieter and philosophical

cards.front: Why does Dharker use humour in 'In Wales, Wanting to be Italian'?
cards.answer: To explore the absurdity of wanting to belong somewhere she has no real connection to.

cards.front: How does the pronoun 'us' show both belonging and exclusion in Kunial's poem?
cards.answer: It is simultaneously a warm term of family and community, and a divisive term separating 'us' from 'them'.

title: Reform Acts and the expansion of the franchise 1832-1928
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three reasons historians give for why women won the vote in 1918.
cards.answer: Women's vital war effort (munitions, nursing, transport) / WSPU had suspended militancy for patriotic service / Need to re-enfranchise servicemen who lost residency-based votes
items: Women's vital war effort (munitions, nursing, transport)
WSPU had suspended militancy for patriotic service
Need to re-enfranchise servicemen who lost residency-based votes

cards.front: Name the four militant tactics the lesson says suffragettes used.
cards.answer: Smashing windows / Chaining themselves to railings / Arson attacks on post boxes and buildings / Hunger strikes in prison
items: Arson attacks on post boxes and buildings

cards.front: Why did industrialisation create pressure for electoral reform before 1832?
cards.answer: A rapidly growing urban working class had no representation, and fear of unrest like the French Revolution made MPs nervous about ignoring calls for change.

cards.front: Why did Disraeli's government extend the vote to working-class men in 1867?
cards.answer: Disraeli calculated the newly enfranchised working class would be grateful and vote Conservative, though this proved partly wrong.

title: Normans, Jews and Medieval Traders, c1066–c1500
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four key factors the lesson uses to compare medieval migrant groups.
cards.answer: Institutions / Religion / Economic influences / Attitudes

cards.front: Name the three similarities the lesson gives between Normans, Jewish migrants and Hanseatic/Flemish migrants.
cards.answer: All relied on royal protection / All faced the legal label of alien in some form / All faced periods of hostility from the population
items: All faced the legal label of alien in some form
All faced periods of hostility from the population

cards.front: How did Norman migration after 1066 lead to the creation of Middle English?
cards.answer: Norman French became the language of court and law while ordinary people kept speaking English, and over centuries the two languages mingled into Middle English.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to say medieval Jews were freely tolerated until the sudden 1290 expulsion?
cards.answer: Royal taxation rose steadily after 1200, the 1190 massacres showed protection was thin, and Edward I's failed 1270s reforms show a long deterioration, not sudden change.

cards.front: Name the three loose ends the lesson says are left unresolved at the play's end.
cards.answer: Hero's silence / Claudio's inadequate penance / Don John's delayed punishment

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says comic conventions require.
cards.answer: obstacles overcome / marriages / dancing

cards.front: Why do some see Claudio's remorse as questionable rather than genuine?
cards.answer: Because he shows the same passivity and obedience to orders that originally led him to shame Hero.

cards.front: Why does the play's formally happy ending still feel uneasy?
cards.answer: Because the audience has witnessed Hero's destruction, Leonato's betrayal, and Claudio's fragile love, undermining the formal happiness.

cards.front: Name the three top party bodies Stalin sat on at once, giving him unmatched oversight of party life.
cards.answer: Politburo / Orgburo / Secretariat

cards.front: Name the four leadership rivals who could have succeeded Lenin in 1924.
cards.answer: Leon Trotsky / Grigory Zinoviev / Lev Kamenev / Nikolai Bukharin

cards.front: Why did Stalin's doctrine of Socialism in One Country appeal to many party members?
cards.answer: It offered a cautious, realistic message to people exhausted by civil war, positioning Stalin as a patriot rather than a reckless adventurer.

cards.front: How did the Lenin Enrolment of 1924 help Stalin's rise to power?
cards.answer: It brought hundreds of thousands of new working-class, ideologically untrained members who saw Stalin as Lenin's loyal, humble disciple.

cards.front: Name the four stages of Henry V's epic structure, in the order they occur.
cards.answer: Invocation (the Muse of fire) / Preparation for war (Acts 1-2) / The campaign itself (Acts 3-4) / Peace and marriage (Act 5)

cards.front: Name the five major speeches that form Henry V's structural spine, in order.
cards.answer: Tennis balls response (Act 1) / Harfleur speech (Act 3) / Harfleur threat (Act 3) / St Crispin's Day speech (Act 4) / Wooing of Katherine (Act 5)

cards.front: Why is the Chorus's apology about the stage's limitations ('wooden O') paradoxical?
cards.answer: By admitting the stage cannot show France or Agincourt, Shakespeare shows how language and the audience's imagination can fill the gap.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare pair each of Henry's public speeches with a complicating moment?
cards.answer: So the audience admires Henry's rhetorical skill while also being invited to question whether his words are honest.

title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four arguments the lesson gives in favour of the death penalty.
cards.answer: Acts as the ultimate deterrent / Provides retribution for the most serious crimes / Permanently protects society from dangerous criminals / Principle of utility may support it if it saves more lives than it takes
items: Provides retribution for the most serious crimes
Permanently protects society from dangerous criminals
Principle of utility may support it if it saves more lives than it takes

cards.front: Name the five arguments the lesson gives against the death penalty.
cards.answer: Violates the sanctity of life / Innocent people may be wrongly executed / Does not allow for reformation / Reduces the state to the level of the murderer / Evidence shows it doesn't deter crime better than prison
items: Innocent people may be wrongly executed
Reduces the state to the level of the murderer
Evidence shows it doesn't deter crime better than prison

cards.front: Why might prison fail to achieve reformation, according to critics?
cards.answer: Critics argue prisons can be 'universities of crime', where offenders learn new criminal skills instead of reforming.

cards.front: How can community service serve both the deterrence and reformation aims of punishment?
cards.answer: The offender must give up their time, which deters, while the work helps them develop skills and a sense of responsibility, which reforms.

title: Global Urbanisation & the Rise of Megacities
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the five push factors the lesson gives for rural-to-urban migration in LICs.
cards.answer: Poor harvests from drought or soil exhaustion / Lack of healthcare / Few schools beyond primary level / Low wages from subsistence farming / Conflict or land disputes
items: Poor harvests from drought or soil exhaustion

cards.front: Name the four pull factors the lesson gives for migration to growing cities.
cards.answer: Chance of paid work in factories or services / Better hospitals and universities / Mains water and electricity / Hope of a better future for children
items: Chance of paid work in factories or services
Hope of a better future for children

cards.front: Why does rural-to-urban migration tend to follow established routes, with relatives joining relatives?
cards.answer: The first migrant takes the biggest risk, but afterwards others follow the same path using contacts from relatives, radio or social media.

cards.front: Why is Lagos able to grow at a much faster rate than London did during its industrial growth?
cards.answer: Lagos is going through the same sprawl-and-migration process as London did, but compressed into fifty years instead of two hundred.

title: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the eight aspects of the Eightfold Path.
cards.answer: Right Understanding / Right Intention / Right Speech / Right Action / Right Livelihood / Right Effort / Right Mindfulness / Right Concentration

cards.front: What three types of suffering does the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta identify?
cards.answer: Obvious physical and mental pain / Suffering caused by change / Subtle suffering of conditioned existence

cards.front: Why does the Buddha's teaching compare the Four Noble Truths to a medical diagnosis?
cards.answer: Like diagnosing an illness, they identify suffering, find its cause, confirm a cure exists, and prescribe the treatment.

cards.front: How do sila, samadhi and panna support each other in the Threefold Way?
cards.answer: Ethical behaviour (sila) creates the conditions for meditation (samadhi), which in turn deepens wisdom (panna).

cards.front: Name the three goddesses who descend to bless Ferdinand and Miranda in Prospero's wedding masque.
cards.answer: Iris / Ceres / Juno

cards.front: The 'Our revels now are ended' speech works on three levels — what are they?
cards.answer: the masque has ended / all life is temporary / theatre itself is an illusion

cards.front: How does Prospero defeat Caliban's conspiracy without using violence?
cards.answer: He sets out fine 'glistering apparel' that Stephano and Trinculo cannot resist stealing, then sends spirit dogs to chase them away.

cards.front: How does the epilogue reverse the power dynamic Prospero held throughout the play?
cards.answer: Having given up his magic, the once-powerful master magician becomes a powerless supplicant, depending entirely on the audience's applause to be set free.

cards.front: Name the five stages of the product life cycle in order.
cards.answer: Research & development / Introduction / Growth / Maturity / Decline

cards.front: Name the five extension strategies the lesson lists for delaying decline.
cards.answer: Updating packaging / Adding more or different features / Changing the target market / Advertising / Price reduction

cards.front: Why might a business still be making a loss during the introduction stage of the PLC?
cards.answer: Sales grow slowly, price may be set low, and heavy advertising costs mean revenue hasn't caught up yet.

cards.front: Why can the Boston Matrix wrongly label an iconic product like the Rolls-Royce Phantom as a Dog?
cards.answer: It only uses two axes, so it ignores things like profit margin, brand value and strategic importance.

title: Case Studies: Bristol Mid-20th Century and Asian Leicester from 1945
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four people who founded the West Indian Development Council in Bristol.
cards.answer: Roy Hackett / Owen Henry / Audley Evans / Prince Brown

cards.front: Name the three inner Bristol areas where the Caribbean community grew from 1948.
cards.answer: St Paul's / Easton / Montpelier

cards.front: Why did the 1980 St Paul's riot happen?
cards.answer: Frustration with policing, particularly ‘sus law’ stop-and-search, led to the riot in Bristol's St Paul's area.

cards.front: Why was the economic impact of East African Asian migration on Leicester so rapid?
cards.answer: As 'twice migrants' they arrived as established business families with British passports, English skills and capital, not starting from zero.

cards.front: Name the three universal characteristics that make up the Three Marks of Existence.
cards.answer: Dukkha (suffering/unsatisfactoriness) / Anicca (impermanence) / Anatta (no fixed self)

cards.front: What are the five khandas that make up what we call 'the self' according to anatta?
cards.answer: physical form / feelings / perceptions / mental formations / consciousness

cards.front: Why does dependent origination mean suffering can cease?
cards.answer: Because suffering arises from causes and conditions, removing those conditions makes suffering cease, giving the logical basis for the Third and Fourth Noble Truths.

cards.front: What does the defeat of Mara beneath the Bodhi tree symbolise?
cards.answer: It symbolises overcoming the three poisons—greed, hatred and delusion—that bind beings to the cycle of rebirth, allowing Enlightenment.

cards.front: Name the three categories the lesson uses to classify feedback in sport.
cards.answer: Emotional tone (positive or negative) / Source (intrinsic or extrinsic) / What it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance)
items: What it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance)

cards.front: Name the four sensory channels through which intrinsic feedback travels.
cards.answer: Proprioception / Vision / Touch / Hearing

cards.front: Why is knowledge of results motivating but limited as a learning tool?
cards.answer: It gives a clear signal like an improved time, but doesn't explain why the result happened or how to change it.

cards.front: Why should beginners not be given detailed knowledge of performance?
cards.answer: Overloading a beginner with detailed KP can cause confusion and undermine their motivation.

title: Musical Styles & Technology Through the Decades
subject: music-technology

cards.front: Name the six building blocks used to describe any musical style.
cards.answer: Structural sections / Form / Melody / Harmony / Rhythm / Instrumentation

cards.front: Name the five major technological developments of the 1980s.
cards.answer: Digital sampler / Digital tape / Digital synthesis / MIDI / Portastudio

cards.front: How did multitrack recording help soul and rock develop their complex sounds in the 1960s?
cards.answer: Multitrack recording made layered arrangements possible, allowing soul and rock to build more complex, layered sounds.

cards.front: How did the digital sampler change what hip hop producers could do in the 1980s?
cards.answer: The digital sampler let hip hop producers record short audio clips and replay them, so they could borrow and rearrange existing recordings.

cards.front: The lesson gives four pieces of evidence for Russell's argument that class determines destiny. Name them.
cards.answer: The policeman scene (same offence, different treatment) / Factory vs university (same genes, different outcomes) / Mickey's cry 'I could have been him!' / The Narrator's final question (superstition or class?)
items: The policeman scene (same offence, different treatment)
Factory vs university (same genes, different outcomes)
Mickey's cry 'I could have been him!'
The Narrator's final question (superstition or class?)

cards.front: Name the four key themes the lesson identifies in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Class & Social Inequality / Superstition & Fate / Motherhood / Violence & Its Roots

cards.front: Why does Mrs Lyons's love for Edward become distorted and lead to violence?
cards.answer: Her love is distorted by guilt and fear, causing her to slap Edward, spy on him and attempt to stab Mrs Johnstone.

cards.front: How does the lesson explain violence in the play as coming from class rather than individual character?
cards.answer: Violence escalates as a symptom of inequality — unemployment and desperation push Mickey into crime, culminating in the shooting.

cards.front: Name the four hazards of UV radiation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sunburn / Premature skin ageing / Increased risk of skin cancer / Eye damage/cataracts

cards.front: Name the three precautions used to reduce X-ray hazards in medical settings.
cards.answer: Lead aprons protect staff / Exposure times are minimised / Number of scans is limited

cards.front: Why does a higher frequency EM wave always have a shorter wavelength in a vacuum?
cards.answer: Since v = fλ and all EM waves travel at the same fixed speed in a vacuum, frequency and wavelength are inversely related.

cards.front: How do microwaves heat up food in a microwave oven?
cards.answer: Water molecules in the food absorb the microwave energy, causing them to heat up.

title: Brahman, the Three Aspects of the Divine and the Deities
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three main deities in Hindu cosmology and their roles.
cards.answer: Vishnu (preserver) / Shiva (destroyer-transformer) / Brahma (creator)

cards.front: Name the four features Shiva is depicted with.
cards.answer: Crescent moon / Ganges flowing from his matted hair / A trident / Seated in meditation
items: Ganges flowing from his matted hair

cards.front: Why is Shiva's role as destroyer not seen as pure annihilation?
cards.answer: Because his destruction represents transformation, not annihilation - the old must end for the new to begin.

cards.front: Why do avatars of Vishnu appear on earth?
cards.answer: Avatars are manifestations of Vishnu who descend to earth to restore dharma when cosmic order is under threat.

cards.front: Name the three fearful reactions Spider shows at Eel Marsh House that prove the haunting is real.
cards.answer: Cowering / Whimpering / Refusing to enter certain rooms

cards.front: Name the three things Sam Daily does to try to help Kipps against the Woman in Black.
cards.answer: Offers veiled warnings / Lends his dog Spider for company / Eventually reveals the full truth of the curse
items: Lends his dog Spider for company
Eventually reveals the full truth of the curse

cards.front: Why does the gap between young and old Kipps create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The reader knows young Kipps's confidence and courage will end in devastation, undercutting every moment of his assurance.

cards.front: Why does Sam Daily fail to save Kipps even though he knows the full truth about the curse?
cards.answer: Hill shows that knowing about the danger isn't enough, because some evils cannot be reasoned with, understood, or defeated.

cards.front: Name the three emotional responses Scrooge shows during Stave 2.
cards.answer: Weeps seeing his lonely childhood self / Feels delight at Fezziwig's party / Begs the ghost to show him no more after Belle scene
items: Weeps seeing his lonely childhood self
Begs the ghost to show him no more after Belle scene

cards.front: Why does young Scrooge find comfort in books like Ali Baba and Robinson Crusoe?
cards.answer: These fictional companions replaced real human relationships, foreshadowing how adult Scrooge substitutes money for love and connection.

cards.front: How does the Ghost of Christmas Past's dual nature as both child and old man reflect the nature of memory?
cards.answer: It reflects the paradox that memory belongs to the past yet has the power to change the present.

cards.front: According to the lesson, name three things drivers do when petrol prices spike, reducing quantity demanded.
cards.answer: Combine journeys / Take public transport more often / Walk short distances

cards.front: Name three examples of normal goods given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Holidays / Restaurant meals / New clothes

cards.front: What is the income effect of a price rise on demand?
cards.answer: A price rise reduces the real purchasing power of a consumer's income, so they can afford to buy less overall.

cards.front: Why can a rise in car insurance prices reduce demand for cars themselves, even though the car's price hasn't changed?
cards.answer: It raises the total cost of motoring, making cars less attractive overall even though the car's own price is unchanged.

cards.front: Name the three reasons Mr Collins gives for wanting to marry Elizabeth.
cards.answer: Lady Catherine de Bourgh advised it / He needs a wife for his position as a clergyman / He feels he should compensate the Bennets for inheriting their estate
items: Lady Catherine de Bourgh advised it
He needs a wife for his position as a clergyman
He feels he should compensate the Bennets for inheriting their estate

cards.front: In his first proposal, what three reasons does Darcy give for why he shouldn't love Elizabeth?
cards.answer: Her family's low connections / Her mother's vulgarity / Her younger sisters' impropriety

cards.front: Why is Darcy's letter described as the novel's climax or turning point?
cards.answer: It reveals the truth about Wickham and Jane, forcing Elizabeth to re-evaluate Darcy, Wickham and herself, starting both characters' change.

cards.front: Why does Austen place Darcy's letter at the novel's midpoint?
cards.answer: To create a before/after divide, where events before the letter are shaped by misunderstanding and events after are a process of correction and growth.

cards.front: Name the five indicators used to measure uneven development in the UK.
cards.answer: Employment / Income / Life expectancy / Educational attainment / Access to digital infrastructure (broadband)

cards.front: Name the four causes of uneven development in the UK.
cards.answer: Geographical location / Economic change / Infrastructure / Government policy

cards.front: Why has 'levelling up' UK regional inequality proved hard to achieve?
cards.answer: The agglomeration effect self-reinforces: skilled workers cluster where jobs are and companies cluster where skilled workers are, pulling growth to London.

cards.front: How did deindustrialisation lead to the North East having the UK's lowest disposable income?
cards.answer: Coal mining, shipbuilding and steel collapsed from the 1970s, and replacement industries like call centres offered fewer, lower-paid jobs.

cards.front: Name the five key past participles for food given in the lesson.
cards.answer: gegessen (eaten) / getrunken (drunk) / bestellt (ordered) / gefunden (found) / geschmeckt (tasted)

cards.front: Name the six typical German dishes given in the food culture section.
cards.answer: Schweinshaxe (pork knuckle) / Bratwurst (fried sausage) / Currywurst / Döner Kebab / Kartoffelsalat (potato salad) / Schnitzel (breaded cutlet)

cards.front: Why does the lesson say using 'Könnte ich...?' instead of 'Ich möchte...' is useful in the restaurant role-play?
cards.answer: Because 'Könnte ich...?' is a polite conditional form that shows higher-level language than the basic 'I would like' phrases.

cards.front: How does the phrase 'es hat mir (nicht) geschmeckt' differ from 'es hat ... geschmeckt' when describing a meal?
cards.answer: 'Es hat ... geschmeckt' describes how the food tasted, while 'es hat mir (nicht) geschmeckt' says whether you liked or disliked it.

title: Joining & Finishing — Permanent and Temporary Fixings
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three heat-treatment processes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Annealing / Hardening / Tempering

cards.front: Name the four finishing methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Painting / Plating / Polishing / Chemical treatment (etching)

cards.front: Why is brazing more suitable for steel and copper than for aluminium?
cards.answer: Brazing needs high temperatures, and aluminium has a melting point too low, so it would melt instead of staying solid.

cards.front: How does hardening make steel hard but brittle?
cards.answer: Steel is heated to the correct temperature then rapidly quenched, which traps its structure in a hard but brittle state.

title: London’s response: government, Royals, propaganda and ‘Dig for Victory’
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four things Mass Observation diaries from 1940-41 recorded about how the Blitz actually felt.
cards.answer: Looting in bombed shops / Panic on the worst nights / Shelter trekking by middle-class families to outer suburbs / Class resentment over West End private deep shelters
items: Shelter trekking by middle-class families to outer suburbs
Class resentment over West End private deep shelters

cards.front: Name the six foods that rationing covered by 1942.
cards.answer: Meat / Butter / Sugar / Cheese / Eggs / Tea

cards.front: Why did the government keep cinemas, dancehalls and theatres open during the Blitz instead of closing them for safety?
cards.answer: Home Intelligence reports concluded closing leisure venues for safety would damage morale more than the casualties from occasional bombing.

cards.front: Why was the documentary London Can Take It! widely shown in the United States?
cards.answer: It packaged one night of the Blitz as cheerful resilience to push American sympathy towards the British cause.

cards.front: Name the three methods of good customer service the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Product knowledge / Customer engagement / Post-sales services

cards.front: Name the three ICT developments the lesson says have transformed customer service.
cards.answer: Websites / E-commerce / Social media

cards.front: Why does strong product knowledge help build customer trust?
cards.answer: Staff who really understand what they sell save the customer time, turning an uncertain shopper into a confident one.

cards.front: Why is customer engagement deliberately kept low at a budget supermarket?
cards.answer: The business competes on price rather than experience, so it keeps staff to a minimum to keep prices low.

cards.front: Name the four rhetorical techniques the lesson says Antony uses in his funeral speech.
cards.answer: Ironic repetition of 'honourable men' / Rhetorical questions / Emotional appeals / Physical props

cards.front: What are the four balanced clauses Brutus uses in his funeral speech to justify killing Caesar?
cards.answer: As Caesar loved me, I weep for him / As he was fortunate, I rejoice at it / As he was valiant, I honour him / As he was ambitious, I slew him
items: As Caesar loved me, I weep for him
As he was fortunate, I rejoice at it
As he was valiant, I honour him
As he was ambitious, I slew him

cards.front: How does Cassius's line about 'ages hence' create metatheatre in Act 3, Scene 1?
cards.answer: He imagines future audiences re-enacting the assassination, which mirrors Shakespeare's real audience watching the scene, blurring Rome and the Elizabethan theatre.

cards.front: Why does Antony shake hands with the conspirators after finding Caesar's body?
cards.answer: It is a calculated political act that appears to signal acceptance while he privately views them as butchers, hiding his true intentions.

cards.front: Name the three couples who celebrate together at the close of The Merchant of Venice.
cards.answer: Bassanio and Portia / Gratiano and Nerissa / Lorenzo and Jessica

cards.front: What four things has Jessica done that make her assimilation into Belmont uneasy?
cards.answer: Betrayed her father / Stole his money / Traded her dead mother's ring for a monkey / Converted to Christianity
items: Traded her dead mother's ring for a monkey

cards.front: How does the ring trick reassert Portia's authority over the marriage?
cards.answer: She has saved Antonio, outperformed the male lawyers, and now proves she controls the marriage by testing the rings.

cards.front: Why does Lorenzo's speech on music seem aimed at Shylock?
cards.answer: Shylock earlier complained about music, so the speech marks him as unfit for treasons and excluded from Belmont's harmonious community.

title: Jewish Beliefs about God and Sacred Place
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What four functions does the synagogue serve in Jewish life?
cards.answer: Prayer / Study / Celebration / Assembly

cards.front: What four things does a Jewish family do at home to mark the start of Shabbat?
cards.answer: Light candles / Say kiddush (blessing over wine) / Bless the challah (bread) / Abstain from creative work

cards.front: Why does Judaism forbid artistic representations of G-d?
cards.answer: Because G-d is transcendent, and images or statues would reduce the infinite to something finite, misrepresenting G-d's true nature.

cards.front: Why is the kippah worn by many Jewish men?
cards.answer: It is a visible reminder that G-d is above, watching over the person's actions.

cards.front: Name the four types of evidence the lesson gives for reconstructing past climate.
cards.answer: Global temperature records / Ice cores / Tree rings (dendrochronology) / Paintings and diaries

cards.front: Name the three natural causes of climate change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Variations in solar output / Changes in the Earth's orbit / Volcanic activity

cards.front: How do ice cores preserve a record of past atmospheres?
cards.answer: Snow falls in annual layers and compresses into ice, trapping tiny air bubbles from the year it fell.

cards.front: Why have sea levels risen since 1900?
cards.answer: Warmer water expands in volume and ice sheets are melting, both adding water and raising sea levels.

cards.front: What three types of cause does the lesson give for insomnia?
cards.answer: Psychological cause (nervous system arousal) / Physical cause (sleeping environment) / Biological cause (brain damage)

cards.front: What four sleep hygiene strategies does the lesson list for improving sleep?
cards.answer: Consistent bedtime and wake-up time / Dark, quiet and cool bedroom / Avoiding screens, caffeine and heavy meals before bed / Using the bed only for sleep and rest
items: Avoiding screens, caffeine and heavy meals before bed
Using the bed only for sleep and rest

cards.front: How do sleep diaries help work out which type of insomnia a person has?
cards.answer: By recording sleep and waking times each night, showing whether the problem is falling asleep or staying asleep.

cards.front: Why is it important to match insomnia treatment to its specific cause rather than treating insomnia as one single problem?
cards.answer: Because insomnia can stem from different causes, so a treatment that works for one cause won't fix a different underlying cause.

cards.front: Name the four aims of punishment described in Muslim thought.
cards.answer: Protection / Retribution / Deterrence / Reformation

cards.front: Name the three reasons non-religious thinkers give for opposing capital punishment.
cards.answer: Violates the right to life / Risks executing an innocent person / Lacks reliable evidence it deters crime
items: Lacks reliable evidence it deters crime

cards.front: Why do many Muslims see crime as a distraction from focusing on Allah?
cards.answer: Because a person absorbed in wrongdoing has stopped directing their life towards worship and obedience.

cards.front: Why do Muslims see punishment as a form of justice?
cards.answer: Because it restores balance after a wrong and is needed to protect people and deter future crime.

cards.front: Name the four independent lines of evidence the lesson gives for climate change.
cards.answer: Ice cores / Temperature records / Sea level measurements / Satellite data (sea ice/glaciers)

cards.front: Name the three sources of methane emissions the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Livestock digestion (enteric fermentation) / Rice paddies / Landfill sites

cards.front: Why does methane have a stronger warming effect per molecule than CO2, despite being present in lower concentrations?
cards.answer: Each molecule of methane traps substantially more heat than a molecule of CO2.

cards.front: Why can reducing methane emissions produce quicker effects on warming than reducing CO2 emissions?
cards.answer: Methane breaks down in the atmosphere in about a decade, whereas CO2 persists for centuries.

cards.front: Name the five types of force and stress covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Bending / Torsion / Shear

cards.front: Name the four reinforcement methods given for strengthening materials.
cards.answer: Lamination / Folding / Webbing / Fabric interfacing

cards.front: Why is corrugated card strong in compression?
cards.answer: Its fluted inner layer acts as a series of small arches that resist compression.

cards.front: Why is a triangulated frame, like a roof truss, efficient at distributing loads?
cards.answer: Triangles cannot be deformed without changing the length of a side.

cards.front: What three broad historical periods do sociologists use to study how family relationships have changed?
cards.answer: Pre-industrial / Industrial / Contemporary

cards.front: Name the four contemporary family issues studied by sociologists mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Quality of parenting / Relationships between teenagers and adults / Care of disabled and elderly family members / Arranged marriage
items: Care of disabled and elderly family members

cards.front: How did industrialisation change the family's economic role?
cards.answer: Paid work moved into factories and offices, separating public and private spheres and shifting the family from a unit of production to a unit of consumption.

cards.front: How does the functionalist view explain historical changes in family relationships?
cards.answer: The family adapted by shedding functions it could no longer perform efficiently to schools, hospitals and the state, keeping primary socialisation and personality stabilisation.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says the pre-frontal cortex is heavily involved in.
cards.answer: Decision-making / Planning ahead / Controlling impulses / Regulating personality and social behaviour

cards.front: According to Damasio et al.'s reconstruction, which four areas of Gage's brain were left untouched by the rod?
cards.answer: Movement / Sensation / Speech / General intelligence

cards.front: Why does visual agnosia show that seeing and recognising an object are separate brain processes?
cards.answer: A person can see an object clearly but not name it, yet recognise it instantly by touch, showing recognition needs separate processing areas.

cards.front: Why does prosopagnosia suggest the brain has a dedicated area for face processing?
cards.answer: The deficit only affects recognising faces, while other objects are still recognised normally, suggesting face processing is separate from general object recognition.

cards.front: The lesson names three types of bullying. What are they?
cards.answer: Physical (hitting, pushing) / Verbal (name-calling, threats) / Cyber (online harassment)

cards.front: Name the five cultural factors covered in the lesson that can affect health and wellbeing.
cards.answer: Religion / Gender roles and expectations / Gender identity / Sexual orientation / Community participation

cards.front: Why might some religious beliefs negatively affect a person's healthcare?
cards.answer: Some religious practices may restrict access to certain treatments, like blood transfusions, or create conflict with family or community beliefs.

cards.front: How does workplace discrimination affect a person economically?
cards.answer: It can limit career progression and reduce a person's income.

cards.front: Name the four earldoms held by the Godwin family and who held each one, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Harold – Wessex / Tostig – Northumbria / Gyrth – East Anglia / Leofwine – south-east

cards.front: Name the four rival claimants to the English throne in January 1066.
cards.answer: Harold Godwinson / William of Normandy / Harald Hardrada / Edgar the Aethling

cards.front: Why was Harold's alleged oath to William on holy relics so damaging to his reputation?
cards.answer: Swearing on holy relics was sacred and binding, so breaking the oath was a sin against God, giving William moral as well as political authority.

cards.front: Why did Harold's decision during the 1065 Northumbrian revolt weaken his family's power?
cards.answer: Harold refused to support his brother Tostig and accepted Morcar as earl instead, losing Godwin control of Northumbria though securing Mercian loyalty.

cards.front: Name the four other anthology poems the lesson pairs with 'A Song' for comparison.
cards.answer: Looking at Your Hands (Martin Carter) / Poem for My Love (June Jordan) / Flirtation (Rita Dove) / The Perseverance (Raymond Antrobus)

cards.front: Name the three stages the six stanzas of 'A Song' move through.
cards.answer: Stanzas I–II: past contentment with the trade / Stanza III: present tense, lover's departure / Stanzas IV–VI: distress once he is gone
items: Stanzas I–II: past contentment with the trade
Stanza III: present tense, lover's departure
Stanzas IV–VI: distress once he is gone

cards.front: How does Williams make the storm metaphor in the final stanza of 'A Song' feel powerful?
cards.answer: The sea stays calm with only a soft breeze, so the storm existing nowhere but her soul shows her turmoil is entirely internal.

cards.front: Why does Williams withhold pathetic fallacy when describing the waves in 'A Song'?
cards.answer: The waves stay calm and 'faithless', offering no pity, so nature refuses to mirror her feelings, emphasising her isolation.

cards.front: Name the five main jobs of an operating system, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Providing a user interface / Managing memory and multitasking / Managing peripherals through drivers / Managing users and their access rights / Managing files
items: Managing users and their access rights

cards.front: Name the three examples of utility software given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Encryption software / Defragmentation / Data compression

cards.front: How does an operating system make it seem like several programs run at the same time?
cards.answer: It gives each running program a tiny slice of processor time in turn, switching between them so quickly they appear simultaneous.

cards.front: Why does data compression count as utility software rather than a job the operating system does by default?
cards.answer: It performs a task—shrinking files by encoding them to use fewer bits—that the operating system does not handle on its own.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the information processing model, in order.
cards.answer: Input / Decision Making / Output / Feedback

cards.front: What three sources of sensory information does the lesson give for the input stage?
cards.answer: Eyes tracking ball and defenders / Ears picking up teammate shouts / Proprioceptors sensing body position and balance
items: Proprioceptors sensing body position and balance

cards.front: Why does Hick's Law say a player with more shot options takes longer to decide?
cards.answer: Reaction time increases with the number of possible responses available, so more choices slow down decision making.

cards.front: Why is a beginner's output slower than an expert's when performing the same skill?
cards.answer: The beginner must consciously direct each element of the movement, while the expert's motor programme runs automatically.

cards.front: Name the eight Boolean algebra laws covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Identity / Annulment (Null) / Idempotent / Complement / Commutative / Associative / Distributive / Absorption

cards.front: What three symbols does standard Boolean notation use for AND, OR and NOT?
cards.answer: dot (·) for AND / plus sign (+) for OR / overbar for NOT

cards.front: Why does the Absorption law let A + A·B simplify straight to A?
cards.answer: Because A is already in the expression, any term multiplying A by something else adds no new information and is redundant.

cards.front: Why does it matter when a Boolean expression simplifies down to a constant like 1?
cards.answer: It means the output never changes, so the circuit can be replaced with a simple connection to logic HIGH or LOW instead of gates.

title: Your Fieldwork Approach for 2027: Change Over Time and Sphere of Influence

cards.front: Name the four change-over-time enquiries listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Retail patterns vs historical data / Weather vs same period in an earlier year / River or coastal landforms vs historical maps/photos / Land use today vs earlier date
items: Weather vs same period in an earlier year
River or coastal landforms vs historical maps/photos
Land use today vs earlier date

cards.front: Name the five sphere-of-influence enquiries listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Urban area's reach over rural hinterland / Externalities of a major event or venue / Visitor pressure at a honeypot site / Impact of a distinctive landscape feature / Impact of a river catchment on flood risk
items: Urban area's reach over rural hinterland
Externalities of a major event or venue
Visitor pressure at a honeypot site
Impact of a distinctive landscape feature
Impact of a river catchment on flood risk

cards.front: Why must the historical evidence in a change-over-time enquiry cover the same location as your fieldwork site?
cards.answer: Because the comparison only works if the 'then' evidence describes the same place, otherwise differences may not show real change.

cards.front: How do you judge the impact side of a sphere-of-influence enquiry?
cards.answer: By identifying the effects found and sorting them into positive impacts (like extra income) and negative impacts (like erosion or litter).

title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Robotics
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson names four possible parties who could be liable when an AI system causes harm. What are they?
cards.answer: The company that developed the AI software / The organisation that deployed the system / The engineer who designed the training process / The dataset provider
items: The company that developed the AI software
The organisation that deployed the system
The engineer who designed the training process

cards.front: What three benefits of AI, machine learning and robotics does the lesson give?
cards.answer: AI diagnosing diseases from scan images / Machine learning detecting banking fraud in milliseconds / Robots doing dangerous or repetitive tasks
items: AI diagnosing diseases from scan images
Machine learning detecting banking fraud in milliseconds
Robots doing dangerous or repetitive tasks

cards.front: How can an adversarial attack cause an AI safety failure?
cards.answer: Small, imperceptible changes to an input can make a well-trained image classifier confidently produce a completely wrong output.

cards.front: Why can developers of deep learning systems not explain a specific prediction for a specific individual?
cards.answer: Predictions come from thousands of weighted calculations that cannot be easily summarised into human-readable rules.

title: Uneven Global Development & Strategies to Address It
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: Name the three broad categories of causes of uneven development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Physical (climate, hazards, landlockedness, resources) / Historic (colonialism, conflict) / Economic (trade, debt, technology)

cards.front: Name the three types of international aid described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Bilateral (government to government) / Multilateral (through organisations like the World Bank or UN) / Non-governmental (charities such as Oxfam)
items: Multilateral (through organisations like the World Bank or UN)

cards.front: How did colonialism cause lasting uneven development in former colonies?
cards.answer: Colonialism reshaped economies to serve imperial powers, leaving newly independent countries with infrastructure built for export rather than internal development.

cards.front: Why do rich-country tariffs on processed cocoa or cotton keep poorer countries poor?
cards.answer: The tariffs make processed exports less profitable, encouraging poorer countries to sell raw materials instead at lower prices.

title: Hernán Cortés and the road to Tenochtitlán
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What did Cortés's expedition consist of when he set out from Cuba in February 1519?
cards.answer: Around 11 ships / About 500-600 soldiers / 16 horses / A handful of artillery pieces

cards.front: What three different ways have historians interpreted La Malinche's role in the conquest?
cards.answer: Spanish chroniclers praised her as essential to Cortés's success / Mexican nationalists condemned her as a traitor / Modern historians see her as enslaved, making strategic choices to survive
items: Spanish chroniclers praised her as essential to Cortés's success
Mexican nationalists condemned her as a traitor
Modern historians see her as enslaved, making strategic choices to survive

cards.front: Why did Moctezuma II likely receive Cortés peacefully at Tenochtitlán in November 1519?
cards.answer: He was probably applying a diplomatic strategy, welcoming a potentially powerful ally while assessing the threat he posed.

cards.front: How did the Cholula massacre affect other cities on the road to Tenochtitlán?
cards.answer: It sent a clear message that resistance would be met with overwhelming violence, showing Cortés's willingness to use terror politically.

cards.front: Name the five types of intermarket relationship the lesson says you must identify when tracing a ripple effect between markets.
cards.answer: Substitute goods / Complementary goods / Joint supply / Competitive supply / Derived demand

cards.front: Name the three uses of farmland given as the example of composite demand for land.
cards.answer: Growing crops / Building houses / Renewable energy projects (solar farms)

cards.front: Why did car manufacturers have to pause production lines during the global semiconductor shortage?
cards.answer: Cars need chips to be built, so demand for chips is derived from demand for cars; fewer chips meant fewer cars could be made.

cards.front: Why does a sharp rise in demand for cheese push up the price of drinking milk?
cards.answer: Milk is in composite demand; more milk is diverted to cheese production, leaving less available for drinking, raising its price.

title: Domino Theory: Eisenhower and Kennedy in Vietnam
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: According to Eisenhower's April 1954 domino warning, which five countries could fall to communism next if South Vietnam fell?
cards.answer: Laos / Cambodia / Thailand / Burma / Indonesia

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson give for why US involvement in Vietnam deepened despite Diem's failures?
cards.answer: Domino Theory framed setbacks as regional collapse / Kennedy feared another perceived defeat / Advisers' combat-like role made escalation feel gradual
items: Domino Theory framed setbacks as regional collapse
Advisers' combat-like role made escalation feel gradual

cards.front: How was the Strategic Hamlets programme meant to defeat the Vietcong?
cards.answer: By moving peasants into fortified compounds, physically separating them from the Vietcong to cut off insurgents' food, intelligence and recruits.

cards.front: How did Thich Quang Duc's self-immolation affect American opinion of Diem?
cards.answer: A press photograph of his self-immolation spread worldwide and turned American opinion sharply against Diem's government.

title: Human Computer Interface (HCI) in Everyday Life
subject: it-ocr

cards.front: Name the four hardware considerations the lesson says shape HCI design.
cards.answer: Display type / Display size / Memory (RAM) / Processing power

cards.front: Name the three things a banking HCI must be, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Secure (two-factor authentication) / Accessible to customers of all ages / Able to handle sensitive transactions reliably
items: Accessible to customers of all ages
Able to handle sensitive transactions reliably

cards.front: Why is the HCI on an embedded system like a washing machine often minimal?
cards.answer: Because the device has a single dedicated purpose, so only a few buttons and an LED display are needed.

cards.front: Why must HCI in entertainment devices like games consoles respond instantly?
cards.answer: Because users expect a smooth, enjoyable experience from entertainment technology.

title: Principles of Training: SPORT and FITT
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson suggests introducing variety to avoid tedium in training.
cards.answer: Different training methods / Different environments / Different partners / Mixed session structures

cards.front: Name the three training types the lesson matches to specific sports.
cards.answer: Continuous training for a long-distance runner / Circuit training with punching drills and HIIT for a boxer / Static stretching sessions for a gymnast
items: Continuous training for a long-distance runner
Circuit training with punching drills and HIIT for a boxer
Static stretching sessions for a gymnast

cards.front: How does the duration (Time) of a session affect which energy system is stressed?
cards.answer: A 30-minute continuous run mainly stresses the aerobic system, while 10-second interval sprints stress the anaerobic system.

cards.front: Why is consistent, year-round training more effective than intense bursts followed by long rest periods?
cards.answer: Because reversibility means fitness losses occur once training stops, so maintaining a training stimulus prevents cardiovascular adaptations being lost.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says high unemployment is costly.
cards.answer: Individuals lose income and purpose / Government pays more benefits and collects less tax / The economy wastes productive capacity
items: Government pays more benefits and collects less tax

cards.front: Name the five conflicts between economic objectives described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Growth vs inflation / Growth vs balance of payments / Unemployment vs inflation / Growth vs environmental sustainability / Growth vs income equality

cards.front: Why can economic growth conflict with environmental sustainability?
cards.answer: More output generally means more energy use, transport and waste, increasing carbon emissions and resource use.

cards.front: Why can economic growth conflict with income equality?
cards.answer: During strong growth, profits and returns to capital often rise faster than wages for low-income workers, widening the gap between rich and poor.

cards.front: Name the four primary research methods named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Questionnaires / Interviews / Trialling / Focus groups

cards.front: Name the four secondary research sources named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Newspapers and magazines / The census / Websites / Internal data

cards.front: Why can a focus group give a biased result?
cards.answer: A small group of 6–10 people is used, and one loud voice can dominate and skew the reactions captured.

cards.front: Why do businesses like Tesco and Netflix use both qualitative and quantitative data?
cards.answer: Quantitative data shows what customers do, while qualitative data explains why, so together they answer the full question.

cards.front: Why does Shelley present Victor's guilt over Justine's death as a moral crime equal to the Creature's violence?
cards.answer: Victor feels the 'never-dying worm' of guilt but only weeps and agonises, doing nothing to save the innocent Justine from execution.

cards.front: How does the framing of Justine show a change in the Creature's behaviour?
cards.answer: It shows the Creature has learned from human society how to manipulate justice, mirroring the cruelty it has received.

cards.front: Name the six long-term sources of finance given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Personal savings / Venture capital / Share capital / Loans / Retained profit / Crowd funding

cards.front: What three factors determine the best source of finance for a business?
cards.answer: The amount needed / How quickly it must be repaid / The implications for ownership and control
items: How quickly it must be repaid
The implications for ownership and control

cards.front: Why does a bank loan make cash-flow planning easier than an overdraft?
cards.answer: A loan has a fixed sum and a predictable repayment schedule, unlike an overdraft which can be withdrawn at short notice.

cards.front: Why might a brand-new start-up struggle to get an overdraft or trade credit?
cards.answer: It has no trading history, so banks are cautious about lending and suppliers may demand upfront payment until trust is established.

cards.front: Name the four logical operators covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: AND / OR / NOT / XOR

cards.front: What are the three common mistakes to avoid in truth table questions, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Confusing XOR with OR / Filling in only the output column for combined gates / Mixing up Boolean notation with arithmetic
items: Filling in only the output column for combined gates
Mixing up Boolean notation with arithmetic

cards.front: Why must you add an intermediate column when building a truth table for the expression NOT A AND B?
cards.answer: Because NOT A must be worked out first before it can be combined with B in the AND stage, so each stage needs its own column.

cards.front: Why are universal gates like NAND practically important for hardware manufacturers?
cards.answer: They let manufacturers produce one gate type in bulk and use it to build every other gate, simplifying chip design and cutting costs.

title: Key Sociological Concepts and the Sociological Approach
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the eight core concepts of GCSE Sociology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Culture / Norms / Values / Roles / Status / Identity / Sanctions / Cultural diversity

cards.front: What three social processes does the lesson give as examples of how society reproduces itself?
cards.answer: Socialisation / Social control / Social stratification

cards.front: Why do sociologists say a social role exists independently of the individual who fills it?
cards.answer: Because the bundle of norms attached to a role, like teacher, existed before that person took it and remains after they leave.

cards.front: How do interactionists explain where social structures come from?
cards.answer: They argue structures are produced by the countless daily face-to-face interactions in which individuals negotiate meaning.

cards.front: Name the three categories of test data the lesson describes for testing input ranges.
