cards.front: Why is Easter treated as Christianity's central festival rather than Christmas?
cards.answer: Because Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15 that if Christ was not raised, Christian preaching and faith are useless.

cards.front: Why do Baptists and many evangelical Christians baptise adults rather than infants?
cards.answer: They see baptism as a public declaration of personal faith, made by full immersion, rather than a means of removing sin.

title: Context: Jacobean World, James I & Witchcraft
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three unnatural events Ross and the Old Man describe in Act 2, Scene 4 after Duncan's murder.
cards.answer: The sun is blocked out ('dark night strangles the travelling lamp') / A falcon is killed by a mousing owl / Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other
items: The sun is blocked out ('dark night strangles the travelling lamp')
A falcon is killed by a mousing owl
Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other

cards.front: According to Jacobean belief under the 1604 Witchcraft Act, what three things were witches thought capable of doing?
cards.answer: Controlling the weather / Cursing livestock / Foretelling the future

cards.front: Why does the falcon being killed by a 'mousing owl' in Act 2, Scene 4 show divine anger at Duncan's murder?
cards.answer: The owl (lower in the Chain of Being) killing the noble falcon (representing Duncan) allegorises a lesser being destroying a greater one, showing God's anger.

cards.front: How does the failure of the Gunpowder Plot help explain why Macbeth's regicide must fail?
cards.answer: The Plot's failure was seen as divine intervention protecting the anointed king, so Macbeth's murder of Duncan must also be destroyed to reassure the audience regicide can never succeed.

title: The Hurt Locker: Bigelow's Iraq Thriller
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three production companies that produced The Hurt Locker.
cards.answer: Voltage Pictures / Grosvenor Park Media / Film Capital Europe Funds

cards.front: What three camera positions does the opening pre-credits disposal sequence cut between?
cards.answer: A wide overhead shot / an extreme telephoto close-up from a rooftop / rapid rack-focus pulls scanning for threats
items: an extreme telephoto close-up from a rooftop
rapid rack-focus pulls scanning for threats

cards.front: Why does Bigelow use long telephoto lenses during the bomb-disposal sequences?
cards.answer: To compress space and create distance, positioning the spectator as an anxious, helpless observer rather than a participant.

cards.front: Why does The Hurt Locker structure itself as escalating disposal episodes rather than building to one climax?
cards.answer: Because bomb disposal has no narrative finish line, so each episode resets tension instead of resolving it.

cards.front: Name the four stages of a device's environmental impact given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Manufacture (mining, fabrication emissions) / Energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks) / Replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded) / Disposal (e-waste and toxic materials)
items: Energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks)
Replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded)

cards.front: Name the four types of intellectual property protection covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Copyright / Patents / Trademarks / Licencing

cards.front: How do cooling systems in data centres add to environmental impact?
cards.answer: They are needed to stop equipment overheating, but they themselves consume additional electricity and water.

cards.front: Why can long, complex privacy policies undermine genuine user consent?
cards.answer: They can obscure the true scope of what data collection and use users are actually agreeing to.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence the lesson pairs with the three eras of policing.
cards.answer: Tithing system (Saxon era) / Parish constable (Tudor era) / Metropolitan Police 1829 (modern era)

cards.front: What three things must a 16-mark thematic essay do?
cards.answer: Identify turning points / Identify continuities / Reach a substantiated conclusion

cards.front: How did the spirit of community-based enforcement survive after it was replaced?
cards.answer: It survived in the Peelian principle of 'policing by consent', even though community-based enforcement itself was replaced.

cards.front: How does the aim behind the Bloody Code connect to deterrence debates today?
cards.answer: Both share the same underlying purpose of punishment — deterring crime — linking the Bloody Code to modern deterrence debates.

cards.front: Name the four deliberate hardships the agoge used to toughen boys, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: Minimal food / Rough sleeping / Endurance tests / Organised fighting

cards.front: Name the five things a Spartan man had to contribute to his syssitia each month.
cards.answer: Barley meal / Wine / Cheese / Figs / A sum for condiments

cards.front: Why was helot labour essential to the Spartan warrior lifestyle?
cards.answer: Helots worked the land assigned to Spartiates, freeing them from manual labour so they could train as warriors continuously.

cards.front: Why did the Spartans reportedly declare war on the helots at the start of each year?
cards.answer: So that helot deaths, such as those during the krypteia, were technically not classed as murder.

cards.front: Name the three things Ed confesses to Christopher in Act 2.
cards.answer: Hiding the letters / Lying about Judy's death / Killing Wellington

cards.front: What five things does the lesson say make the journey to London terrifying for Christopher?
cards.answer: Crowds / Strangers / Unpredictable sensory environments / Trains / The Underground

cards.front: Why did Ed choose to tell Christopher his mother was dead rather than that she had left?
cards.answer: He wrongly believed saying she had died was kinder than telling Christopher she had chosen to leave him.

cards.front: How does Stephens contrast Judy's and Christopher's love when they reunite in London?
cards.answer: Judy shows emotional, demonstrative love by weeping and holding him, while Christopher's love is shown through competence and simply arriving.

cards.front: Name the three main types of system software given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Operating system / Utility programs / Device drivers

cards.front: Name the three example utility programs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: File compression tool / Disk cleanup tool / Encryption software

cards.front: Why is antivirus software classed as system software rather than application software?
cards.answer: Because its purpose is to maintain the health of the system, not to help the user complete a personal task.

cards.front: Why does a compiled program run faster than an interpreted one once it is finished?
cards.answer: Because the whole program is translated to machine code in advance, so no further translation is needed at run time.

cards.front: Name the four things a real fortress would have that Acton Burnell lacks.
cards.answer: A moat / A curtain wall of any strength / A gatehouse / Room for a garrison
items: A curtain wall of any strength

cards.front: In the exam answer, name the four features the lesson says to read as evidence about Edward's England.
cards.answer: Large windows and thin defences / The licence to crenellate / The barn parliament and statute / The builder's career

cards.front: Why did Edward grant licences to crenellate like Burnell's if they weren't needed for real defence?
cards.answer: By Edward's reign such licences were largely honours showing royal favour, so a licence said publicly that a man mattered to the king.

cards.front: Why did a merchants' debt law matter to a warrior king like Edward?
cards.answer: Edward's wars ran on credit from merchant-bankers, who would only lend and trade freely if debts could actually be collected, so the statute was war finance by other means.

title: Focuses of Worship and the Murti
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five focuses of Hindu worship covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: The many deities, the guru and elders / One God (personal or non-personal) / Holy land, hills and rivers / Sacred plants and animals / The murti as a representation of God
items: The many deities, the guru and elders
The murti as a representation of God

cards.front: What four things count as personal focuses of worship in Hindu practice?
cards.answer: Deities such as Vishnu, Shiva or Ganesha / The guru / The murti / Sacred places linked to a deity's story
items: Deities such as Vishnu, Shiva or Ganesha
Sacred places linked to a deity's story

cards.front: Why is worshipping many different deities not seen as contradictory in Hindu thought?
cards.answer: Because Hindu teaching holds that all deities are ultimately manifestations of the one Brahman.

cards.front: Why is Varanasi considered the most sacred city in Hinduism?
cards.answer: Because it lies on the Ganges and dying there is believed to bring moksha.

cards.front: Name the four criticisms intellectuals raised about the Party during the Hundred Flowers Campaign.
cards.answer: Party corruption / Privileges enjoyed by cadres / Poor treatment of intellectuals / Rigid application of Soviet-style policies

cards.front: What three methods did the Anti-Rightist Campaign use to enforce punishments?
cards.answer: Public denunciations / Political study sessions / Pressure on colleagues and family to denounce
items: Pressure on colleagues and family to denounce

cards.front: How did running the Anti-Rightist Campaign benefit Deng Xiaoping's later political career?
cards.answer: Running it efficiently with Mao's backing cemented his reputation as a loyal enforcer, aiding his rehabilitation after his own later purge.

cards.front: Why did the Anti-Rightist Campaign create a lasting chilling effect on Chinese intellectual life?
cards.answer: Intellectuals who avoided being labelled rightists learned that silence was safer than honest appraisal, so they stopped speaking out for a decade.

cards.front: Name the four safety features the lesson gives for protecting against mains electrical dangers.
cards.answer: Fuses in the live wire / Earth wires on metal-cased appliances / Circuit breakers / Double insulation on plastic-cased devices

cards.front: What are the potential differences between the three wire pairs in a plug (live-neutral, live-earth, neutral-earth)?
cards.answer: Live to neutral: about 230 V / Live to earth: about 230 V / Neutral to earth: about 0 V

cards.front: Why must a fuse be placed in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?
cards.answer: If it were in the neutral wire, a blown fuse would leave the live wire connected, so the casing could stay at 230 V, causing electrocution risk.

cards.front: Why does the UK use alternating current for its mains supply instead of direct current?
cards.answer: A.c. can be stepped up and down by transformers, which only work with a.c., allowing efficient high-voltage transmission and safe domestic use.

title: Plot and Structure: A Dystopian Two-Act Tragedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What are the six stages of the play's structural arc, from the opening scene to the epilogue?
cards.answer: Opening beach scene (childhood) / School integration scenes / Family fractures / Liberation Militia sequences / Hostage scene (brief hope) / Execution and epilogue

cards.front: Why does the dual-narrator device create dramatic irony in Noughts & Crosses?
cards.answer: Because the audience often knows more about each character's private feelings than the other character does.

cards.front: Why does Cooke use episodic structure to adapt the novel for the stage?
cards.answer: It allows him to compress years of narrative into stage time using short scenes marked by sound and lighting transitions rather than elaborate set changes.

title: A Divided Society: Prohibition, Crime, the Klan and the Red Scare
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three types of campaigners who pushed for Prohibition.
cards.answer: Anti-Saloon League / Women's Christian Temperance Union / Evangelical Protestant churches

cards.front: Name the four groups the revived Ku Klux Klan targeted.
cards.answer: African-Americans / Catholics / Jews / Recent immigrants

cards.front: Why did Prohibition create a huge illegal alcohol economy?
cards.answer: Most Americans did not want to give up alcohol, and only about 1,500 federal agents could not police a country that refused to be policed.

cards.front: Why did the WASP backlash of Prohibition, the Klan and immigration laws happen in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Urbanisation and the 1920 census made growing numbers of immigrants, Catholics, Jews and Black southerners visible, threatening rural Protestant dominance, so it reached for laws to reverse this.

title: The Skeletal System: Bones and Functions
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Name the six functions of the skeleton.
cards.answer: Support / Posture / Protection / Movement / Blood cell production / Storage of minerals

cards.front: How do muscles and bones work together to produce movement in sport?
cards.answer: Muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints.

cards.front: How does weight-bearing exercise affect bone strength over time?
cards.answer: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

cards.front: Name the four details Ishiguro uses to build the reader's suspicions in 'A Family Supper'.
cards.answer: Mother's death from fugu / Watanabe's murder-suicide / Father's belief his wife's death was no accident / The model battleship and talk of the pilot's 'final weapon'
items: Father's belief his wife's death was no accident
The model battleship and talk of the pilot's 'final weapon'

cards.front: Name the three symbols the lesson identifies in 'A Family Supper'.
cards.answer: The fugu fish / The empty rooms of the house / The old well the narrator believed haunted
items: The empty rooms of the house
The old well the narrator believed haunted

cards.front: How does the narrator's tone contribute to the story's ambiguity?
cards.answer: His calm, matter-of-fact tone even describing his mother's death or Watanabe's killings means nothing is flagged as alarming, leaving the reader unsure if suspicions are reasonable.

cards.front: Why does Ishiguro's use of a limited first-person narrator suit the story's themes?
cards.answer: Because the story is about failed understanding, the reader only knows what the son knows, and the son cannot fully read his father's intentions.

cards.front: Name the six minerals covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Calcium / Iron / Sodium / Fluoride / Iodine / Phosphorus

cards.front: Name the five ways given to minimise vitamin loss when cooking vegetables.
cards.answer: Use the minimum water possible / Steam rather than boil / Use short cooking times / Prepare vegetables just before cooking / Avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods
items: Avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods

cards.front: Why does eating too much sodium increase the risk of stroke and heart disease?
cards.answer: Excess sodium raises blood pressure (hypertension), which increases the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease.

cards.front: Why don't fat-soluble vitamins need to be eaten every day?
cards.answer: They are stored in the liver and body fat, so the body can draw on reserves instead of needing daily intake.

cards.front: Name the three types of maps the lesson gives for presenting spatial fieldwork data.
cards.answer: Choropleth map / Flow-line map / Proportional symbols map

cards.front: Name the five skills the lesson says a hand-drawn map should show.
cards.answer: Title / Scale bar / North arrow / Key / Accurate labelling

cards.front: Why must the categories in a pie chart add up to 100%?
cards.answer: A pie chart shows shares of a whole, so its segments must represent parts of one total.

cards.front: How does evaluating fieldwork differ from describing it?
cards.answer: Describing states what happened, while evaluating judges whether the method or data was reliable.

cards.front: Name the three types of force the lesson says police and army used against Soweto protesters.
cards.answer: Tear gas / Rubber bullets / Live ammunition

cards.front: As protests spread nationwide after Soweto, what three types of targets were attacked?
cards.answer: Schools burned / Government buildings attacked / Police stations stoned

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the Afrikaans decree as the trigger, not the cause, of the Soweto uprising?
cards.answer: Black Consciousness ideas had circulated in schools for years and students formed an action committee before the march, showing deeper organisation behind it.

cards.front: How did the Soweto uprising change the ANC exile leadership's view of resistance inside South Africa?
cards.answer: It showed resistance inside the country was self-generating, not dependent solely on direction from Lusaka, reconnecting the internal and external movements.

title: Planning Assets, Hardware, Software & File Management
subject: cambridge-nationals-creative-imedia

cards.front: Name the four things a creator should note about each asset during the planning stage.
cards.answer: what the asset is / whether it will be created, sourced from stock, or provided by client / who is responsible for obtaining or creating it / any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements
items: whether it will be created, sourced from stock, or provided by client
who is responsible for obtaining or creating it
any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements

cards.front: Name the six sub-folders a project's top-level folder structure might contain.
cards.answer: images / audio / video / graphics / exports / working-files

cards.front: Why is it important to list all required assets during the planning stage of a media project?
cards.answer: To prevent discovering at the editing phase that a critical file is missing, unavailable or in the wrong format.

cards.front: How can choosing the wrong software for an asset type affect the finished product?
cards.answer: It can lead to poor-quality outputs or unnecessary file conversions.

cards.front: Name the three ways fossils can be dated, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Position in rock layers (older strata lie deeper) / Radiometric dating techniques / Comparison with other fossils of known age
items: Position in rock layers (older strata lie deeper)
Comparison with other fossils of known age

cards.front: Name the five causes of extinction given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Climate change / New predators or competitors / New diseases / Habitat destruction / Catastrophic events

cards.front: Why is variation essential for natural selection to occur?
cards.answer: Without variation all individuals would respond identically to environmental pressures, leaving nothing for selection to act on.

cards.front: Why did the proportion of dark peppered moths increase during industrial pollution?
cards.answer: Soot darkened tree bark and killed lichens, so dark moths were better camouflaged, survived predation more and reproduced more.

title: Area of Study 4: Western Classical Tradition since 1910 — Unfamiliar Listening
subject: music-aqa

cards.front: Name the four movements of Bartók's Hungarian Sketches set for study (movement 3 is not included).
cards.answer: An Evening in the Village / Bear Dance / Slightly Tipsy / Swineherd's Dance

cards.front: Name the three pieces given in the British strand.
cards.answer: Peterloo Overture (Arnold) / Song for Athene (Tavener) / An Orkney Wedding, with Sunrise (Maxwell Davies)
items: An Orkney Wedding, with Sunrise (Maxwell Davies)

cards.front: How does Reich's Music for 18 Musicians change over any five-minute stretch of listening?
cards.answer: It changes very little, and only very gradually, even across a five-minute listen.

cards.front: What four income categories does the World Bank use to classify countries by GNI per capita?
cards.answer: Low-income / Lower-middle income / Upper-middle income / High-income

cards.front: Besides GNI and HDI, what four other measures does the lesson mention for judging development?
cards.answer: Literacy rates / Doctors per 1,000 people / Infant mortality / Access to safe water

cards.front: Why can China be called the world's second-largest economy but only a middle-income country per person?
cards.answer: China's total GDP is huge because of its large population, but dividing by that population gives a much lower per-capita figure.

cards.front: Why can a country's GDP grow quickly while quality of life or the environment gets worse?
cards.answer: GDP only measures market output and ignores unpaid care work, subsistence farming and environmental damage.

title: Holy Books, Angels, Predestination and Akhirah
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four earlier holy books Muslims believe Allah revealed before the Qur'an.
cards.answer: Tawrat / Zabur / Injil / Sahifah

cards.front: What is the sequence of events in Muslim teaching about Akhirah, from death onwards?
cards.answer: Death / Barzakh / Resurrection / Judgement of deeds / Jannah or Jahannam

cards.front: Why does belief in al-Qadr not remove a Muslim's moral responsibility for their actions?
cards.answer: Although Allah already knows what a person will choose, Muslims are still judged on the basis of their actual choices, not a fixed fate.

cards.front: How does Islamic teaching on judgement after death differ from Christian teaching?
cards.answer: Islam has no purgatory, only barzakh, and judgement rests on weighing deeds plus Allah's mercy rather than a mediating figure like Christ's atoning death.

title: Dramatic Methods: Cross-Cutting and Stage Directions
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three signals Turnly's stage directions combine to mark a leap in time between scenes.
cards.answer: A change in lighting state / A costume change visible to the audience / A change in the physical bearing of performers
items: A costume change visible to the audience
A change in the physical bearing of performers

cards.front: Name the three design approaches the lesson gives for realising the sea on stage in The Great Wave.
cards.answer: A soundscape of waves fading in and out / A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey / Gobos throwing fragmented water-light patterns
items: A soundscape of waves fading in and out
A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey

cards.front: Why is cross-cutting in The Great Wave described as a political act rather than just an editing device?
cards.answer: It refuses to let the audience follow only one storyline, forcing them to hold both in mind and creating dramatic irony and moral pressure.

cards.front: How can blocking at the start of a new scene signal that time has passed in The Great Wave?
cards.answer: Quick movement to a new position suggests arrival in a new moment, while stillness as lights rise signals the scene begins mid-thought.

cards.front: William James identified four features common to mystical experiences. Name them.
cards.answer: Noetic (conveys knowledge) / Transient (short-lived) / Passive (person feels acted upon) / Ineffable (impossible to put into words)

cards.front: Name the four forms of religious experience discussed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Conversion / Mystical experience / Charismatic and ecstatic experience / Visions

cards.front: How do believers respond to Hume's argument that belief in miracles is almost never justified?
cards.answer: They say his argument presupposes naturalism and begs the question, since if God exists, miracles are entirely possible.

cards.front: Why do non-believers think religious experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality?
cards.answer: Because experiences are shaped by culture — a Christian sees Jesus, a Muslim encounters Allah — suggesting belief shapes the experience.

cards.front: Name the five codes Barthes identified at work in narratives and texts.
cards.answer: Enigma code / Action code / Semantic code / Symbolic code / Referential code

cards.front: Name the three types of sign semioticians distinguish.
cards.answer: Iconic sign / Index sign / Symbolic sign

cards.front: Why do media producers use anchorage on an ambiguous image?
cards.answer: Because an image is polysemic and could be read in multiple ways, so text pins down the preferred meaning.

cards.front: What is a key limitation of the linear model of communication?
cards.answer: It implies a passive audience who simply receive meaning and ignores noise, mediation and context shaping understanding.

cards.front: Name the four areas the WJEC specification groups hospitality job roles into.
cards.answer: Front of house / Housekeeping / Kitchen brigade / Management

cards.front: Name the three management roles listed for a hospitality business.
cards.answer: Food and beverage manager / Housekeeping manager / Marketing manager

cards.front: Why is the kitchen brigade structure important in a busy restaurant serving hundreds of covers a night?
cards.answer: It prevents confusion and ensures dishes are prepared consistently, since everyone knows their role and who they report to.

cards.front: How do smaller kitchens adapt the traditional kitchen brigade hierarchy?
cards.answer: They use a simplified version, with the head chef taking on multiple senior roles instead of separate staff.

cards.front: Name the five key threats to biodiversity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Deforestation / Habitat destruction / Climate change / Pollution / Overexploitation

cards.front: Name the five kingdoms organisms are traditionally divided into.
cards.answer: Animals / Plants / Fungi / Protists / Prokaryotes (Bacteria)

cards.front: Why were dolphins historically classified as fish?
cards.answer: Their body shape resembled fish due to convergent evolution, before DNA evidence showed they are actually mammals.

cards.front: Why would a decline in UK pollinators threaten more than just the pollinators themselves?
cards.answer: Almost nine in ten flowering plant species depend on animal pollinators, so losing them would cascade through food chains, threatening crop yields and wild plants.

title: Methods of punishment: medieval to early modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names four specific mutilations used in Anglo-Saxon punishment. What were they and which crimes did they punish?
cards.answer: Hands cut off for theft / Ears cut off for false witness / Tongues cut off for slander / Blinding for particularly serious offences
items: Ears cut off for false witness

cards.front: Name the three aims of punishment that stayed constant across the medieval and early modern periods.
cards.answer: Deterrence / Retribution / Incapacitation

cards.front: How did the wergild system help prevent blood feuds?
cards.answer: It gave families a cash compensation alternative to private revenge, so violence between families was not needed to settle a killing.

cards.front: Why did authorities make executions at Tyburn public spectacles?
cards.answer: The public nature of execution was deliberate, meant to demonstrate the power of the state and deter crime among onlookers.

cards.front: Name the six themes the lesson gives for pairing poems in a comparison essay.
cards.answer: Power of nature / Effects of conflict / Power and control / Identity and place / Memory and loss / Attitudes to war

cards.front: Which three poem pairings does the lesson recommend for the theme 'memory and loss'?
cards.answer: Poppies + Remains / The Prelude + Kamikaze / War Photographer + The Emigrée

cards.front: Why should you plan your exam time to leave a few minutes spare at the end?
cards.answer: Planning, writing and proofreading are all part of a strong response, so time must be saved for checking.

cards.front: Why does 'eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers' show bitter irony in War Photographer?
cards.answer: It reflects Duffy's anger that society treats real human suffering as a momentary inconvenience rather than something to act on.

title: Binary, BCD and Decade Counters with 7-Segment Displays
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Which six segments are ON to display the letter 'A' on a 7-segment display?
cards.answer: a / b / c / e / f / g

cards.front: Which four segments are ON to display the letter 'C' on a 7-segment display?
cards.answer: a / d / e / f

cards.front: Why does a decade counter automatically reset after reaching binary 1001 (9)?
cards.answer: Internal logic detects the forbidden state above 9 and fires a reset pulse that clears all flip-flops back to 0000.

cards.front: How does wiring a chosen Q output to the 4017's reset pin (MR) create a modulo-N counter?
cards.answer: When that Q output goes HIGH it immediately triggers reset, so the counter only stably counts through the earlier states before starting again.

title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Name the four components that make up blood.
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Why do red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape and no nucleus?
cards.answer: The biconcave shape increases surface area and having no nucleus allows the cell to carry more haemoglobin.

cards.front: Why are heart transplants a limited treatment option for coronary heart disease?
cards.answer: They are limited by the availability of donor hearts and the risk of the immune system rejecting the transplant.

title: Post-war problems and the Treaty of Versailles
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of burden the Treaty of Versailles placed on Germany.
cards.answer: Territorial losses / Military restrictions / Financial costs (reparations) / Moral burden (war guilt)

cards.front: Name the four territorial losses Germany suffered under the Treaty of Versailles.
cards.answer: Alsace-Lorraine to France / Saar coalfield to League of Nations control / Parts of Posen to Poland / All overseas colonies
items: Saar coalfield to League of Nations control

cards.front: Why did the Dolchstosslegende (stab-in-the-back myth) matter politically for Weimar Germany?
cards.answer: It transferred blame for losing the war from the generals, where it belonged, to the politicians who signed the armistice and Versailles.

cards.front: Why did Weimar governments print money instead of paying reparations through taxation in the early 1920s?
cards.answer: Paying meant accepting Versailles, raising taxes on the rich and losing voters, so governments printed money instead.

title: The Norman Church, Lanfranc & the Domesday Book
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why the Church was essential to William's rule.
cards.answer: Educated administrators / Moral authority / A network of parish churches reaching every community
items: A network of parish churches reaching every community

cards.front: Name the four key areas of Church reform Lanfranc carried out.
cards.answer: Replacing English churchmen with Normans / Ending corruption (simony and pluralism) / Reorganisation of the Church hierarchy / Separating Church courts from secular courts
items: Separating Church courts from secular courts

cards.front: Why did Pope Alexander II support William's invasion of England?
cards.answer: Stigand's irregular, uncanonical position as Archbishop made the English Church seem corrupt, giving William religious justification for reform through conquest.

cards.front: How did the Domesday Book confirm feudal landholding?
cards.answer: Once ownership was recorded in Domesday it became legally fixed, settling disputes and stopping lords claiming more land than they were entitled to.

title: Tet, My Lai and the War at Home, 1968-70
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four events of 1968-70 that the lesson says broke the credibility of the Johnson administration and divided American society.
cards.answer: The Tet Offensive / Walter Cronkite's CBS broadcast / The My Lai Massacre / The Kent State shootings

cards.front: Name the four students killed in the Kent State shootings of 4 May 1970.
cards.answer: Allison Krause / Jeffrey Miller / Sandra Scheuer / William Schroeder

cards.front: Why did the Tet Offensive damage American public opinion even though it was a tactical US-South Vietnamese victory?
cards.answer: It so completely contradicted Westmoreland's 'light at the end of the tunnel' assurances that the gap between official optimism and televised reality opened the credibility gap.

cards.front: How did helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson Jr intervene during the My Lai massacre?
cards.answer: He landed between US troops and fleeing Vietnamese, ordered his crew to fire on their own side if they advanced, and rescued around eleven civilians.

cards.front: Name the six adverbs of frequency given for talking about how often you do hobbies in French.
cards.answer: toujours (always) / souvent (often) / quelquefois / parfois (sometimes) / de temps en temps (from time to time) / rarement (rarely) / ne…jamais (never)
items: de temps en temps (from time to time)

cards.front: Name the five opinion phrases given for saying how you feel about a free-time activity in French.
cards.answer: J'adore (I love) / J'aime (I like) / Je préfère (I prefer) / Je n'aime pas (I don't like) / Je déteste (I hate)

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use faire, jouer à or jouer de when talking about a hobby in French?
cards.answer: Use faire de for sports/activities, jouer à for games and team sports, and jouer de for musical instruments.

cards.front: How can you build a high-level sentence about a free-time activity for the writing or speaking exam?
cards.answer: Combine a time phrase, a frequency adverb, the activity, an opinion, and a reason introduced by parce que/car.

cards.front: Why does Clarke describe Catrin's birth using battle language like 'our first Fierce confrontation'?
cards.answer: To show that love and conflict are inseparable, even in the tender moment of birth.

cards.front: Why does Clarke leave the poem's ending argument unresolved?
cards.answer: To suggest the push and pull between a mother's need to protect and a daughter's need for independence is permanent.

cards.front: Name the three levels of the Edwardian class hierarchy described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Landed aristocracy (e.g. the Crofts) / Industrial capitalists (e.g. Birling) / The working class (e.g. Eva Smith)

cards.front: What three things does Priestley achieve by setting the play in 1912 instead of 1945?
cards.answer: Dramatic irony discredits Birling's capitalist worldview / The 1945 audience sees themselves reflected in the selfishness shown / Creates urgency that disasters will repeat if attitudes don't change
items: Dramatic irony discredits Birling's capitalist worldview
The 1945 audience sees themselves reflected in the selfishness shown
Creates urgency that disasters will repeat if attitudes don't change

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Eva Smith's death is a direct consequence of the class system?
cards.answer: As a working-class woman she depended entirely on her employers' goodwill, and every Birling systematically removed that goodwill, leading to her death.

cards.front: Why was the play's Moscow premiere in 1945 significant?
cards.answer: The Soviet Union was a socialist state, and its ideology aligned with Priestley's themes of collective responsibility and critique of capitalism.

title: Crime, Courts and Punishment in Edward's England
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five crimes classified as felonies in Edward I's England.
cards.answer: Murder / Robbery / Rape / Arson / Treason

cards.front: Name the three punishments used for petty offences (trespasses) in this period.
cards.answer: Fines / The pillory / The stocks

cards.front: Why did the Statute of Winchester require hedges and undergrowth near major roads to be cleared?
cards.answer: So that highwaymen had nowhere to hide, making roads safer for travellers.

cards.front: Why did English judges turn to trial by jury after 1215?
cards.answer: Because the Pope banned clergy from taking part in trial by ordeal, so jury trial replaced it.

title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the three dimensions across which the lesson says deviance is relative.
cards.answer: Time / Place / Situation

cards.front: Name the four sociological perspectives the lesson uses to explain the social construction of crime.
cards.answer: Functionalist / Marxist / Feminist / Interactionist

cards.front: Why did Durkheim argue that some level of crime is functional for society?
cards.answer: Punishing crime helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and reaffirms a society's shared values.

cards.front: According to interactionists like Becker, how does an act become deviant?
cards.answer: An act is not deviant in itself; it becomes deviant only when someone with power successfully applies a label to it.

title: Notting Hill, c1948–c1970: The Local Context
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four tactics Rachman used to drive sitting tenants out of regulated properties.
cards.answer: Removing front doors / Cutting off water and gas / Sending heavies to bang on doors at night / Moving in disruptive lodgers
items: Sending heavies to bang on doors at night

cards.front: Name the four dangerous conditions recorded by London County Council inspectors in Notting Hill HMOs.
cards.answer: Damp walls / Faulty wiring / Blocked drains / Broken sash windows

cards.front: Why did some Notting Hill streets end up with more and more Caribbean households over time?
cards.answer: Chain migration through family contacts produced clusters street by street, not a deliberate wish for segregation.

cards.front: Why couldn't Rachman's Caribbean tenants simply move elsewhere despite paying three or four times the regulated rent?
cards.answer: The colour bar meant no white landlord further west would let to them, so they had nowhere else to go.

cards.front: Name the four main drivers of Amazon deforestation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cattle ranching / Soya farming / Logging / Road building

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says monoculture farming changes ecosystem processes.
cards.answer: Cuts evapotranspiration, so regional rainfall falls / Exposes soil to erosion by heavy rain / Removes plant variety, leaving fewer food web species
items: Cuts evapotranspiration, so regional rainfall falls
Exposes soil to erosion by heavy rain
Removes plant variety, leaving fewer food web species

cards.front: How does farming on degraded rainforest soil end up causing algal blooms in rivers?
cards.answer: Degraded soil needs more fertiliser, which then runs off into rivers and triggers algal blooms downstream.

cards.front: Why does the London Array offshore wind farm still have an ecosystem cost despite producing clean energy?
cards.answer: Its construction creates noise that disturbs harbour porpoises and seabirds.

title: Waves: Properties, Wave Equation and Behaviour
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four properties used to describe any wave.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: What four things can happen when a wave reaches a boundary between two materials?
cards.answer: Reflected / Refracted / Transmitted / Absorbed

cards.front: Why does a floating object on water bob up and down but not travel along with the wave?
cards.answer: Because the particles of the medium oscillate about their rest positions, so only energy transfers, not matter.

cards.front: Why is the metal rod method more precise than the ripple tank for measuring wave speed?
cards.answer: Because water waves are affected by surface tension and depth variations, while the rod is not.

cards.front: Name the three consumer/medical applications the lesson gives for SMA wire.
cards.answer: Medical stents / Self-straightening eyeglass frames / Thermostatic valves

cards.front: Name the three composite materials described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) / Kevlar (para-aramid fibre) / Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP)

cards.front: Why does QTC change from an insulator to a conductor when compressed?
cards.answer: Compression forces the conductive metal particles close enough for electrons to tunnel through the gaps between them.

cards.front: Why is CFRP used for aircraft frames and racing car bodies?
cards.answer: Because it is stiffer and lighter than steel.

cards.front: The lesson gives four benefits person-centred care brings to workers and services. Name them.
cards.answer: Job satisfaction / Saves time / Saves money / Reduces complaints

cards.front: Why does ignoring a person's wishes make them less likely to follow a care plan?
cards.answer: Because the plan no longer reflects what they actually want, so it feels imposed rather than owned by them.

cards.front: Why do health and social care workers often feel greater job satisfaction with person-centred care?
cards.answer: They see individuals engaging with care plans and making real progress, which improves morale and knowing their work makes a difference.

title: Characters: Sheila, Eric, Gerald and Mrs Birling
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three actions Gerald takes after the Inspector leaves that show he aligns with the older generation.
cards.answer: Leads the investigation into the Inspector's identity / Telephones the infirmary / Tries to convince Sheila everything can return to normal
items: Leads the investigation into the Inspector's identity
Tries to convince Sheila everything can return to normal

cards.front: Name the three qualities the lesson uses to describe Mrs Birling's rigid character.
cards.answer: Cold / Snobbish / Completely lacking in empathy

cards.front: Why does Mrs Birling's insistence that the father of Eva's child be punished backfire on her?
cards.answer: She unknowingly condemns her own son Eric, who was the father of Eva's unborn child.

cards.front: Why is Gerald's relationship with Eva/Daisy presented as more than simple exploitation?
cards.answer: He genuinely cared for her, driven by attraction and some compassion, not just using her.

cards.front: Name the three main functions of protein given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Growth and repair of body tissues / Production of enzymes, hormones and antibodies / Secondary energy source when carbohydrate is depleted
items: Growth and repair of body tissues
Production of enzymes, hormones and antibodies
Secondary energy source when carbohydrate is depleted

cards.front: Name the four consequences of protein deficiency given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stunted growth / Poor wound healing / Muscle wasting / Impaired immunity

cards.front: Why does combining lentils and rice give a vegan a complete amino acid profile?
cards.answer: Lentils are low in methionine, which rice provides, and rice is low in lysine, which lentils provide.

cards.front: Why can a very low-fat diet cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiency even if those vitamins are eaten?
cards.answer: Without dietary fat, vitamins A, D, E and K cannot be absorbed in the small intestine.

cards.front: Name the three advantages of bus topology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cheap to install / Easy to add new devices / Simple to set up

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages of star topology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Central switch is a single point of failure / More cable required than bus topology / Cost of the central switch
items: Central switch is a single point of failure
More cable required than bus topology

cards.front: Why does performance degrade in a bus topology as more devices are added?
cards.answer: All devices share the same bandwidth, so collisions become more frequent on a busy network.

cards.front: Why can traffic on the internet's core infrastructure be automatically re-routed around a failed link?
cards.answer: Because it uses a partial mesh, giving devices multiple connections and alternative paths for data.

cards.front: Name the three traditional industries the lesson says were allowed to collapse under Thatcherism.
cards.answer: Steel / Shipbuilding / Coal mining

cards.front: Name the four things the post-war welfare state provided, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: The NHS / Council housing / Free education / Unemployment benefit

cards.front: How does Russell use the contrasting settings of the Johnstone and Lyons households to make his political point?
cards.answer: He shows the class divide physically — a cramped council estate versus a spacious private house — so the audience can see the argument, not just hear it.

cards.front: Why does Russell show the catalogue man and milkman cutting off Mrs Johnstone's credit?
cards.answer: To make the audience feel the humiliation of poverty and understand that it is structural, caused by the system, not her personal failings.

title: The Trinity, Creation, the Incarnation and the Last Days of Jesus
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: What are the three distinct roles the lesson gives for each person of the Trinity?
cards.answer: Father: source, creator and sustainer of all things / Son: reveals God by taking human form / Holy Spirit: guides and strengthens believers today
items: Father: source, creator and sustainer of all things
Son: reveals God by taking human form
Holy Spirit: guides and strengthens believers today

cards.front: Name the seven events of Jesus's last days listed in the lesson, from Last Supper to ascension.
cards.answer: Last Supper / betrayal / arrest / trial / crucifixion / resurrection / ascension

cards.front: How do the crucifixion and resurrection together confirm that Jesus is both human and divine?
cards.answer: The crucifixion shows his full humanity because he genuinely suffered and died; the resurrection shows his full divinity because only God has power over death.

cards.front: Why does the incarnation matter to Christians today?
cards.answer: It means God is not distant, since Jesus showed what God is like and, having experienced human life fully, can identify with human suffering.

cards.front: Name the nine two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen) given in the lesson.
cards.answer: in / an / auf / über / unter / vor / hinter / neben / zwischen

cards.front: Name the four dative contractions with articles given in the lesson.
cards.answer: in dem = im / an dem = am / zu dem = zum / zu der = zur

cards.front: How do you say how you travel somewhere in German?
cards.answer: Use mit plus the dative case, e.g. mit dem Zug (by train).

cards.front: How do you know whether to use dative or accusative with a two-way preposition?
cards.answer: Use dative for location, answering 'Wo?' (where), and accusative for movement to a place, answering 'Wohin?' (where to).

cards.front: Name the five key sequences the lesson identifies for micro/representation analysis in Wadjda.
cards.answer: The opening classroom recitation / The toy-shop bicycle reveal / The rooftop sequence with Wadjda and her mother / The Quran-competition prize-announcement / The closing street-traversal
items: The rooftop sequence with Wadjda and her mother

cards.front: Why does Al-Mansour keep the camera close to Wadjda's physical point of view with low angles and child-eye perspective?
cards.answer: So the spectator inhabits the restricted world from inside a child's experience, rather than observing it as an adult outsider.

cards.front: Why does the closing street-traversal represent ambiguous freedom rather than full liberation?
cards.answer: The structural conditions that restricted Wadjda remain in place, so the tracking shot shows agency within those conditions, not their removal.

cards.front: Name the three main forms of sponsorship in sport described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Financial sponsorship / Clothing and equipment sponsorship / Facility sponsorship

cards.front: Name the five types of media described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Television / Radio / Press / Internet / Social media

cards.front: How does commercialisation increase pressure on officials?
cards.answer: Broadcasters replay errors in slow motion and millions of viewers scrutinise decisions, which can affect officials' decision-making.

cards.front: Why do less commercially viable sports struggle to attract sponsorship?
cards.answer: Sponsors want visibility with large audiences, so sports with smaller audiences receive little sponsorship and become under-resourced compared to football or tennis.

cards.front: Why does a small campaign group's influence depend on consistency rather than numbers?
cards.answer: A minority has no power in numbers, so if its message changes or members disagree, the majority dismisses it as unreliable.

cards.front: How did the Time to Change campaign use both minority and majority influence to reduce stigma?
cards.answer: People sharing lived experience acted as a consistent minority challenging stereotypes, then public figures, schools and workplaces joining in made openness the majority norm.

cards.front: What five things does the lesson say you can compare between two poems in Part (ii)?
cards.answer: Tone / Imagery / Structure / Perspective / Ending

cards.front: How should you choose which points to compare in a Part (ii) answer?
cards.answer: Choose three or four strong points of comparison and develop them fully, rather than trying to cover everything.

cards.front: Why does 'same technique, different effect' analysis create the strongest comparisons?
cards.answer: It shows that both poems might use the same technique, like metaphor, but create opposite effects, revealing deeper understanding of methods.

title: Mary, Queen of Scots arrives in England, 1568–69
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four options did Elizabeth have for dealing with Mary in 1568?
cards.answer: Restore Mary by force / Allow Mary to return to France / Help Mary go to Spain / Keep Mary in England
items: Allow Mary to return to France

cards.front: What five overlapping reasons made Mary's presence in England a permanent threat?
cards.answer: Ready-made Catholic alternative / Political magnet for the disaffected / Foreign support / Marriage games / Public sympathy

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth rule out sending Mary to Spain in 1568?
cards.answer: King Philip II of Spain was already a potential enemy, so helping Mary reach him was even riskier than France.

cards.front: Why was the 'not proven' verdict at York and Westminster politically useful to Elizabeth?
cards.answer: It kept Mary tarnished enough to justify continued custody, but innocent enough that her royal status wasn't openly attacked.

cards.front: Name the three examples of giant covalent structures given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Diamond / Graphite / Silicon dioxide

cards.front: Name the three properties described for graphene in the lesson.
cards.answer: Very strong / Light / Excellent conductor of electricity and heat
items: Excellent conductor of electricity and heat

cards.front: Why do larger molecules tend to have higher boiling points than smaller molecules?
cards.answer: As molecules get bigger, the intermolecular forces between them become stronger, needing more energy to overcome.

cards.front: Why do giant covalent structures have very high melting points?
cards.answer: They contain millions of atoms joined by many strong covalent bonds, which all need breaking to melt them.

cards.front: Name the three men whose failures toward Hero the lesson describes in Act 4 Scene 1.
cards.answer: Claudio shames her / Don Pedro condemns her / Leonato wishes her dead

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things does Beatrice's 'Kill Claudio' reveal about her?
cards.answer: her fierce loyalty to Hero / her frustration at the patriarchal system / her willingness to use her relationship with Benedick
items: her frustration at the patriarchal system
her willingness to use her relationship with Benedick

cards.front: Why does Beatrice's cry 'O God, that I were a man!' expose structural injustice?
cards.answer: She has the moral authority to act against Claudio but lacks the social permission to do so because of her gender.

cards.front: Why is Don Pedro complicit in Hero's public shaming?
cards.answer: He supports Claudio's accusation and public shaming of Hero without ever investigating whether it is true.

title: Concerto Detective Work: Identifying Period and Style in an Unfamiliar Extract
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the five things the checklist tells you to listen for when identifying the period of an unfamiliar concerto extract.
cards.answer: Forces (size/make-up of ensemble) / Continuo / Dynamics / Harmony / Soloist writing

cards.front: What does the quick forces checklist say about ensemble size and period?
cards.answer: Harpsichord continuo audible = Baroque / Pairs of woodwind, horns, no harpsichord = Classical / Large strings, expanded brass/woodwind, possibly harp = Romantic
items: Pairs of woodwind, horns, no harpsichord = Classical
Large strings, expanded brass/woodwind, possibly harp = Romantic

cards.front: How does ritornello form work in a Baroque concerto movement?
cards.answer: A returning tutti theme played by the full orchestra alternates with contrasting solo episodes featuring the soloist's decorated version of similar material.

cards.front: Why is the presence of clarinets a useful clue when dating an unfamiliar concerto extract?
cards.answer: Clarinets were not used before the Classical period, so hearing them rules out Baroque and points to Classical or later.

title: The Liturgical Year and Catholic Sacraments
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven stages/seasons the Catholic liturgical year moves through, from Advent to Pentecost.
cards.answer: Advent / Christmas / Epiphany / Lent / Easter / Ascension / Pentecost

cards.front: Name the six key features of a Catholic church building given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Altar / Font / Lectern / Lady Chapel / Confessionals / Statues and votive candles

cards.front: Why does Lent last forty days?
cards.answer: It recalls Jesus' forty days of fasting in the wilderness before his public ministry began.

cards.front: Why is no Mass celebrated on Good Friday?
cards.answer: Because it is the day of the crucifixion; instead the Liturgy of the Word and Veneration of the Cross take place.

title: Film Music: Writing About an Unfamiliar Cue and Composing to a Brief
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: What musical choices does the lesson suggest for scoring a chase scene?
cards.answer: Fast tempo / Driving string or brass ostinato / Syncopated rhythms / Gradual crescendo and thickening texture / Mickey-moused sting for a near-miss

cards.front: What musical choices does the lesson suggest for scoring a quiet romantic reunion?
cards.answer: Slow tempo / Solo instrument like oboe or violin / Lyrical, mostly stepwise melody / Consonant harmony / Thin, gentle texture with soft dynamics / Brief swell as characters embrace
items: Solo instrument like oboe or violin
Thin, gentle texture with soft dynamics

cards.front: Why does the opening of John Williams' Jaws theme create dread?
cards.answer: A quiet, narrow semitone ostinato in low strings and tuba is repetitive, making it unsettling from the start.

cards.front: How does Bernard Herrmann's Psycho shower cue create terror using only strings?
cards.answer: High shrieking violin figures with rapid repeated bowing mimic stabbing, while dissonant, tightly-spaced pitches create harsh, jarring harmony.

title: Theories of Dreaming: Freud and Activation Synthesis
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three processes involved in Activation Synthesis Theory of dreaming.
cards.answer: Random activation / Sensory blockade / Movement inhibition

cards.front: Why is Freud's theory of dreaming seen as low in scientific validity?
cards.answer: Because the latent content is hidden, interpretations are subjective, and two psychoanalysts could disagree with no way to prove which is correct.

cards.front: How did Freud interpret Little Hans's phobia of horses?
cards.answer: As a repressed fear connected to his father, unconsciously displaced onto horses because the real fear was too disturbing to face.

title: Data on Crime and the Dark Figure
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the three main sources of crime data in England and Wales.
cards.answer: Police-recorded crime / The Crime Survey for England and Wales / Self-report studies
items: The Crime Survey for England and Wales

cards.front: Name the three reasons the police may not record a reported crime.
cards.answer: They judge it insufficiently serious / The victim withdraws the complaint / Recording practices are inconsistent

cards.front: Why does the Crime Survey for England and Wales consistently record higher crime levels than police-recorded figures?
cards.answer: It surveys victims directly, capturing many incidents that go unreported to and unrecorded by the police.

cards.front: Why do interactionists argue that crime statistics measure policing activity rather than actual criminal behaviour?
cards.answer: Because police have discretion over whom to stop, search, arrest and charge, so statistics reflect who is labelled criminal, not who offends.

cards.front: Why does Kelman refuse to give Harri a last-minute rescue at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: To confront the reader with the brutal reality that children die on estates like this and the system does nothing to prevent it.

cards.front: Why does Harri speak a form of pidgin English in the novel?
cards.answer: He blends Ghanaian English, London slang and his own inventions, communicating across cultures in a world that does not always listen.

cards.front: Name the four ways a person could become enslaved in Rome, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Capture in war / Born to an enslaved mother / Punishment for certain crimes / Enslaved through debt (abolished early)

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why Roman owners might free their slaves.
cards.answer: Reward for long service / Provision in the owner's will / Act of affection / To avoid supporting ageing slaves

cards.front: Why did wealthy Roman aristocrats often run their businesses through freedmen agents?
cards.answer: Because direct involvement in trade was considered beneath the social status of aristocrats, so freedmen conducted transactions on their behalf.

cards.front: Why does Tacitus's account of a household's execution after their master's murder (Annals 14.42) matter to historians?
cards.answer: It shows Roman anxiety about slave resistance and the legal violence used to maintain control over the enslaved population.

cards.front: Name the five things each Birling family member did that contributed to Eva Smith's death.
cards.answer: Birling sacked her / Sheila had her fired / Gerald used and abandoned her / Mrs Birling rejected her plea for help / Eric assaulted her and stole to support her
items: Mrs Birling rejected her plea for help
Eric assaulted her and stole to support her

cards.front: Name the three assessment objectives tested on the An Inspector Calls exam question.
cards.answer: AO1: understanding and response / AO2: analysis of language, form and structure / AO4: accurate written English
items: AO2: analysis of language, form and structure

cards.front: Why can the older Birlings not change while Sheila and Eric can?
cards.answer: The older generation are too embedded in the class system, too invested in status, and too emotionally closed to feel genuine remorse.

cards.front: Why does the class system stop Mrs Birling from helping Eva?
cards.answer: The class system creates a psychological distance between rich and poor, so Mrs Birling cannot see Eva as a fellow human being.

cards.front: Name the four freedoms the lesson lists as part of what underpins democracy.
cards.answer: Freedom to express opinions / Freedom to hold a religion / Freedom to assemble peacefully / Freedom to access information

cards.front: Name the four shortcomings critics point to when arguing the UK's democracy has significant weaknesses.
cards.answer: Unelected House of Lords has legislative power / First Past the Post limits impact of many votes / Falling voter turnout in recent elections / Uncodified constitution gives too much power to the executive
items: Unelected House of Lords has legislative power
First Past the Post limits impact of many votes
Falling voter turnout in recent elections
Uncodified constitution gives too much power to the executive

cards.front: Why is representative democracy used in most large modern societies like the UK?
cards.answer: Because it would be impractical for citizens to vote directly on every issue in a large, complex society, so elected representatives decide instead.

cards.front: Why is the rule of law essential for a genuine democracy?
cards.answer: Without it, a government could change or ignore laws to suit itself, allowing arbitrary power that harms citizens.

title: The Arms Race & the Hungarian Uprising 1956
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons Hungarians resented Soviet control before 1956.
cards.answer: Secret police terrorised the population / Living standards were poor / Hungarian resources were exported to the USSR
items: Hungarian resources were exported to the USSR

cards.front: Name the three demands made by Hungarian students and workers in 1956.
cards.answer: Free elections / Withdrawal of Soviet troops / Return of Imre Nagy

cards.front: Why did the development of ICBMs increase the danger of the nuclear arms race?
cards.answer: ICBMs meant each superpower could destroy the other in minutes, raising the stakes of any conflict.

cards.front: Why could the United Nations not take action over the Soviet invasion of Hungary?
cards.answer: Because the USSR used its veto in the Security Council, blocking any UN action.

cards.front: Name the four categories of cyber-security threats the lesson groups attacks into.
cards.answer: Denial of Service (DoS) / Hacking / Malware / Social engineering

cards.front: Name the six social engineering methods covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phishing / Pretexting / Baiting / Quid pro quo / Scareware / Shoulder surfing

cards.front: Why is a DDoS attack more powerful and harder to block than a single-machine DoS attack?
cards.answer: It uses many computers at once, often via a botnet, making it stronger and harder to block.

cards.front: Why is a grey hat hacker still breaking the law even when they report a vulnerability with good intentions?
cards.answer: Because they accessed the system without permission, and legality depends on permission, not just intent.

cards.front: How do the audience learn about the window deception, since Shakespeare never stages it directly?
cards.answer: Through Borachio's drunken confession to Conrade, which the Watch overhears.

cards.front: Why is the Watch overhearing Borachio's confession a 'turning point' that doesn't immediately save Hero?
cards.answer: The truth is now known, but Dogberry's incompetence delays it reaching Leonato before the wedding.

cards.front: Name the three things that can happen when a wave meets a material.
cards.answer: Transmitted (passes through) / Absorbed (energy transferred to material) / Reflected and scattered

cards.front: Name the three uses of convex lenses given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cameras / Eyes / Magnifying glasses

cards.front: Why does a red object appear dark when lit only by blue light?
cards.answer: The object only scatters red wavelengths, and there is no red light present for it to scatter.

cards.front: Why do thick, dense walls transmit less sound than thin partitions?
cards.answer: More of the sound wave's energy is absorbed within the denser material, so less passes through.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says Pip cannot do after Magwitch's revelation.
cards.answer: Cannot send Magwitch away (execution risk) / Cannot continue living as a gentleman (money is tainted) / Cannot return to the forge (burned bridge through snobbery)
items: Cannot continue living as a gentleman (money is tainted)
Cannot return to the forge (burned bridge through snobbery)

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson says have genuine moral worth because they never pretended to be anything other than what they are.
cards.answer: Joe / Biddy / Herbert

cards.front: Why does Magwitch want to 'make a gentleman' out of Pip?
cards.answer: Partly genuine gratitude for Pip's childhood kindness, and partly to prove a convict can create something the class system says he cannot.

cards.front: How does the repeated phrase 'in jail and out of jail' explain Magwitch's criminal past?
cards.answer: It emphasises the cycle of poverty and criminality that Victorian society created in Magwitch and then punished him for.

cards.front: Name St John Rivers' three roles that the lesson tracks in his arc.
cards.answer: Rescuer / Cousin / Suitor

cards.front: Name the five minor characters the lesson identifies as moral instruments.
cards.answer: Helen Burns / Miss Temple / Mrs Reed / Grace Poole / Adèle

cards.front: Why should Rochester's change across the novel be credited to Brontë's purpose rather than his own decision?
cards.answer: Brontë uses him to interrogate Victorian ideas of male dominance, so he is rebalanced by authorial design, not personal choice.

cards.front: Why must biographical detail about Brontë's life be avoided in a character paragraph?
cards.answer: It becomes a detour that wastes time unless the biography directly illuminates the specific line quoted.

title: Decline, Regeneration & Sustainability in UK Cities
subject: geography-edexcel-b

cards.front: Name the four main drivers of urban decline in UK cities.
cards.answer: De-industrialisation / De-population / De-centralisation of retail and services / Shift to e-commerce

cards.front: Name the three common regeneration approaches used in UK cities.
cards.answer: Flagship redevelopment / Culture-led regeneration / Education-led innovation districts

cards.front: Why does de-population often follow de-industrialisation in a city area?
cards.answer: When factory or industrial jobs leave, working-age residents move away too, leaving an older and poorer remaining population.

cards.front: Why is London's ULEZ charge seen as politically contentious?
cards.answer: The charge for entering with older vehicles falls hardest on lower-income drivers who cannot afford newer, cleaner cars.

cards.front: Name the four ways Nanima communicates with Meena despite not speaking English.
cards.answer: Touch / Food / Stories / The sheer force of her presence
items: The sheer force of her presence

cards.front: What sequence of events leads to Meena's broken leg at the stables?
cards.answer: Finds out Anita is going out with Sam / Tries to ride away / Is thrown from the horse / Spends a long time in hospital
items: Finds out Anita is going out with Sam
Spends a long time in hospital

cards.front: Why does Sam Lowbridge's 'This is our patch' outburst devastate Meena?
cards.answer: It shatters her illusion of belonging, proving that people like Sam will never accept her because of her race.

cards.front: How does the closing of Tollington's mines lead to racism against immigrant families?
cards.answer: Job losses and shrinking prospects create resentment which is misdirected onto immigrant families seen as competition for scarce resources.

title: Why and How Aims and Objectives Change
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five triggers the lesson gives for why business aims and objectives change.
cards.answer: Market conditions / Technology / Performance / Legislation / Internal reasons

cards.front: Name the four practical ways the lesson gives in which aims and objectives change.
cards.answer: Shift between survival and growth / Change which markets it operates in / Change the size of the workforce / Change the product range
items: Change which markets it operates in
Change the size of the workforce

cards.front: Why has technology encouraged businesses to set global expansion objectives?
cards.answer: Technology reduces barriers to international trade, making global expansion objectives feasible that weren't possible before.

cards.front: How does a merger or takeover change a business's objectives?
cards.answer: It changes the business's size, culture and capabilities, so objectives must be rebuilt from the ground up.

cards.front: Name the four types of keyword used in pseudocode, as listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Assignment / Input and output / Selection / Iteration

cards.front: Name the six standard symbols used in a flowchart.
cards.answer: Terminal / Process / Input/output / Decision / Sub program / Flow line

cards.front: Why is it useful to design an algorithm before writing real program code?
cards.answer: Planning first means you can spot mistakes in the logic before spending time typing real code.

cards.front: How does a trace table help you find a logic error in an algorithm?
cards.answer: You work through the algorithm step by step recording each variable's value, so the table shows exactly where the logic went wrong.

cards.front: Name the five prevention measures against cyber threats covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Biometric measures / Password systems / CAPTCHA / Email confirmation / Automatic software updates

cards.front: What four features make a password strong, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: At least 12 characters long / Mix of upper/lower case, numbers and symbols / Not a dictionary word or predictable modification / Unique to each account
items: Mix of upper/lower case, numbers and symbols
Not a dictionary word or predictable modification

cards.front: How does CAPTCHA tell the difference between a human and a bot?
cards.answer: It sets tasks like reading skewed text or picking images, which are easy for humans but computationally hard for automated programs.

cards.front: Why are automatic software updates more effective at closing vulnerabilities than manual updates?
cards.answer: Manual updating is unreliable because users often delay or ignore update prompts, leaving software unpatched and vulnerable.

cards.front: Name the four distinctive Marian dogmas held by Catholic teaching.
cards.answer: Immaculate Conception / Perpetual Virginity of Mary / Divine Motherhood (Theotokos) / Assumption

cards.front: Name the four Mysteries meditated on during the Rosary.
cards.answer: Joyful Mysteries / Sorrowful Mysteries / Glorious Mysteries / Luminous Mysteries

cards.front: Why is the Rosary described as a deeply Marian prayer?
cards.answer: The Hail Mary is at its heart and it contemplates Jesus's life through Mary's perspective as mother and disciple.

cards.front: Why do Catholics move through the Stations of the Cross?
cards.answer: To pause and reflect at each scene, entering imaginatively into Christ's suffering and redemptive love.

cards.front: What were the three stages of a Greek funeral?
cards.answer: Prothesis (laying-out of the body) / Ekphora (funeral procession) / Burial or cremation

cards.front: What four types of grave goods does the lesson mention being placed in Greek tombs?
cards.answer: Pottery / Jewellery / Weapons / Figurines

cards.front: Why did Athens pass laws limiting extreme mourning behaviour at funerals?
cards.answer: Because ritualised mourning had become a competitive display of grief among wealthy families.

cards.front: Why was the Greek ekphora (funeral procession) held before dawn?
cards.answer: The timing was probably intended to prevent excessive public display of the funeral.

cards.front: Name the four contact forces the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Friction / Air resistance / Tension / Normal contact force

cards.front: Name the three non-contact forces the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Gravity / Magnetic forces / Electrostatic forces

cards.front: Why does an astronaut have the same mass but a smaller weight on the Moon than on Earth?
cards.answer: Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight depends on gravitational field strength, which is weaker on the Moon.

cards.front: Why are the weight and normal contact force on a person NOT a Newton's Third Law pair?
cards.answer: Because they act on the same object (the person), not on two different objects, so they can't be a pair.

cards.front: Name the six main endocrine glands mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pituitary gland / Thyroid gland / Adrenal glands / Pancreas / Ovaries / Testes

cards.front: Name the four effects adrenaline has on the body during fight-or-flight.
cards.answer: Increases heart rate / Raises blood pressure / Increases blood flow to skeletal muscles / Stimulates liver to convert glycogen into glucose
items: Increases blood flow to skeletal muscles
Stimulates liver to convert glycogen into glucose

cards.front: How does adrenaline raise blood glucose levels?
cards.answer: It stimulates the liver to convert stored glycogen into glucose, raising blood sugar for energy.

cards.front: (Higher tier) Why does thyroxine inhibit TRH and TSH once levels return to normal?
cards.answer: This stops the pituitary and hypothalamus stimulating more thyroxine production, preventing overproduction as part of negative feedback.

cards.front: Name the three senses McKay uses to structure the poem's three quatrains, with an example image for each.
cards.answer: Sight - "wonder-eyes", "sapphire skies" / Motion - "waters rushing down the mountain passes" / Sound - "fiddle and fife", "dear delicious tunes"
items: Motion - "waters rushing down the mountain passes"

cards.front: Why is the lack of a volta in 'I Shall Return' significant?
cards.answer: Instead of a dramatic turn, the poem builds steadily towards its closing promise, suggesting quiet resolve rather than sudden realisation.

cards.front: Why does McKay's use of future tense make 'I Shall Return' different from most anthology memory poems?
cards.answer: Most memory poems look backward with nostalgia, but McKay's future-tense promise of homecoming gives the poem a determined, not nostalgic, tone.

title: Historic environment: Royal Dockyards, Chatham c.1567-1984
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for the closure of Chatham Dockyard in 1984.
cards.answer: Declining Royal Navy fleet size / Thatcher government's defence spending review / Competition from other naval bases

cards.front: Name the three types of dockyard infrastructure the lesson says enabled permanent building, repair and supply of warships.
cards.answer: Dry docks / Storehouses / Rope houses

cards.front: Why was the ability to work on a ship's hull below the waterline essential for maintaining a wooden warship fleet?
cards.answer: Wooden warships were vulnerable to marine worms, rot and battle damage, so hulls needed regular access for repair.

cards.front: Why did the covered slips built for wooden warships become redundant in the Victorian period?
cards.answer: Because iron-hulled ships could not be built in the same way as wooden ships, making the old covered slips unsuitable.

cards.front: The lesson names four qualities in Anita that first attract Meena. What are they?
cards.answer: Bold / Loud / Fearless / Unconcerned with what adults think

cards.front: Name the three ways Meena adapts herself to please Anita, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Laughs at jokes she doesn't find funny / Joins in cruelty she knows is wrong / Suppresses her own intelligence and curiosity
items: Laughs at jokes she doesn't find funny
Joins in cruelty she knows is wrong
Suppresses her own intelligence and curiosity

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the Meena-Anita friendship as unequal rather than a real friendship?
cards.answer: Anita leads and decides everything while Meena constantly adapts, laughs along, and hides her true self to earn approval.

cards.front: How does Meena's final realisation lead her to reject what Anita represents?
cards.answer: She learns that belonging comes from wherever she stands, rejecting the idea she must be white, working-class and tough to have value.

cards.front: What three conditions does Maggie set for returning to help Hobson in Act 4?
cards.answer: Willie becomes master of the shop / Hobson takes a half-share as a sleeping partner with no say / Hobson lives there as a dependent, not the boss
items: Willie becomes master of the shop
Hobson takes a half-share as a sleeping partner with no say
Hobson lives there as a dependent, not the boss

cards.front: What three roles has Willie proven himself in, earning his authority as master?
cards.answer: A craftsman / A businessman / A husband

cards.front: Why does Maggie use the trespass case at the wedding party instead of taking it to court?
cards.answer: She uses it as leverage to pressure Hobson into settling out of court, releasing the marriage settlements he had refused to provide.

cards.front: Why is the ending of the play considered ambiguous regarding Hobson's character?
cards.answer: He accepts the new arrangement because he has no alternative, not because he recognises his faults, showing people don't always learn from mistakes.

cards.front: Name the three ways energy can transfer 'by heating', as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Conduction / Convection / Evaporation

cards.front: Name the three stores or pathways energy goes to when a car crashes into a barrier.
cards.answer: Thermal store of the car and barrier / Elastic potential store as the car body deforms / Sound waves to the thermal store of the surroundings
items: Thermal store of the car and barrier
Elastic potential store as the car body deforms
Sound waves to the thermal store of the surroundings

cards.front: Why does an object's kinetic energy decrease as it rises upwards, ignoring air resistance?
cards.answer: Kinetic energy is transferred to the gravitational potential energy store as the object gains height, until all kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy at the highest point.

cards.front: How is energy transferred when a constant force accelerates a car along a road?
cards.answer: Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store of the car, with some dissipated to the thermal store via friction and air resistance.

title: Act 3: The Ending and the Phone Call
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does Mr Birling say 'the whole thing's different now' after learning the Inspector was a fake?
cards.answer: He believes that if the Inspector was fake, no real harm was done, so there is nothing to worry about.

cards.front: Why does Eric say it doesn't matter whether the Inspector was real?
cards.answer: Because what they did was wrong regardless of whether the consequences were real.

cards.front: Name the three core functions of the UK Parliament.
