cards.answer: Making laws (legislative function) / Scrutinising the work of the government (accountability function) / Representing citizens and debating matters of public concern
items: Scrutinising the work of the government (accountability function)
Representing citizens and debating matters of public concern

cards.front: Name the three ways MPs scrutinise the government, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Parliamentary questions / Select committees / Debates

cards.front: Why is the door of the House of Commons shut in Black Rod's face during the State Opening of Parliament?
cards.answer: It symbolises the Commons' independence from the Crown, before the door is opened after three knocks.

cards.front: Why is the King's Speech written by the government rather than the monarch?
cards.answer: It reflects the convention that the monarch acts on the advice of ministers.

title: Technology and the Form of Media Products
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four practical techniques used to create visual effects before digital/CGI production.
cards.answer: Miniature models / Matte paintings / Puppetry / Practical in-camera techniques

cards.front: Name the three features of 'streaming-era' narrative form described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Complex characters / Slow-burn development / Cliff-hanger episode endings

cards.front: Why can make-up, prosthetics and sets that looked convincing in standard definition appear artificial in HD?
cards.answer: HD delivers extreme clarity, so imperfections invisible in standard definition become visible and artificial in HD close-ups.

cards.front: Why do some music video and advertising directors deliberately use lo-fi, grainy aesthetics despite HD being available?
cards.answer: They use it as a countercultural signal against the corporate smoothness associated with high-definition commercial media.

cards.front: Name the three views used in orthographic projection.
cards.answer: Front elevation / Side elevation / Plan view (from above)

cards.front: In a flow diagram, name the three standard shapes and what each represents.
cards.answer: Rectangles for processes / Diamonds for decisions / Ovals for start/end points

cards.front: Why does orthographic projection remove ambiguity for manufacturers?
cards.answer: Each view is drawn to scale and fully dimensioned, so exact shape, hole size and wall thickness can be read without visual interpretation.

cards.front: Why is sketching described as a 'thinking tool' rather than a draft?
cards.answer: The act of drawing forces designers to make implicit ideas explicit, exposing problems not apparent when the idea was only a thought.

cards.front: Name the three ranks of the Regency social hierarchy described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Aristocracy / Landed gentry / Professional classes and tradespeople

cards.front: Name the three things gentry women in the Regency period could not do.
cards.answer: Enter professions / Own property after marriage / Attend university

cards.front: Why does Caroline Bingley show snobbery towards the Bennets?
cards.answer: Because she is trying to distance herself from her own family's commercial (trade) origins.

cards.front: Why does Austen use Darcy's initial pride and Lady Catherine's outrage at Elizabeth?
cards.answer: To expose the absurdity of judging people by birth rather than character.

title: Flood Management & the River Severn Scheme
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four hard engineering strategies for flood management described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dams and reservoirs / Channel straightening / Embankments / Flood relief channels

cards.front: What are the three levels of flood warning issued by the Environment Agency?
cards.answer: Flood alert / Flood warning / Severe flood warning

cards.front: Why can channel straightening make flooding worse further downstream?
cards.answer: Cutting through meanders speeds up river flow, so the problem is passed on and can speed up flooding lower down the river.

cards.front: Why does Bewdley flood so quickly after heavy rain falls in mid-Wales?
cards.answer: Heavy winter rain falls on steep, impermeable Welsh uplands and reaches the lowland Severn at Bewdley within hours.

title: The October Revolution: The Bolshevik Seizure of Power
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why the Bolsheviks won in October 1917.
cards.answer: Their opponents were exhausted / Slogans answered urgent demands / Trotsky organised the seizure via the MRC / Lenin pushed the party into action
items: Trotsky organised the seizure via the MRC
Lenin pushed the party into action

cards.front: Name the five key locations MRC units seized in the early hours of 25 October 1917.
cards.answer: Railway stations / The State Bank / The Central Telegraph Office / The bridges / The General Staff building

cards.front: Why did the July Days demonstrations break out in Petrograd?
cards.answer: Kronstadt sailors and Petrograd soldiers, fearing transfer to the front, demonstrated for 'All Power to the Soviets'.

cards.front: Why did the Bolshevik uprising have to happen quickly after the 10 October Central Committee vote?
cards.answer: Kamenev and Zinoviev, who had opposed the vote, leaked the decision to a Menshevik newspaper.

title: Viewpoints, Self-Representation and the Social Significance of Representation
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five news values identified by Galtung and Ruge.
cards.answer: Proximity / Magnitude / Negativity / Continuity / Elite persons or nations

cards.front: Name the four sources the lesson gives for where contested representations can emerge from.
cards.answer: Alternative or independent media / Social media campaigns / Documentary film-making / Community-led journalism

cards.front: How does a representation come to feel like a natural description of reality rather than a constructed choice?
cards.answer: It is repeated across news, drama, advertising and social media simultaneously, so it seems to come from everywhere at once.

cards.front: Why does the news as a whole represent a particular kind of world?
cards.answer: News values prioritise drama, crisis and power, systematically excluding small positive stories, long-term problems and non-elite groups.

cards.front: During Kipps's first crossing of the causeway, what three beautiful elements of the landscape does Hill describe?
cards.answer: The wide sky / The call of birds / The vast openness of the marshes
items: The vast openness of the marshes

cards.front: During Kipps's first crossing of the causeway, what three unsettling details does Hill describe alongside the beauty?
cards.answer: The sucking mud / The rising mist / The sense the landscape could swallow him whole
items: The sense the landscape could swallow him whole

cards.front: Why does Hill rely on sound rather than visual description for the pony and trap scene?
cards.answer: The absence of anything to see makes it worse, forcing the reader's imagination to do the work, which is more disturbing than graphic description.

cards.front: Why does Hill build sympathy for Kipps through his brave rescue of Spider from the marsh?
cards.answer: Showing Kipps as brave and compassionate makes his eventual destruction far more painful and devastating for the reader.

cards.front: What three things does the body do to respond to increased energy demand during exercise, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Increase heart rate / Increase breathing rate and depth / Break down glycogen stores into glucose
items: Break down glycogen stores into glucose

cards.front: What five life processes does the lesson say are powered by energy from respiration?
cards.answer: Muscle contraction / Nerve impulse transmission / Active transport across membranes / Protein synthesis / Cell division

cards.front: Why does lactic acid cause the burning sensation and fatigue felt during intense exercise?
cards.answer: Lactic acid builds up in muscles, lowering pH and interfering with enzyme function, causing burning and fatigue.

cards.front: Why do cells with high energy demands, like muscle, liver and sperm cells, contain large numbers of mitochondria?
cards.answer: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens, and it produces the largest yield of ATP to meet high energy demand.

cards.front: What four practical issues does the lesson identify in researching families?
cards.answer: Access to private family homes / Time and cost of longitudinal studies / Representativeness of participating families / Changing composition of families over time
items: Time and cost of longitudinal studies
Changing composition of families over time

cards.front: What three approaches does the lesson suggest for addressing ethical issues when researching children in families?
cards.answer: Briefing participants on limits of confidentiality / Using independent child welfare advisers / Letting children speak to researchers separately from parents
items: Briefing participants on limits of confidentiality
Letting children speak to researchers separately from parents

cards.front: Why did Ann Oakley criticise Willmott and Young's survey findings on the domestic division of labour?
cards.answer: Their survey used a low threshold for counting male participation, so respondents may have overstated how much housework men did.

cards.front: Why might trends in divorce and marriage statistics not reflect real changes in family behaviour?
cards.answer: These statistics can shift because of legal reforms, such as the Divorce Reform Act 1969, rather than actual changes in how families live.

cards.front: What three pieces of metadata does the lesson say are stored for a bitmap image?
cards.answer: Width / Height / Colour depth

cards.front: Name the three colour depths and their colour counts given in the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: 4-bit = 16 colours / 8-bit = 256 colours / 24-bit = 16,777,216 colours

cards.front: Why does zooming into a low-resolution image reveal visible pixel squares?
cards.answer: Because fewer pixels are packed into the same display area, making each one visible.

cards.front: Why does CD-quality audio typically need compression, such as MP3, for streaming?
cards.answer: Because CD-quality audio produces very large file sizes, making it impractical to stream uncompressed.

title: Silver, the Slave Trade and the Government of Empire
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four levels of colonial administration below the Council of the Indies, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Viceroys / Audiencias / Governors and corregidores / Encomenderos, missions and mita rotas

cards.front: Name the five American crops the lesson says slowly transformed European agriculture and cuisine.
cards.answer: Maize / The potato / The tomato / The chilli pepper / Cocoa

cards.front: Why did mercury use in silver refining kill Indigenous mine workers?
cards.answer: Workers used mercury to refine the silver ore, and repeated exposure to it poisoned them slowly.

cards.front: How could the Spanish empire be powerful and economically weak at the same time?
cards.answer: Silver made the crown a great-power military machine, but inflation and reliance on extraction, forced labour and foreign bankers hollowed out Spanish manufacturing and left it dependent.

title: The Urban-Rural Continuum in the UK
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main flows that link rural and urban areas in the UK.
cards.answer: Commuting (people travelling to work) / Shopping (people travelling to retail) / Services (healthcare, education, leisure) / Communications (digital and transport networks)

cards.front: Name the four things rural areas supply to UK cities.
cards.answer: Food / Water / Energy / Recreation

cards.front: Why are accessible rural areas growing while remote rural areas are losing services?
cards.answer: Accessible rural areas are within easy commuting reach of a city so gain population and new houses, while remote areas thin out and lose services.

cards.front: Why is fuel poverty higher in rural households than the urban average?
cards.answer: Partly because off-grid rural homes rely on expensive heating oil instead of mains gas.

cards.front: The lesson says a news editor makes three choices when selecting stories for a front page. What are they?
cards.answer: Which stories run / What order they appear in / How much space each receives

cards.front: In the lesson's example of a constructed TV report on local flooding, what four elements are shown in sequence?
cards.answer: Aerial drone footage of submerged streets / Close-up of a tearful resident / Statement from a local councillor / Graphic showing predicted rainfall
items: Aerial drone footage of submerged streets

cards.front: Why can two media outlets covering the same event produce meanings that feel almost unrecognisable to each other?
cards.answer: Because mediation filters the event through different backgrounds, cultural contexts, employer expectations and commercial pressures, even though the event itself hasn't changed.

cards.front: Why does high verisimilitude make it easier for a product to communicate an ideology to its audience?
cards.answer: Because the more real a product feels, the less audiences question it, so it can position them more powerfully.

cards.front: Name the four converging crises the lesson says drive Scenes 5–8.
cards.answer: Del at Mai's / Enid searching for her / Brod's revelation / the final reconciliation

cards.front: Name the five deliberate choices the lesson says shape the play's meaning.
cards.answer: the eight-scene structure / the two physical settings / domestic realism / the hybrid incorporation of Obeah / the technique of gradual revelation

cards.front: Why does gradual revelation of Enid's backstory create dramatic tension?
cards.answer: It engages the audience as active interpreters, since in Scene 1 we sense something is wrong before we know what.

cards.front: What is the effect of the play opening and closing at Mai's bedsit?
cards.answer: The Caribbean spiritual world frames the entire action, since it is both where the story begins and where it resolves.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson says affect energy supply.
cards.answer: Physical factors like climate and geology / Cost of exploitation / Technology / Political factors
items: Physical factors like climate and geology

cards.front: Name the five consequences of energy insecurity listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Exploration of difficult areas / Economic costs / Environmental costs / Food production impacts / Industrial output falls

cards.front: Why did European gas prices rise sharply in 2022?
cards.answer: Russia cut gas supplies after invading Ukraine, while sanctions and pipeline sabotage cut flow further, pushing wholesale prices over fivefold.

cards.front: How did fracking change the US energy supply?
cards.answer: Hydraulic fracturing technology unlocked shale gas reserves that were previously inaccessible, boosting US gas production.

title: Case Studies, Correlations and Types of Data
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Name the three dot patterns scatter diagrams show for the three types of correlation.
cards.answer: Positive correlation: dots trend bottom-left to top-right / Negative correlation: dots trend top-left to bottom-right / Zero correlation: scattered cloud with no clear pattern
items: Positive correlation: dots trend bottom-left to top-right
Negative correlation: dots trend top-left to bottom-right
Zero correlation: scattered cloud with no clear pattern

cards.front: Name the four benefits the lesson gives for quantitative, qualitative, primary and secondary data.
cards.answer: Quantitative data allows comparison / Qualitative data allows depth / Primary data is tailored to the study / Secondary data saves time and resources
items: Primary data is tailored to the study
Secondary data saves time and resources

cards.front: Why might a case study researcher's interpretation of their findings be biased?
cards.answer: The researcher may grow close to the person being studied over time, risking a subjective or biased interpretation.

cards.front: Why does the correlation between ice cream sales and drowning rates not mean ice cream causes drowning?
cards.answer: Hot weather is a third variable that affects both ice cream sales and drowning rates, causing the correlation.

title: Practitioner Application: Naturalism vs Heightened Style
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What three key questions does Stanislavski's system ask for every moment on stage?
cards.answer: What does my character want? (objective) / What is stopping them? (obstacle) / What action do they take?

cards.front: The lesson says a director's choice between naturalism and heightened style affects which six departments?
cards.answer: performer training / voice work / blocking / set design / lighting / costume

cards.front: Why does the prologue of Romeo and Juliet work as a Brechtian framing device?
cards.answer: It tells the audience the ending before it begins, so they cannot be surprised and must think about why the tragedy happens, not whether it will.

cards.front: How does Frantic Assembly's physical theatre style externalise Romeo and Juliet's desire?
cards.answer: It makes emotional force literal and spatial through the physics of the performers' bodies, weight, momentum and proximity, such as a run ending in a catch.

title: Popular entertainment in the Jazz Age
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four Hollywood stars the lesson names as household names in the 1920s.
cards.answer: Charlie Chaplin / Mary Pickford / Douglas Fairbanks / Rudolph Valentino

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson describes flappers defying social convention.
cards.answer: Wore short skirts / cut their hair short / wore make-up / drank and smoked publicly

cards.front: Why did talkies give Hollywood a special commercial advantage in Britain and other English-speaking markets?
cards.answer: Because talkies used English-language dialogue, making American films especially influential and popular in English-speaking countries.

cards.front: Why was jazz controversial among conservatives in 1920s America?
cards.answer: Many conservatives condemned jazz as immoral and associated it with Black culture.

cards.front: Name the five narrative techniques the lesson says Syal uses in Anita and Me.
cards.answer: Child narrator / Humour / Code-switching / Episodic structure / Foreshadowing

cards.front: What three events make up the 'crisis' phase of Meena's bildungsroman arc?
cards.answer: Sam's racism / the attack / the riding accident

cards.front: Why does Meena's narration wander, circle back and sometimes contradict itself?
cards.answer: It mimics the way memory actually works, reflecting the instability of childhood identity.

cards.front: How does the split between Punjabi and English mirror Meena's identity?
cards.answer: Punjabi dominates at home while English is required outside, mirroring the tension between her two identities.

title: Valor Ecclesiasticus and Visitation of the Monasteries
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four types of misconduct the Comperta alleged monasteries were guilty of.
cards.answer: Sodomy / Keeping of concubines / Superstitious relics / Financial corruption

cards.front: Name the four obligations the Valor Ecclesiasticus recorded monasteries owed in return for holding their lands.
cards.answer: Charitable distributions / Almsgiving / Hospitality / Maintenance of bridges and roads

cards.front: Why did the Valor and Comperta together give Parliament a strong case for the 1536 Suppression Act?
cards.answer: The Valor showed monasteries were wealthy, giving an economic reason, while the Comperta alleged corruption, giving a moral reason to dissolve them.

cards.front: Why did some monks and nuns, like Abbot Whiting, risk execution during the dissolution?
cards.answer: Those who surrendered voluntarily typically received a pension, but those who refused to accept dissolution risked execution instead.

cards.front: Name the four features that always describe a Newton's third law force pair.
cards.answer: Act on two different objects / Equal in size / Opposite in direction / Same type of force

cards.front: According to F = ma, what three things does the equation tell us about force, mass and acceleration?
cards.answer: A larger force produces a greater acceleration / A larger mass needs a greater force for the same acceleration / If resultant force is zero, there is no acceleration
items: A larger force produces a greater acceleration
A larger mass needs a greater force for the same acceleration
If resultant force is zero, there is no acceleration

cards.front: Why can a rocket still accelerate even though the force it exerts on the gas equals the force the gas exerts on it?
cards.answer: The two equal and opposite forces act on different objects (rocket and gas), so they don't cancel out for either object.

cards.front: Why does a skydiver's acceleration decrease as they fall, before reaching terminal velocity?
cards.answer: Air resistance increases with speed while weight stays constant, so the resultant force and acceleration get smaller.

title: From Hastings to Coronation: William Takes the Throne
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five places William's army moved through as it circled London during the March of Submissions (mid-October to December 1066).
cards.answer: Romney / Dover / Canterbury / Wallingford / Berkhamsted

cards.front: Name the five towns where motte-and-bailey castles were built within months of Hastings.
cards.answer: London / Dover / Canterbury / Winchester / Wallingford

cards.front: Why did William adopt moderate, conciliatory policies in the early months after his coronation?
cards.answer: Conciliation was a tool of conquest that bought time while William consolidated power, built castles and brought over Norman lords.

cards.front: Why couldn't the Witan's chosen king, Edgar Atheling, stop William taking the throne?
cards.answer: Edgar had no army, the northern earls Edwin and Morcar had returned home, and the archbishops could not raise London to fight.

cards.front: Name the four non-ferrous metals the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Aluminium / Copper / Lead / Zinc

cards.front: Name the four ferrous metals the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Cast iron / Low carbon steel / High carbon steel / Stainless steel

cards.front: How does alloying make a metal harder and stronger than the pure metal alone?
cards.answer: The extra atoms disrupt the regular crystal lattice, making it harder for dislocations to move.

cards.front: Why does reducing grain size increase a metal's strength?
cards.answer: Finer grains create more grain boundaries, which impede the movement of dislocations.

cards.front: Name the three poems studied as 'dark places' poems in this lesson, with their poets.
cards.answer: London - Blake / Nothing's Changed - Afrika / In Romney Marsh - Davidson

cards.front: Name the three institutions Blake's 'London' attacks for allowing suffering.
cards.answer: The Church / The monarchy / The marriage laws

cards.front: Why does Afrika write 'Nothing's Changed' in short, clipped stanzas with no regular rhyme?
cards.answer: The fragmented form mirrors the speaker's controlled anger at continuing racial injustice.

cards.front: Why does Davidson use regular quatrains and an ABAB rhyme scheme in 'In Romney Marsh'?
cards.answer: The regular form creates a hymn-like quality, as if the speaker is worshipping the overwhelming landscape.

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say the total supply of labour in an economy depends on?
cards.answer: Size of the working-age population / Participation rate (proportion willing to work) / Number of hours worked

cards.front: How does capital increase the productive capacity of labour?
cards.answer: Capital equipment, like a mechanical mixer or combine harvester, lets workers produce far more output per hour than working by hand.

cards.front: Why does low occupational mobility cause structural unemployment?
cards.answer: When an industry declines, workers whose skills don't transfer easily to other jobs are left behind and unable to find new work.

cards.front: Name the four models of faith the lesson identifies across the novel.
cards.answer: Brocklehurst's hypocrisy / Helen's patience / St John's rigour / Jane's marriage as affectionate honesty

cards.front: Name the four earlier settings the lesson says Jane must walk through before the happy ending is possible.
cards.answer: Gateshead / Lowood / Thornfield / Moor House

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Rochester's blindness and injury are a 'humbling' rather than a punishment?
cards.answer: His new dependence on Jane rebalances their relationship, lowering his once-dominant status to create moral equality between them.

cards.front: How does Brontë's use of the Gothic setting at Ferndean differ from its earlier use at Thornfield?
cards.answer: At Ferndean the wilderness marks Rochester's humility and reduced state, whereas at Thornfield the Gothic setting had hidden Bertha's secret.

cards.front: What four things did Cortés lose during La Noche Triste?
cards.answer: About half his Spanish soldiers / Most of his horses / Virtually all his artillery / Virtually all his gold

cards.front: What three things combined to defeat Tenochtitlán in 1521?
cards.answer: Naval blockade with thirteen brigantines / Systematic demolition of the city / A vast allied indigenous army (mainly Tlaxcalan)
items: A vast allied indigenous army (mainly Tlaxcalan)

cards.front: Why was Moctezuma's death in June 1520 so damaging to the Spanish position?
cards.answer: It removed the last possibility of negotiating through the emperor, and the Aztecs elected Cuitláhuac, who organised an assault on the Spanish.

cards.front: Why did Cortés have Mexico City built directly on top of the ruins of Tenochtitlán?
cards.answer: It was a deliberate act of symbolic erasure, physically overwriting the Aztec city as a statement about the permanence of Spanish power.

title: Astronomy: Solar System, Stars and the Big Bang
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six types of bodies that make up the Solar System.
cards.answer: The Sun / Eight planets / Moons (natural satellites) / Dwarf planets / Asteroids / Comets

cards.front: Give the six stages in the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun, in order.
cards.answer: Nebula / Protostar / Main sequence star / Red supergiant / Supernova / Neutron star or black hole

cards.front: Why do communication satellites in high geostationary orbit move more slowly than the International Space Station in low orbit?
cards.answer: A stable circular orbit needs a specific radius for each speed; a lower orbital speed requires a larger orbital radius, so high satellites move slower.

cards.front: Why does an 80 kg astronaut weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
cards.answer: Weight depends on gravitational field strength, which is lower on the Moon (about 1.6 N/kg) than on Earth (about 10 N/kg), even though mass stays the same.

cards.front: Why was the killing at Glencoe seen as especially shocking, beyond the number of dead?
cards.answer: Soldiers had been billeted with the MacDonalds under Highland hospitality customs before killing their own hosts.

cards.front: How did the failure of the Darien Scheme push Scotland towards union with England?
cards.answer: It left Scotland economically desperate and proved it could not trade independently while England blocked it, driving both sides towards union.

title: Divorce: Causes, Consequences and Theoretical Perspectives
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: What four main reasons does the lesson give for the rise in divorce since 1945?
cards.answer: Legal change (1969 Divorce Reform Act) / 2022 no-fault divorce reform / Secularisation reducing religious stigma / Changing social attitudes and status of women
items: Changing social attitudes and status of women

cards.front: What are the main consequences of divorce listed in the lesson?
cards.answer: Financial hardship, particularly for women / Social isolation, particularly for men / Varied impacts on children's wellbeing / Disruption of extended family relationships / Significant increase in lone parent families
items: Significant increase in lone parent families

cards.front: Why do men tend to experience greater social isolation after divorce than women?
cards.answer: Men are less likely to have primary care of children and may have weaker social networks outside the family.

cards.front: How do Marxists explain the causes of marital breakdown?
cards.answer: They argue it stems from capitalism's economic conditions, including poverty, financial stress, work alienation and housing insecurity.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why reported incidence of mental health problems has risen.
cards.answer: Increased challenges of modern living / Increased recognition of mental health problems / Lessening of social stigma
items: Increased recognition of mental health problems

cards.front: How can updates to the ICD classification system make it look like mental illness has risen, even if it hasn't?
cards.answer: As the system is updated, conditions can be redefined, merged or added, changing how many cases are officially recorded.

cards.front: Why does research suggest higher rates of mental health difficulty among LGBTQ+ groups?
cards.answer: It is often linked to discrimination and minority stress.

title: Bush's War on Terror and Operation Enduring Freedom
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three aims did Bush state for launching Operation Enduring Freedom?
cards.answer: Destroy al-Qaeda's leadership and training camps / Capture or kill Osama bin Laden / Remove the regime that protected him
items: Destroy al-Qaeda's leadership and training camps
Capture or kill Osama bin Laden
Remove the regime that protected him

cards.front: What three factors explain why the Taliban regime collapsed so quickly in 2001?
cards.answer: Air force and air defences destroyed within ten days / US paid local commanders huge sums to switch sides / Northern Alliance had prepared for five years
items: Air force and air defences destroyed within ten days
US paid local commanders huge sums to switch sides
Northern Alliance had prepared for five years

cards.front: Why did NATO's invocation of Article 5 in September 2001 matter symbolically?
cards.answer: An alliance built to deter the Soviet Union was now mobilised against a stateless network of religious radicals.

cards.front: Why couldn't the quick US-led military victory in Afghanistan be turned into lasting political stability?
cards.answer: Because the Western ground footprint was deliberately kept small, giving a fast military win but little control on the ground.

cards.front: Name the four things standardisation keeps identical for every participant except for the IV condition.
cards.answer: Procedure / Instructions / Materials / Environment

cards.front: Name the six planning decisions the lesson says you need to work through when designing an investigation.
cards.answer: Hypothesis / Independent variable / Dependent variable / Extraneous variables / Standardisation / Design

cards.front: How does counterbalancing reduce the effect of practice or fatigue in a repeated measures design?
cards.answer: Half the participants complete condition A first and half complete condition B first, so the practice or fatigue effect balances out across the sample.

cards.front: In the flashcard revision study, why must a difference in participants' baseline memory be controlled as an extraneous variable?
cards.answer: Because better baseline memory in one group could explain the recall difference instead of the revision method used.

cards.front: Name the four nutrients UK law requires bread flour to be fortified with.
cards.answer: Calcium / Iron / Thiamin (B1) / Niacin (B3)

cards.front: Name the five main categories of food additives the lesson covers.
cards.answer: Preservatives / Colourings / Flavour enhancers / Emulsifiers / Stabilisers

cards.front: Why does steaming vegetables preserve more vitamins than boiling them?
cards.answer: The food does not sit in water, so water-soluble vitamin C and B vitamins do not leach out into the cooking water.

cards.front: How does adding nitrates to cured meat like bacon extend its shelf life?
cards.answer: Nitrates inhibit the growth of Clostridium botulinum and other spoilage bacteria, dramatically extending shelf life.

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for how Squealer uses propaganda.
cards.answer: Emotional manipulation / Statistics that contradict lived experience / The 'Jones would come back' threat / Gradual rewriting of the commandments

cards.front: Name the four elements of Napoleon's rise to power that mirror Stalin's, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Eliminating a charismatic rival / Using secret police / Rewriting history / Building a cult of personality

cards.front: Why does Orwell deliberately make Napoleon less charismatic than Snowball?
cards.answer: Because Stalin was not a great orator but a ruthless operator, so Napoleon's power comes from fear and manipulation, not inspiration.

cards.front: How do Boxer's blind loyalty and Benjamin's cynical inaction both enable tyranny?
cards.answer: Boxer's trust is exploited by the pigs while Benjamin sees the truth but stays silent, so neither awareness nor action alone stops the pigs' power.

cards.front: Name the seven stock forms the lesson gives for metals.
cards.answer: Bar / Sheet / Plate / Pipe/tube / Castings / Wire / Powder

cards.front: Name the four stock forms the lesson gives for natural and manufactured timbers.
cards.answer: Regular sections / Mouldings / Dowels / Sheets

cards.front: Why can extrusion only be used to make certain stock forms?
cards.answer: Because extrusion needs a shaped die to push or pull material through, creating a length of constant cross-section.

cards.front: Why is it important to choose a stock size close to what a design actually needs?
cards.answer: It reduces waste and expense, and cuts the amount of scrap material sent to landfill, making the process more sustainable.

title: Food as a Display of Wealth and Power
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four Roman writers this lesson discusses in relation to food, wealth and power.
cards.answer: Petronius / Martial / Pliny / Seneca

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things could a host's food reveal about their guests' status?
cards.answer: Boast about wealth / Humiliate guests / Sort guests into ranks

cards.front: Why does Trimalchio tell his guests that yesterday he served worse wine to more respectable men?
cards.answer: He is deliberately reminding this evening's guests that they rank below the guests he entertained yesterday.

cards.front: Why does Seneca include the story of Vedius Pollio in his treatise?
cards.answer: The treatise urges Nero to show clementia, and Pollio is held up as the extreme opposite, a man who abused power to commit cruelty.

cards.front: Name the four processes that transport sediment along the coast.
cards.answer: Traction / Saltation / Suspension / Solution

cards.front: Give the five-stage sequence in which erosional landforms evolve on a headland.
cards.answer: Crack / Cave / Arch / Stack / Stump

cards.front: Why do constructive waves build up a beach?
cards.answer: Their swash is strong and pushes sediment up the beach, while their backwash is weak so little is dragged back.

cards.front: Why does the Holderness coast erode much faster than the Cornish coast?
cards.answer: Holderness is made of soft boulder clay that erodes easily, while Cornwall's coast is hard rock that resists erosion.

cards.front: What four consequences does the lesson say flow from Romeo killing Tybalt?
cards.answer: Triggers his banishment / Separates him from Juliet / Sets the Friar's desperate plan in motion / Leads directly to the deaths in the tomb
items: Sets the Friar's desperate plan in motion
Leads directly to the deaths in the tomb

cards.front: What four events does the lesson say flow from the Act 3 Scene 1 turning point?
cards.answer: The forced marriage to Paris / The sleeping potion / The missed letter / The double suicide

cards.front: How does Romeo's attempt to make peace directly cause Mercutio's death?
cards.answer: Romeo tries to intervene between the fighting Mercutio and Tybalt, and in that moment Tybalt stabs Mercutio under Romeo's arm.

cards.front: Why does Mercutio's death show the feud destroys more than just the two families?
cards.answer: Mercutio belongs to neither the Montagues nor Capulets yet is killed by their feud, proving it consumes participants and bystanders alike.

cards.front: Name the three ways of changing a repeated cell described in this lesson.
cards.answer: Additive process / Phasing / Layering

cards.front: Name the three textural features that build the sound of Reich's Music for 18 Musicians.
cards.answer: Pulsing chords / Tuned percussion interlocking in hocket / Very slow harmonic rhythm

cards.front: How does the texture in Short Ride in a Fast Machine grow from a few instruments to a full orchestra?
cards.answer: Layer after layer is added on top of the pulse, thickening the sound gradually until it reaches a full ensemble.

cards.front: How can you tell from an unfamiliar extract whether it is sonata form or minimalism?
cards.answer: If a clear tune returns transformed, it's sonata form; if a short pattern repeats and mutates with little melody, it's minimalism.

title: Opposition, persecution and the racial state
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson identifies as persecuted by the racial state.
cards.answer: Jews / Disabled people / Homosexuals / Jehovah's Witnesses

cards.front: What three things did Jehovah's Witnesses refuse to do, leading to their persecution?
cards.answer: Give the Hitler salute / Swear loyalty oaths / Serve in the military

cards.front: Why couldn't left-wing parties organise effective opposition to the Nazis after 1933?
cards.answer: They had been destroyed by mid-1933, and remaining underground Communist and Social Democrat networks were continually disrupted by Gestapo raids.

cards.front: How does eugenics ideology link the persecution of Jews and disabled people?
cards.answer: Both drew on eugenics, which defined the German nation biologically and sought to remove 'undesirable' hereditary and racial traits.

title: The UK in the Wider World
subject: geography-ocr

cards.front: Name the five international organisations the lesson says the UK is a member of.
cards.answer: United Nations / NATO / G7 / G20 / Commonwealth

cards.front: What four factors does the lesson give for why London is a primary node in the global financial network?
cards.answer: Time-zone overlap with Asian and American markets / English language / Common-law legal system / Concentration of professional services
items: Time-zone overlap with Asian and American markets

cards.front: Why did the 2021 container shipping crisis cause goods to stockpile at the Port of Felixstowe?
cards.answer: Imports keep British shelves stocked, but supply chains can be disrupted by events thousands of miles away.

cards.front: Why does soft power matter for the UK's trade and diplomacy?
cards.answer: Soft power underpins trade and diplomacy because countries are more willing to do business with a place they admire.

title: Arguments For the Existence of God
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three main arguments for God's existence covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Design argument / First Cause argument / Argument from miracles

cards.front: What three objections did Hume raise against Paley's watchmaker analogy?
cards.answer: An analogy is not proof / The universe might have many designers, not one / Poor design suggests an imperfect or uncaring designer
items: The universe might have many designers, not one
Poor design (disease, disasters) suggests an imperfect or uncaring designer

cards.front: Why did Aquinas argue there must be an uncaused First Cause?
cards.answer: Because an infinite chain of causes could never have got started, so something must have begun it without itself being caused.

cards.front: Why do humanists reject miracles as evidence for God's existence?
cards.answer: They explain seemingly miraculous events through natural causes like misdiagnosis or spontaneous remission, believing the world is governed entirely by natural laws.

cards.front: Name the six stages of linear design, in order, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Analyse the brief / Research / Write a specification / Generate ideas / Make a prototype / Evaluate

cards.front: What four steps make up one cycle of iterative design?
cards.answer: Produce an idea / Test or evaluate it / Identify weaknesses / Redesign and test again

cards.front: Why does user-centred design reduce the risk of a product failing in the market?
cards.answer: Designers gather detailed user research and continually involve users, so the final product is highly likely to meet real user needs.

cards.front: Why is ergonomic design essential for tools and equipment used repeatedly over long periods?
cards.answer: Poor fit between the product and the human body leads to injury or error, so ergonomic design improves safety and comfort.

cards.front: Name the three March zones used to administer each side of the Anglo-Scottish border.
cards.answer: West March / Middle March / East March

cards.front: Name the five reiver families given in the lesson as raiding across the Anglo-Scottish border.
cards.answer: Armstrongs / Elliots / Grahams / Nixons / Scotts

cards.front: Why did the English victory at the Battle of Pinkie (1547) fail to produce a political settlement with Scotland?
cards.answer: The Scots gained French support and sent Mary to France, frustrating English plans for a marriage union.

cards.front: Why did the Union of Crowns in 1603 end border reiving?
cards.answer: It removed the frontier between two rival states that had let reivers operate, allowing one Crown to suppress the clans.

cards.front: Name the three strict conditions that must be met for lesser jihad to be permitted in Islam.
cards.answer: Declared by a legitimate authority / Proportionate / A last resort

cards.front: Name the three names given for Allah linked to peace, mercy and forgiveness.
cards.answer: As-Salaam (source of peace) / Ar-Rahman (the most merciful) / Al-Ghaffar (the most forgiving)

cards.front: Why do some Christians accept violence despite Jesus's teaching of non-violence?
cards.answer: Some Christians believe violence may sometimes be justified as a last resort when all peaceful options have failed.

cards.front: What is the key contrast between Christian and Muslim views on violence?
cards.answer: Christianity has a stronger tradition of absolute pacifism (e.g. Quakers), while Islam more explicitly permits defensive violence under strict conditions.

cards.front: Name the three ways bootleggers supplied speakeasies with alcohol during Prohibition.
cards.answer: Domestic illegal distillation / Smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean / Diversion of industrial alcohol
items: Smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean

cards.front: Name the three signs that Prohibition succeeded in its early years.
cards.answer: Cirrhosis death rates dropped / Arrests for public drunkenness declined / Reduced domestic violence in some areas
items: Reduced domestic violence in some areas

cards.front: Why was Prohibition so difficult to enforce across the USA?
cards.answer: The federal Prohibition Bureau was chronically underfunded, had only about 1,500 agents nationwide, and agents were often bribed.

cards.front: How did Prohibition cause organised crime to grow in American cities?
cards.answer: Criminal networks expanded massively into the alcohol trade, using violence to control territory and corruption to neutralise law enforcement.

cards.front: Name the six indirect object pronouns used with doler, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: me (to me) / te (to you) / le (to him/her/you formal) / nos (to us) / os (to you all) / les (to them/you all formal)

cards.front: Why does 'me duele' change to 'me duelen' in some sentences?
cards.answer: Doler works like gustar, so it agrees with the body part: singular body part uses duele, plural uses duelen.

cards.front: Why does Spanish say 'tengo fiebre' instead of using a verb like 'to be' as English does?
cards.answer: Spanish uses tener (to have) for many conditions where English uses 'to be', so tengo fiebre literally means 'I have a fever'.

cards.front: Name the three core ideas in the Peelian Principles drafted by Rowan and Mayne.
cards.answer: Police power comes from public approval, not force / The goal is prevention of crime, not punishment after the fact / The police officer is a citizen in uniform, not a separate class
items: Police power comes from public approval, not force
The goal is prevention of crime, not punishment after the fact
The police officer is a citizen in uniform, not a separate class

cards.front: Name the three continuities that persisted in policing despite the changes after 1829.
cards.answer: Policing remained locally administered / Policing by public consent linked back to community tradition / Poverty remained the underlying driver of crime
items: Policing by public consent linked back to community tradition
Poverty remained the underlying driver of crime

cards.front: Why did reform of London's policing get blocked for decades before 1829?
cards.answer: Vested interests defended the old system and there was deep suspicion of a standing police resembling continental state spies and arbitrary arrest.

cards.front: What were Robert Peel's two main arguments for setting up a professional police force?
cards.answer: Urban crime was too large for amateur enforcement, and a disciplined uniformed force would be less threatening to liberty than the existing chaotic mix of watchmen and thief-takers.

title: Bombs over London: Black Saturday, the East End and the V-weapons
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four types of bombs used by Germany against London during the war.
cards.answer: Incendiary bombs (magnesium sticks) / High-explosive bombs (50–1,800kg) / V1 doodlebugs (jet-powered) / V2 rockets (supersonic ballistic missiles)

cards.front: What four types of goods did the London docks handle that made them a key bombing target?
cards.answer: Food / Oil / Timber / Munitions

cards.front: Why did the East End suffer disproportionate damage compared to wealthier boroughs during the Blitz?
cards.answer: Dockers and factory workers had to live within walking distance of the docks and factories, so bombing the targets also destroyed the surrounding housing.

cards.front: Why couldn't water be used to fight fires started by incendiary bombs?
cards.answer: Magnesium sticks burned at roughly 2,200°C, so water could not put them out and only sand or smothering worked.

title: The Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan & Berlin Blockade
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three major consequences did the Berlin Blockade crisis produce?
cards.answer: Germany formally divided into FRG and GDR / NATO formed in April 1949 / Cold War division of Europe became permanent
items: Germany formally divided into FRG and GDR
Cold War division of Europe became permanent

cards.front: What three methods did Stalin use to install communist governments in Eastern Europe's satellite states?
cards.answer: Rigged elections / Intimidation / Presence of the Red Army

cards.front: How was Stalin able to block Western access to West Berlin in 1948?
cards.answer: West Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, so Stalin could cut all road, rail and canal links into it.

cards.front: Why did the USA believe economic aid through the Marshall Plan would stop communism spreading?
cards.answer: The USA believed poverty and instability made countries vulnerable, since hungry, desperate people found communist ideas attractive.

title: Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide and Climate Feedbacks
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of proxy evidence geologists use to reconstruct CO2 levels beyond the 800,000-year ice core record.
cards.answer: Sediment cores / Carbon isotope ratios in fossil shells / Stomatal density of fossil leaves
items: Carbon isotope ratios in fossil shells

cards.front: Name the three negative feedbacks the lesson describes that remove CO2 from the atmosphere.
cards.answer: Chemical weathering of silicate rocks / Marine storage in shells and carbonate sediment / Subduction of carbon-rich ocean crust
items: Marine storage in shells and carbonate sediment

cards.front: Why does the water vapour feedback amplify warming?
cards.answer: Warming increases atmospheric water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas, causing further warming.

cards.front: Why did the Carboniferous coal measures help trigger glaciation?
cards.answer: Organic carbon was buried at an enormous rate, drawing down atmospheric CO2 and helping trigger the Carboniferous–Permian glaciation.

cards.front: Name the four poems given as comparison partners for Rita Dove's 'Flirtation'.
cards.answer: Robert Browning's Now / James Fenton's In Paris With You / John Keats's Bright Star / Liz Lochhead's I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine
items: James Fenton's In Paris With You
Liz Lochhead's I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says to read for when practising a comparison with an unseen poem.
cards.answer: ideas and attitudes each poem explores / tone and atmosphere each creates / effects of language and structure each poet chooses
items: ideas and attitudes each poem explores
effects of language and structure each poet chooses

cards.front: Why does Dove use enjambment across an early stanza break in 'Flirtation'?
cards.answer: It lets one idea flow into the next without a full stop, fitting a moment that is itself unresolved and still unfolding.

cards.front: How does sibilance and alliteration affect the atmosphere of 'Flirtation'?
cards.answer: They build a hushed, sensuous soundscape that matches the poem's quiet, night-time setting.

cards.front: Two heterozygous Bb parents have children. What are the three possible genotype ratios among the offspring?
Why are most human characteristics not controlled by a single gene?
cards.answer: Because most characteristics are polygenic, meaning they are controlled by several genes working together.

cards.front: Why is embryo screening during IVF considered controversial?
cards.answer: Some argue it prevents suffering by avoiding faulty alleles, while others think selecting embryos is unethical or could lead to designer babies.

cards.front: Name the three biographical connections between Dickens's own life and A Christmas Carol.
cards.answer: His father was imprisoned for debt / He worked in a factory as a child / He was driven to change conditions for the poor, especially children
items: His father was imprisoned for debt
He worked in a factory as a child
He was driven to change conditions for the poor, especially children

cards.front: Name the three Christmas traditions that became popular during the Victorian era.
cards.answer: Cards / Crackers / Christmas trees

cards.front: Why did Dickens decide to write a story instead of a political pamphlet about child labour?
cards.answer: He believed a novella could reach people's hearts and make his argument hit harder than statistics or a political essay ever could.

cards.front: How does the Ghost of Christmas Present challenge Scrooge's Malthusian view of the poor in Stave 3?
cards.answer: The Ghost throws Scrooge's own words about decreasing the 'surplus population' back at him, forcing him to confront the cruelty of his views.

cards.front: Name the four bases found in DNA nucleotides.
cards.answer: Adenine (A) / Thymine (T) / Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)

cards.front: Name the four potential applications of the Human Genome Project given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying genes linked to inherited diseases / Developing personalised medicines / Understanding evolutionary relationships between species / Advancing forensic science
items: Identifying genes linked to inherited diseases

cards.front: Why is each gamete produced by meiosis genetically different from the others?
cards.answer: Meiosis involves shuffling of genetic material, so each gamete ends up with a different combination of alleles.

cards.front: Why does a zygote have the full set of 46 chromosomes?
cards.answer: It forms when two haploid gametes, each with 23 chromosomes, fuse together at fertilisation.

cards.front: Name the four atomic models, in order, that led to our current model of the atom.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere model / Thomson's plum pudding model / Rutherford's nuclear model / Bohr's energy levels model

cards.front: State the maximum number of electrons that can occupy each of the first three electron shells.
cards.answer: First shell: 2 / Second shell: 8 / Third shell: 8

cards.front: Why does losing electrons turn an atom into a positive ion?
cards.answer: Because there are now more protons than electrons, giving the atom an overall positive charge.

cards.front: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table react in similar ways?
cards.answer: Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which determines how they react.

title: The end of austerity: 'never had it so good'
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three consumer goods the lesson says ordinary working people could newly afford in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Televisions / Washing machines / Cars

cards.front: Name the three types of school under the 1944 tripartite system.
cards.answer: Grammar school / Technical school / Secondary modern school

cards.front: Why did Beeching recommend closing many rural railway lines in his 1963 report?
cards.answer: Because many rural branch lines were lossmaking and it was cheaper to let cars and lorries carry passengers and freight.

cards.front: Why did critics argue the tripartite system should be replaced?
cards.answer: It locked children into a track at eleven, disadvantaged working-class pupils, and wasted talent.

title: Causes of war across the eras
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four recurring causes of war identified across British history in this lesson.
cards.answer: Religion / Politics / Nationalism / Ideology

cards.front: What three things did the Treaty of Versailles do to Germany?
cards.answer: Stripped it of territory / Imposed heavy reparations / Limited its armed forces

cards.front: How did nationalism act as both an aggressive and a defensive cause in the Second World War?
cards.answer: German nationalism drove aggressive territorial expansion, while British national identity motivated resistance to defend freedom and treaty commitments.

cards.front: Why had religion largely stopped being the main cause of large-scale war by the twentieth century?
cards.answer: Religion was displaced as the primary driver of war by nationalism and ideology, which became the dominant causes.

cards.front: Name the three main types of chemical bonding covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: Name the three types of covalent bond based on how many electron pairs are shared, with an example gas for each.
cards.answer: Single bond - one shared pair / Double bond - two shared pairs (e.g. O2, CO2) / Triple bond - three shared pairs (e.g. N2)
items: Double bond - two shared pairs (e.g. O2, CO2)
Triple bond - three shared pairs (e.g. N2)

cards.front: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not, even though both are giant covalent structures made of carbon?
cards.answer: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom that can move and carry charge, but diamond uses all its electrons in bonding.

cards.front: Why does an ionic compound conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water but not when solid?
cards.answer: When molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry charge, but in a solid the ions are fixed in position.

title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four core Jewish moral principles the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Tzedek (justice) / Tikkun olam (repair the world) / Tzedakah (charity) / Chesed (loving kindness)

cards.front: Give the three examples the lesson gives of chesed in British Jewish community life.
cards.answer: Weekly food bank / Visiting housebound elderly members / Clothing collections for asylum seekers

cards.front: Why does Judaism teach that Pikuach Nefesh overrides almost all the mitzvot?
cards.answer: Because every human being is created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim), reflecting the absolute sanctity of human life.

cards.front: How did Maimonides resolve the tension between free will and God's foreknowledge?
cards.answer: He taught that free will is given to every human being and that God's foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility.

title: Wall Street Boom and the Inequalities Beneath It
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says happened at once to cause the Wall Street boom.
cards.answer: Republican tax cuts left wealthy Americans with billions to invest / Mass production generated record corporate profits / New buying rules let small investors join in
items: Republican tax cuts left wealthy Americans with billions to invest
Mass production generated record corporate profits
New buying rules let small investors join in

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says the Boom left out.
cards.answer: Farmers (collapsing crop prices) / Sharecroppers (debt to landlords) / African-Americans (Jim Crow segregation) / Native Americans (reservations) / Unskilled industrial workers (wages rose far less than profits)
items: Unskilled industrial workers (wages rose far less than profits)

cards.front: Why did buying shares on the margin become dangerous if share prices fell?
cards.answer: The loan from the stockbroker still had to be repaid in full, even though the shares bought with it had lost value.

cards.front: Why did the Great Migration not bring full equality for African-Americans in northern cities?
cards.answer: Restrictive covenants enforced white-only neighbourhoods and trade unions refused black members, confining them to overcrowded areas and the lowest-paid jobs.

title: Global Food Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the six factors the lesson gives that commonly limit food production.
cards.answer: Climate / Technology / Pests and disease / Water stress / Conflict / Poverty

cards.front: Name the five impacts of food insecurity described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Famine / Undernutrition / Soil erosion / Rising prices / Social unrest

cards.front: How did rising meat consumption in China drive deforestation in Brazil's Cerrado?
cards.answer: China's meat consumption doubling required more grain imports for animal feed, raising demand for soya and causing forest clearance in Brazil's Cerrado.

cards.front: Why do conflict and food insecurity reinforce each other in the Sahel?
cards.answer: Climate-driven drought reduces pasture, pushing herders onto cropland and sparking clashes with farmers, while resulting conflict further disrupts food production.

cards.front: Name the four arguments given in the lesson for wearing school uniform.
cards.answer: Cheaper than other clothes / Don't waste time choosing clothes / Gives a sense of belonging to a community / Dressed the same so less bullying
items: Gives a sense of belonging to a community
Dressed the same so less bullying

cards.front: Name the three arguments given in the lesson against wearing school uniform.
cards.answer: Not fashionable / Can't show your personality / Not comfortable especially when hot

cards.front: How does the article change after the negative expression 'il n'y a pas' in French?
cards.answer: The article changes to de/d' regardless of gender, e.g. il y a une piscine becomes il n'y a pas de piscine.

cards.front: Why do some students argue that wearing a uniform reduces bullying?
cards.answer: Because everyone is dressed the same way, so people are less likely to be bullied.

cards.front: Name the three common flat-roof finishes given in the lesson.
cards.answer: EPDM rubber-based sheeting / GRP fibreglass / Single-ply membranes

cards.front: Name the five cladding options given for a framed building's external skin.
cards.answer: Brick slips on backing board / Rendered blockwork / Profiled steel sheeting / Aluminium-faced insulated panels / Curtain walling

cards.front: How does a cavity wall keep a building warm and dry?
cards.answer: Two leaves of masonry with an insulated air gap between them stop rain crossing while the insulation reduces heat loss.

cards.front: Why is a ventilated void included beneath a suspended ground floor?
cards.answer: It prevents moisture building up under the floor, which would otherwise cause timber decay.

cards.front: Name the four kinds of wartime roles the lesson says Soviet women took on.
cards.answer: Drove tractors / Ran lathes / Served as pilots in the 'Night Witches' bomber regiment / Worked as front-line snipers and medics
items: Served as pilots in the 'Night Witches' bomber regiment
Worked as front-line snipers and medics

cards.front: Name the three ethnic groups the lesson says were deported en masse during the war.
cards.answer: Volga Germans / Chechens and Ingush / Crimean Tatars

cards.front: Why did Stalin order 1,500 factories moved east of the Urals in 1941?
cards.answer: To move industry beyond the reach of German bombers so weapons production could continue safely.

cards.front: Why did the Battle of Stalingrad become the war's turning point?
cards.answer: A Soviet pincer, Operation Uranus, encircled the German Sixth Army, forcing its surrender and confirming Soviet military recovery.

title: Trench Warfare on the Western Front
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three combined defensive advantages that caused the Western Front stalemate.
cards.answer: Machine guns firing 500 rounds a minute / Barbed wire belts slowing attackers / Pre-registered artillery destroying attacks
items: Machine guns firing 500 rounds a minute

cards.front: What four elements made up the BEF's 'steep learning curve' by 1918?
cards.answer: Creeping artillery barrages / Combined-arms tactics / Accurate counter-battery fire / Tanks and aircraft used together

cards.front: Why did cavalry become useless as a weapon of breakthrough on the Western Front?
cards.answer: Cavalry, the traditional arm of breakthrough, could not overcome entrenched infantry defended by machine guns and artillery.

cards.front: Why did poison gas rarely produce a decisive breakthrough on the Western Front?
cards.answer: Prevailing winds were unreliable and gas masks improved quickly, so gas caused suffering but not lasting advantage.

cards.front: The lesson identifies seven factors affecting life chances alongside social class. Name them.
cards.answer: Gender / Race and ethnicity / Sexuality / Age / Disability / Religion and belief

cards.front: How does the social model of disability explain the disability employment gap?
cards.answer: It argues inequalities come from social barriers, such as employer attitudes and inaccessible workplaces, rather than from impairment alone.

cards.front: Why are women more likely to experience poverty in old age despite living longer than men?
cards.answer: Career breaks reduce women's pension accumulation, leaving them with lower incomes than men in retirement.

cards.front: Name the six arithmetic operators covered in this lesson, with what each does.
cards.answer: + (add) / − (subtract) / * (multiply) / / (real division, decimal result) / DIV (integer division, whole quotient) / MOD (remainder after integer division)

cards.front: Name the six relational operators used for comparisons in conditions.
cards.answer: = (equal to) / ≠ (not equal to) / (greater than) / ≤ (less than or equal to) / ≥ (greater than or equal to)

cards.front: Why should you use a WHILE loop, not REPEAT...UNTIL, for reading GPS data while a car is moving?
cards.answer: The car might already be stopped when the program starts, so the loop body may never need to run, and only WHILE can skip it.

cards.front: In a nested IF checking for Pass (score ≥40) then Merit (score ≥70), why might a student wrongly output 'Merit'?
cards.answer: They check the inner condition without first confirming the outer IF's condition was also met.

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that increase thinking distance.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Alcohol / Drugs / Distractions / Higher speed

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that increase braking distance.
cards.answer: Higher speed / Wet or icy roads / Worn tyres / Worn or overheated brakes

cards.front: Why does a spacecraft drifting in deep space keep moving at the same velocity?
cards.answer: No force such as friction or air resistance acts on it to slow it down, not because a force keeps pushing it.

cards.front: Why are weight and normal contact force on a person NOT a Newton's Third Law pair?
cards.answer: Both forces act on the same object (the person), but a Third Law pair must act on two different objects.

title: Arguments Against the Existence of God
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence the lesson gives that support the Big Bang theory.
cards.answer: Observed expansion of the universe / Cosmic microwave background radiation / Relative abundance of light elements

cards.front: Why does the free will defence fail to fully solve the problem of evil, according to the counter-argument in the lesson?
cards.answer: Free will explains moral evil but does not explain natural evil, since events like earthquakes and disease are not caused by human choice.

cards.front: Why does Richard Dawkins argue that evolution removes the need for a designer God?
cards.answer: Once complex life is explained through natural selection, the Design argument loses its force, so the universe is explicable through natural causes alone.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say science cannot disprove the existence of God?
cards.answer: Science only describes how the universe operates through natural processes and cannot disprove a being that exists outside or beyond the universe.

cards.front: What are the three ways the lesson says information can be encoded?
cards.answer: Visually (as an image) / Acoustically (as a sound or word in your head) / Semantically (by meaning)
items: Acoustically (as a sound or word in your head)

cards.front: Name the three types of long-term memory the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Episodic memory / Semantic memory / Procedural memory

cards.front: Why does surface encoding produce weaker memories than deep encoding?
cards.answer: Surface encoding just repeats information without thinking about its meaning, so it produces weaker memories that fade quickly, unlike deeper, meaningful encoding.

cards.front: Why can retrieval fail even when a memory has been stored?
cards.answer: Retrieval can fail because the right retrieval cue is missing, so without that trigger the stored memory stays out of reach.

title: Historic environment: Policing in Liverpool c.1787-1900
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three specialist branches Liverpool Police developed during the Victorian era.
cards.answer: Detective branch (1844) / River police (1865) / Mounted division (1886)

cards.front: Why was Liverpool's pre-1836 watch and ward system unable to cope with the city's needs?
cards.answer: Because rapid population growth created a large, transient, impoverished dock community that overwhelmed the old elderly, poorly paid watchmen.

cards.front: Why did Liverpool's new police force suffer high staff turnover in its early years after 1836?
cards.answer: Because officer numbers and pay were low and discipline was poor, causing men to resign or be dismissed for drunkenness, bribery and other misconduct.

title: England in 1216: John's Death, Succession and William Marshal as Regent
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four castles that made up the network of loyalist-held territory in October 1216.
cards.answer: Dover / Windsor / Corfe / Nottingham

cards.front: What three immediate problems did the succession face after John's death?
cards.answer: Legal status of a child king needing a regent / Political legitimacy against Louis's rebel claim / Finance to pay mercenaries
items: Legal status of a child king needing a regent
Political legitimacy against Louis's rebel claim

cards.front: Why was nine-year-old Henry chosen as king rather than an adult Plantagenet?
cards.answer: No plausible adult Plantagenet candidate existed, so his weak personal authority but indisputable legitimacy was an asset against Louis's foreign claim.

cards.front: How did reissuing Magna Carta in November 1216 help the loyalist cause?
cards.answer: It stripped the rebels of their political programme, since Magna Carta was now the new king's own law, drawing wavering moderates back.

cards.front: Name the five planning elements that must be agreed before a recording session.
cards.answer: Time constraints/timeline / Session length / Agreed goals / Hardware/software requirements / Artist requirements

cards.front: Name the three rules of good file management given for a recording project.
cards.answer: Naming audio files clearly / Labelling folders by song/instrument/date / Naming projects with song title and date
items: Naming projects with song title and date

cards.front: How does recording each overdubbed part onto its own track help later in production?
cards.answer: It allows each part to be edited and mixed independently of the others.

cards.front: Why must audio files be kept within the project folder rather than moved or renamed outside the DAW?
cards.answer: If files are moved or renamed outside the DAW, the project loses its links and the audio goes missing.

cards.front: The lesson gives four different forms of silence in DNA. Name them.
cards.answer: Phil's silence is strategic / The group's silence is self-protective / Leah's silence is defeat / Adam's absence is imposed

cards.front: How does Kelly link Phil's leadership to Milgram's obedience experiment?
cards.answer: Phil acts like the authority figure in the white coat while the group act as willing participants, showing power flows to whoever seems most confident and competent.

cards.front: Why does the debate over whether Phil is a manipulator or a pragmatist remain unresolved in the play?
cards.answer: Phil never lies or flatters the group, but his calm authority still overrides their moral judgement, so the effect matches manipulation regardless of his intent.

cards.front: Why is a binary search much faster than a linear search on large sorted lists?
cards.answer: Because each comparison rules out half of the remaining items at once, instead of checking them one by one.

cards.front: Why might a linear search still be the sensible choice for a small or frequently changing data set?
cards.answer: Because sorting takes time and effort, and for small lists the speed gain from a binary search is too small to be worth it.

title: Sacred Texts, the Covenant and Jewish Identity
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the first five of the Ten Commandments, which Jewish tradition groups as duties to G-d.
cards.answer: I am the Lord your God / No other gods or images / Not misusing the divine name / Keeping Shabbat / Honouring parents
items: I am the Lord your God

cards.front: Name the second five of the Ten Commandments, which Jewish tradition groups as duties to other people.
cards.answer: No murder / No adultery / No theft / No false witness / No coveting

cards.front: Why is a yad used when reading from the Torah scroll?
cards.answer: So that human fingers never touch the sacred text, reflecting the Torah's highest status.

cards.front: Why does the Talmud preserve minority opinions and ongoing debate rather than settling every question?
cards.answer: Because it works on the principle that honest disagreement is itself sacred.

cards.front: Name the five types of internal force found in structural members.
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Bending / Torsion / Buckling

cards.front: What five ports does a 5/2 directional control valve have?
cards.answer: One air inlet / Two cylinder ports / Two exhaust ports

cards.front: Why are dynamic loads often more damaging than static loads of the same size?
cards.answer: Because the rapid change in the load creates additional stress within the material.

cards.front: Why does a beam loaded in the middle have its top surface in compression and bottom surface in tension?
cards.answer: The load makes the beam curve (bend), squeezing the top surface and stretching the bottom surface.

cards.front: Name the four dietary changes recommended in the lesson for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD).
cards.answer: Replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats / Increase NSP intake / Reduce salt intake / Limit free sugars
items: Replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats

cards.front: Name the three haem iron food sources given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Red meat / Liver / Sardines

cards.front: Why is someone with iron deficiency anaemia advised not to drink tea or coffee with iron-rich meals?
cards.answer: Tannins in tea and coffee inhibit iron absorption, so drinking them alongside iron-rich meals reduces how much iron the body absorbs.

cards.front: Why can switching to unfortified almond milk cause someone with lactose intolerance to miss their calcium needs?
cards.answer: Unfortified almond milk contains far less calcium than cow's milk, so a fortified plant milk must be chosen to match cow's milk calcium levels.

cards.front: Name the five poems the lesson compares with Plath's 'You're'.
cards.answer: Baby Song by Thom Gunn / My First Weeks by Sharon Olds / Theme for English B by Langston Hughes / Happy Birthday Moon by Raymond Antrobus / Equilibrium by Theresa Lola
items: My First Weeks by Sharon Olds
Theme for English B by Langston Hughes
Happy Birthday Moon by Raymond Antrobus

cards.front: What five comparisons open the lesson's description of the unborn child in 'You're'?
cards.answer: clown / fish / turnip / prawn / eel

cards.front: How does 'You're' change the usual riddle poem tradition?
cards.answer: It removes the suspense of guessing by naming the subject in the title, so the poem's energy comes from tone instead.

cards.front: How does the poem's two-stanza structure show the passage of time?
cards.answer: The break falls after 'Farther off than Australia', but time passes through the dates buried in the list, not the stanza break.

cards.front: Name the four features of a manic episode in bipolar depression.
cards.answer: Abnormally elevated or irritable mood / Increased energy / Reduced need for sleep / Impulsive or risky behaviour

cards.front: Name the three parts of Beck's cognitive triad.
cards.answer: Negative view of the self / Negative view of the world / Negative view of the future

cards.front: How do SSRIs work to treat depression?
cards.answer: They block the reabsorption of serotonin after it crosses the synapse, increasing serotonin availability in the brain.

cards.front: Why is clinical depression treated as different from everyday sadness?
cards.answer: It is persistent and debilitating, significantly impairing how a person thinks, feels and functions, requiring professional assessment.

title: Program Structure, Data Types and Variables
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four primitive data types in Python.
cards.answer: Integer / Real / Boolean / Char

cards.front: Name the four techniques that make code easy to read.
cards.answer: Meaningful identifier names / Correct indentation / Useful comments / Consistent use of white space

cards.front: Why does "5" + "3" give "53" instead of 8 in Python?
cards.answer: Because input() returns a string by default, so + joins (concatenates) the strings instead of adding numbers.

cards.front: Why is a name like livesRemaining better than x or temp for a variable?
cards.answer: Meaningful identifier names make the variable's purpose clear, making code readable and maintainable, unlike vague single-letter names.

cards.front: What three main routes do UK firms use to compete internationally (other than cheap labour)?
cards.answer: Better designs / Higher quality products / Clever pricing that makes quality feel affordable
items: Clever pricing that makes quality feel affordable

cards.front: Name the four benefits of globalisation for UK businesses given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Access to larger markets / Lower costs from global supply chains / Specialisation (focus on what they do best) / Economies of scale from global volumes
items: Lower costs from global supply chains
Specialisation (focus on what they do best)
Economies of scale from global volumes

cards.front: Why did many British factories close in the 1990s and 2000s because of globalisation?
cards.answer: Asian manufacturers had much lower labour costs and undercut British factories on price, taking their business.

cards.front: How do global supply chains lower costs for UK firms?
cards.answer: Firms can buy materials like steel, circuit boards or packaging from whichever country offers the best price.

title: Energy Transforming Matter — States and Heating
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: In the school experiment to measure specific heat capacity, name the four quantities you record.
cards.answer: Current / Voltage / Time / Temperature rise

cards.front: Why does the sea help moderate coastal climates compared to inland areas?
cards.answer: Water's high specific heat capacity lets the sea absorb large amounts of energy in summer and release it slowly in winter.

cards.front: Why does density change when a substance changes state?
cards.answer: Mass stays the same during a change of state, but the volume usually changes, so density changes too.

cards.front: Name the four features of ordinary estate life Kelman uses to show it is also Harri's home.
cards.answer: Neighbours who look out for each other / Children playing in stairwells / The market / The chicken shop
items: Neighbours who look out for each other

cards.front: What three stages does Jordan pass through in his gradual drift towards the Dell Farm Crew?
cards.answer: Vandalism / Stealing for the Crew / Carrying a knife

cards.front: Why does Harri's happiness on the estate make his eventual fate more devastating?
cards.answer: He is shown as a genuinely happy child who loves his flat, school and friends, not a child trapped in misery, so his danger feels crueller.

cards.front: Why does Harri's outsider status put him at risk on the estate?
cards.answer: Belonging on the estate requires knowledge of its codes that Harri, as a Ghanaian newcomer, does not yet have, leaving him exposed to danger.
