cards.answer: They pressed a single chief to sign, assuming his signature bound every band, when no chief could speak for others.

cards.front: Why did the Comanche become the dominant power of the southern Plains?
cards.answer: After horses spread across the Plains by 1750, the Comanche built an empire of horse breeders and raiders.

cards.front: Name the four main parts of the CPU described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) / Control Unit (CU) / Cache / Registers

cards.front: Name the four special registers used in Von Neumann architecture.
cards.answer: Program Counter / Memory Address Register / Memory Data Register / Accumulator

cards.front: Why does the CPU only handle one instruction at a time?
cards.answer: Because instructions and data share the same memory and travel along the same route, so the processor deals with them in order, one at a time.

cards.front: Why does the Program Counter increase by one during the fetch stage?
cards.answer: So it points to the following instruction, ready to be fetched during the next cycle.

title: The Armistice and the Aims of the Peacemakers
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three countries and leaders that made up the 'Big Three' at the Paris Peace Conference.
cards.answer: Woodrow Wilson (USA) / Georges Clemenceau (France) / David Lloyd George (Britain)

cards.front: What four things did Clemenceau demand from Germany to secure French safety?
cards.answer: Heavy reparations / Return of Alsace-Lorraine / A demilitarised Rhineland buffer zone / Stripping Germany's army, navy and air force
items: Stripping Germany's army, navy and air force

cards.front: Why did many Germans believe they had not really been defeated on the battlefield in 1918?
cards.answer: Because the armistice was signed before any Allied soldier set foot on German soil.

cards.front: Why did Lloyd George not want Germany crippled economically at the peace conference?
cards.answer: He feared a weakened Germany would let Soviet revolution spread west, and knew Germany was an essential trading partner.

cards.front: Name the four steps in treating waste water before it's released, in order.
cards.answer: Screening (removes large objects) / Sedimentation (solids settle as sludge) / Biological treatment (aerobic bacteria break down effluent) / Final treatment (water tested and released)
items: Biological treatment (aerobic bacteria break down effluent)

cards.front: Name the four stages of a product's life a life cycle assessment looks at.
cards.answer: Extracting raw materials / Manufacturing and packaging / Use / Disposal (landfill, recycling or incineration)

cards.front: How does reverse osmosis turn sea water into potable water?
cards.answer: It forces the water through a membrane that blocks salt from passing through.

cards.front: Why isn't recycling a perfect solution for saving resources?
cards.answer: Recycling has its own costs, such as collection, sorting and processing energy.

cards.front: Name the three qualities (Three Marks of Existence) that the five khandas are all said to be subject to.
cards.answer: Impermanent (anicca) / Contribute to suffering (dukkha) / No fixed self, alone or together (anatta)
items: No fixed self, alone or together (anatta)

cards.front: Name the six qualities that make up the Six Perfections (paramitas) cultivated by a Bodhisattva.
cards.answer: Generosity / Ethics / Patience / Energy / Meditation / Wisdom

cards.front: Why is it intention, rather than the outcome of an action, that determines whether kamma is generated?
cards.answer: Buddhist teaching holds that it is the intention behind an action, not just its result, that determines its kamma-generating quality.

cards.front: Why does a Bodhisattva deliberately delay their own final liberation?
cards.answer: Motivated by karuna and metta, a Bodhisattva vows to remain in the cycle of existence until all beings are liberated.

cards.front: Name the four stages the lesson gives for developing new medicines.
cards.answer: Discovery / Development / Preclinical testing / Clinical testing

cards.front: Name the three types of treatment for cardiovascular disease given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lifestyle changes / Life-long medication / Surgical procedures

cards.front: How does hydrochloric acid in the stomach protect the body from pathogens?
cards.answer: It has a pH of 1–2, which kills most pathogens swallowed with food or drink.

cards.front: Why can a weakened immune system from HIV make someone more likely to catch TB?
cards.answer: HIV destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system, making the person more vulnerable to other infections like TB.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says legal structure affects.
cards.answer: How much control owners keep / How profits are shared / Where the business can raise money / What happens if things go wrong
items: Where the business can raise money
What happens if things go wrong

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson says decide which ownership structure suits a business.
cards.answer: The size of the business / The risk it faces / How much outside finance it needs
items: How much outside finance it needs

cards.front: Why does becoming a Plc mean owners lose some control of the business?
cards.answer: Shares are sold to the public, diluting ownership, making takeovers possible and exposing results to shareholder and press scrutiny.

cards.front: Why can one partner's mistake financially harm the other partners in a partnership?
cards.answer: Partners have unlimited liability, so if one partner makes a costly mistake, all partners share responsibility for the debt.

cards.front: The lesson gives three examples of casual racism faced by the Kumars/Meena in the novel. Name them.
cards.answer: Neighbours assume the Kumars eat 'strange food' / The shopkeeper watches Meena more closely than white children / People are surprised she speaks with a Black Country accent, not a 'foreign' one
items: Neighbours assume the Kumars eat 'strange food'
The shopkeeper watches Meena more closely than white children
People are surprised she speaks with a Black Country accent, not a 'foreign' one

cards.front: Name the four historical background elements the lesson says help explain why the characters in Anita and Me behave as they do.
cards.answer: The Windrush generation / Powell's speech / The decline of mining communities / The experience of second-generation immigrants

cards.front: Why does Syal set Anita and Me in a declining Black Country mining community?
cards.answer: The mines closing left white working-class communities anxious about lost jobs, so they scapegoated immigrant families for their changing world.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say casual racism is more insidious than Sam Lowbridge's open hostility?
cards.answer: Casual racism is normalised and embedded in everyday assumptions, making it harder to identify and challenge than overt hostility.

title: Music Video from the Past: Duran Duran and TLC
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three members of TLC.
cards.answer: Tionne 'T-Boz' Watkins / Lisa 'Left Eye' Lopes / Rozonda 'Chilli' Thomas

cards.front: What four mise-en-scène elements does 'Waterfalls' use to contrast its drugs and HIV narrative strands?
cards.answer: Baggy tracksuits / Inner-city streets / Silk stockings / Tangled sheets

cards.front: How does the 'Rio' video construct an aspirational, escapist star image for Duran Duran?
cards.answer: It combines a luxury yacht setting with bright pastel fashion, encoding meanings of glamour, wealth and desirability rather than everyday realism.

cards.front: How does TLC's costume in 'Waterfalls' create a hybrid gender representation?
cards.answer: Their make-up and colourful cropped tops follow feminine codes, but their loose combat-style trousers cover their legs unlike typical R&B videos of the period.

cards.front: Name the four sampling methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Random sampling / Opportunity sampling / Systematic sampling / Stratified sampling

cards.front: Why must a hypothesis be operationalised before a study is conducted?
cards.answer: Without clearly defining both the IV and DV in measurable terms, the hypothesis cannot be properly tested.

cards.front: Why is it important to control extraneous variables in an experiment?
cards.answer: So that any difference in the DV reflects the effect of the IV rather than another uncontrolled factor.

title: The Multi-Store Model and Peterson & Peterson
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: What three features does the multi-store model use to describe how each memory store differs?
cards.answer: Coding (how information is stored) / Capacity (how much it can hold) / Duration (how long it lasts)

cards.front: Why is Peterson and Peterson's study seen as a strength for the multi-store model?
cards.answer: Its controlled lab procedure, using a standardised trigram and fixed counting task, reliably showed STM decays rapidly without rehearsal, as the model predicts.

cards.front: Why might Peterson and Peterson's study lack validity as evidence for STM duration?
cards.answer: Recalling meaningless consonant trigrams differs from remembering meaningful everyday information, limiting how far the findings can be generalised.

cards.front: Name the five details revealed through Scene One's dialogue and action that show how poor the flat is.
cards.answer: No working heating / A leaking roof / One bed to share / A view over a slaughterhouse / A tugboat horn near the river
items: A tugboat horn near the river

cards.front: What three-part plan does Jo tell Jimmie about her future in Scene Two?
cards.answer: Leave school / Work part-time in a bar / Find full-time work and move out
items: Find full-time work and move out

cards.front: Why does Jo taunt Peter about the photographs of other women and his eye patch?
cards.answer: She is not really interested in his past; she is testing whether she can drive him away before he takes her mother from her.

cards.front: Why did Delaney build A Taste of Honey around one composite set instead of changing scenery for each location?
cards.answer: So scene changes happen through lighting, sound or performer movement instead of new scenery, since the same set serves the whole play.

title: Rise and consolidation of Nazi power, 1933-1934
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four messages the Nazis used to attract voters in the early 1930s.
cards.answer: A strong Germany restored to greatness / Punishment of Jews, communists and Weimar politicians / Full employment / National unity
items: A strong Germany restored to greatness
Punishment of Jews, communists and Weimar politicians

cards.front: Name the four changes brought about by Gleichschaltung during 1933.
cards.answer: Trade unions banned / All other political parties banned / State governments stripped of independence / Press, radio and film put under Propaganda Ministry control
items: Press, radio and film put under Propaganda Ministry control

cards.front: Why did the Reichstag Fire help the Nazis remove their main political rivals?
cards.answer: Hitler claimed the fire proved a communist plot, so Hindenburg's Fire Decree allowed arrest without trial and over 4,000 communists were arrested.

cards.front: Why was Nazi control not fully complete in practice by August 1934, even though Hitler held all formal power?
cards.answer: The regime still depended on cooperation from the civil service, judiciary and army, many of whose members were not committed Nazis.

title: Staging and Design: Verona Then and Now
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three approaches to staging Verona that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Traditional Renaissance Verona / Modern-dress Verona / High-concept symbolic Verona

cards.front: Name the four design departments the lesson says must all speak the same production language.
cards.answer: Set / Lighting / Sound / Costume

cards.front: Why does the tomb scene use cold, unforgiving lighting instead of the warm tones used earlier in the play?
cards.answer: It contrasts with the warm amber used in the love scenes, so the shock of cold blue-white shows the audience the warmth is gone.

cards.front: How can a concept production recreate the balcony's sense of separation without building a physical balcony?
cards.answer: By placing Romeo and Juliet at the same level inside a single tight lighting special, using intimacy of light to create private, suspended time.

title: P.W. Botha's State of Emergency and total strategy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three elements of P.W. Botha's 'total strategy'.
cards.answer: Military force / Limited political reform / Regional destabilisation

cards.front: Name the three forms of mass protest that paralysed townships during the 1984–1986 revolt.
cards.answer: Rent boycotts / School boycotts / Strikes

cards.front: Why was the 1983 Church Street bombing controversial even within the anti-apartheid movement?
cards.answer: It targeted a military building but also killed 19 people and injured over 200, many of them civilians.

cards.front: Why did the UDF matter even though the ANC remained banned?
cards.answer: It acted as a legal front inside South Africa, reviving the ANC's internal organising network while the ANC itself stayed banned.

cards.front: What three stages does Mrs Lyons use to manipulate Mrs Johnstone into the pact?
cards.answer: Sympathy / Practical arguments / Threat of superstition

cards.front: Name the three superstitions Mrs Johnstone fears throughout the play.
cards.answer: Broken mirrors / Shoes on tables / The number thirteen

cards.front: Why does the Bible oath scene create dramatic irony for the audience?
cards.answer: The audience sees that Mrs Lyons has invented the superstition and is manipulating Mrs Johnstone, but Mrs Johnstone cannot see this exploitation herself.

cards.front: How does Russell use the musical form of the songs to present Mrs Johnstone?
cards.answer: Songs let her express feelings she cannot say in dialogue, staying hopeful and warm despite her desperate situation, making her sympathetic to the audience.

cards.front: Name the three components involved in every homeostatic control system.
cards.answer: Receptor / Coordination centre / Effector

cards.front: Name the three types of neurone described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sensory neurone / Relay neurone / Motor neurone

cards.front: Why is a reflex action so fast compared to a conscious response?
cards.answer: The brain is bypassed, so the impulse travels a short pathway through the spinal cord without conscious processing.

cards.front: Why must internal conditions stay close to normal for enzymes to keep working?
cards.answer: If conditions drift too far from an enzyme's optimum temperature or pH, it denatures and can no longer catalyse reactions.

cards.front: Name the four conditions bacteria need in order to multiply, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Warmth within the danger zone (5°C–63°C) / Near-neutral pH (6.5–7.5) / Moisture (available water) / Time

cards.front: Name the three types of cross-contamination described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Direct cross-contamination / Indirect cross-contamination / Drip contamination

cards.front: Why doesn't freezing food make it safe from bacteria?
cards.answer: Freezing stops bacteria from reproducing, but it does not kill the bacteria already present in the food.

cards.front: Why can't you tell if food is contaminated just by looking or smelling it?
cards.answer: Bacteria like Salmonella, Campylobacter and E. coli produce no obvious odour, colour change or slimy texture at levels that cause illness.

cards.front: Name the four non-ohmic components described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Filament lamp / Diode / Thermistor / LDR

cards.front: Why does everything stop working if one component breaks in a series circuit?
cards.answer: There is only one path for current, so a break makes the circuit incomplete and stops current flowing anywhere.

cards.front: Why does a parallel circuit keep working if one branch breaks?
cards.answer: There are multiple paths for current, so it can still flow through the other unbroken branches.

title: Sculpture, Statuary and Popular Catholic Devotion
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four sets of Mysteries into which the Rosary is grouped.
cards.answer: Joyful Mysteries / Luminous Mysteries / Sorrowful Mysteries / Glorious Mysteries

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things do pilgrims do at Lourdes?
cards.answer: Bathe in or drink the spring water / Attend candlelit processions / Celebrate Mass at the Basilica / Pray for healing
items: Bathe in or drink the spring water

cards.front: Why do Catholics say using statues in worship is not idolatry?
cards.answer: Because Catholics venerate the person depicted, not the statue itself, using it as a visual aid for prayer and meditation.

cards.front: How does Mary's expression in the Pietà offer a model for Catholics facing suffering?
cards.answer: Her serene grief shows sorrow held with trust in God's providence rather than despair, modelling how believers should receive suffering.

cards.front: Name the six groups exempt from fasting during Ramadan.
cards.answer: Young children / The elderly / Pregnant or breastfeeding women / People who are ill / Travellers / Those menstruating

cards.front: What four benefits does fasting (Sawm) bring, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Develops taqwa (God-consciousness) / Strengthens willpower / Creates empathy with those who go hungry / Brings the community together through iftar
items: Creates empathy with those who go hungry
Brings the community together through iftar

cards.front: Why is praying in congregation at the mosque considered more rewarding than praying alone?
cards.answer: Muhammad said congregational prayer is twenty-seven times more rewarding than praying individually.

cards.front: Why do some Shi'a Muslims place a turbah on the ground when they pray?
cards.answer: They believe the forehead should touch natural earth rather than carpet when prostrating.

cards.front: Name the six reasons the lesson gives for carrying out fitness testing.
cards.answer: Identify strengths and weaknesses / Monitor improvement over time / Establish a baseline fitness level / Inform training requirements / Compare results to norms or personal bests / Motivate athletes and set realistic goals
items: Compare results to norms or personal bests
Motivate athletes and set realistic goals

cards.front: Name the three tests the lesson lists for assessing cardiovascular endurance.
cards.answer: Cooper 12-minute run test / Cooper 12-minute swim test / Harvard Step Test

cards.front: How is jump height calculated in the vertical jump test?
cards.answer: It is the difference in centimetres between the marked standing reach and the mark touched at the peak of the jump.

cards.front: Why is a lower recovery heart rate in the Harvard Step Test seen as a better result?
cards.answer: A lower recovery heart rate indicates a more efficient cardiovascular system.

cards.front: Why is video described as highly engaging but expensive to produce?
cards.answer: It combines moving images, audio and text making it engaging, but this makes it expensive and time-consuming to produce and needs fast internet to stream.

cards.front: Why can social media communication be risky for an organisation's message?
cards.answer: It allows rapid two-way communication with large audiences, so organisations lose control over how their message is interpreted and inaccurate content spreads quickly.

cards.front: Name the three things Enid does as part of her assimilation strategy.
cards.answer: Speaks 'proper' English / Dismisses Obeah as superstition / Suppresses reference to Jamaican culture

cards.front: Name the three facts the lesson gives about Brod's circumstances in England.
cards.answer: Has a serious drinking problem / Has a wife and children still in Jamaica / Deeply disenchanted with life in England
items: Has a wife and children still in Jamaica
Deeply disenchanted with life in England

cards.front: Why did Enid end her marriage to her husband?
cards.answer: To protect her daughters from the abuse rooted in the racism and humiliation her husband suffered at work.

cards.front: How does Del's final palm-reading of Enid help her mother?
cards.answer: It offers Enid a bridge to reconnect with the Jamaican heritage she suppressed, which she could never build alone.

cards.front: Name the four factors a designer should reference when justifying a choice of printing process.
cards.answer: Volume of production / Substrate type / Print quality required / Set-up cost

cards.front: Name the three purposes every surface finish serves.
cards.answer: Protection / Aesthetics / Function

cards.front: How does the rubber blanket cylinder in offset lithography improve print quality?
cards.answer: It conforms to the surface of the substrate, giving sharper results than direct plate-to-paper printing.

cards.front: Why might a designer choose digital spot varnish instead of UV spot varnish at low production volumes?
cards.answer: Digital spot varnish is cheaper at low volumes, though it gives slightly less tactile relief than UV spot varnish.

title: Explaining Addiction: Genes and Learning Theory
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why identical twins might share a more similar environment than non-identical twins.
cards.answer: Treated more alike by parents / Dress similarly / Spend more time together

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says explanations of addiction can be evaluated using.
cards.answer: Validity / Reliability / Objectivity

cards.front: Why is addiction running in families not strong evidence for the genetic explanation on its own?
cards.answer: Because family members also share the same environment and habits, not just their genes.

cards.front: How can a genetic vulnerability and a person's environment interact to produce addiction?
cards.answer: A person may inherit a genetic vulnerability, but whether it develops into addiction depends on their environment and reinforcement patterns, such as substance exposure and stress relief.

cards.front: Name the four main types of employment contract the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Full-time contract / Part-time contract / Job share / Zero-hour contract

cards.front: Name the four extra selection methods the lesson gives besides the interview.
cards.answer: Skills tests / Presentations / Group tasks / Assessment centres

cards.front: Why can interviews be an unreliable selection method?
cards.answer: Good talkers may not actually be good workers, so interview performance doesn't reliably show job ability.

cards.front: How does effective recruitment raise a business's productivity?
cards.answer: It hires skilled staff who match the role, so they complete more tasks to a higher standard.

cards.front: Name the four events in the connected sequence of Jesus's life described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Incarnation - God becomes human / Crucifixion - Jesus dies for sin / Resurrection - Jesus conquers death / Ascension - Jesus returns to heaven

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for why the incarnation matters to Christians?
cards.answer: Shows God loves humanity enough to become human / Means God understands human suffering personally / Gives Jesus's teachings the full authority of God / Was necessary for salvation
items: Shows God loves humanity enough to become human
Means God understands human suffering personally
Gives Jesus's teachings the full authority of God

cards.front: Why did the incarnation need to happen for salvation, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Only someone who was both fully God and fully human could bridge the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity.

cards.front: How did the ascension prepare the way for the Holy Spirit?
cards.answer: It showed Jesus's mission on Earth was complete and cleared the way for the Holy Spirit to come at Pentecost, empowering the disciples.

cards.front: The lesson says Olds gives three pieces of precise physical detail instead of sentimental description of infancy. What are they?
cards.answer: Breast milk / Bottles / A nurse's measured ounces of water
items: A nurse's measured ounces of water

cards.front: Which three poems does the lesson suggest as a second-poem comparison choice alongside 'My First Weeks'?
cards.answer: Baby Song / You're / Equilibrium

cards.front: How does Olds use enjambment to present birth in 'My First Weeks'?
cards.answer: The sentence runs across several lines without a break, so the reader feels the same forward momentum and rush as the baby being born.

cards.front: How does the poem link the strict feeding schedule to the shaping of the speaker's adult character?
cards.answer: The nurses believed the four-hourly rationing taught the baby to give up, building self-control before she could consciously remember it.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says market research collects information about.
cards.answer: Demand / Competition / The target market

cards.front: Name the four typical sources of secondary research given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Internet research (competitor websites, review sites, social media) / Government statistics (ONS) / Market reports (e.g. Mintel) / Printed press (newspapers, trade magazines)
items: Internet research (competitor websites, review sites, social media)

cards.front: Why would asking shoppers outside Waitrose not tell you what Aldi shoppers think?
cards.answer: It causes sampling bias, because that group only represents Waitrose customers, not the wider market.

cards.front: Why could Costa be losing market share even though its sales rose 3%?
cards.answer: Because the total coffee market grew 10%, faster than Costa's sales, so rivals grew faster and took a bigger slice.

title: Principles of Food Safety — Buying, Storing and Preparing
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: What four things should you do when buying food at the shop to keep it safe?
cards.answer: Check date marks before buying / Pack raw meat and fish separately from ready-to-eat foods / Choose chilled and frozen foods last / Transport them in insulated bags
items: Pack raw meat and fish separately from ready-to-eat foods
Choose chilled and frozen foods last

cards.front: Name six times you should wash your hands during food preparation.
cards.answer: Before handling food / After handling raw meat or fish / After visiting the toilet / After touching your face or hair / After handling waste / After touching pets
items: After handling raw meat or fish
After touching your face or hair

cards.front: Why is a damp cloth not sufficient for cleaning work surfaces during food prep?
cards.answer: A damp cloth spreads bacteria around rather than removing it, so surfaces should be wiped with antibacterial cleaner and paper towels or a freshly laundered cloth.

cards.front: Why must a food temperature probe be cleaned and sanitised before checking another food?
cards.answer: To avoid cross-contamination between the food just tested and the next food it is used on.

cards.front: Name the five core maths techniques covered in this lesson for retail calculations.
cards.answer: Percentages / Averages / Profit / Mark-up / Footfall

cards.front: Name the three types of average used to summarise retail data.
cards.answer: Mean / Median / Mode

cards.front: How does gross profit differ from net profit?
cards.answer: Gross profit is revenue minus the cost of goods sold, while net profit also subtracts other costs like rent, wages and utilities.

cards.front: Why does mark-up always give a higher percentage than profit margin for the same product?
cards.answer: Mark-up divides the profit by the lower cost price, whereas profit margin divides the same profit by the higher selling price.

title: Media Audiences: Targeting, Categorisation and Uses & Gratifications
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What are the four categories of need in Blumler and Katz's Uses and Gratifications theory?
cards.answer: Information (surveillance) / Personal identity / Integration and social interaction / Entertainment

cards.front: Why is Uses and Gratifications theory seen as an active-audience model?
cards.answer: Because the same product can gratify different needs for different people, showing meaning depends on what the audience brings, not just producer intent.

cards.front: Why can two audience members interpret the same media product differently at the same point in time?
cards.answer: Social factors like age, gender, class or cultural background, and individual factors like personal experience and belief, shape how they read it.

cards.front: Name the four routes to organic growth listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Increasing output / Gaining new customers / Developing new products / Increasing market share

cards.front: Name the three types of external growth covered in the specification.
cards.answer: Horizontal integration / Vertical integration / Diversification

cards.front: Why is organic growth generally lower-risk than external growth?
cards.answer: It is funded internally from retained profit or a loan, growing gradually rather than committing to a large, risky purchase.

cards.front: Why does decision-making often slow down as a business grows through external growth?
cards.answer: More managers are added and have to sign off on decisions, and communication becomes harder across scattered staff.

cards.front: Name the six factors you must apply when selecting a material for a design context.
cards.answer: Aesthetic factors / Environmental factors / Availability factors / Cost factors / Social factors / Cultural/ethical factors

cards.front: What three things drive the cost of a material, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Quality of material needed / Manufacturing processes required / Market factors such as commodity price
items: Market factors such as commodity price

cards.front: Why do designers often prefer recycled steel and aluminium over virgin ore, for environmental reasons?
cards.answer: Producing steel from raw ore uses large amounts of energy and can cause pollution, so recycled metal has a smaller footprint.

cards.front: How do fast-fashion textiles create built-in obsolescence?
cards.answer: They use cheap synthetic fabrics that wear out quickly, driving repeat purchases.

cards.front: Name the three types of pesticide described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Herbicides / Insecticides / Fungicides

cards.front: Name the three minerals fertilisers provide to plants.
cards.answer: Nitrates / Phosphates / Potassium

cards.front: Why is insect farming considered a sustainable source of protein?
cards.answer: Insects need far less land, water and feed than livestock, produce fewer greenhouse gases, and can be fed on organic waste.

cards.front: Why might locally grown food sometimes have a bigger carbon footprint than imported food?
cards.answer: Heated greenhouses used to grow food locally can use more energy than transporting food from a country where it grows naturally outdoors.

cards.front: Name the four digital tools for civic participation the lesson identifies, besides voting.
cards.answer: E-petitions on the Parliament website / Direct contact with MPs by email or social media / Online access to council meetings / Crowdfunding platforms for community campaigns
items: Direct contact with MPs by email or social media

cards.front: Which three groups does the lesson say historically faced barriers to participation but can now engage digitally?
cards.answer: Young people / Disabled citizens / Those in rural areas

cards.front: Why does the e-petition system lower the barrier to entry for political participation?
cards.answer: A citizen does not need party membership, a personal MP contact, or financial resources to trigger a parliamentary response.

cards.front: Why might low-effort digital actions like signing a petition still be valuable, according to one viewpoint in the lesson?
cards.answer: They can build political confidence and act as a gateway to more sustained, deeper participation later.

cards.front: Name the three planes of movement described in this lesson.
cards.answer: Sagittal plane / Frontal plane / Transverse plane

cards.front: Name the three axes of rotation used in OCR's system.
cards.answer: Transverse axis / Frontal axis / Longitudinal axis

cards.front: Why does running count as sagittal-plane movement while a cartwheel does not?
cards.answer: Running limbs swing forward and backward (sagittal plane), but a cartwheel moves the body sideways, rotating around the frontal axis instead.

cards.front: Why do movement analysts use a system of planes and axes to describe sporting actions?
cards.answer: To describe exactly which direction a movement occurs in and around which line the body rotates.

cards.front: Name the three motives the lesson gives for Khrushchev placing missiles in Cuba.
cards.answer: Deter a future US invasion of Cuba / Close the nuclear gap with the USA / Use Cuba as a bargaining chip over Turkey missiles
items: Deter a future US invasion of Cuba
Close the nuclear gap with the USA
Use Cuba as a bargaining chip over Turkey missiles

cards.front: Name the three immediate outcomes of the Cuban Missile Crisis given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Soviet withdrawal of missiles from Cuba / Secret US commitment to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey / Establishment of the Moscow–Washington hotline
items: Soviet withdrawal of missiles from Cuba
Secret US commitment to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey

cards.front: Why did Kennedy avoid calling the naval action a 'blockade'?
cards.answer: Because 'blockade' is a legal term implying an act of war, so he called it a quarantine instead.

cards.front: Why was Castro furious at the resolution of the crisis?
cards.answer: He was not consulted in the back-channel negotiations and felt the Soviet Union had betrayed Cuba by withdrawing missiles without Cuban input.

cards.front: Name the four social and economic factors the lesson gives that increase coastal vulnerability.
cards.answer: Population density / Income / Infrastructure / Government and education

cards.front: Name the three climate change processes the lesson gives that drive sea levels higher.
cards.answer: Thermal expansion / Melting glaciers / Stronger storms

cards.front: How does the shape of a coastline affect its vulnerability to erosion and flooding?
cards.answer: Bays focus wave energy on headlands, estuaries channel storm surges inland, and low-lying flat coasts have no high ground to break the sea's power.

cards.front: Why do the Netherlands and the Maldives face very different levels of risk despite both being extremely low-lying?
cards.answer: The Netherlands is wealthy enough to invest heavily in defences, while the Maldives has low income and no high ground to retreat to.

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages of computer networks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cost of hardware and maintenance / Risk of malware spreading to every connected device / Need for security measures to protect shared data
items: Risk of malware spreading to every connected device
Need for security measures to protect shared data

cards.front: Name the four network characteristics the lesson says matter most.
cards.answer: Speed / Range / Latency / Bandwidth

cards.front: Why does the internet have no single point of failure?
cards.answer: Each router makes its own forwarding decision, so if one route is blocked, traffic can be rerouted another way.

cards.front: Why are wireless connections considered less secure than wired ones?
cards.answer: Wireless signals travel through the air and can be intercepted by anyone within range, unlike signals confined to a cable.

title: Terror and persuasion: how the Nazis controlled Germany
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four things Heinrich Himmler controlled by the late 1930s.
cards.answer: The SS / The Gestapo / The concentration camp system / Most of Germany's police forces

cards.front: What three-part combination of responses among Germans made Nazi control stable through the 1930s?
cards.answer: Genuine support among many / Passive compliance among most / Terror-induced silence among the rest

cards.front: Why was the Gestapo so feared even though it had only around 32,000 officers for 80 million people?
cards.answer: People never knew who might denounce them, so many avoided expressing any dissent even in private, making Germans police themselves.

cards.front: Why was Nazi propaganda often especially effective at winning genuine support?
cards.answer: It worked best not by forcing belief but by reinforcing things Germans already wanted to believe, like economic recovery and reversed national humiliation.

title: Act 2: The Balcony Scene and Secret Marriage
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why is Romeo in real physical danger during the balcony scene?
cards.answer: He is trespassing in the Capulet orchard, where discovery by Juliet's kinsmen would mean he is killed.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use Juliet's age to criticise the adult world around her?
cards.answer: Juliet is only thirteen, so her courage and maturity are remarkable, making the adults' failure to protect her more damning.

cards.front: Why is the secret marriage ending Act 2 dramatically ironic?
cards.answer: The audience already knows from the Prologue that the marriage will end in death, contrasting the wedding's joy with the doom awaiting them.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why an ordered list is easier to work with.
cards.answer: Quicker to scan by eye / Quicker to search with a computer / Some fast search methods only work once data is sorted
items: Quicker to search with a computer
Some fast search methods only work once data is sorted

cards.front: Name the three sorting algorithms covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Bubble sort / Insertion sort / Merge sort

cards.front: In merge sort, why is a sub-list of just one item already sorted?
cards.answer: A single value cannot be out of order.

cards.front: Why do bubble sort and insertion sort become slow on large lists?
cards.answer: As the list grows, the number of comparisons they must make rises steeply, making them slow on large data.

cards.front: Name the five renewable energy sources the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Hydroelectric power (HEP) / Wind / Solar / Geothermal / Tidal

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson says shape a country's energy mix.
cards.answer: Population (size of demand) / Wealth (capacity to invest) / Natural availability of resources

cards.front: Why did Germany shut down its nuclear power plants after 2011?
cards.answer: Germany shut its nuclear plants after the Fukushima nuclear accident in 2011 changed government policy.

cards.front: Why was fracking near Blackpool paused in 2019?
cards.answer: Fracking there was paused after it was linked to a 2.9 magnitude tremor near Blackpool.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three challenges did Windrush generation immigrants face when they came to Britain seeking a better life?
cards.answer: Racism / Cultural displacement / The challenge of raising children between two worlds
items: The challenge of raising children between two worlds

cards.front: What three aspects of Caribbean-British women's experience does Leave Taking centre, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Motherhood / Cultural identity / Generational conflict

cards.front: Why did many first-generation Caribbean immigrants feel they had to suppress their cultural identity, language and spiritual practices?
cards.answer: To survive in a racist Britain, many felt forced to suppress their cultural identity, language and spiritual practices.

cards.front: Why was the 1994 National Theatre production of Leave Taking historically significant?
cards.answer: It was the first time a Black British woman's play had been staged at the National Theatre.

cards.front: Name the three classic examples of negative externalities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Air and water pollution from factories / Congestion from extra cars on the road / Passive smoking in a public space
items: Air and water pollution from factories
Congestion from extra cars on the road
Passive smoking in a public space

cards.front: Name the three classic examples of positive externalities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Education / Vaccination / Public health services

cards.front: How does a firm planting trees for timber create a positive externality of production?
cards.answer: Making the timber also creates woodland habitats, absorbs carbon and improves local air quality for nearby residents, benefits outside the firm's profit calculation.

cards.front: Why do externalities cause resources to be misallocated in a market?
cards.answer: Market price only reflects private costs and benefits, not external ones, so too much or too little of a good gets produced.

title: Comparing the Anthology: Themes & Exam Technique
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven stories in the AQA Telling Tales anthology.
cards.answer: Chemistry / Odour of Chrysanthemums / My Polish Teacher's Tie / Korea / A Family Supper / Invisible Mass of the Back Row / The Darkness Out There
items: Invisible Mass of the Back Row (Claudette Williams)

cards.front: What are the five dominant recurring themes across the Telling Tales anthology?
cards.answer: Family and relationships / Death and mortality / Secrets, revelation, and concealment / Injustice and powerlessness / Appearance versus reality

cards.front: Why is death presented as an ongoing presence rather than a clean ending across the anthology?
cards.answer: Deaths like the grandfather's in Chemistry are anticipated then replayed in memory, and A Family Supper leaves further death open, so mortality shapes the living rather than simply concluding.

cards.front: Why is secrecy in the anthology more complex than simple deliberate deception?
cards.answer: Secrets arise from limited self-knowledge, cultural codes preventing openness, or power structures silencing the voiceless, not from characters choosing to hide things.

title: Pilgrimage, Festivals, Mission and the Worldwide Church
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four pilgrimage sites named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Jerusalem / Iona / Taizé / Walsingham

cards.front: Name the five days/events of Holy Week in order.
cards.answer: Palm Sunday / Maundy Thursday / Good Friday / Holy Saturday / Easter Sunday

cards.front: Why were Protestant reformers like Luther and Calvin cautious about pilgrimage?
cards.answer: They rejected the idea that visiting a physical location earns spiritual credit, arguing God is present everywhere.

cards.front: Why is Walsingham significant for relations between Christian denominations today?
cards.answer: After being destroyed at the Reformation it was restored and is now visited by both Catholics and Anglicans, representing healed divisions.

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that increase a driver's reaction time.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Alcohol / Drugs / Distractions such as mobile phone use / Poor visibility
items: Distractions such as mobile phone use

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that affect braking distance.
cards.answer: Speed of the vehicle / Mass of the vehicle / Condition of the brakes / Condition of the road surface / Friction between tyres and road

cards.front: Why does increasing a vehicle's speed have such a dramatic effect on its stopping distance?
cards.answer: Both thinking distance and braking distance increase with speed, and braking distance increases with the square of the speed.

cards.front: (Higher tier) Why does stopping very quickly in a crash produce a very large force on passengers?
cards.answer: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, so if the time taken to stop is very short, the force must be very large.

cards.front: What three stark contrasts does Kelman present on the estate in Pigeon English?
cards.answer: Children play alongside drug dealers / Residents look out for each other while fearing neighbours / Everyday life exists in the shadow of gang violence
items: Residents look out for each other while fearing neighbours
Everyday life exists in the shadow of gang violence

cards.front: What three factors does Kelman say draw younger boys from bystander into gang participation?
cards.answer: Fear / Peer pressure / Desire to belong

cards.front: Why does Kelman present the opening murder outside the chicken shop as almost routine?
cards.answer: To critique a society that allows certain communities to exist in a state of constant, normalised danger.

cards.front: Why does Kelman show the estate's warmth and solidarity alongside its danger and deprivation?
cards.answer: Because reducing estate life to violence alone would be dishonest and dehumanising.

cards.front: The mercy speech rises through three levels of authority to show mercy is the highest virtue — name them in order.
cards.answer: Nature (the rain) / Divinity (God) / Monarchy (the throned monarch)

cards.front: Why can't Venice simply void Shylock's bond to save Antonio?
cards.answer: Breaking a foreign merchant's contract would undermine trust in Venetian law and damage the whole commercial system the city depends on.

cards.front: Why does Antonio present Shylock's forced conversion to Christianity as an act of mercy?
cards.answer: Antonio claims the conversion saves Shylock's soul, framing it as spiritual salvation rather than punishment.

cards.front: Name the six types of media/platform the lesson gives as an example of convergence promoting the same artist.
cards.answer: A website / A YouTube channel / Instagram / Facebook / A streaming platform / A physical tour

cards.front: Name the four features of Stormzy's website the lesson uses to show how he builds his brand online.
cards.answer: Tag-style logo font / Main image dominated by one music video / Pop-up newsletter sign-up advert / Hyperlinks to merchandise, tickets and albums
items: Main image dominated by one music video
Hyperlinks to merchandise, tickets and albums

cards.front: Why does Stormzy's website use a pop-up advert inviting visitors to sign up to a newsletter?
cards.answer: It gives fans a simple form of interaction while capturing data the artist and label can use for marketing.

cards.front: How did Lizzo's song Good as Hell become a sleeper hit?
cards.answer: Released in 2016, it gained success years later after featuring in the film Barbershop: The Next Cut, then her MTV Awards performance boosted it as an opinion leader moment.

cards.front: Name the three groups of Greek fighters Leonidas kept with him for the last stand at Thermopylae.
cards.answer: Three hundred Spartans / Thespians who stayed voluntarily / Theban contingent (possibly detained)

cards.front: Name the two prescribed visual sources for the Thermopylae period.
cards.answer: Spartan bronze warrior figure / Corinthian-type helmet dedicated at Olympia

cards.front: Why did the narrow pass at Thermopylae neutralise the Persians' huge numerical advantage?
cards.answer: The pass was so narrow that cavalry charges were impossible and only a small number of Persian infantry could engage at once.

cards.front: Why did Leonidas send most of the Greek allied forces away on the third day at Thermopylae?
cards.answer: He realised the position was now encircled after the betrayal, so staying meant certain death for everyone, and he sent most away to fight another day.

cards.front: Name the six benefits training brings to a business, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Raises productivity / Improves product quality / Improves customer service / Helps adapt to new technology / Improves staff retention / Motivates staff

cards.front: Name the three drawbacks of on-the-job training given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Trainer is less productive while training / Trainee may pick up bad habits from trainer / Rushed training may miss important knowledge
items: Trainer is less productive while training
Trainee may pick up bad habits from trainer
Rushed training may miss important knowledge

cards.front: Why is off-the-job training generally more expensive than on-the-job training?
cards.answer: It involves course fees, travel costs and lost output, as the trainee produces no useful work while away.

cards.front: How does training help a business adapt to technological change?
cards.answer: Staff who aren't retrained on new technology are left behind, so businesses that plan training in adapt faster than rivals.

cards.front: What four grievances did Saddam publicly give for turning on Kuwait in 1990?
cards.answer: Unpaid war debts / Kuwaiti oil overproduction / Bubiyan and Warbah border dispute / slant-drilling accusations at Rumaila
items: Unpaid Iraqi war debts to Kuwait
Kuwaiti oil overproduction pushing down prices
Border dispute over Bubiyan and Warbah islands

cards.front: From inside Baghdad, what four benefits did the invasion of Kuwait seem to offer Iraq?
cards.answer: Cancelled Iraq's debts / doubled Iraq's oil reserves / intimidated the Gulf states / offered a pan-Arab nationalist triumph
items: Doubled Iraq's share of world oil reserves
Intimidated the rest of the Gulf

cards.front: How did Iraq's original invasion plan change before the attack on Kuwait was launched?
cards.answer: It grew from a limited operation to seize Bubiyan, Warbah and Rumaila into a plan for full annexation of Kuwait.

cards.front: Why did outside powers unite against Iraq after the invasion of Kuwait?
cards.answer: Saudi Arabia feared its own oil fields were next, the US saw a state seizing a fifth of world oil reserves, and even the Soviet Union would not defend annexation at the UN.

cards.front: Name the five types of structure the lesson describes for substances.
cards.answer: Giant ionic lattices / Simple molecular structures / Giant covalent structures / Polymers / Metallic structures

cards.front: Name the three limitations of dot-and-cross diagrams given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Don't show 3D shape of molecules / Don't show relative sizes of atoms / Don't show distances between atoms
items: Don't show relative sizes of atoms

cards.front: Why do most atoms bond with other atoms?
cards.answer: Most atoms don't naturally have a full outer shell of electrons, and bonding lets them achieve one, making them more stable.

cards.front: Why don't Group 0 elements readily form bonds?
cards.answer: Group 0 elements already have full outer shells of electrons, so they don't need to lose, gain or share electrons.

title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the six key structures of a synovial joint.
cards.answer: Synovial membrane / Synovial fluid / Joint capsule / Bursae / Cartilage / Ligaments

cards.front: Name the six movements possible at the shoulder joint (ball-and-socket).
cards.answer: Flexion / Extension / Abduction / Adduction / Rotation / Circumduction

cards.front: Why do cartilage injuries take so long to heal and can end sporting careers?
cards.answer: Cartilage has no blood supply of its own, relying on synovial fluid for nourishment, so damage heals very slowly.

cards.front: Why does warming up reduce the risk of ligament and tendon tears?
cards.answer: Higher body temperature during a warm-up makes ligaments and tendons more pliable, reducing the risk of tears.

cards.front: What three types of documents does Kipps find among Mrs Drablow's papers that reveal the truth?
cards.answer: Letters / Birth certificates / Adoption records

cards.front: The curse's child deaths appear as what three kinds of accidents?
cards.answer: Drownings / Falls / Illnesses

cards.front: Why does Jennet's revenge as the Woman in Black target innocent children rather than those who actually wronged her?
cards.answer: Her grief has become so vast and indiscriminate that she punishes the innocent, inflicting on others the same loss that destroyed her.

cards.front: Why does Hill refuse to give the novel a conventional, comforting ending?
cards.answer: The ghost cannot be defeated because Jennet's grief can never be resolved, since her child is dead and nothing can undo that.

cards.front: Name the four impulsive actions that define Romeo's character in the play.
cards.answer: Falls in love instantly / Marries within a day / Kills Tybalt in a rage / Buys poison without confirming Juliet's death
items: Buys poison without confirming Juliet's death

cards.front: From the balcony scene onwards, name the three ways Juliet drives the relationship.
cards.answer: Proposes marriage / Challenges the power of names / Makes practical plans

cards.front: Why does Mercutio's death change the tone of the play?
cards.answer: Without his irreverent energy the tone becomes unrelentingly tragic, marking the end of comedy in the play.

cards.front: How does Tybalt's aggression directly cause tragedy at the ball?
cards.answer: He insists on duelling Romeo despite Capulet's orders, which directly causes Mercutio's death and his own.

cards.front: Name the six circuit parameters covered in this course.
cards.answer: Potential difference / Current / Resistance / Capacitance / Power / Frequency

cards.front: Name the six unit prefixes used in circuit calculations, from largest to smallest.
cards.answer: Mega (M) / Kilo (k) / Milli (m) / Micro (µ) / Nano (n) / Pico (p)

cards.front: Why is 'potential difference' considered more precise than 'voltage'?
cards.answer: Potential difference always refers to the difference in electrical potential energy per unit charge between two specific points, never a single point.

cards.front: Why is confusing the prefix milli (m) with mega (M) such a serious mistake?
cards.answer: They differ by a factor of one billion, so mistaking 1 mW for 1 MW changes the value hugely and causes a serious error.

cards.front: What two symbolic items does a baby receive during infant baptism?
cards.answer: White garment symbolising purity / Candle symbolising the light of Christ
items: Candle symbolising the light of Christ

cards.front: How does full immersion in believers' baptism symbolise dying and rising to new life?
cards.answer: Being submerged under water mirrors dying to the old sinful life, and being raised up mirrors Jesus's death and resurrection into new life.

cards.front: Why do Baptists see believers' baptism as a more meaningful commitment than infant baptism?
cards.answer: It is a personal choice and public declaration of faith made by someone old enough to understand the commitment, unlike a baby.

title: Active and Passive Audiences and Uses & Gratifications Theory
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four audience needs identified by Blumler and Katz in Uses and Gratifications theory.
cards.answer: Information (surveillance of the world) / Personal identity (reinforcing values and self-image) / Integration and social interaction (maintaining relationships) / Entertainment (diversion and pleasure)

cards.front: Why did the two-step flow model weaken the hypodermic needle model?
cards.answer: It showed audiences were not uniform, as opinion leaders interpreted media first and social relationships filtered messages before reaching the wider group.

cards.front: Why can the same media product satisfy different needs for different audiences, according to Uses and Gratifications theory?
cards.answer: Because audiences use media purposefully, so one viewer might watch for information, another for identity reinforcement, and another for social interaction.

cards.front: Name the three characteristics that have the biggest effect on CPU performance.
cards.answer: Clock speed / Cache size / Number of cores

cards.front: In what order does a CPU check the three levels of cache before going to RAM?
cards.answer: L1 cache / L2 cache / L3 cache

cards.front: Why does a higher clock speed usually give better CPU performance?
cards.answer: More cycles per second means the CPU can carry out more instructions per second.

cards.front: Why might a CPU with a very high clock speed but a tiny cache still perform poorly?
cards.answer: It keeps stalling waiting for data from RAM because the small cache gives few cache hits.

cards.front: Name the three generations held at once in 'Partition'.
cards.answer: The aunt who acts / The mother who listens but stays home / The poet who receives the story decades later
items: The mother who listens but stays home
The poet who receives the story decades later

cards.front: What four short quotations does the lesson suggest learning from 'Partition'?
cards.answer: the cries of the people / she felt afraid / I still feel guilty about that / a man who knew nothing about geography
items: I still feel guilty about that
a man who knew nothing about geography

cards.front: Why does Bhatt never give the young woman in 'Partition' a name?
cards.answer: It is a distancing device that makes her feel like any woman living through Partition, not one unique individual.

cards.front: Why does Bhatt keep the horror of Partition off-page, heard only as distant cries?
cards.answer: It makes the reader share the young woman's own limited, frightened perspective on events she cannot see.

title: Propaganda, the police state and Nazi culture
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five main propaganda tools the lesson lists for the Nazi regime.
cards.answer: Radio / Film / Press / Posters / Rallies

cards.front: What were the four core elements of the Nazi propaganda message, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Hitler as saviour / The Volk as racial community / Versailles 'stab in the back' as a wound to reverse / Communism and Jewry as threats
items: Versailles 'stab in the back' as a wound to reverse

cards.front: Why did the lesson describe radio as the regime's most powerful single propaganda tool?
cards.answer: The Volksempfanger and public loudspeakers reached almost every household, spreading Nazi messages while blocking foreign broadcasts.

cards.front: How did self-policing let the Nazi regime control the population despite having only 32,000 Gestapo officers?
cards.answer: Fearing unknown informers, most Germans policed their own conversations, so terror worked through self-censorship as much as actual surveillance.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Jekyll's tragic arc, from voluntary transformation to his final escape.
cards.answer: Transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom / Hyde grows stronger / Transformations become involuntary / The potion stops working / Jekyll is trapped as Hyde and commits suicide
items: Transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom
Jekyll is trapped as Hyde and commits suicide

cards.front: Why does trying to separate good and evil make Jekyll's situation worse rather than better?
cards.answer: Separating good from evil makes both sides more extreme, so repressing his evil side only intensifies it.

cards.front: According to Stevenson, why did Jekyll really need the experiment in the first place?
cards.answer: Victorian society's pressure for respectability forced Jekyll to suppress his desires entirely instead of finding a healthy balance.

title: Castles: Instruments of Conquest and Control
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five kinds of buildings the lesson says were found inside a bailey.
cards.answer: Stables / Kitchens / A chapel / A hall / Quarters for the garrison

cards.front: The lesson gives three things Norman castles were sited to control. What are they?
cards.answer: Movement (rivers, roads, town gates) / People (rebellious regions, urban populations) / Patronage networks (centre of a tenant-in-chief's lands)
items: Patronage networks (centre of a tenant-in-chief's lands)

cards.front: Why did William need castles that could be built quickly after 1066?
cards.answer: The Normans were a tiny ruling minority controlling millions of Anglo-Saxons, so fast timber castles let them project control and crush rebellions immediately.

cards.front: Why did William replace timber castles with stone in places like the White Tower?
cards.answer: Wood could rot, burn or be chopped down, so stone gave permanence and made a visible, lasting statement of Norman power in major centres.

cards.front: Name the three factors the specification says designers must consider when selecting materials and components.
cards.answer: Functional need / Cost / Availability

cards.front: Name the five marking out methods the specification requires understanding of.
cards.answer: Reference datum points / Coordinates / Templates / Jigs / Patterns

cards.front: Why must designers plan the cutting and shaping of materials to minimise waste?
cards.answer: Wasted material is wasted money (economic), and less waste means a smaller environmental footprint.

cards.front: Why does the grain direction of fabric matter when cutting pattern pieces?
cards.answer: Cutting across the grain can affect the way the garment hangs and stretches.

cards.front: What are the five central themes of Boys Don't Cry, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Masculinity / Prejudice and acceptance / Family / Responsibility / Identity

cards.front: What features of the novel's setting reflect the realities of many British families?
cards.answer: Council estates / Stretched finances / Single-parent households / Pressure to succeed academically

cards.front: Why does dual narration create dramatic irony in Boys Don't Cry?
cards.answer: The reader sees both Dante's and Adam's inner worlds, so notices connections and parallels between their struggles that the brothers themselves miss.

cards.front: Why was Blackman's focus on Dante as a teen father socially significant when she wrote the novel?
cards.answer: Government campaigns focused on young mothers while teen fathers were largely invisible, so centring Dante challenged that assumption.

cards.front: Name three comic details Wells uses to show the crowd's complacency at Horsell Common.
cards.answer: People arrive by carriage and bicycle / Boys throw stones / A man sells apples
items: People arrive by carriage and bicycle

cards.front: Name three ways Wells shows social order dissolving during the evacuation.
cards.answer: People trample one another / People steal food / People abandon the weak

cards.front: How does Wells's simile describing Heat-Ray victims dehumanise them?
cards.answer: Saying each man was 'turned to fire' reduces people to fuel, stripping their dignity, mirroring how colonial powers described conquered peoples.

cards.front: Why does the narrator keep expecting the army and government to restore order?
cards.answer: His mind clings to normality, showing denial and confusion, mirroring how real people respond to disaster by refusing to accept the world has changed.

cards.front: Name the four institutions the SS controlled by 1939, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Gestapo / Concentration camps / SD (Security Service) / RSHA (Reich Security Main Office)

cards.front: Which four groups were concentration camps initially set up for in 1933?
cards.answer: Communists / Social Democrats / Trade unionists / Clergy who criticised the regime

cards.front: Why were the SD's frank reports on public opinion useful to Hitler?
cards.answer: SD officers reported discontent accurately, giving Hitler information about where public support for the regime was weak.

cards.front: How did the SS's self-image make it capable of committing extreme crimes?
cards.answer: Its combination of an elite self-image (racially pure, ideologically trained) with unconstrained power let it act where ordinary bureaucracies might resist.

cards.front: Name the five categories of customer requirement the lesson identifies for hospitality and catering.
cards.answer: Customer needs / Customer rights and inclusion / Lifestyle and dietary needs / Customer expectations / Customer demographics

cards.front: Name the seven factors the lesson says shape customer expectations.
cards.answer: Service quality / Value for money / Current trends / Awareness of competition / Media influence / Environmental concerns / Seasonality

cards.front: Why does failing to be inclusive harm a hospitality business itself, not just excluded customers?
cards.answer: It breaks equality legislation and also loses the business potential customers, damaging its reputation.

cards.front: How can media influence affect a hospitality business's bookings?
cards.answer: A positive review or TV feature can boost bookings, while a negative social media post can cause lasting damage.

cards.front: Name the three levels on which dramatic irony operates in An Inspector Calls.
cards.answer: Historical - audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong / Investigative - audience sees implications before characters do / Structural - audience knows the investigation will repeat
items: Historical - audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong
Investigative - audience sees implications before characters do
Structural - audience knows the investigation will repeat

cards.front: What three things does the cyclical ending of An Inspector Calls achieve, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Punishes the older generation for wasting their chance / Validates the younger generation's belief in accountability / Extends the warning to the real audience
items: Punishes the older generation for wasting their chance
Validates the younger generation's belief in accountability
Extends the warning to the real audience

cards.front: How does confining the play to one room in real time affect the audience watching it?
cards.answer: It makes the audience feel the same trapped pressure as the characters, with no time jumps, scene changes or relief from the revelations.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector's power not depend on documents or institutional evidence?
cards.answer: He has only a photograph and no files, so his power comes entirely from moral authority and the characters' guilty consciences.

cards.front: Name the seven Spanish phrases the lesson gives for talking about relationships with friends.
cards.answer: Me llevo bien con / No me llevo bien con / Me llevo mal con / Nos llevamos bien / Nos peleamos a veces / Tenemos mucho en común / Somos muy diferentes

cards.front: Name the eight opinion phrases the lesson gives for reaching higher marks in speaking and writing.
cards.answer: Creo que / Pienso que / En mi opinión / A mi modo de ver / Me parece que / Lo mejor es que / Lo peor es que / Me da la impresión de que

cards.front: Why is it important to use a variety of opinion phrases, not just me gusta, in Spanish speaking and writing exams?
cards.answer: Using a range of opinion phrases like a mi modo de ver demonstrates sophisticated language use needed for higher mark bands.

cards.front: How does the form of llevarse bien/mal con change depending on who is speaking?
cards.answer: It is a reflexive verb, so it changes form with the subject, e.g. me llevo bien or se lleva mal.

cards.front: Name the five types of accommodation given in the lesson vocabulary list.
cards.answer: un hotel / un hotel de lujo / un albergue juvenil / un camping / una casa rural

cards.front: Name the four hotel problems given as example complaint phrases.
cards.answer: air conditioning doesn't work / no hot water / the room is dirty / the lift doesn't work

cards.front: Why is quisiera preferred over quiero when booking a hotel room in a role-play?
cards.answer: Quisiera is more formal and polite than quiero, showing you can vary your register.

cards.front: How are the preterite and imperfect tenses used together to describe past accommodation?
cards.answer: The preterite describes the action of staying there, while the imperfect describes what the hotel or room was like.

title: Exchange, Transport and the Circulatory System
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four components of blood.
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right ventricle?
cards.answer: It must generate higher pressure to pump blood all the way around the entire body, not just to the lungs.

cards.front: Why is extra oxygen needed after intense exercise (oxygen debt)?
cards.answer: It is needed to break down the lactate that has accumulated from anaerobic respiration during exercise.

title: Characters: Sephy, Callum and Their Families
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things a sophisticated costume design answer should specify, according to the lesson, to avoid the 'black and white' misconception.
cards.answer: The fabric type / The fit / The colour palette / The condition of the clothing

cards.front: What three physical adjustments might a director ask the performer playing Callum to make in Cross spaces?
cards.answer: Keep arms closer to the body / Reduce gesture / Avoid direct eye contact with Cross characters
items: Keep arms closer to the body
Avoid direct eye contact with Cross characters

cards.front: Why does Callum reduce his physical expressiveness in Cross spaces?
cards.answer: He has learned to make himself smaller as self-policing to appear safe, contrasting with his freer physicality around Sephy or in nought spaces.

cards.front: How could lighting design signal Sephy's emotional arc across the play?
cards.answer: Early scenes use a warm overhead wash suggesting unexamined confidence, shifting later to a cooler, isolating lighting state showing her contracted world.

cards.front: Name the four elements of Hitler's ideology that Mein Kampf outlined.
cards.answer: Extreme nationalism / Anti-Semitism / Lebensraum / The need for a dictatorial leader
items: The need for a dictatorial leader

cards.front: Name the three crises that converged in Germany during 1923.
cards.answer: The Ruhr occupation / Hyperinflation / The Munich Putsch

cards.front: Why did Stresemann call off passive resistance in September 1923?
cards.answer: He recognised the printing presses had to stop, accepting the political cost of appearing to surrender to France.

cards.front: Why did the Munich Putsch fail within 24 hours?
cards.answer: The Bavarian government and the army did not support it, as Hitler had miscalculated loyalty to the republic.

cards.front: Name the three components a mains-powered PSU chain contains to produce stable DC.
cards.answer: Step-down transformer / Bridge rectifier / Smoothing capacitor

cards.front: Name the four factors that decide the choice between a mains and a battery power supply.
cards.answer: Power requirement / Portability / Safety / Cost

cards.front: Why do transformers only work with AC and not DC?
cards.answer: DC creates a static (unchanging) magnetic field in the core, which induces no voltage in the secondary coil.

cards.front: How does a bridge rectifier produce full-wave rectification?
cards.answer: It uses four diodes arranged in a diamond so both the positive and negative half-cycles contribute to the output.

cards.front: Name the three social factors the lesson gives that affect conformity.
cards.answer: Group size / Anonymity / Task difficulty

cards.front: Give the three weaknesses of Asch's study mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sample limited to male American students, reducing generalisability / Artificial lab task lacks ecological validity / Deception raised ethical concerns about consent
items: Sample limited to male American students, reducing generalisability
Artificial lab task lacks ecological validity
Deception raised ethical concerns about consent

cards.front: Why does a strong need for social approval increase conformity?
cards.answer: People who need social approval fear rejection, so they are more likely to go along with the group.

cards.front: Why is a controlled lab experiment considered a strength of Asch's study?
cards.answer: The conditions could be carefully controlled and repeated, and confederates gave consistent behaviour across trials.

title: War Communism, Kronstadt and the NEP
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four measures that made up War Communism (1918-21).
cards.answer: Nationalised all industry above smallest workshops / Banned private trade / Drafted workers into labour battalions paid in rations / Grain requisitioning at fixed low prices
items: Nationalised all industry above smallest workshops
Drafted workers into labour battalions paid in rations
Grain requisitioning at fixed low prices

cards.front: Name the four features of the New Economic Policy introduced in 1921.
cards.answer: Tax in kind replacing requisitioning / Small private workshops and shops legalised / Foreign concessions granted for capital / State kept the commanding heights of the economy
items: Small private workshops and shops legalised
State kept the commanding heights of the economy

cards.front: Why did peasants stop growing surplus grain under War Communism?
cards.answer: Armed detachments seized any surplus at fixed low prices, so peasants had no reason to grow more than they needed.

cards.front: Why did the Kronstadt Rising frighten Lenin more than other revolts like Tambov?
cards.answer: The demands came from Bolshevik-loyal sailors once called the revolution's pride, showing the regime's own base had turned against it.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why celebrities can be good role models.
cards.answer: They work hard and show success is possible / They support charitable causes and donate money / They inspire young people to follow their dreams
items: They work hard and show success is possible
They support charitable causes and donate money
They inspire young people to follow their dreams

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why celebrities can be bad role models.
cards.answer: They show an unrealistic lifestyle / Young people compare themselves and feel low self-esteem / There is too much pressure to look perfect
items: Young people compare themselves and feel low self-esteem
There is too much pressure to look perfect

cards.front: How can comparing yourself to celebrities affect young people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It can lead to low self-esteem.

cards.front: How does using 'einerseits ... andererseits' improve a German opinion answer?
cards.answer: It lets you present a balanced argument by showing both sides of an issue.

cards.front: Name the four types of synovial joint covered for GCSE PE.
cards.answer: Pivot joint / Hinge joint / Condyloid joint / Ball-and-socket joint

cards.front: Name the three hinge joints relevant to sport.
cards.answer: Elbow / Knee / Ankle

cards.front: Why do ligament sprains heal slowly compared to muscle injuries?
cards.answer: Ligaments have a relatively poor blood supply, so the limited blood flow makes the repair process slow.

cards.front: Why can't the wrist rotate like a screwdriver even though it's a moveable joint?
cards.answer: The wrist is a condyloid joint which only flexes, extends, abducts and adducts; rotation actually comes from the radioulnar pivot joint.

cards.front: Name the five main agencies of informal social control listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: The family / The peer group / Education / Religion / The media

cards.front: Name the four stated purposes of prison given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Punishment / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: How does feminist theory say family-based informal control differs for boys and girls?
cards.answer: Daughters are typically given less freedom of movement, face earlier curfews and are held to different standards than sons.

cards.front: How can the peer group encourage deviance rather than conformity, according to subcultural theorists like Cohen?
cards.answer: Peer groups can exert control towards deviance when their shared norms actually celebrate breaking rules.

title: Communist Control: Propaganda, Censorship and the Cult of Mao
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four pillars the lesson says communist control in Mao's China rested on.
cards.answer: Propaganda / Cult of Mao / Censorship / Forced labour (laogai)

cards.front: Name the four types of prisoner the lesson says were held in laogai camps.
cards.answer: Former GMD officials / Denounced 'rightists' / Religious clergy / 'Capitalist roaders'

cards.front: Why did the CCP rely on propaganda rather than just police control to rule China?
cards.answer: Because ruling around 600 million people, mostly illiterate peasants across vast countryside, made direct rule by police alone impossible.

cards.front: How did censorship work alongside propaganda to control what people believed?
cards.answer: By banning and removing alternative narratives, censorship made the regime's own propaganda message the only one in circulation.

title: Act 1: The Ball & Love at First Sight
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: What three driving forces does the Prologue establish in its opening quatrain?
cards.answer: The feud ('ancient grudge') / The doomed love ('star-cross'd lovers') / The link between love and death ('fatal loins')
items: The link between love and death ('fatal loins')

cards.front: Name the four Petrarchan oxymorons Romeo uses to describe his love for Rosaline.
cards.answer: Feather of lead / Bright smoke / Cold fire / Sick health

cards.front: Why does the Prologue's dramatic irony affect how the audience experiences the play?
cards.answer: It reveals the lovers' deaths before the action starts, so every joyful moment is filled with foreboding.

cards.front: Why is Prince Escalus's decree in Act 1 Scene 1 crucial to the plot?
cards.answer: It threatens death for further street violence, making Romeo's later killing of Tybalt punishable by banishment or death.

title: Quantitative Chemistry: Moles, Mass and Yield
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three steps used to find the mass of a product from a known mass of reactant in a balanced equation.
cards.answer: Calculate moles of the reactant / Use the equation ratio to find moles of product / Convert moles of product to mass
items: Use the equation ratio to find moles of product
Convert moles of product to mass

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why percentage yield is lowered.
cards.answer: Incomplete reactions / Reversible reactions reaching equilibrium before completion / Losses during filtration or evaporation
items: Reversible reactions reaching equilibrium before completion

cards.front: Why is the amount of product in a reaction calculated from the limiting reactant rather than the excess reactant?
cards.answer: The limiting reactant runs out first, so it caps the maximum amount of product that can form.

cards.front: Why do addition reactions have a high atom economy?
cards.answer: All the reactants combine into one single product, so no atoms are wasted in by-products.

cards.front: According to Greek myth, name the three ways the Amazons were said to differ from ordinary women.
cards.answer: Cut off one breast to improve their aim with a bow / Rejected men except for reproduction / Chose to fight rather than to weave
items: Cut off one breast to improve their aim with a bow
Chose to fight rather than to weave
