His home country is violent and persecuting
He can never return to his old life

cards.front: How does Sissay build suspense before the tribunal's verdict?
cards.answer: Through pacing — the hearing concludes, there is a wait, then the verdict is delivered, heightening emotional weight.

cards.front: Why does testimony work differently on stage than in a novel?
cards.answer: A real person stands before real people, so the audience cannot look away, skip ahead, or close the book.

cards.front: Name the four major international agreements of the 1920s, with their dates.
cards.answer: Dawes Plan (August 1924) / Locarno Treaties (December 1925) / Kellogg-Briand Pact (August 1928) / Young Plan (June 1929)

cards.front: Name the three acts of aggression the lesson gives as breaches of the Kellogg-Briand Pact.
cards.answer: Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) / Italy invaded Abyssinia (1935) / Germany remilitarised the Rhineland (1936)

cards.front: Why did the Ruhr occupation lead to hyperinflation in Germany?
cards.answer: Germany responded with 'passive resistance', ordering workers to strike, which disrupted the economy and caused hyperinflation.

cards.front: Why did the Dawes Plan create a dangerous dependency for Germany?
cards.answer: It worked by bringing American capital into the system through US loans, making Germany reliant on continued US lending.

cards.front: Name the three modern materials the lesson identifies as key examples.
cards.answer: Graphene / Metal foams / Titanium

cards.front: Name the five technical textiles or textile treatments the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Conductive fabrics / Fire-resistant fabrics / Kevlar / Microfibres / Micro encapsulation

cards.front: Why do metal foams work well for crash protection in vehicles?
cards.answer: They are lightweight but strong, and absorb energy well, cushioning impact during a crash.

cards.front: Why do photochromic pigments make good reactive sunglasses lenses?
cards.answer: They change colour in response to light, darkening in bright sunlight and returning to clear indoors.

cards.front: Besides ship money, name the three other financial measures Charles I used during the Personal Rule.
cards.answer: Distraint of knighthood / Revived forest laws / Granting of monopolies

cards.front: Why did Charles I dissolve the Short Parliament after only three weeks in 1640?
cards.answer: MPs insisted on discussing their grievances before granting him money, so Charles dissolved it.

cards.front: Why did the mutilation of Prynne, Burton and Bastwick in 1637 backfire on Charles and Laud?
cards.answer: The brutal censorship generated public outrage rather than submission, increasing opposition to Laud's reforms.

cards.front: The lesson gives five factors that affect BMR. Name them.
cards.answer: Age / Gender / Body composition / Hormones / Pregnancy

cards.front: How many kilocalories per gram do carbohydrate, protein, fat and alcohol each supply?
cards.answer: Carbohydrate: 4 kcal/g / Protein: 4 kcal/g / Fat: 9 kcal/g / Alcohol: 7 kcal/g

cards.front: Why does BMR increase during pregnancy?
cards.answer: Because the body is supporting fetal development and preparing for breastfeeding.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that eating fat, rather than carbohydrate, is what causes weight gain?
cards.answer: Weight gain comes from positive energy balance (eating more total kcal than you use), and high-sugar carbohydrate diets can cause this too.

cards.front: Name the three forms of exploitation Hari faces as a lascar sailor.
cards.answer: Low pay / Dangerous work / Racial abuse from white sailors

cards.front: What three key dynamics has Gupta established by the end of the opening scenes?
cards.answer: Hope versus reality / Exploitation versus resistance / Power imbalance between British employers and Indian workers
items: Power imbalance between British employers and Indian workers

cards.front: Why does Gupta give the ayahs a collective voice rather than focusing only on Rani's story?
cards.answer: So the audience cannot dismiss Rani's experience as an isolated case, showing exploitation is the systemic norm, not an exception.

cards.front: How does Susan Matthews justify owing Rani nothing once the ship docks?
cards.answer: She points out there was no written contract between them, so she owes Rani nothing.

cards.front: Name the four main forms of UK taxation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Income tax / National Insurance / VAT / Corporation tax

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says governments can manage unplanned spending risk.
cards.answer: Hold reserves / Borrow by issuing government bonds (gilts) / Adjust tax rates

cards.front: Why do local councils have less room to manage budget risk than central government?
cards.answer: Because, unlike central government, councils cannot borrow freely or print money, so must cut services when grants are reduced.

cards.front: Why is there significant political debate about social care funding compared to the NHS?
cards.answer: Because social care isn't entirely free at the point of use, so individuals may have to contribute based on their savings, unlike the NHS.

title: Funeral Rites and Evaluating Life and Death
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three religions the lesson states have burial as the traditional funeral practice.
cards.answer: Christianity / Judaism / Islam

cards.front: Name the three religions the lesson states have cremation as the traditional funeral practice.
cards.answer: Hinduism / Sikhism / Buddhism

cards.front: Why are Muslim graves positioned facing the direction of Makkah (qiblah)?
cards.answer: Because it reflects the belief that at the resurrection the dead will rise facing Makkah.

cards.front: Why do Protestant funerals typically not include prayers for the dead, unlike Catholic funerals?
cards.answer: Because most Protestant traditions reject the doctrine of purgatory, which such prayers are linked to.

cards.front: Name the three uses given for acrylic.
cards.answer: Display cases / Light diffusers / Rear lights of vehicles

cards.front: Name the four uses given for silicone.
cards.answer: Baking moulds / Sealants / Medical-grade implants / Gaskets

cards.front: Why can't thermosetting plastics be re-melted after they have been cured?
cards.answer: Curing forms permanent chemical cross-links between chains, so heating causes charring or decomposition rather than melting.

cards.front: How does woven Kevlar fabric absorb a sudden impact?
cards.answer: The fibres resist stretching, so impact energy is absorbed and spread across the fibres rather than concentrated at one point.

cards.front: Name the five separate actions each Birling character took against Eva Smith.
cards.answer: Birling sacked her / Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards / Gerald used and discarded her / Eric assaulted her / Mrs Birling denied her charity
items: Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards

cards.front: What three class layers does Priestley present in the play?
cards.answer: Landed aristocracy / Industrial middle class / Working class

cards.front: Why does Priestley argue that society, not just individuals, killed Eva Smith?
cards.answer: Each character's actions formed a chain, and a society letting the powerful exploit the vulnerable without consequence is ultimately to blame.

cards.front: How does class privilege enable each Birling character to exploit Eva?
cards.answer: Each uses their social or economic power over her: profit motive, spending power, wealth, status, or class immunity, leaving her no recourse.

cards.front: Besides Sam, name the three examples of everyday racism in Tollington the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Mr Christmas's 'jokes' about Indians / Neighbours' comments on the smell of Mama's cooking / The Kumars treated as exotic curiosities
items: Neighbours' comments on the smell of Mama's cooking
The Kumars treated as exotic curiosities

cards.front: Name the three effects of the racist attack on the Indian man that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Meena's parents are shaken / The Indian community draws closer together / Meena understands racism is physical danger, not just words
items: The Indian community draws closer together
Meena understands racism is physical danger, not just words

cards.front: How does dramatic irony work in the Spring Fete scene?
cards.answer: The reader can sense the danger in Sam's presence, but Meena, caught up in the excitement, cannot.

cards.front: Why is Papa's controlled, restrained anger after the attack more powerful than an outburst?
cards.answer: His restraint highlights the exhausting emotional labour of being an immigrant in a hostile environment.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the conch's decline through the novel, with their chapters.
cards.answer: Established in Chapter 1 / Challenged in Chapter 2 / Ignored by Chapter 8 / Destroyed in Chapter 11

cards.front: Name the four dictator tactics Jack mirrors from real-world dictatorships.
cards.answer: Uses fear of the beast to unify the group / Provides meat as reward / Demands absolute obedience / Employs Roger as his enforcer
items: Uses fear of the beast to unify the group

cards.front: Why does Jack's authoritarian leadership defeat Ralph's democratic leadership in the novel?
cards.answer: It appeals to primal emotions like fear and hunger with immediate rewards, while democracy requires patience and deferred gratification.

cards.front: Why does Golding describe civilisation as a 'veneer' in the novel?
cards.answer: Boys arrive with civilised habits like politeness, rules and democracy but quickly become murderers once adult restraints are removed.

cards.front: Name the six pieces of evidence the lesson gives for the theme of power and corruption in Animal Farm.
cards.answer: The milk and apples (early privilege) / Dogs chasing Snowball (violence) / Confessions and executions (terror) / Pigs sleeping in beds (breaking their own rules) / Boxer's sale to the knacker's (exploitation) / Final scene with humans (becoming the oppressor)
items: Pigs sleeping in beds (breaking their own rules)
Final scene with humans (becoming the oppressor)

cards.front: What five-step pattern should each main paragraph of an Animal Farm essay follow?
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Explanation / Context / Link back to the question

cards.front: Why does Orwell argue that power always corrupts those who hold it in Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Because systems without accountability, such as no free press, judiciary or educated citizens, will always produce corruption.

cards.front: How does controlling language allow the pigs to control what the animals believe is true?
cards.answer: By rewriting the commandments, the rules change and with them the animals' own understanding of what is right and wrong.

title: Ending the Bloody Code: Howard, Fry and Pentonville
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four recommendations did John Howard make to reform prisons?
cards.answer: Prisoners paid for, not made to pay fees / Classified by crime and by sex / Cells clean, ventilated and inspected / Chaplains and surgeons should attend
items: Prisoners paid for, not made to pay fees
Classified by crime and by sex

cards.front: What three things did 'reform' actually mean to Victorians like Howard and Fry?
cards.answer: Religious instruction / Work / Separation from corrupting company

cards.front: Why did reformers think keeping prisoners separate at Pentonville would reform them?
cards.answer: Separation stopped hardened criminals corrupting first offenders and forced each prisoner to confront his conscience without distraction.

cards.front: Why was public execution abolished in 1868?
cards.answer: After decades of complaint that the spectacle attracted huge drunken crowds and brutalised onlookers rather than deterring crime.

cards.front: Name the six key areas that an operating system manages.
cards.answer: CPU scheduling / Memory management / Backing store (file system) management / Peripheral management / User interface / Security

cards.front: Name the six main utility software programs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Anti-virus software / Backup software / Disk defragmenter / Disk compression / Data recovery software / File manager

cards.front: Why does excessive paging cause a system to slow down dramatically (thrashing)?
cards.answer: Because accessing the backing store is much slower than accessing RAM, so too much swapping of pages badly slows the system.

cards.front: Why is First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling considered unfair?
cards.answer: Because a long process that arrives first can block shorter processes from running for a long time.

title: Stalin's Response: Cominform, Comecon and Yugoslavia
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things Cominform did in practice, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Coordinated propaganda against the Marshall Plan / Enforced ideological discipline, denouncing deviation / Told local parties when to obstruct, strike, or stand for office
items: Coordinated propaganda against the Marshall Plan
Told local parties when to obstruct, strike, or stand for office

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of Comecon deciding national specialisation.
cards.answer: Bulgaria grew tomatoes / Hungary built buses / East Germany made chemicals

cards.front: Why did industrial unrest break out in France in autumn 1947?
cards.answer: Cominform ordered the French Communist Party, forced out of government, to fight the Marshall Plan from opposition.

cards.front: How did Comecon's trade rules disadvantage Eastern European countries?
cards.answer: They were forced to sell goods to Moscow below world prices and buy Soviet goods above world prices.

cards.front: Name the three types of hormonal contraception the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Oral contraceptive pill / Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch / Intrauterine device (IUD)
items: Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal methods of contraception the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragms) / Spermicidal agents / Surgical methods (sterilisation) / Abstinence or natural family planning

cards.front: How does oestrogen affect FSH and LH release once it reaches a high level?
cards.answer: At high levels, oestrogen stimulates LH release and inhibits FSH production.

cards.front: Why do contraceptive injections, implants or patches give long-term contraception without daily action?
cards.answer: They slowly release progesterone over weeks or months, so no daily action is needed.

title: Women, education and the One Child Policy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three areas of social policy under Deng that the lesson says stand out for the exam.
cards.answer: Education (restoration of merit-based university entrance) / The family (the One Child Policy) / The role of women (the 1980 Marriage Law)
items: The role of women (the 1980 Marriage Law)

cards.front: Name the three broad perspectives on the One Child Policy the lesson says should be understood.
cards.answer: PRC government's demographic and economic rationale / Human rights concerns about state coercion of reproduction / Demographic concerns about sex ratio imbalance and ageing population
items: PRC government's demographic and economic rationale
Human rights concerns about state coercion of reproduction
Demographic concerns about sex ratio imbalance and ageing population

cards.front: Why was restoring the gaokao in 1977 more than just an educational reform?
cards.answer: It was also a political statement, signalling that expertise and academic merit mattered again after political credentials had determined entry under Mao.

cards.front: How did rural areas gain some flexibility under the One Child Policy from 1984?
cards.answer: From 1984 many provinces allowed rural families a second child if the first child was a girl, unlike stricter urban enforcement.

cards.front: Name the four biotic factors the lesson gives.
cards.answer: food availability / predators / pathogens / competition

cards.front: Name the four threats to food security the lesson gives.
cards.answer: growing global population / climate change affecting crop yields / spread of new crop diseases / limited freshwater supplies

cards.front: Why can fish farming be more energy-efficient than catching wild fish?
cards.answer: Farmed fish don't lose energy swimming long distances or maintaining body temperature in cold water, unlike wild fish.

cards.front: Why does high biodiversity make an ecosystem more stable and resilient?
cards.answer: If one species declines, other species can take over some of its roles, keeping the ecosystem functioning.

title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four classification continuums used to describe skills in PE.
cards.answer: Basic – Complex / Open – Closed / Self-Paced – Externally Paced / Gross – Fine

cards.front: Name the four examples of abilities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reaction time / Balance / Limb coordination / Explosive power

cards.front: Why is a basketball lay-up placed between the basic and complex ends of the continuum?
cards.answer: It has a set pattern, making it less random, but needs coordination of running, jumping and release angle, making it more demanding.

cards.front: Why is serving in tennis classed as self-paced?
cards.answer: The server decides exactly when to toss the ball and begin the swing, so no external factor dictates their timing.

title: Act 1: The Feud and the Party
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: What pattern does the contrast between Benvolio and Tybalt establish for the rest of the play?
cards.answer: Those who try to make peace are overwhelmed by those who choose violence.

cards.front: Why does light/dark imagery become a significant recurring motif in the play?
cards.answer: It shows their love as a point of light surrounded by the darkness of the feud, violence, and death.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson states about Barzakh.
cards.answer: Intermediate state between death and Day of Judgement / Described as a barrier between living and afterlife / Soul remains conscious but cannot return to the world / A waiting period, not permanent reward or punishment
items: Intermediate state between death and Day of Judgement
Described as a barrier between living and afterlife
Soul remains conscious but cannot return to the world
A waiting period, not permanent reward or punishment

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson describes as happening on the Day of Judgement.
cards.answer: All souls are resurrected and brought before Allah / Each person's book of deeds is opened / The scale of deeds decides paradise or punishment / The angel Israfil blows the trumpet to begin it
items: All souls are resurrected and brought before Allah
Each person's book of deeds is opened
The scale of deeds decides paradise or punishment
The angel Israfil blows the trumpet to begin it

cards.front: Why does Allah's foreknowledge of a person's choice not force them to make it, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because Allah's knowledge simply reflects the choice the person freely makes, rather than causing it.

cards.front: Why do Muslim scholars disagree about whether descriptions of al-Jannah and Jahannam are literal or metaphorical?
cards.answer: Some take the vivid imagery at face value as real, while others see it as pointing to spiritual realities beyond human language.

title: Life Factors — What Shapes Health Across the Lifespan
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven family types the lesson names as life factors.
cards.answer: Nuclear / Extended / Single-parent / Step / Foster / Adoptive / Same-sex parent

cards.front: Name the five barriers to accessing services given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Geography (rural areas) / Financial cost (transport, prescriptions) / Language barriers / Disability / Lack of knowledge about services

cards.front: How does neglect during infancy affect a child's development across the PIES domains?
cards.answer: It disrupts attachment formation (emotional), impairs brain development (intellectual), delays physical growth, and limits socialisation (social).

cards.front: Why does unemployment damage an adult's emotional wellbeing, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Unemployment causes loss of routine, social contacts, and sense of purpose, alongside financial hardship, which damages emotional wellbeing.

title: Notting Hill: Riots, Racism and Policing
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three national stories the lesson says met at Notting Hill in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Post-war reconstruction and labour demand / The end of Empire (Windrush migration) / Wider cultural change (the 'Swinging Sixties')

cards.front: Name the four weapons the lesson says attackers used during the 1958 Notting Hill riots.
cards.answer: Iron bars / Knives / Milk bottles / Homemade petrol bombs

cards.front: Why did Caribbean migrants become concentrated in Notting Hill after the war?
cards.answer: Post-war labour demand pulled them to London, the 1948 British Nationality Act gave them the right to come, and the housing colour bar concentrated them in Notting Hill.

cards.front: Why shouldn't the 1958 Notting Hill attacks be described as a two-sided race riot?
cards.answer: Crowds of up to 400 white men, including outsiders, attacked Caribbean homes while residents only formed defence committees to protect themselves reactively.

title: The Treaty of Tordesillas and Rivalry with Portugal
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three long-term investments Portugal had made in the African route to Asia before 1493.
cards.answer: The fort at El Mina / Decades of royally funded voyages under Prince Henry / Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope (1488)
items: Decades of royally funded voyages under Prince Henry
Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope (1488)

cards.front: Give the three ways the lesson says Tordesillas mattered for the whole period.
cards.answer: Gave Spain unchallenged Catholic title west of the line / Embedded a religious framing later used in the Requerimiento / Became the template for later European imperial agreements
items: Gave Spain unchallenged Catholic title west of the line
Embedded a religious framing later used in the Requerimiento
Became the template for later European imperial agreements

cards.front: Why was Pope Alexander VI willing to back Spain in Inter caetera?
cards.answer: He was Spanish-born and depended on Ferdinand and Isabella's backing in Italian politics, so favouring Spain cost him nothing and earned their gratitude.

cards.front: Why did King John II push for the Tordesillas line to be moved further west?
cards.answer: Portugal had gathered reports that land lay much closer to the African coast in the southern Atlantic than Inter caetera's line assumed.

title: West Germany: economic recovery and politics
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four countries the lesson says West Germany recruited Gastarbeiter (guest workers) from.
cards.answer: Italy / Spain / Greece / Turkey

cards.front: What four things did the CDU offer voters, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Western integration / Social market economics / Firm opposition to communism / Conservative Christian social order

cards.front: How did the 'constructive vote of no confidence' make West German governments more stable?
cards.answer: It meant a chancellor could only be removed if parliament simultaneously agreed on a replacement, making governments harder to topple.

cards.front: Why did West Germany's economic growth slow down from the 1970s?
cards.answer: The rapid growth of the 1950s–60s relied on easy gains from post-war reconstruction, which ran out as the economy matured.

cards.front: Name the three things Victor has lost by the end, leaving the pursuit as his only identity.
cards.answer: His family / His friends / His health

cards.front: What three things does the Arctic ice symbolise the loss of for both Victor and the Creature?
cards.answer: Love / Warmth / Human connection

cards.front: Why does the Creature leave food and clues for Victor during the Arctic pursuit instead of killing him quickly?
cards.answer: The Creature wants Victor to suffer prolonged misery rather than die quickly, so it keeps him alive.

cards.front: Why does the Creature choose the frozen Arctic as the setting for the final pursuit?
cards.answer: The Creature picks terrain where its superior physical endurance gives it the advantage over Victor.

cards.front: Name the four meals of the day given in the lesson, in Spanish.
cards.answer: el desayuno / la comida / el almuerzo / la cena / la merienda

cards.front: Which three tenses does the model paragraph on food and mealtimes use?
cards.answer: present / preterite / conditional

cards.front: Why does the model paragraph on food use three different tenses?
cards.answer: Using present, preterite and conditional tenses together is essential for accessing higher mark bands in writing and speaking.

cards.front: How do you use 'me gustaría' to say what you would like to do?
cards.answer: Me gustaría is the conditional form of gustar, followed by an infinitive, to politely say 'I would like to...'.

cards.front: Name the four things animals compete for within a community.
cards.answer: Food / Territory / Mates / Water

cards.front: Name the four things plants compete for within a community.
cards.answer: Light / Water / Space / Mineral ions from the soil

cards.front: Why did producing insulin using genetically modified bacteria replace the older method of extracting it from animals?
cards.answer: Because extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases sometimes caused allergic reactions in patients.

cards.front: How does the predator-prey cycle work as prey numbers rise?
cards.answer: More prey gives predators more food so predator numbers rise, which then reduces prey numbers, causing predators to decline.

cards.front: Name the three options Victorian society gave middle-class women for their lives, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Marriage / Becoming a governess / Dependence on relatives

cards.front: Name the three Gothic features of Thornfield Hall described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dark corridors / A mysterious third-floor room / Unexplained laughter in the night

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Jane occupies an 'impossible position' in the Victorian class system as a governess?
cards.answer: She is educated enough to teach the family's children but too poor to be considered their social equal.

cards.front: Why does Brontë use Gothic elements in Jane Eyre, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: She uses them not just for atmosphere but to externalise Jane's inner psychological conflicts.

cards.front: Name the three ways every adult fails Juliet by the end of Act 3.
cards.answer: Capulet threatens to disown her / Lady Capulet withdraws support / The Nurse advises her to marry Paris (bigamy)
items: The Nurse advises her to marry Paris (bigamy)

cards.front: Name the five characters the feud goes on to destroy, fulfilling Mercutio's curse.
cards.answer: Romeo / Juliet / Tybalt / Paris / Lady Montague

cards.front: Why does Romeo's cry 'O, I am fortune's fool!' raise the fate vs free will debate?
cards.answer: Romeo blames fortune for Tybalt's death, but the audience has just watched him choose to fight.

cards.front: How does the Queen Mab speech show Mercutio's cynical worldview?
cards.answer: It presents dreams, and by extension love, as dangerous illusions, offering a rational alternative to Romeo's romanticism.

title: England in the fourteenth century: society, church and trade
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three institutions the lesson says shaped most people's lives in 1337 England.
cards.answer: The manor / The parish church / The serf system

cards.front: Name the four great festivals that gave the medieval agricultural year its rhythm.
cards.answer: Christmas / Easter / Midsummer / Harvest

cards.front: Why did the Church's wealth make it a powerful landlord as well as a spiritual authority?
cards.answer: It owned about a third of English land and collected tithes plus fees for baptisms, marriages and burials.

cards.front: Why were some peasants able to improve their economic position despite serfdom?
cards.answer: Some free peasants accumulated land to become yeomen, skilled tradesmen rose in towns, and the wool trade created a wealthy merchant class.

cards.front: Name the five data types the lesson says you must know.
cards.answer: Integer / Real (float) / Character / String / Boolean

cards.front: Name the three number systems described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Denary (base 10) / Binary (base 2) / Hexadecimal (base 16)

cards.front: Why does every piece of data stored in a computer need a data type?
cards.answer: The type tells the computer how many bytes to reserve, which operations are allowed, and how to interpret the binary pattern's meaning.

cards.front: How do you convert an 8-bit binary number into hexadecimal?
cards.answer: Split the bits into groups of four from the right, then replace each group of four bits with its matching hex digit.

cards.front: Name the four settings the lesson uses to map the clones' emotional journey.
cards.answer: Hailsham – protected innocence / The Cottages – drift and false freedom / Recovery centres – clinical despair / Norfolk field at the end – emptiness and acceptance
items: The Cottages – drift and false freedom
Norfolk field at the end – emptiness and acceptance

cards.front: Name the four losses the lesson gives to show every character is losing something.
cards.answer: Kathy loses Tommy / Tommy loses hope / Ruth loses time / The clones lose their lives

cards.front: Why are Ishiguro's symbols effective even though they are ordinary objects and places?
cards.answer: They are not dramatic but accumulate meaning through repetition and association across the novel.

cards.front: How does the physical narrowing of settings mirror the clones' emotional journey?
cards.answer: The settings move from Hailsham's relative openness to the stark emptiness of the final field, mirroring the shift from hope to acceptance.

cards.front: Name the three overlapping conspiracies against authority in the play.
cards.answer: Antonio's past usurpation of Prospero in Milan / Antonio and Sebastian's plot to murder Alonso / Caliban's alliance with Stephano and Trinculo to murder Prospero
items: Antonio's past usurpation of Prospero in Milan
Antonio and Sebastian's plot to murder Alonso
Caliban's alliance with Stephano and Trinculo to murder Prospero

cards.front: Who are the 'three men of sin' Ariel denounces as a harpy?
cards.answer: Alonso / Antonio / Sebastian

cards.front: Why does Caliban offer to serve Stephano and show him the island?
cards.answer: He is repeating the cycle of colonisation, offering his knowledge of the island to a new master to escape the old one.

cards.front: What does the vanishing banquet symbolise about Antonio, Alonso and Sebastian's treachery?
cards.answer: It shows that the material rewards of treachery are ultimately empty.

cards.front: Name the four 'Sugar Islands' Britain held by 1750.
cards.answer: Barbados / Jamaica / Antigua / St Kitts

cards.front: What four methods did the abolitionist movement combine to campaign against slavery?
cards.answer: Eyewitness testimony / Statistical research / Parliamentary lobbying / Consumer boycotts of West Indian sugar
items: Consumer boycotts of West Indian sugar

cards.front: Why did Barbados planters turn to enslaved Africans instead of indentured servants for sugar production?
cards.answer: Sugar farming was extremely labour-intensive and indentured English servants and Irish convicts couldn't supply enough workers or endure the conditions.

cards.front: Why did the Middle Passage kill so many enslaved Africans in transit?
cards.answer: Captives were chained into coffin-sized hold space with foul food and no sanitation, causing outbreaks of dysentery and smallpox.

cards.front: Why does Harri's reaction to the murder create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: He processes the blood, police tape and flowers as exciting and scary, not realising it is a life-destroying tragedy the reader understands.

cards.front: How does Kelman build tension through Harri's clue collection?
cards.answer: Each piece of evidence Harri gathers brings him closer to real danger, while the reader sees the threat building though Harri stays oblivious.

cards.front: What are the three main types of chemical bond?
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: What three things do dot-and-cross diagrams NOT show?
cards.answer: 3D shape / Relative atom sizes / Bond lengths

cards.front: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
cards.answer: Atoms are most stable with a full outer electron shell, and bonding lets them achieve this.

cards.front: Why do metals conduct electricity?
cards.answer: Because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the metal structure.

title: Staging and Design: Ships, Palaces and the Ayahs' Home
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three staging configurations considered for staging The Empress.
cards.answer: Proscenium arch / Thrust stage / Traverse staging

cards.front: Name the three objects that function as design symbols across The Empress.
cards.answer: Silver compass / Golden egg cup / Jewelled spice box

cards.front: Why did Emma Rice choose to use music and song throughout her production of The Empress?
cards.answer: To reinforce the play's clash and blend of cultures by mixing classical Indian and contemporary Western musical styles.

cards.front: Why might a designer track one object, like the compass, consistently across the whole play?
cards.answer: It gives the audience a physical thread through a story that otherwise leaps years at a time.

cards.front: Name the five rhetorical techniques Orwell gives Old Major in his speech.
cards.answer: Inclusive pronouns / Rhetorical questions / Repetition / Emotive language / Rule of three

cards.front: Why does Orwell make the Rebellion happen because Mr Jones forgets to feed the animals, rather than from ideology?
cards.answer: It shows revolutions are often triggered by immediate suffering like hunger rather than ideology alone, mirroring Russian bread shortages.

cards.front: How does dramatic irony work in the opening chapters of Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Readers know history shows the revolution will be betrayed, so the animals' hopeful optimism becomes poignant and tragic.

cards.front: Name the four levels at which Orwell's moral message can be read.
cards.answer: Political / Universal / About language / About responsibility

cards.front: Why is the reversal of 'Four legs good, two legs bad' into 'two legs better' the novella's most powerful moment of political irony?
cards.answer: The slogan that once defined the revolution is reversed to serve the new oppressors, showing language can be weaponised to mean the opposite of its original intent.

cards.front: How does renaming the farm back to 'Manor Farm' show that the revolution has failed?
cards.answer: The name 'Animal Farm' represented the revolution's promise of a new beginning, so its erasure means the revolution was entirely undone by the animals who led it.

cards.front: Name the five stages of photo etching, in order.
cards.answer: Print photomask / UV exposure / develop / etch / strip resist
items: Strip remaining resist to reveal tracks

cards.front: Name the three types of PCB covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Single-sided / Double-sided / Flexible

cards.front: How does CAM milling create the copper tracks on a PCB?
cards.answer: A CNC machine with a cutting bit physically cuts away copper between the tracks, leaving only the desired conductive paths.

cards.front: Why can't a complex circuit be routed on a single-sided PCB?
cards.answer: Complex circuits need tracks to cross, which isn't possible on one side without bridges or extra wiring.

title: Applied Methods: Interpreting Data and Crime Research
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: What are the three steps for systematically reading a table of crime rates by social group?
cards.answer: Identify what the columns and rows represent / Note the units used (rate, percentage or raw number) / Identify the highest and lowest values and any standout groups
items: Identify what the columns and rows represent
Note the units used (rate, percentage or raw number)
Identify the highest and lowest values and any standout groups

cards.front: What are the four common errors students make when reading crime tables and charts?
cards.answer: Confusing raw numbers with rates / Confusing an increase with a high level / Over-interpreting small differences / Ignoring the data source
items: Confusing an increase with a high level

cards.front: How does the functionalist perspective explain the age-crime curve?
cards.answer: It links the peak in youth offending to reduced social responsibility during adolescence and early adulthood.

cards.front: How does the structural explanation account for ethnic minority overrepresentation in crime statistics?
cards.answer: Ethnic minorities are disproportionately poor and in insecure work, so material deprivation, not ethnicity itself, may explain elevated offending.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says food can be produced.
cards.answer: Grown (vegetables and cereals in soil) / Reared (livestock like cattle, sheep, pigs on farms) / Caught (fish and shellfish, wild or farmed)
items: Reared (livestock like cattle, sheep, pigs on farms)
Caught (fish and shellfish, wild or farmed)

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson gives for why understanding food's origin matters.
cards.answer: Affects nutritional quality and freshness / Has environmental consequences (land, water, energy use) / Raises ethical questions (animal welfare, worker conditions, fair trade)
items: Has environmental consequences (land, water, energy use)
Raises ethical questions (animal welfare, worker conditions, fair trade)

cards.front: How does food waste cause economic harm, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Wasting food wastes the land, water, energy and labour used to produce it, leading to higher food prices for consumers.

cards.front: How can someone be food-insecure even in a wealthy country?
cards.answer: Food may be physically available, but the person cannot afford or access nutritious food despite living in a wealthy country.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson links to the appearance versus reality theme in Much Ado.
cards.answer: Masked ball (literal disguise) / Gulling scenes (staged appearances create new emotional realities) / Window plot (staged scene destroys a reputation) / Final wedding (masks conceal Hero's identity until the reveal)
items: Gulling scenes (staged appearances create new emotional realities)
Window plot (staged scene destroys a reputation)
Final wedding (masks conceal Hero's identity until the reveal)

cards.front: Name the three qualities the lesson says Beatrice and Benedick's love is built on.
cards.answer: Verbal equality / Mutual knowledge / Tested commitment

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare avoid presenting deception as simply good or bad in Much Ado?
cards.answer: Because he shows deception as a tool whose moral value depends entirely on the intention behind it.

cards.front: Why is Beatrice's cry 'O God, that I were a man!' significant?
cards.answer: It exposes that she has the moral authority to defend Hero but not the social permission, revealing patriarchy's structural injustice.

title: Jewish Worship: Synagogue, Prayer and Sacred Texts
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three daily times Jews pray, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Shacharit (morning) / Mincha (afternoon) / Maariv (evening)

cards.front: What three things does a synagogue service involve, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Prayer / Readings from the Torah and Haftarah / A rabbi's sermon
items: Readings from the Torah and Haftarah

cards.front: Why is the Amidah recited standing and facing Jerusalem?
cards.answer: It reflects the direction of the ancient temple and the Almighty's presence during this central prayer.

cards.front: Why do many kosher homes keep separate crockery and utensils for meat and dairy?
cards.answer: Because Exodus 23:19 commands not cooking a young goat in its mother's milk, so meat and dairy must be kept apart.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives for a firm to raise revenue.
cards.answer: Selling more units / Raising prices / Launching new products

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives for a firm to reduce costs.
cards.answer: Switching to cheaper suppliers / Automating tasks to cut labour costs / Producing on a larger scale to spread fixed costs
items: Automating tasks to cut labour costs
Producing on a larger scale to spread fixed costs

cards.front: How does predatory pricing differ from penetration pricing?
cards.answer: Penetration pricing sets low prices to attract customers and build market share, while predatory pricing illegally sets prices below cost to drive rivals out.

cards.front: How does profit act as an incentive in a market economy?
cards.answer: The prospect of profit motivates entrepreneurs to set up businesses, take risks and innovate.

cards.front: Name the three stereotypes Elizabethan culture associated with Jewish people.
cards.answer: Usury (money-lending at interest) / Devilry / Ritual murder of Christian children

cards.front: Name the two medieval sources Shakespeare combined to create The Merchant of Venice.
cards.answer: The 'pound of flesh' story (Il Pecorone) / The 'three caskets' story (Gesta Romanorum)

cards.front: Why is Antonio's treatment of Shylock in Venice seen as hypocritical?
cards.answer: Antonio insults Shylock as 'dog' and 'misbeliever' and spits on him, yet borrows his money whenever he needs it.

cards.front: How does the play's dual setting of Venice and Belmont create structural opposition?
cards.answer: It sets commerce against romance, law against love, and outsiders against insiders, since Shylock is never seen in Belmont.

cards.front: Name the three types of aid described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / Tied aid

cards.front: Name the three examples of top-down development projects given in the lesson.
cards.answer: China's Three Gorges Dam / Egypt's Aswan High Dam / India's nationwide rail network

cards.front: Why can globalisation make export-dependent economies vulnerable?
cards.answer: Because economies that depend on exports can crash when global demand falls, as happened in the 2008 financial crisis.

cards.front: Why can tied aid lock developing countries into expensive contracts?
cards.answer: Because tied aid requires the recipient to spend it on goods or services from the donor country.

title: The Home Front: recruitment, DORA and propaganda
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name four jobs (other than munitions work) that women moved into during the First World War.
cards.answer: Bus conductresses / Delivery drivers / Police officers / Civil servants / Bank clerks

cards.front: Name four forms of propaganda the government used to sustain support for the war.
cards.answer: Recruitment posters / Cinema newsreels / Censored newspaper reports / Stories about German atrocities

cards.front: Why did Pals battalions devastate entire communities when they suffered heavy casualties?
cards.answer: Because whole battalions were made up of men from the same town or workplace, so heavy losses wiped out a generation from one community at once.

cards.front: Why did public disillusionment with the war grow by 1916-1917?
cards.answer: Somme casualties, food shortages from the German submarine campaign, and endless newspaper casualty lists eroded initial patriotism.

title: The Great Depression and the retreat to nationalism
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three interconnected threats to the international order that the Depression had produced by 1933.
cards.answer: Germany had a fascist government rejecting Versailles / Japan had defied and left the League / Economic nationalism had destroyed 1920s trade relationships
items: Germany had a fascist government rejecting Versailles
Japan had defied and left the League
Economic nationalism had destroyed 1920s trade relationships

cards.front: What three structural factors are given for why Germany was more vulnerable to authoritarianism than its western neighbours?
cards.answer: Short democratic experience since 1919 / Hyperinflation trauma of 1923 / Humiliating legacy of Versailles

cards.front: How did the Depression drive the Nazi Party's vote share up between 1928 and July 1932?
cards.answer: Economic catastrophe led unemployed workers and anxious middle-class voters to turn to radical alternatives like the Nazis.

cards.front: Why did Brüning's deflationary policies prove politically catastrophic?
cards.answer: Cutting government spending and wages to fight the crisis actually worsened unemployment in the short term.

cards.front: Name the five external storage devices named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Portable HDD / Portable SSD / NAS device / Portable USB flash drive / Portable wireless drive

cards.front: Name the four consequences of not testing an IT system, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Data loss / Financial damage / Reputational harm / Potential harm to people in safety-critical systems
items: Potential harm to people in safety-critical systems

cards.front: Why would a business with ten employees benefit from cloud storage or a NAS device?
cards.answer: So everyone can access the latest version of shared files from any device.

cards.front: Why is a portable HDD or NAS device suitable for a photographer backing up thousands of RAW image files?
cards.answer: Because the task needs high storage capacity, which these devices provide.

cards.front: Name the four processes that cause coastal erosion.
cards.answer: Hydraulic action / Abrasion / Attrition / Solution (corrosion)

cards.front: Name the three ingredients needed to explain any UK coastal landscape.
cards.answer: Geology / Marine processes (waves and tides) / Sub-aerial processes

cards.front: How does abrasion wear away a cliff?
cards.answer: Waves throw sand and pebbles against the cliff, sandpapering and wearing away the rock surface.

cards.front: Why does longshore drift move beach material in a zigzag path along the coast?
cards.answer: Swash carries material diagonally up the beach at an angle, but gravity pulls the backwash straight back down the slope.

title: Rebel Without a Cause and Ferris Bueller's Day Off: Teen Rebellion
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four Chicago locations the lesson says were used for location shooting in Ferris Bueller's Day Off.
cards.answer: Sears Tower / Art Institute of Chicago / Wrigley Field / Downtown parade staged for the production
items: Downtown parade staged for the production

cards.front: Why does the chickie-run sequence use dissonant non-diegetic music rather than a heroic score?
cards.answer: It refuses to glamorise the danger, generating unease so the spectator fears for the characters instead of enjoying the race.

cards.front: Why is Plato repeatedly framed at the edges of the composition in the abandoned-mansion scene?
cards.answer: To show he is physically marginalised in the mise-en-scene even though the scene is nominally about inclusion in a makeshift family.

cards.front: Name the six design features Howard's garden city plan included.
cards.answer: Low-density housing set in gardens / Ample green belt land / No slums / Community-owned land / Smoke-free industry separated from housing / Full range of civic amenities

cards.front: Name the four civic institutions Letchworth's founders created for community life.
cards.answer: A co-operative store / Allotments for growing food / Public baths / A theatre

cards.front: Why was early Letchworth criticised for failing to help the working-class poor it was meant to benefit?
cards.answer: Rents, though lower than London, were still beyond the reach of the very poorest workers, so it attracted middle-class reformers instead.

cards.front: How did Letchworth pass into public ownership in 1963?
cards.answer: Parliament passed the Letchworth Garden City Act 1962, creating a statutory corporation that took the estate into public ownership, with compensation paid to shareholders.

cards.front: Name the six changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Boiling (evaporation) / Condensing / Freezing / Sublimation / Deposition

cards.front: How does melting change the arrangement of particles in a solid?
cards.answer: Particles gain energy and overcome some of the forces holding them in fixed positions, so they can slide past each other.

cards.front: Why is burning magnesium in air a chemical change?
cards.answer: It forms magnesium oxide, a new substance with different properties, and this cannot easily be reversed.

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth's visit to Pemberley change her view of Darcy?
cards.answer: The estate's beauty without ostentation mirrors Darcy's character, revealing an admirable nature beneath his proud exterior.

cards.front: Why does Darcy's secret rescue of Lydia prove his transformation is complete?
cards.answer: He saves the Bennets from ruin purely out of love for Elizabeth, seeking no credit or gratitude, showing pride replaced by generosity.

cards.front: Name the three rhetorical stages Henry's Harfleur speech moves through, in order.
cards.answer: Personal appeal ("dear friends") / National identity ("noblest English") / Divine mission ("God for Harry, England, and Saint George")
items: Divine mission ("God for Harry, England, and Saint George")

cards.front: Name the three visceral atrocities Henry threatens will happen to Harfleur if it doesn't surrender.
cards.answer: Naked infants spitted upon pikes / Mad mothers' howls breaking the clouds / Pure maidens falling into forcing violation
items: Mad mothers' howls breaking the clouds
Pure maidens falling into forcing violation

cards.front: How does Henry's threat to Harfleur work as a rhetorical strategy rather than just a description of violence?
cards.answer: He distances himself from the atrocities by blaming the governor, using the threat itself to force surrender without the violence occurring.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use Fluellen's honourable conduct in contrast to Pistol's cowardice?
cards.answer: To show that genuine honour exists among the common soldiers, even when the nobles' motives are questionable.

cards.front: Name the four transport expressions in the lesson that use 'à' instead of 'en'.
cards.answer: à vélo (by bike) / à pied (on foot) / à cheval (on horseback) / à moto (by motorbike)

cards.front: Name the four weather expressions in the lesson that use 'il fait'.
cards.answer: il fait beau (it's nice) / il fait mauvais (it's bad weather) / il fait chaud (it's hot) / il fait froid (it's cold)

cards.front: Why does 'parce que' change to 'parce qu'il' before 'il'?
cards.answer: Because 'que' drops its final vowel before 'il', giving 'parce qu'il' (and 'même si' becomes 'même s'il').

cards.front: Why must you include the definite article when a verb of opinion is followed by a country name, e.g. 'J'aime la France'?
cards.answer: Because in French, verbs of opinion followed by a country name always require the definite article before the country.

title: Barriers to Participation — and How to Remove Them
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-studies

cards.front: Name the four types of adapted provision the lesson gives for people with disabilities.
cards.answer: Wheelchair-accessible changing rooms and pool hoists / Hearing loops at reception and in fitness studios / Braille signage for visually impaired users / Coaching qualifications covering disability sport
items: Wheelchair-accessible changing rooms and pool hoists
Hearing loops at reception and in fitness studios
Braille signage for visually impaired users

cards.front: Name the three solutions the lesson gives for the family commitments barrier.
cards.answer: Buggy fitness classes / Family membership schemes / On-site crèche provision

cards.front: Why does unequal media coverage create a repeating cycle that limits participation in women's and disability sport?
cards.answer: Less coverage means fewer visible role models, so fewer people try those sports, leaving fewer stories for broadcasters to cover.

cards.front: Why is crèche provision at a leisure centre so important for removing the family commitments barrier?
cards.answer: It is frequently cited by mothers as the single most important factor enabling them to exercise.

cards.front: Name the three caskets Portia's suitors must choose between.
cards.answer: Gold / Silver / Lead

cards.front: Name the three ways Portia outsmarts the patriarchal system while technically obeying its rules.
cards.answer: Manipulates the casket test / Disguises herself as a male lawyer / Saves Antonio's life through legal brilliance
items: Disguises herself as a male lawyer
Saves Antonio's life through legal brilliance

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Shylock's demand for his 'pound of flesh' as more than simple villainy?
cards.answer: It is a response to systematic abuse, asserting his legal rights within a system that otherwise denies him justice.

cards.front: How does Antonio's behaviour towards Shylock expose Christian hypocrisy in Venice?
cards.answer: Antonio lends money without interest and spits on Shylock, yet Christian Venice depends on the Jewish money-lending it despises.

title: The Conquistadors Begin: Balboa, Cuba and Magellan
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three steps the lesson describes as building Spain's conquistador launch platform by 1520.
cards.answer: Balboa reaches the Pacific (1513) / Conquest of Cuba (1511-15) / Magellan's voyage (1519-22)

cards.front: What three groups made up Balboa's 1513 expedition across Panama?
cards.answer: Around 190 Spaniards / several hundred Indigenous porters / a pack of war dogs

cards.front: Why does the lesson say it is wrong to treat 'the Spanish' conquistadors as one united team?
cards.answer: Because conquistadors like Velazquez and Pedrarias Davila competed bitterly with each other for governorships, encomiendas, royal favour and the right to launch expeditions.

cards.front: How did Balboa's 1513 discovery help make Pizarro's later conquest of Peru possible?
cards.answer: Rumours of a southern empire of gold that Balboa collected became official intelligence at the Spanish court, planting the seed Pizarro harvested in 1532.

title: Socialisation, Identity and Agents of Socialisation
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three key dimensions of identity the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Gender identity / Class identity / Ethnic identity

cards.front: Name the four official institutions the lesson gives as examples of formal social control.
cards.answer: Police / Courts / Schools / Government

cards.front: How, according to Bowles and Gintis, does education's hidden curriculum socialise children?
cards.answer: Teachers model authority and students learn to follow instructions without question, preparing them to accept a hierarchical workplace.

cards.front: Why is informal social control usually more powerful than formal control in everyday life?
cards.answer: The desire to belong, be respected and avoid shame strongly motivates people to conform to norms without legal sanction.

cards.front: Name the three categories the lesson organises feedback into.
cards.answer: Emotional tone (positive or negative) / Source (intrinsic or extrinsic) / What it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance)
items: What it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance)

cards.front: Name the four sensory channels through which intrinsic feedback travels.
cards.answer: Proprioception / Vision / Touch / Hearing

cards.front: Why do elite performers often welcome negative feedback rather than seeing it as a threat?
cards.answer: They are confident enough to use precise detail on errors as a tool to refine already high-level technique.

cards.front: Why does a sprinter need extrinsic feedback to correct her block start angle?
cards.answer: She cannot feel the exact angle herself, but a coach can see it on camera and give precise corrections.

cards.front: Name the three key biographical links the lesson gives between Dickens and the novel.
cards.answer: His father was imprisoned for debt / He worked in a blacking factory and felt shame about class / He became wealthy but never lost sensitivity to how the poor were treated
items: His father was imprisoned for debt
He worked in a blacking factory and felt shame about class
He became wealthy but never lost sensitivity to how the poor were treated

cards.front: Name the three tiers of the Victorian class system described in the lesson, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Landed gentry and aristocracy / Professional and merchant classes / Labouring poor

cards.front: How does the criminal justice system expose class hypocrisy in Great Expectations?
cards.answer: Magwitch, treated as subhuman by the law, shows more genuine love and generosity than the 'respectable' Miss Havisham or Compeyson.

cards.front: Why does Dickens show Pip's education at Matthew Pocket's as limited?
cards.answer: It makes Pip more polished on the surface but does not make him a better person, unlike morally educated Joe and Biddy.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things do the spirits force Scrooge to confront?
cards.answer: His past choices / His present isolation / His potential future

cards.front: The lesson says Christmas in the novella embodies three things — what are they?
cards.answer: Generosity / Family unity / Social harmony

cards.front: How does Dickens use setting to contrast wealth and poverty?
cards.answer: Scrooge's counting house is cold with only one coal for warmth, while the poor Cratchit home is filled with warmth, love and Christmas spirit.

cards.front: Why is Fred's invitation to Scrooge for Christmas dinner significant?
cards.answer: Despite years of rejection from Scrooge, Fred still invites him, demonstrating unconditional love and forgiveness.

cards.front: Name the four sleep stages the brain cycles through during one sleep cycle.
cards.answer: Light sleep / Deeper sleep / Deep (slow-wave) sleep / REM sleep

cards.front: What four things happen to the body during REM sleep?
cards.answer: Eyes move rapidly beneath closed lids / Brain activity looks similar to being awake / Major muscles are temporarily paralysed / Heart rate and breathing become faster and irregular
items: Eyes move rapidly beneath closed lids
Brain activity looks similar to being awake
Heart rate and breathing become faster and irregular

cards.front: Why is chronic short sleep linked to poorer memory and mood?
cards.answer: Waking early or cutting sleep short loses a disproportionate amount of REM sleep, since REM is concentrated in later cycles.

cards.front: Why do shift workers who sleep by day and work by night often struggle to sleep well?
cards.answer: Their light exposure is the opposite of what their circadian rhythm expects, so their body clock falls out of sync.

title: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four ways of presenting data in sport that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Table / Bar chart / Line graph / Pie chart

cards.front: Name the three common errors students make when interpreting data.
cards.answer: Copying numbers without saying what they show / Forgetting to include units in calculations / Confusing the mean with the range
items: Copying numbers without saying what they show
Forgetting to include units in calculations
Confusing the mean with the range

cards.front: Why does a line graph of resting heart rate over 12 weeks of training show a downward trend?
cards.answer: It shows bradycardia adaptation, where the heart becomes stronger and more efficient, lowering resting heart rate.

cards.front: Why is qualitative data harder to compare statistically than quantitative data?
cards.answer: Because it is open-ended and two observers watching the same performance might write different notes, making objective comparison difficult.

cards.front: Name the four main settings the lesson analyses as symbolic in Great Expectations.
cards.answer: The marshes / Satis House / London / The forge

cards.front: Name the three key symbols/motifs the lesson highlights beyond setting itself.
cards.answer: Mist / Chains / Light and dark

cards.front: Why does Dickens have Pip return to the marshes at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: To show that true identity is found by going back to your origins, not by running from them.

cards.front: How does the destruction of Satis House after Miss Havisham's death work symbolically?
cards.answer: Its physical ruin mirrors the end of her poisonous influence, and Pip and Estella walking out together symbolises liberation from the past.

cards.front: Name the five strict conditions Islamic teaching sets before lesser jihad can be declared.
cards.answer: Must be defensive / Must be a last resort / Must be declared by a recognised religious authority / Must be proportionate / Must stop when the enemy seeks peace
items: Must be declared by a recognised religious authority
Must stop when the enemy seeks peace

cards.front: Name the three Islamic festivals covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Id-ul-Adha / Id-ul-Fitr / Ashura

cards.front: Why is greater jihad considered more important than lesser jihad?
cards.answer: Because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle involving daily efforts to study the Qur'an, follow the Five Pillars and improve oneself spiritually.

cards.front: How does the Shi'a belief in the occultation of the twelfth Imam affect when lesser jihad can be declared?
cards.answer: Some Shi'a scholars teach only a divinely appointed Imam can declare lesser jihad, so it cannot be declared while he remains hidden.

cards.front: Name the three terminals of an operational amplifier.
cards.answer: Inverting input (−) / Non-inverting input (+) / Single output

cards.front: Name the three circuit connections that define an inverting amplifier.
cards.answer: Input signal via R1 to the − input / Feedback resistor Rf from output to the − input / + input connected to 0V (ground)
items: Input signal via R1 to the − input
Feedback resistor Rf from output to the − input

cards.front: Why is negative feedback added around an op-amp instead of using it open-loop?
cards.answer: Open-loop gain is enormous and unstable, so resistors are added to form negative feedback, setting a stable, predictable gain.

cards.front: Why must you check for clipping when calculating an op-amp's output voltage?
cards.answer: The output can never exceed the supply rail voltage, so a calculated output close to it may actually be clipped.

title: Operating Systems, Utility Software and Robust Software
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five utility programs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: File repair / Backup / Data compression / Disk defragmentation / Anti-malware

cards.front: What four things does an audit trail record about each action on a system?
cards.answer: Which user logged in / Which files were accessed / What data was changed / When it happened

cards.front: How does process management make several programs appear to run at the same time?
cards.answer: The OS switches the CPU between processes so quickly that they all seem to run simultaneously.

cards.front: Why is anti-malware classed as utility software rather than application software?
cards.answer: It maintains the health and security of the system rather than performing a task for the user directly.

cards.front: Why does Winterson report the exorcism in flat, ordinary sentences?
cards.answer: The calm, restrained telling makes it obvious this is not spiritual healing but physical and psychological abuse.

cards.front: How does the church's earlier binary worldview shape its reaction to Jeanette's relationship?
cards.answer: Because the church only recognises 'righteous' or 'demonic', there's no category for a good person who happens to be gay.

title: Newspaper Front Pages: The Guardian and The Sun (2022/2021 editions)
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four clothing items Boris Johnson wears in The Guardian's jogging photo.
cards.answer: Beanie hat / Jumper / Fish-print shorts / Leather-effect trainers

cards.front: What three light workplace stereotypes appear in The Guardian's G2 skyline entertainment feature?
cards.answer: The office romance / The geek / The joker

cards.front: Why does the caption on The Guardian's jogging photo act as anchorage?
cards.answer: It names the dog and location so readers interpret the image exactly as intended, as evidence of Johnson's ineptitude.

cards.front: Why does The Sun frame Covid-19 vaccination volunteers as an 'army'?
cards.answer: Calling volunteers an army frames Covid-19 as a common enemy readers can help defeat, turning a medical story into a military one.

title: Relational Databases: Tables, Keys and Relationships
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three types of organisation the lesson gives as database users, with what each stores.
cards.answer: Schools store pupil records / Hospitals track patient appointments / Online shops manage product stock

cards.front: Name the two rules a primary key field must always follow.
cards.answer: No two records can share the same value / The field can never be left blank
items: No two records can share the same value
The field can never be left blank

cards.front: Why did storing all student and course data in one big flat table cause problems?
cards.answer: Repeating a student's name and year group for every course caused redundancy, and changing year group meant updating every row or risking inconsistency.

cards.front: Why is the foreign key always placed in the table on the 'many' side of a one-to-many relationship?
cards.answer: Each record on the many side belongs to only one record on the one side, so it needs a field pointing back to that single matching record.

cards.front: The lesson names four common exam mistakes to avoid in a modern-text essay. What are they?
cards.answer: Narrative retelling / Bolted-on context / Ignoring the prompt / Vague analysis

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, what three roles does music play in connecting to the novel's themes?
cards.answer: A class leveller / An identity marker / A symbol of redemption

cards.front: Why does Gavin use childhood as the lens through which every other theme in the novel is examined?
cards.answer: Because how each adult character treats children reveals and tests their moral character.

cards.front: Why does 'good' always come at a cost in Coram Boy?
cards.answer: Because doing good requires sacrifice, shown through Meshak's sacrifice, Handel's charity and Thomas Coram's decades of campaigning.

cards.front: Name the four stages that life cycle analysis (LCA) breaks a product's environmental impact into.
cards.answer: Extracting raw materials / Manufacturing and processing / Use by the consumer / Final disposal or recycling

cards.front: Name the five contemporary and future scenarios the lesson gives for evaluating a new technology.
cards.answer: Natural disasters / Medical advances / Travel / Global warming / Communication

cards.front: Why might a cheap, ethically sourced material with a low carbon footprint still fail as a design solution?
cards.answer: It might not survive the stresses the product faces, or the factory may lack the machinery to shape it accurately.

cards.front: Why does life cycle analysis (LCA) consider all four stages of a product's life rather than just manufacturing?
cards.answer: A product could score well at manufacturing but still have a poor overall impact if it cannot be recycled or safely disposed of.

cards.front: Name the four steps in the systematic debugging routine described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Read the error message carefully / Narrow down the fault by checking each module's output / Trace the suspect section by hand / Make one change at a time and re-test
items: Narrow down the fault by checking each module's output
Trace the suspect section by hand
Make one change at a time and re-test

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says refining can improve a program.
cards.answer: Correcting an error / Tightening up the logic / Adding a check for input not thought of / Rewriting a clumsy section to run faster or read more clearly
items: Adding a check for input not thought of
Rewriting a clumsy section to run faster or read more clearly

cards.front: Why does iterative testing save so much time compared with testing only at the very end?
cards.answer: Because you already know earlier parts work, so any new bug caught is almost certainly in the code you just added.

cards.front: Why is final testing still needed even after every module has been tested individually?
cards.answer: Because some faults only appear when different parts of the program interact, which module-by-module testing can miss.

cards.front: Name the three types of interdependence relationships in a community.
cards.answer: Predation / Mutualism / Parasitism

cards.front: Name the three types of adaptations organisms can have.
cards.answer: Structural / Behavioural / Functional

cards.front: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
cards.answer: Energy is lost at each trophic level through respiration, movement and heat, leaving too little energy to support further levels.

cards.front: Why do pyramids of biomass give a more accurate picture of energy flow than pyramids of numbers?
cards.answer: Pyramids of numbers can be inverted, like one oak tree supporting thousands of insects, but biomass reflects the actual mass of living matter at each level.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says Helen uses humour.
cards.answer: Deflect criticism / Avoid emotional honesty / Belittle Jo

cards.front: Name the three domestic concerns that fill Geof's dialogue.
cards.answer: Questions about the baby / Suggestions about seeing the doctor / Offers to cook

cards.front: Why is Jo's invented word 'geniused' significant?
cards.answer: It is grammatically 'wrong' but asserts Jo's creativity and intelligence despite her lack of formal education.

cards.front: How did Littlewood shape the play's rapid-fire dialogue?
cards.answer: She sharpened the rhythm in rehearsals using the music hall tradition of quick exchanges between a straight man and a funny man.

cards.front: Name the three broad categories of protecting information that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Logical protection / Physical protection / Security policies

cards.front: Name the three main security policies covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Disaster recovery plan / Staff responsibilities policy / Acceptable use policy

cards.front: Why is multi-factor authentication harder for an attacker to bypass than a single password?
cards.answer: Because stealing a password alone is not enough; the attacker also needs the second check, like a one-time code.

cards.front: Why are backup systems classed as physical protection rather than logical protection?
cards.answer: Because decisions like where to store backups and how many copies to keep concern physical hardware and location, guarding against physical threats.

cards.front: Name the five things the lesson says a child needs that Silas could not provide while living in isolation.
cards.answer: Food / Clothing / Medical care / Company / Guidance

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says community acceptance requires from Silas.
cards.answer: Vulnerability / Need / Reciprocity

cards.front: How does telling Eppie stories about Lantern Yard help Silas deal with his past?
cards.answer: The act of narrating his history to Eppie is itself a form of healing that processes his trauma.

cards.front: How does Eliot show Godfrey's guilt getting worse through his silence about Eppie?
cards.answer: Each act of concealment makes the next easier, until he loses the capacity to act honestly.

cards.front: What four advantages does CNC routing have over manual routing, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Accuracy (tolerances of ±0.1 mm) / Speed (sheets cut in minutes) / Complexity (curves, pockets, joints in one setup) / Nesting (arranges parts to cut waste)
items: Complexity (curves, pockets, joints in one setup)

cards.front: What four safety precautions does the lesson give for using a circular saw or band saw?
cards.answer: Guards correctly adjusted and in place / Appropriate PPE worn / Timber fed steadily without forcing / Dust extraction connected and running
items: Guards correctly adjusted and in place

cards.front: Why must you always mark and cut on the waste side of a line rather than exactly on it?
cards.answer: The saw kerf removes some material, so cutting on the wrong side leaves the finished component slightly undersize.

cards.front: Why is a rip saw not suitable for cutting across the grain?
cards.answer: Its large, widely spaced teeth cut along the grain by a chiselling action rather than cleanly severing cross-grain fibres.

cards.front: Name the six territories Russia lost under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
cards.answer: Poland / Lithuania / Latvia / Estonia / Finland / Ukraine

cards.front: What four sets of reasons explain why the Reds won the Civil War?
cards.answer: Geography (interior lines, central railway hub) / Leadership (Lenin and Sovnarkom unified, Whites divided) / The Red Army (Trotsky's conscript force with ex-Tsarist officers) / Propaganda (land, peace, bread vs monarchists and foreign agents)
items: Leadership (Lenin and Sovnarkom unified, Whites divided)
The Red Army (Trotsky's conscript force with ex-Tsarist officers)
Propaganda (land, peace, bread vs monarchists and foreign agents)

cards.front: Why did Lenin overrule Trotsky and sign the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918?
cards.answer: 'No war, no peace' failed as Germany marched deeper into Russia unopposed, so Lenin judged a breathing space at any price better than a doomed revolutionary war.

cards.front: Why did the Whites lose the Civil War for structural reasons rather than unpopularity?
cards.answer: They could not coordinate Denikin, Kolchak and Yudenich, had no common political programme, relied on alienating monarchist symbols, and lacked the Reds' central railway hub.

cards.front: Name the five categories that official statistics on clinical depression are broken down by.
cards.answer: Prevalence / Differences across age groups / Differences between men and women / Differences across ethnic groups / Recovery rates

cards.front: Name the four symptoms clinicians check for using ICD criteria to diagnose clinical depression.
cards.answer: Persistent low mood / Loss of interest in normal activities / Disrupted sleep and appetite / Reduced energy
items: Loss of interest in normal activities

cards.front: How does social rank theory explain low energy and reduced activity as symptoms of depression?
cards.answer: They limit further competitive behaviour that could provoke conflict with higher-ranking individuals.

cards.front: Why do critics argue social rank theory doesn't fully explain human depression?
cards.answer: Because grief, trauma, chronic stress and negative thinking can trigger depression without any loss of social rank.

cards.front: Name the four common imperfect tense phrases used for describing sport at Foundation tier.
cards.answer: c'était (it was) / il y avait (there was/were) / j'étais (I was) / il faisait (it was - weather)

cards.front: Name the three jerseys given for the Tour de France.
cards.answer: maillot jaune (yellow, overall leader) / maillot vert (green, best sprinter) / maillot à pois (polka dot, best climber)
items: maillot à pois (polka dot, best climber)

cards.front: How do you form the imperfect tense in French for most verbs?
cards.answer: Take the nous form of the present tense, remove -ons, then add the endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

cards.front: Why combine the perfect and imperfect tenses when describing a past sporting event?
cards.answer: The perfect tense describes completed actions or results, while the imperfect describes the atmosphere and feelings at the time.

cards.front: Name the four themes Act 1 Scene 1 introduces in miniature, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Poverty (the flat) introduces class / Helen's drinking introduces self-destruction / Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men / Jo left alone introduces abandonment
items: Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men

cards.front: What three details does the opening stage direction give about the flat?
cards.answer: a comfortless flat / large, sagging furniture / a view of the gasworks

cards.front: Why does Delaney write Jo and Helen's dialogue as rapid-fire exchanges?
cards.answer: It reflects music hall influence, giving sharp wit that masks pain and showing their bickering is habitual rather than new.

cards.front: Why does Jo react calmly rather than crying when Helen leaves her alone with Peter?
cards.answer: Abandonment has become normalised for Jo because she has been left before many times, showing resilience that is also her tragedy.

cards.front: Name the four muscles/muscle groups the lesson describes at the shoulder joint.
cards.answer: Deltoid / Rotator cuffs / Pectorals / Latissimus dorsi

cards.front: Name the three types of muscle contraction the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Isotonic concentric / Isotonic eccentric / Isometric

cards.front: Why must every joint be controlled by at least two muscles working in opposite directions?
cards.answer: Because muscles can only pull, never push, so one muscle contracts to move a joint while its partner relaxes to allow that movement.

cards.front: How do the gluteals and hip flexors act as an antagonistic pair at the hip?
cards.answer: Gluteals are the agonist during hip extension, while hip flexors are the agonist during hip flexion, each relaxing when the other contracts.

cards.front: Name the three domains in which Heidensohn argued women face tighter control than men.
cards.answer: Control in the home / Control in public / Control at work

cards.front: Name the four stated purposes of prison given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Punishment / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: Why do interactionist sociologists say formal social control produces unequal outcomes?
cards.answer: Discretion at every stage (police, prosecutors, judges) is shaped by stereotypes and social power, not just evidence, producing selective enforcement.

cards.front: How does Carlen extend Heidensohn's feminist explanation of female crime?
cards.answer: Carlen argues that when the class deal and gender deal both fail working-class women, crime becomes a rational alternative.
