cards.answer: When all karma is exhausted and the atman recognises its true nature as identical with Brahman or eternally related to Bhagavan, rebirth ends.

cards.front: Name the three ways Tollington's neighbours react to the racist attack, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Horrified / Indifferent / Sympathetic to Sam

cards.front: How does the Spring Fete change Meena's understanding of racism?
cards.answer: She realises racism isn't just awkward comments or curiosity, but physical, violent danger to her family.

cards.front: Why does Meena's hospital recovery bring her closer to her Punjabi heritage?
cards.answer: Separated from Anita's influence, Meena reconnects with Punjabi stories, food and family instead of chasing Anita's approval.

cards.front: Name the four main categories of renewable technology used in buildings, as covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Solar / Wind / Heat pumps / Water technologies

cards.front: Name the four water technologies described for reducing mains water use or generating power.
cards.answer: Rainwater harvesting / Grey water re-use / Hydro-generation / Tidal generation

cards.front: Why are heat pumps considered highly efficient?
cards.answer: They move existing heat from a natural source to the building rather than generating heat by burning fuel.

cards.front: Why does a solar thermal system usually still need a backup heating source?
cards.answer: Its output depends on sunshine, so a boiler or immersion heater must top up water temperature in cold or cloudy periods.

cards.front: Name the three things Christopher does as part of his investigation into Wellington's death.
cards.answer: Interviews neighbours methodically / Creates a list of suspects / Reasons about motive and opportunity

cards.front: Why does Christopher keep investigating Wellington's death after Ed tells him to stop?
cards.answer: Not out of defiance, but because he cannot stop applying logic to an unsolved problem.

cards.front: Why does Christopher admire Sherlock Holmes?
cards.answer: Holmes uses logic and deduction rather than emotional intuition, a way of understanding the world Christopher can access.

cards.front: The lesson names four environmental impacts caused by burning fossil fuels. What are they?
cards.answer: CO2 causing the greenhouse effect and climate change / Sulfur dioxide causing acid rain / Particulates causing respiratory problems / Oil spills damaging marine ecosystems
items: CO2 causing the greenhouse effect and climate change

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages of wind power given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Intermittent (only generates when wind blows) / Visual and noise impact / Can harm birds

cards.front: Why is natural gas sometimes called a 'transition fuel'?
cards.answer: It has about half the carbon footprint of coal per unit of energy, helping countries move towards renewables.

cards.front: How is biomass considered carbon-neutral in theory?
cards.answer: The CO2 absorbed by plants as they grow equals the CO2 released when the biomass is burned.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things lured most of the boys to defect to Jack's tribe?
cards.answer: The promise of meat / Excitement / Protection from the beast

cards.front: Why does Golding use sexually violent language to describe the killing of the sow?
cards.answer: To show the hunters are no longer killing for food but for pleasure and dominance.

cards.front: How does Ralph's reaction to Simon's death differ from Piggy's, and why does this matter?
cards.answer: Ralph admits "That was murder" and confronts the horror, while Piggy rationalises it as an accident to protect himself, showing even good characters are complicit.

title: The Position of Women: Flappers and Their Limits
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson, what jobs were 1920s American women concentrated in as 'women's work'?
cards.answer: Secretarial work / Teaching (especially young children) / Nursing / Telephone operating / Retail

cards.front: What factors does the lesson give for why the 19th Amendment passed when it did?
cards.answer: Wyoming gave women the vote in 1869 as a territory / Fifteen states had given women the vote by 1918 / Women's war work in WWI shifted politics / Wilson told the Senate in 1918 it was vital to winning the war
items: Wyoming gave women the vote in 1869 as a territory
Fifteen states had given women the vote by 1918
Women's war work in WWI shifted politics
Wilson told the Senate in 1918 it was vital to winning the war

cards.front: Why did the First World War help persuade politicians to grant women the vote?
cards.answer: Around 25,000 women served as nurses and tens of thousands more did factory work, farming and Red Cross work, proving their contribution and shifting political opinion.

cards.front: Why is the flapper an unreliable image of what life was like for most 1920s American women?
cards.answer: The flapper lifestyle was confined to a small group of young, urban, middle-class white women, while most women were rural, working-class, immigrant or African-American with barely changed lives.

title: Causes of illness and disease over time
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three years the lesson gives for major cholera epidemics in Britain.
What three responses did people use against the Black Death, based on mistaken beliefs?
cards.answer: Burning herbs / Flagellation / Quarantine of towns

cards.front: Why did quarantine accidentally help slow the spread of the Black Death?
cards.answer: It separated infected people from healthy people, reducing contact, even though the real cause (fleas and rats) was unknown.

cards.front: How did killing cats and dogs during the Great Plague possibly make the outbreak worse?
cards.answer: It removed some natural predators of rats, which may have helped the plague spread further.

cards.front: Name the four yugas (ages) in Hindu cosmology, in order.
cards.answer: Satya Yuga / Treta Yuga / Dvapara Yuga / Kali Yuga

cards.front: Name the four main paths of Hindu yoga.
cards.answer: Karma yoga / Jnana yoga / Raja yoga / Bhakti yoga

cards.front: Why does karma explain suffering in Hindu thought?
cards.answer: Because actions performed in previous lives shape a person's present experience, so present suffering results from past karma.

cards.front: Why do worshippers cup their hands over the flame after arti?
cards.answer: To bring the flame's warmth to their faces, symbolising receiving the deity's blessing.

cards.front: Name the four layers of a tropical rainforest, from tallest to shortest.
cards.answer: Emergent layer / Canopy / Understorey / Forest floor

cards.front: Name the five animal adaptations to rainforest life given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Howler monkeys' prehensile tails / Sloths' algae-covered fur for camouflage / Poison dart frogs' bright warning colours / Toucans' huge bills to reach fruit / Jaguars' strong swimming ability
items: Poison dart frogs' bright warning colours
Toucans' huge bills to reach fruit

cards.front: Why does slash-and-burn farming quickly destroy rainforest fertility?
cards.answer: Most nutrients are stored in the living trees, not the soil, so cutting and burning them removes the nutrients entirely.

cards.front: How does cutting down rainforest trees reduce rainfall in the region?
cards.answer: Fewer trees means less transpiration, so less water vapour rises to form clouds, causing less rain and drier conditions.

cards.front: Name the three causes of crime the lesson says many Jews recognise alongside the spiritual dimension.
cards.answer: Poverty / Family breakdown / Lack of moral education

cards.front: Name the three aims of punishment that Jews hold divergent views about.
cards.answer: Retribution / Deterrence / Reformation

cards.front: Why does Isaiah 55:6-8 support restorative justice for offenders?
cards.answer: Because God freely pardons those who turn back to him, so Jews believe offenders should be given the chance to repair harm and rejoin the community.

cards.front: Why do Jews hold divergent views on the death penalty today?
cards.answer: Some see Exodus 21 as justifying it as proportionate retribution for murder, while others follow the Mishnah's caution that courts should rarely execute.

cards.front: Name the four marriages in the novel's resolution.
cards.answer: Elizabeth and Darcy / Jane and Bingley / Charlotte and Collins / Lydia and Wickham

cards.front: What three things does Lady Catherine say Elizabeth lacks?
cards.answer: family / connections / fortune

cards.front: Why does Darcy's secret rescue of Lydia prove his moral transformation is genuine?
cards.answer: He acts out of love, not for public credit, saving the family at great personal cost and asking for nothing in return.

cards.front: Why is Lydia's elopement more than just a romantic subplot?
cards.answer: It is the mechanism that tests whether Darcy's transformation, glimpsed at Pemberley, is genuine.

cards.front: Name the six main factors in material selection the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Functionality / Aesthetics / Availability / Cost / Environmental impact / Social & ethical considerations

cards.front: Name the five material categories the lesson compares for cost.
cards.answer: Timber / Metals / Polymers / Textiles / Papers & boards

cards.front: Why is beech commonly used for kitchen chopping boards?
cards.answer: It is a food-safe, durable hardwood that resists scoring and does not taint food.

cards.front: Why is recycled aluminium seen as a strong environmental choice for drinks cans?
cards.answer: It uses only 5% of the energy needed to produce virgin aluminium.

title: Global Water Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four impacts of water insecurity described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Waterborne disease and water pollution / Reduced food production / Reduced industrial output / Potential for conflict

cards.front: Name the six factors the lesson gives that affect water availability.
cards.answer: Climate / Geology / Pollution of supply / Over-abstraction / Limited infrastructure / Poverty

cards.front: Why is improving irrigation efficiency seen as the biggest lever for cutting global water demand?
cards.answer: Agriculture uses about 70% of freshwater withdrawals, far more than domestic use, so efficiency gains there cut demand most.

cards.front: Why did Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam create a crisis with Egypt?
cards.answer: Egypt depends on the Nile for about 97% of its fresh water, so filling the dam upstream threatened to reduce its supply.

cards.front: Name the four everyday examples the lesson gives of situations where compression is used.
cards.answer: Streaming music and video / Sending email attachments / Loading images on a web page / Backing up large amounts of data
items: Loading images on a web page
Backing up large amounts of data

cards.front: Name the four benefits the lesson gives of compressing a file.
cards.answer: Downloads and uploads more quickly / Uses less bandwidth / Web pages load sooner / More files fit in an attachment limit or backup drive
items: More files fit in an attachment limit or backup drive

cards.front: How does Huffman coding reduce the number of bits a file needs?
cards.answer: It gives the most common characters the shortest binary codes and rarer characters longer codes, so the file needs fewer bits overall.

cards.front: Why do photographers and musicians keep a lossless master copy instead of only saving a lossy version?
cards.answer: Because lossy compression is not reversible, so re-saving a lossy file repeatedly loses more detail each time.

title: Prison reform: Howard, Fry and the silent and separate systems
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four key proposals John Howard made for prison reform.
cards.answer: Separating different categories of prisoner / Adequate food and healthcare without extortion / Ending the fee system for warders / Ensuring regular inspection
items: Adequate food and healthcare without extortion
Ending the fee system for warders

cards.front: Name the three competing visions of what prison was for in the Victorian debate.
cards.answer: Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: Why did transportation shift from America to Australia?
cards.answer: The American Revolution in 1776 ended transportation to the American colonies, causing a prison overcrowding crisis, so Botany Bay was used instead.

cards.front: Why did Pentonville prisoners wear masks when moved between cells?
cards.answer: To prevent recognition between prisoners, keeping them isolated so they could reflect without contamination by other criminals.

cards.front: Name the four core perspectives GCSE Sociology requires you to know, compare and apply.
cards.answer: Functionalism / Marxism / Feminism / Interactionism

cards.front: Name the three types of feminism described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Liberal feminism / Marxist feminism / Radical feminism

cards.front: Why did Davis and Moore argue that social inequality can serve a functional purpose?
cards.answer: Higher rewards for more demanding roles act as incentives for talented individuals to train for them, filling important positions effectively.

cards.front: Why does Marxist feminism argue women's oppression is tied to capitalism?
cards.answer: Women provide unpaid domestic labour that sustains the workforce, which benefits the capitalist class.

title: Customs and Daily Life in German-Speaking Countries
subject: german-aqa

cards.front: Name the five categories Germans sort their rubbish into.
cards.answer: Restmüll (general waste) / Bioabfall (organic waste) / Papier (paper) / Gelber Sack (packaging/plastics) / Glas (glass, sorted by colour)

cards.front: Name the three tracks of the German school system.
cards.answer: Gymnasium (grammar school, leads to Abitur) / Realschule (middle school) / Hauptschule (vocational school)

cards.front: Why are most shops in Germany closed on Sundays?
cards.answer: Because of Sonntagsruhe, a legal requirement for Sunday rest, so only bakeries, petrol stations and some tourist shops can open.

cards.front: How does the Pfand deposit system lead to Germany's high bottle recycling rates?
cards.answer: Customers pay a small deposit on bottles/cans which is refunded when returned, giving recycling rates above 90%.

cards.front: How do you know overflow has occurred when adding two 8-bit binary numbers?
cards.answer: If the addition produces a carry out from the leftmost (most significant) bit, the 8-bit result cannot fit and overflow has occurred.

cards.front: Why do arithmetic and logical right shifts give the same result for a positive number?
cards.answer: A positive number's sign bit is 0, so filling vacated positions with 0 or with a copy of the sign bit is identical.

cards.front: What two things does Mickey discover in the final scene, right before he confronts Eddie?
cards.answer: Eddie is his twin brother / Linda has been seeing Eddie

cards.front: What three 'false stories' does Russell suggest society uses to explain away class inequality?
cards.answer: the myth of meritocracy / the idea poverty is caused by laziness / the belief that the system is fair
items: the idea poverty is caused by laziness
the belief that the system is fair

cards.front: Why does the superstition seem to 'come true' when the twins learn the truth?
cards.answer: Because decades of damage caused by class inequality cannot be undone by a single revelation, not because of supernatural forces.

cards.front: How does the presence of police marksmen deepen Russell's point about the class system?
cards.answer: It suggests the working class are ultimately destroyed by the same institutions that were meant to protect them.

cards.front: Name the four types of grievance that combined to cause the Pilgrimage of Grace.
cards.answer: Religious anger over the dissolution of the monasteries / Fiscal anger at the Subsidy and Statute of Uses / Agrarian protest against rents and enclosures / Northern political resentment of Cromwell and lost autonomy
items: Religious anger over the dissolution of the monasteries
Fiscal anger at the Subsidy and Statute of Uses
Agrarian protest against rents and enclosures
Northern political resentment of Cromwell and lost autonomy

cards.front: What six demands did the Pontefract Articles make in December 1536?
cards.answer: Restore the dissolved monasteries / Repeal the Statute of Uses / Dismiss Cromwell and Cranmer / Condemn heresy / Hold a free Parliament in the north / Recognise Princess Mary as legitimate
items: Hold a free Parliament in the north

cards.front: Why did Robert Aske call the rising a 'pilgrimage' rather than a rebellion?
cards.answer: Because motives among rebels varied, so a religious banner could unite groups with different grievances and mobilise them quickly.

cards.front: How did Bigod's rising give Henry legal cover to crush the Pilgrimage of Grace survivors?
cards.answer: It let Henry rule the first pardon broken by association, justifying martial law and Norfolk's return to punish the rebels.

title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-studies

cards.front: Name the six criteria a successful Olympic or World Cup bid must address, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Venue and infrastructure / Transport / Security / Accommodation / Legacy planning / Financial viability

cards.front: Name the four pre-event negatives of hosting a major sporting event given in the lesson.
cards.answer: High hosting costs / Displacement of residents / Construction disruption to communities / Political opposition

cards.front: Why are cities becoming increasingly reluctant to enter Olympic bidding races?
cards.answer: Bid campaigns can cost tens of millions of pounds, and cities that lose have spent that money for nothing.

cards.front: Why does infrastructure built for a major event still benefit residents after the event has finished?
cards.answer: New roads, rail lines, airports and broadband built to meet event requirements continue to be used by locals long afterwards.

cards.front: Name the three examples of aerobic activity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: A 10 km run / A long swim / A cycling time trial

cards.front: Name the five recovery methods the lesson describes for after vigorous exercise.
cards.answer: Cool down / Rehydration / Carbohydrate consumption / Ice baths / Massage

cards.front: Why is eating carbohydrates important for recovery after exercise?
cards.answer: It replenishes glycogen stores in the muscles and liver, replacing the glucose fuel broken down during activity.

cards.front: Why is massage particularly valuable for endurance athletes?
cards.answer: They repeatedly use the same muscle groups over long durations, creating chronic tightness that massage relieves by improving circulation and reducing tension.

title: Engagement Patterns in Physical Activity and Sport
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: What four barriers do older adults face in participating in physical activity, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Declining physical capacity / Fewer social networks / Fewer accessible activities / Negative stereotypes about older people

cards.front: Name the four examples of adaptive provision the lesson gives for increasing disabled participation.
cards.answer: Boccia / Sitting volleyball / Goalball / Deaf-friendly coaching

cards.front: Why did grassroots girls' football registrations rise after Beth Mead's hat-trick at the 2022 Women's Euros?
cards.answer: It showed how a visible role model can directly translate into increased grassroots participation among girls.

cards.front: Why are adult women disproportionately affected by caring commitments in relation to sport participation?
cards.answer: Caring responsibilities compete with leisure time, partly explaining why adult women have lower participation in formal sport.

cards.front: Name the four levels of ecosystem organisation, from smallest to largest.
cards.answer: Individual organism / Population (one species) / Community (many species) / Ecosystem (community + abiotic environment)

cards.front: Name the four trophic levels in a food chain, in order.
cards.answer: Producer / Primary consumer (herbivore) / Secondary consumer (carnivore) / Tertiary consumer (top predator)

cards.front: Why did reintroducing wolves to Yellowstone lead to riverside vegetation recovering?
cards.answer: Wolves reduced elk numbers and changed their grazing behaviour, so elk ate less riverside vegetation, allowing it to recover.

cards.front: Why has the introduction of grey squirrels contributed to the decline of red squirrels in the UK?
cards.answer: Grey squirrels are larger and more competitive, so they outcompete red squirrels for the same food sources (interspecific competition).

cards.front: Name the three common soldiers Henry meets in disguise before Agincourt.
cards.answer: Williams / Bates / Court

cards.front: In his soliloquy, name the six things Henry says people lay on the king.
cards.answer: Our lives / Our souls / Our debts / Our careful wives / Our children / Our sins

cards.front: Why does Henry order the killing of the French prisoners?
cards.answer: He gives the order on hearing the French have rallied their scattered men, though Gower later cites the killing of the boys as the reason.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Agincourt through fragmented scenes rather than one continuous battle?
cards.answer: The stage cannot hold real armies, so he shows individual encounters like Pistol's capture and the Boy's commentary instead.

title: The Western Front and the Somme 1916
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says gave defenders an overwhelming advantage on the Western Front by the end of 1914.
cards.answer: Quick-firing artillery / Machine guns / Magazine rifles / Barbed wire

cards.front: Name the four new weapons technologies the lesson says appeared on the Western Front between 1914 and 1918.
cards.answer: Chemical weapons / Aircraft / Tanks / Artillery (creeping barrage)

cards.front: How did new weapons technology cause the Western Front to become a fortified stalemate by the end of 1914?
cards.answer: Quick-firing artillery, machine guns, magazine rifles and barbed wire gave defenders such an advantage that open-order assault became almost impossible, forcing both sides to dig in.

cards.front: Why did tanks fail to produce a breakthrough when first used on the Somme in September 1916?
cards.answer: They were too few in number and too unreliable to break through the German line.

title: Performance Interpretation: The Balcony and the Tomb
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, what three things must a strong performance answer name, all anchored to a specific moment?
cards.answer: A body part (hands, gaze, posture, feet) / A spatial choice (proxemics to another character or the set) / A vocal quality (pace, pitch, volume, pause)
items: A body part (hands, gaze, posture, feet)
A spatial choice (proxemics to another character or the set)
A vocal quality (pace, pitch, volume, pause)

cards.front: Why might a performer speak Romeo's 'sun' lines quietly and almost to himself in the balcony scene?
cards.answer: Because the lines are an act of private worship, not a declaration to Juliet, so a hushed, private delivery suits the moment.

cards.front: Why does the lesson suggest staging Romeo below and Juliet above on the balcony?
cards.answer: The physical relationship stages an argument about their love: Juliet is the fixed point while Romeo is the one reaching upward.

title: The Almighty, Shekhinah, the Messiah and the Covenant with Abraham
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: What are the four key characteristics of the Almighty in Jewish belief?
cards.answer: One / Creator / Law-Giver / Judge

cards.front: What four things happen when the Messianic Age arrives, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Exiled Jews gathered back to Israel / The Temple is rebuilt / War and injustice end / All nations recognise the Almighty
items: Exiled Jews gathered back to Israel

cards.front: Why does the Genesis 2 account of forming humanity from dust matter for Jewish belief about the Almighty?
cards.answer: It shows a close, personal relationship between the Almighty and humanity from the very beginning of creation.

cards.front: Why is the covenant with Abraham described as unconditional?
cards.answer: The Almighty commits to keeping his promise regardless of Israel's later failures, though obedience is still expected.

cards.front: Name the five Bennet sisters and the trait the lesson gives each.
cards.answer: Jane - gentle and trusting / Elizabeth - witty and independent / Mary - pedantic / Kitty - easily led / Lydia - reckless

cards.front: What four themes does the Meryton ball introduce, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Pride (Darcy's refusal to dance) / Prejudice (Elizabeth's instant judgment) / Class (the Bennet family's social embarrassments) / Marriage as a public performance

cards.front: Why does Austen position Elizabeth as the heroine rather than one of her sisters?
cards.answer: Not because she is perfect, but because she combines intelligence with moral seriousness, qualities the other sisters lack in different ways.

cards.front: Why is Jane and Bingley's simple romance disrupted?
cards.answer: Darcy and Caroline Bingley separate them to protect Bingley from a 'disadvantageous' match, showing even gentle love is vulnerable to class interference.

title: Diet, Nutrition and Health — Diet-Related Disease
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four dietary risk factors the lesson gives for obesity.
cards.answer: Diet high in energy-dense foods / Large portion sizes / Frequent processed snacks, fast food and sugary drinks / Low fibre intake
items: Frequent processed snacks, fast food and sugary drinks

cards.front: Name the five risk groups the lesson gives for iron-deficiency anaemia.
cards.answer: Teenage girls / Adult women / Pregnant women / Young children / Vegetarians and vegans

cards.front: Why can a calcium-rich diet still fail to protect bones if vitamin D is deficient?
cards.answer: Without vitamin D, calcium cannot be absorbed from the gut, so even a calcium-rich diet does not fully protect bones.

cards.front: Why does obesity increase the risk of type 2 diabetes?
cards.answer: Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, is strongly associated with insulin resistance, keeping blood glucose elevated.

cards.front: Name the four purposes Odimba achieves by grounding Princess & The Hustler in the 1963 boycott.
cards.answer: Gives voice to untold stories / Shows the personal within the political / Connects past to present / Celebrates community resilience
items: Shows the personal within the political

cards.front: What three types of support networks did Caribbean communities in St Pauls build?
cards.answer: Churches / Social clubs / Informal economies

cards.front: Why was institutional racism harder to challenge in Britain than segregation in America?
cards.answer: British racism was hidden behind unofficial practices and social attitudes rather than law, so authorities could deny it existed.

cards.front: Why did Odimba choose a child, Princess, as her protagonist?
cards.answer: A child lets the audience see systemic racism with fresh eyes, shocked by injustice that adults have learned to accept.

cards.front: Name the five advantages of social media given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stay in contact with friends / It's free and easy to use / Share photos and videos / Useful for revision and homework / Discover new things
items: It's free and easy to use

cards.front: Name the five disadvantages of social media given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Spend too much time online / Cyberbullying is a serious problem / Dangerous - don't know who's behind the screen / Can create an addiction / Bad for mental health
items: Dangerous - don't know who's behind the screen

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use qui or que in a French sentence?
cards.answer: Use qui if a verb comes straight after the gap; use que if a subject/pronoun comes after the gap.

cards.front: Why is que always followed by a subject plus a verb?
cards.answer: Que replaces the object of the second clause, so a subject and verb must still follow it.

title: Guidance for Beginners and Elite Performers
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of guidance the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Visual / Verbal / Manual / Mechanical

cards.front: Why is manual guidance rarely used with elite performers?
cards.answer: Elite performers have established, well-grooved movement patterns, so physical input would likely disrupt rather than improve their performance.

cards.front: Why are manual and mechanical guidance mainly used with beginners?
cards.answer: Safety is the main reason — they allow safe learning of dangerous or complex skills without risk of injury, not for long-term skill development.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says happen as civilisation collapses in the invasion.
cards.answer: Social hierarchies dissolve / Laws become meaningless / Survival depends on individual resourcefulness

cards.front: Why does Wells position humanity 'in the middle' between the Martians and the bacteria?
cards.answer: Martians are more evolved but horrifying, bacteria are less evolved but equally powerful, showing humans are not special or permanent.

cards.front: Why does class become irrelevant during the Martian invasion?
cards.answer: The wealthy cannot buy safety and the poor are no more vulnerable than anyone else, so wealth offers no protection.

cards.front: According to the lesson's key fact, what four effects does competition have on a market?
cards.answer: Drives prices down towards costs / Squeezes profits / Raises quality / Widens consumer choice

cards.front: Why can a firm in a market with high barriers to entry keep prices above average cost indefinitely?
cards.answer: High barriers block new entrants even when profits are very high, so the price can stay well above average cost with no competition forcing it down.

cards.front: Why is competition a mixed story for workers in a competitive market?
cards.answer: Tight profit margins give firms strong incentives to cut labour costs and keep wages low, but competing for skilled staff can push wages up.

cards.front: Name the three levels of traits in Allport's (1936) theory of personality.
cards.answer: Cardinal trait / Central traits / Secondary traits

cards.front: What four things did the questionnaires in Van Houtte and Jarvis's (1995) study measure?
cards.answer: Autonomy / Self-concept / Self-esteem / Attachment to animals

cards.front: Why is Allport's trait theory considered hard to test scientifically?
cards.answer: Traits are identified through case studies and personal judgement, not standardised testing, so psychologists may disagree on which level a trait belongs to.

cards.front: Why is trait theory criticised as reductionist?
cards.answer: It reduces a complex personality to a fixed set of numbers, ignoring how much behaviour changes depending on the situation.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that determine whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
cards.answer: Availability of substitutes / Necessity versus luxury / Proportion of income / Time period

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that determine whether supply is elastic or inelastic.
cards.answer: Spare capacity / Stocks and storage / Ease of switching production / Time period

cards.front: Why does a good that takes up a large proportion of a consumer's income tend to have more elastic demand?
cards.answer: Even a small percentage price change feels significant when the good costs a lot relative to income, making consumers more sensitive to price.

cards.front: Why can inelastic housing supply keep prices high for years even when demand is strong?
cards.answer: Supply cannot quickly expand to match rising demand, so a price rise fails to bring enough new homes onto the market to lower prices.

cards.front: What three elements make up the comic plot in The Merchant of Venice?
cards.answer: The caskets / The wooing / The ring trick

cards.front: What three elements make up the tragic subplot in The Merchant of Venice?
cards.answer: The bond / The trial / The forced conversion

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use prose for Venice's commercial scenes and verse for Belmont's romantic scenes?
cards.answer: To reinforce the play's structural opposition between commerce and romance, and between outsiders and insiders.

cards.front: How does Portia actually defeat Shylock in the trial scene?
cards.answer: By finding a legal technicality (flesh but no blood), not through superior moral argument, so law rather than mercy resolves the play.

cards.front: Name the four drawing types that show the logic, sequence or electrical connections of a system rather than its physical shape.
cards.answer: Block diagram / Flowchart / Circuit diagram / Wiring diagram

cards.front: What three symbol shapes are used in a flowchart, and what does each represent?
cards.answer: Oval terminals / Rectangular process steps / Diamond decision points

cards.front: Why can't an isometric drawing be used directly for manufacture?
cards.answer: Because it cannot show hidden detail accurately and its dimensions are not annotated in a standard manufacturing format.

cards.front: Why can oblique drawings look unrealistic, especially for long objects?
cards.answer: Because the receding edges are drawn at 45°, which exaggerates depth and distorts the object's appearance.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says obesity limits sporting performance.
cards.answer: Limits cardiovascular endurance / Limits flexibility / Limits agility / Limits speed and power

cards.front: Why does obesity limit flexibility?
cards.answer: Excess fat tissue around joints and the abdomen physically restricts the range of movement at key joints.

cards.front: Why might someone with a high BMI, like a rugby prop, not actually be obese?
cards.answer: Their high BMI comes from large muscle mass rather than excess body fat, so body composition suits their sport.

title: Post-Industrial UK: Science Parks & Rural Change
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for South Cambridgeshire's rapid population growth.
cards.answer: Commuter access to Cambridge and London / Quality of life (cheaper houses, good schools, less traffic) / Remote work due to faster broadband
items: Commuter access to Cambridge and London
Quality of life (cheaper houses, good schools, less traffic)
Remote work due to faster broadband

cards.front: Name the three causes the lesson gives for population decline in the Outer Hebrides.
cards.answer: Lack of jobs / Out-migration of young people / Declining services

cards.front: Why do firms benefit from clustering together in a science park?
cards.answer: Co-locating lets staff share ideas, recruits and equipment, an effect economists call agglomeration.

cards.front: Why is the ICT industry attractive compared to heavy industry like mining or shipbuilding?
cards.answer: It requires only modest physical infrastructure such as offices, fast broadband and skilled workers, not coal supplies and railway lines.
